events.title: Dollar dips with US midterm results in focus
events.summary: The yen strengthened to 158.30 per US dollar in early trading. SHANGHAI/SINGAPORE – The dollar fell against most major currencies on Nov 4 ahead of results from US midterm elections, with investors bracing for a potentially strong Democratic showing. The first results in the US midterm elections began trickling in, with Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff winning reelection in Georgia in the first major race to be called. The question of whether Democrats can wrest control of Congress from Donald Trump’s Republicans, though was likely still hours away from a definitive answer. The euro firmed 0.2% to US$1.1212, while the yen strengthened to 158.30 per US dollar in early trading. The dollar index, which measures the greenback against a basket of six currencies, edged down 0.2% to 101.7. The yield on the benchmark US 10-year Treasury note fell 4 basis points to 4.919%. “Given the Democrats are favoured right now, our expectation is that they will take control of both the House and the Senate,” said Carol Kong, currency strategist at Commonwealth Bank of Australia. “If that pans out, the US dollar could sell off further from here, because a Democratic sweep would limit government spending over Trump’s term.” As of 7.30 pm ET (8.30am Singapore time), US media outlets had projected winners in a handful of House races after polls closed in 10 states, with voting still under way across much of the country. Kong said investors were also watching the risk of an escalation in the Middle East depending on the election outcome. “If the Republicans do lose control of the House and the Senate, what will the President do? He previously flagged that he will restart a bombing campaign in Iran after the election, so we are watching that very closely,” she said. “If he does ramp up the aggression in the conflict, then we could see oil prices jump sharply higher, and that will support the US dollar.” Oil prices were little changed at US$103.85 a barrel after easing about 1% on Nov 3 to the lowest in nearly four weeks. The market is weighing talks to end the wars in Iran and Ukraine against worries that recent attacks in both conflicts could further disrupt supplies. Sterling edged higher to US$1.3440, with traders eyeing the Bank of England’s policy announcement on Nov 5 . The central bank’s Monetary Policy Committee is expected to raise interest rates for the first time since August 2023. China’s offshore yuan last traded at 6.6673 per dollar, stabilising after suffering its biggest one-day drop since May 15 on Nov 3 , when the People’s Bank of China raised the amount of foreign currency that financial institutions must hold in reserve in a move to slow the yuan’s rally. REUTERS

events.title: Republicans underperform as first midterm votes are counted
events.summary: The first midterm votes counted on Tuesday night suggest a tough night for Republicans, in line with polling that has put Democrats well ahead in the battle for Congress on the strength of public frustration with President Donald Trump’s agenda. In Indiana and Kentucky, where most polls closed at 6 pm ET, Democrats ran well ahead of their early vote totals two years ago. They were competitive in Indiana’s 5th Congressional District, outside of Indianapolis — where Trump won by 17 points in 2024 — and in Kentucky’s 6th District, which went for Trump by 15 points. Neither of those seats was a Democratic target at the start of this election cycle, but both races saw later investment as the environment appeared to degrade for Republicans. Indiana Rep. Victoria Spartz, an erratic candidate in the 5th District who has underperformed the party before, faced a last-minute spend from the Invest in Tomorrow Coalition, a green energy PAC working to beat Republicans who voted to revoke energy credits last year. House Majority PAC, the Democrats’ super PAC, spent nearly $400,000 for their candidate, JD Ford. The Kentucky seat became a target after Rep. Andy Barr left it to run for Senate. Republicans nominated former state Sen. Ralph Alvarado, while Gov. Andy Beshear campaigned for Democratic nominee Zach Dembo, a federal prosecutor. Republicans expected their numbers to improve as Election Day votes came in, but in both Indiana and Kentucky, the party’s vote share has universally fallen since 2024. Indiana Democrat Beau Bayh, the son and grandson of former senators, led in the early count for secretary of state, the one statewide race his party was competing for. Yet Democrats remain wary about overreading the meaning of early votes, recalling that they banked votes for Kamala Harris two years ago before getting overwhelmed on Election Day. — David Weigel

events.title: AMD sales forecast tops estimates on soaring AI chip demand
events.summary: Fourth-quarter revenue will be US$17 billion (S$21.7 billion), plus or minus 3%, the chipmaker said in a statement on Nov 3. AMD forecast fourth-quarter revenue of US$17 billion, above estimates, as strong AI chip demand and data centre sales stayed high. The result calmed worries about an AI bubble. AMD shares rose about 6% after the report, and the company’s value hit US$1 trillion in September. AMD’s data centre sales nearly doubled to US$8.5 billion, but PC and gaming sales fell 8%. Gross margin is set to narrow to about 55%. CALIFORNIA – Advanced Micro Devices, a key challenger to Nvidia in artificial intelligence chips, gave a revenue forecast that exceeded analysts’ estimates, indicating that demand for data centre processors remains strong. Fourth-quarter revenue will be US$17 billion (S$21.7 billion), plus or minus 3%, the chipmaker said in a statement on Nov 3 . That compares with an average analyst estimate of US$16.3 billion. The outlook provided fresh evidence that AI spending is sustainable, potentially helping soothe jittery investors. Under chief executive officer Lisa Su, AMD has become one of the most important suppliers of processors and computers that operate at the heart of AI facilities, underpinning a flood of new services. “Our fourth-quarter outlook reflects accelerating revenue and earnings growth, driven by strong demand across our data centre portfolio,” chief financial officer Jean Hu said in the statement. AMD shares gained about 6% in late trading after the report was released. Even with recent turbulence, the stock has more than doubled in 2026 . The company’s valuation reached US$1 trillion in September, putting it in an elite group. The data centre growth has helped AMD offset a slump in the personal computer market, where rising memory-chip costs have slowed production and depressed user demand. Intel, AMD’s top rival in that field, suffered its worst stock decline in decades after a downbeat earnings report last week. One possible weak spot for AMD: Its gross margin will narrow to about 55% in the fourth quarter. That measure – the percentage of sales after removing production costs – had been 56% in the previous period. AMD’s third-quarter sales rose 45% to US$13.4 billion. Profit climbed to US$2.09 a share, minus certain items. Analysts on average had predicted revenue of US$13.1 billion and earnings of US$1.97 a share. AMD continues to deliver record results and now boasts sales that are twice as big as they were two years ago. It has also been outperforming longtime nemesis Intel in the market for central processing units, or CPUs. But the company is still well behind Nvidia in so-called AI accelerators, which are used to train and run artificial intelligence models. Sales at AMD’s data centre business nearly doubled to US$8.5 billion. Analysts had predicted a total of US$8.2 billion. PC and gaming-related sales shrank 8% to US$3.7 billion. Like other makers of components for PCs, AMD is suffering from a side effect of the data centre boom. AI servers require a massive amount of memory. That’s cut into the supply of chips available for laptops and desktop machines – and forced prices up. AMD is debuting new product ranges in both the CPU and accelerator markets. The Santa Clara, California-based company is also taking on Nvidia more directly with its Helios server design. But Nvidia, the largest chipmaker and world’s most valuable company, hasn’t been standing still. It is updating its own line up at a fast pace and branching out into everything from software to networking to complete computers. BLOOMBERG

events.title: Midterm elections could jolt stocks if Democrats sweep Congress
events.summary: Investors are not yet fully accounting for the Democrats winning both the House and Senate, a blue wave scenario that could weigh on share prices in the short term on Wednesday. History says any dip should be bought as the post-midterms market move is usually upward. But big gains already this year, may have stolen that momentum. Big Democrat gains could further weigh on an already-ailing AI trade on fear restrictions on data centers gain traction nationwide. The stock market is not yet pricing in a Democratic sweep of Congress — despite some polls and most prediction markets pointing that way — so that scenario could weigh on share prices Wednesday, according to investors and analysts. Follow CNBC's live coverage of the 2026 midterm elections Republicans managing to keep control could cause a short-term relief rally, they said. Short-term moves aside, the typical post-midterm pattern in the months ahead is bullish. But some wonder if the market could buck the positive historical trend this time because the S&P 500 is already up so much this year going into the election. As far as certain stocks to watch, a big Democratic win on Tuesday night — especially in the Texas governor race — could add fuel to an artificial intelligence stock sell-off on the notion that more data center restrictions would gain momentum nationally. Defense stocks could come under pressure on fears of limits on spending. Polls are pointing to a Democratic victory in the House and a toss-up in the Senate. Prediction markets have been more favorable to Democrats, calling for a blue sweep . While investors are signaling "begrudging acceptance" to a base-case scenario that there will indeed be a Democratic sweep, that's not how they're positioning, said Tobin Marcus, head of U.S. policy and politics at Wolfe Research. The firm's recent survey data among more than 100 institutional investors suggests they are not strongly positioned for any particular result. "Investors seem to have a significant dose of skepticism about whether the final outcome is going to be quite as favorable to Democrats as the polling suggests," Marcus told CNBC, noting that the firm shares the view that the "polling is likely overstating Democratic strength." JPMorgan sees a blue wave knocking the S&P 500 by about a half percent on Wednesday. On the other hand, if Republicans end up retaining both chambers of Congress, that could spur a rally, said Sameer Samana, head of global equities and real assets at the Wells Fargo Investment Institute. "From a certainty standpoint, the market knows what to do with Republicans holding both chambers," he said. Citigroup strategists said Monday that Republicans losing the House but managing to keep the Senate could be "a tailwind for equities into year-end." JPMorgan traders predict up to a 1% pop on Wednesday if Republicans hold on to that chamber. Looking past any short-term move, stocks tend to rally after the midterms have concluded. In fact, the S&P 500 was up one year out after all midterm elections going back to the early 1980s. But the S&P 500 has already recorded double-digit gains so far in 2026, so some on Wall Street worry that investors are being overly complacent heading into this year's elections. During midterm election years, the S&P 500 has typically averaged a 14% drawdown at some point in the second half of the year found Jonathan Krinsky, chief market technician at BTIG. "The reason stocks often perform well in November during midterms is because [the S&P 500] typically is weak INTO the elections. We have the opposite setup this year," Krinsky wrote last week. "Therefore, while consensus is that we see a post midterm rally, we think the opposite is actually more likely." It's not helping that the broader market has recently come under significant pressure due to turbulence in the artificial intelligence trade, which led the Nasdaq Composite to post its worst day since June on Friday. AI shares led the market lower again on Monday. A strong showing from Democrats in Tuesday's midterm elections could pressure the trade even more . At the state level, increased Democratic control is probably a headwind for stocks associated with data centers and technological capital equipment, analysts said. "It [would solidify] the early kind of cautionary signs in different states around the advancement of AI infrastructure," Rob Rains at Washington Analysis told CNBC. Goldman Sachs strategists said this week that a Democratic Congress "might limit data center tax incentives, but a national moratorium looks unlikely in any election outcome." One example would be Texas — a key hub of the data center buildout. A surprise loss there by Republican Gov. Greg Abbott has the "potential to spook" the market in the short term, Wolfe's Marcus said. A blue wave might pressure defense shares, while boosting healthcare stocks, analysts and investors said.

events.title: Meta says automation wrongly took down No Kings and a Senate candidate’s page. It’s automating more anyway
events.summary: Meta has spent the last year handing more of its content moderation to artificial intelligence. In the last few weeks, Facebook and Instagram’s parent company has fended off election-interference accusations in Brazil and the U.S. It has largely blamed these errors on its automated systems. Those accusations have come from a sitting president, a national protest movement and a U.S. Senate candidate. Each landed as Meta, a Fortune 500 company that reported $201 billion in revenue last year , speeds up a shift from human reviewers to large language models. Meta announced in March that it would roll out more advanced AI content-enforcement systems. By June, large language models had replaced human reviewers for about half of review requests, with a goal of 90% or more automation for some violation categories by the end of 2026, according to the Financial Times . Meta told the paper its models make 13% fewer errors than human reviewers and catch 10% more violations; some employees have warned that the shift is happening too fast with too little oversight. In 2018, ahead of elections in Brazil and the U.S., Facebook set up a “war room” of more than two dozen experts to fight election interference. Eight years later, both countries are voting again, and Meta now calls its war room the Election Operations Center. But more of the work of policing its platforms has shifted from people to software. According to an October report by the Institute for Strategic Dialogue, a research organization, platforms are increasingly relying on “crowdsourced and automated systems” rather than human oversight. The report found that platforms have disclosed little about how these systems work or are tested, and said: “relying on them as the primary means of oversight during a fast-moving election cycle remains an untested proposition.” This fall’s cases show what happens when those systems misfire in the middle of an election, and why Meta’s explanations have satisfied few affected people. Meta did not respond to Fortune ‘s request for comment. How Meta ended up in Brazil’s electoral court Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won a fourth term in an Oct. 25 runoff despite what his campaign said were Meta’s efforts to restrict his online reach. Meta blamed technical errors. Lula’s campaign went to Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court on Oct. 10, accusing Meta of favoring opponent Flávio Bolsonaro through biased algorithms and AI restrictions. In that petition and later filings, the campaign cited cases in which Meta’s automatic translation rendered comments such as “Flávio futuro presidiário!!” (“Flávio, future prisoner!!”) as “Flávio future president!!” and alleged that Meta restricted sharing for some of Lula’s posts. The newspaper Folha de S. Paulo reported that Meta staff acknowledged in internal messages that Lula’s accounts were restricted compared with Bolsonaro’s. On Oct. 15, the court ordered Meta to treat both candidates equally under threat of a daily fine of 500,000 reais, about $98,000. After finding Meta’s initial response insufficient, the court on Oct. 19 gave the company 24 hours to prove it had not restricted either candidate. Meta’s filing listed 17 measures, Reuters reported, including human review within two hours of any automatic restriction on the presidential campaigns’ ad accounts . The company denied treating the candidates unequally and said the problems arose from technical errors. Bolsonaro’s campaign later joined the case, saying it had also been treated unfairly. Brazil’s electoral prosecutor’s office told the court that Meta had not fully complied with the rulings, including a requirement to explain how its AI tool treats content about each candidate. It argued that errors varied by candidate, undermining Meta’s explanation of technical errors. Lula won the runoff with 51.8% of valid votes. The electoral court has yet to decide whether to fine Meta, and federal prosecutors, who opened an inquiry into account takedowns on Oct. 14, filed a civil suit against Meta on Oct. 21. Why No Kings went dark at the height of its day of action On Oct. 17, during the fourth national No Kings day of action, aimed at encouraging early voting, Meta suspended the coalition’s Instagram account, MS NOW reported. Organizers said the account went down at about 1:30 p.m. ET, at the height of the day’s events, for about 90 minutes. Even after it became viewable again, administrators couldn’t access it for several hours. The coalition also said on Threads that it had received reports that “#NoKings and early voting content was inaccessible, restricted, or seemed suppressed across Meta platforms.” Meta’s explanation changed overnight. That day, Meta’s vice president of communications, Andy Stone, attributed the suspension to unusually high rates of posting, sharing or commenting. The next day, he wrote on X that Meta’s network security systems had detected “the use of a Claude tool reading profiles, posts, and hashtags” in intense bursts, and that the company’s “automated protections” had wrongly taken the account offline. “We want to reiterate our sincere apology for the error,” Stone wrote. The coalition’s social media team later told Ars Technica it had used Claude, Anthropic’s AI model, to search keywords and hashtags to track online conversation. The coalition sent an open letter to Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg asking whether Meta had communicated with the Trump administration about the event or the 2026 midterms. It also asked how Meta’s “whitelist protocols,” which protect certain high-profile accounts from automated removal, treat Trump and his allies compared with No Kings and other “civil society efforts to encourage voter participation.” In an Oct. 21 reply, the coalition posted that Meta apologized again and offered a meeting with its technical experts. The coalition answered with a second letter saying the company had not given a substantive response and demanding a meeting with Meta leadership. On Oct. 22, five Democratic senators led by Chris Van Hollen of Maryland demanded Meta’s records of any communications with the Trump administration about No Kings and called the company’s “shifting explanations” alarming. On Oct. 30, the coalition said it met with senior Meta executives, but the meeting ended without substantive commitments to change Meta’s practices or establish safeguards. events.title: Democrats take Senate seats as Republicans underperform in midterms
events.summary: The News Democrats scored three quick Senate victories on Tuesday night as they appeared on track to hold several Florida congressional seats redrawn to get redder, a sign of significant Republican underperformance across the map. Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff, who Republicans had hoped to unseat this year, easily blew past GOP rival Rep. Mike Collins to win re-election. New Hampshire Rep. Chris Pappas prevailed over former GOP Sen. John Sununu in another race that Republicans had initially hoped to contest. In North Carolina, former Gov. Roy Cooper scored the party’s first pickup, flipping a Republican-held seat. House Republicans were also faltering in Florida, where three seats drawn to elect Republicans have so far gone to Democrats — re-elections for Reps. Jared Moskowitz and Kathy Castor, plus a victory for Rep.-elect Pia Dandiya. The GOP initially redistricted to try to gain four new House seats. All three of the Florida districts that Democrats have won so far on Tuesday night backed President Donald Trump in 2024. Urged to embark on mid-decade redistricting by Trump, Florida GOP Gov. Ron DeSantis has warned that his party was losing some of its advantages, driven by voter anger about the war in Iran. The Earliest Signs In Indiana and Kentucky, where most polls closed at 6 pm ET, Democrats ran well ahead of their early vote totals two years ago. They were competitive in Indiana’s 5th Congressional District, outside of Indianapolis — where Trump won by 17 points in 2024 — and in Kentucky’s 6th District, which went for Trump by 15 points. Neither of those seats were a Democratic target at the start of this election cycle, but both races saw later investment as the environment appeared to degrade for Republicans. Indiana Rep. Victoria Spartz, an erratic candidate in the 5th District who has underperformed the party before, faced a last-minute spend from the Invest in Tomorrow Coalition, a green energy PAC working to beat Republicans who voted to revoke energy credits last year. House Majority PAC, the Democrats’ super PAC, spent nearly $400,000 for their candidate, JD Ford. The Kentucky seat became a target after Rep. Andy Barr left it to run for Senate. Republicans nominated former state Sen. Ralph Alvarado, while Gov. Andy Beshear campaigned for Democratic nominee Zach Dembo, a federal prosecutor. Republicans expected their numbers to improve as Election Day votes came in, but in both Indiana and Kentucky, the party’s vote share has universally fallen since 2024. Indiana Democrat Beau Bayh, the son and grandson of former senators, led in the early count for secretary of state, the one statewide race his party was competing for. Yet Democrats remain wary about overreading the meaning of early votes, recalling that they banked votes for Kamala Harris two years ago before getting overwhelmed on Election Day. David’s view Democrats were feeling giddy early Tuesday night, and I can’t blame them. The first few hours of counting looked like the repudiation of Trump that their party wanted, and didn’t get, in 2020, when a surge of Election Day voters helped Republicans trim their Senate losses. That’s an easy story to tell in Georgia. Republicans were hoping to turn Ossoff into an accidental senator, benefiting from the president’s obsession with overturning the election, which depressed their vote. But the state is clearly shifting left, and the rural Republican vote is sagging everywhere — Florida, South Carolina, Ohio, places where the GOP had begun to believe in a possible permanent red shift of working-class voters. Republican turnout this year was never going to match what happened when Trump was on the ballot. But so far, the president’s dismal popularity is clearly depressing his base in red states.

events.title: Trump turns his ire toward Fox News on election night
events.summary: President Trump lashed out at Fox News on Election Night, attacking the network's personalities, polling and coverage as voters awaited midterm election results. Why it matters: Trump, who has repeatedly dined with Fox News patriarch Rupert Murdoch and hired talent from the network, has come to expect favorable coverage. But Fox's editorial decisions this election cycle suggest it isn't always willing to oblige. Driving the news: Trump began the night by criticizing Jessica Tarlov, a Fox co-host and Democratic strategist, saying he'd "go somewhere else" until she was off the air. He went as far as to reportedly text her co-host, Greg Gutfeld, to complain. His ire then turned toward Fox's political polling , claiming that "[e]very question is a hit job, and every answer is 'BULLSHIT!'" Around half an hour later, he posted that Fox's ratings were down "because they're spending too much time covering the Trump Deranged Dumocrats!" Trump pointed to a "new CNN Poll" as an alternative, touting data demonstrating his strength among MAGA Republicans. But the two CNN polling segments he posted earlier in the night were both well over a month old. State of play : Trump's rocky relationship with Fox News has been a source of tension this election season and in previous elections. Fox's coverage of Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed has fueled tensions for months, Axios' Alex Isenstadt recently reported . Republicans reportedly worried that Fox was undercutting efforts to brand El-Sayed as far outside the mainstream. In late October, Trump posted that Fox was "spending far too much time putting on the OPPONENTS of Republican Party Candidates, people that love our Country, and have Great Policies and Ideas." He added, "That's the only reason this Race is close, if it is indeed close." The White House and Fox did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. Meanwhile, Trump's former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt, now a Fox pundit, appeared on the network's Election Night coverage and said she had just spoken with the president. Reality check: Murdoch, while he is a conservative, has always been passionate about the news business. Fox News did, after all, spark Trumpworld's ire by calling Arizona early for former President Biden in 2020. events.title: No more rice grains in Kellogg's Rice Krispies due to changing weather
events.summary: Published 4 November 2026, 01:14 GMT Breakfast cereal giant Kellogg's has stopped using rice grains in Rice Krispies and Coco Pops in the UK due to "changing weather conditions" that have disrupted supplies. Corn flour and rice flour are being used instead, a Kellogg's spokesperson said on Tuesday, adding that the updated recipes have been "carefully assessed" and the firm has taken customer feedback into consideration. Those ingredients are replacing rice grains as crops have been hit by dry weather in key producing countries in Asia, reducing harvests and driving up prices. The new recipes mean cereal packaging will now include a "contains wheat gluten" warning. Rice Krispies products in the US and Canada will continue to be made with real rice with no changes to their recipes expected, a spokesperson for Kellogg's North American business told the BBC. The recipe change in the UK will help "maintain consistent quality at a time when changing weather conditions are affecting the quality and availability of some of the rice and grains used in our cereals," a Kellogg's spokesperson told the BBC. "We appreciate that even small changes to a much-loved product can feel noticeable and that's why we have approached this with a lot of care and consideration." The company also said that Rice Krispies and Coco Pops will continue to meet UK food standards on levels of fat, salt and sugar in food. The cereals also contain no artificial colours, flavours or sweeteners and the nutritional benefits in each bowl, such as fibre, Vitamin D and iron are staying the same, the spokesperson added. Watch: How does El Niño affect world weather? Published 21 August The Kellogg company separated into two distinct firms in 2023. The largest is Kellanova, which focuses on snacks, cereals, noodles and other food products like Eggo, Pringles and Pop-Tarts sold globally. It is now owned by Mars, which makes confectionery and pet food. The other business, WK Kellogg's, operates in North America and has since been taken over by Italian chocolate giant Ferrero . Most of the world's rice comes from Asia, many parts of which has been impacted by droughts, floods and heatwaves due to the El Niño weather phenomenon. The weather event is expected to severely impact crop production from South East Asia in particular. The region produces more than a quarter of the world's rice. The World Meteorological Agency expects the record-breaking El Niño will last until at least 2027. events.title: Gold steadies as traders track Iran talk prospects, US midterms
events.summary: The precious metal’s movement has been choppy this week on conflicting signals on the progress of US-Iran talks. Gold stayed near US$3,930 as traders watched US-Iran talks and US midterm elections for clues on interest rates, inflation, and fiscal policy. Oil swung on mixed signals from diplomacy, with fresh mediator proposals and reported US strikes on Qeshm raising tensions, but hopes of a peaceful deal eased prices. Gold has fallen about 25% since late February and nearly 7% in October, as higher energy costs and tighter policy hurt demand for the non-yielding metal. Gold held a decline as traders tracked diplomacy efforts in the Middle East and the outcome of US midterm elections for clues on the path for interest rates and American fiscal policy. Bullion was hovering around US$3,930 an ounce, following a modest retreat in the previous session that came after a jump of almost 2% on Nov 2 . The precious metal’s movement has been choppy this week on conflicting signals on the progress of US-Iran talks, making the impact of energy prices on inflation difficult to gauge. Oil continued to fluctuate after shifting in a range of around US$5 a barrel on Nov 3 . Tehran and Washington are reviewing fresh proposals from mediators on how to resolve their differences and avoid a return to all-out war, according to a diplomat briefed on the matter. That came after limited US airstrikes reportedly hit targets on the Iranian island of Qeshm inside the Strait of Hormuz the night of Nov 2 . Oil prices had soared over October on worsening tensions but sharply reversed course this week on signs the White House is willing to allow more time for a diplomatic resolution. Crude and gold have mostly moved in opposite directions in recent weeks, with elevated energy prices fuelling expectations of tighter monetary policy – a headwind for the non-yielding metal. The precious metal slumped almost 7% in October, slipping below the US$4,000 an ounce threshold at the end of the month when a retreat from AI prompted investors to liquidate bullion holdings to cover losses elsewhere. It is down around 25% since the US-Iran conflict erupted in late February, as accelerating inflation has spurred tighter monetary policy. Americans are casting their votes in midterm elections that will determine who controls the House and the Senate. The outcome is likely to shape the US fiscal policy outlook, indirectly affecting gold. Spot gold was 0.2% higher at US$3,938.47 an ounce at 8.17am in Singapore, while silver was steady at US$49.81. Platinum and palladium edged higher. The Bloomberg Dollar Spot Index, a gauge of the US currency, was 0.1% lower after rising 0.3% in the previous session. BLOOMBERG

events.title: Democrat Roy Cooper flips North Carolina Senate seat
events.summary: Democrat Roy Cooper has defeated President Trump's handpicked candidate, Michael Whatley, flipping one of North Carolina's two GOP-held U.S. Senate seats. Why it matters : Cooper, the popular two-term governor, delivered Democrats one of their best shots at flipping a Republican-held Senate seat. Even in a state that voted all three times for Trump, Cooper has never lost an election. The big picture: While the race was originally expected to be tight and expensive, Cooper consistently widened his polling lead throughout campaign season. His name recognition boosted his chances against Whatley, a lawyer who served as Republican National Committee chair but had never run for office himself. As enthusiasm lagged behind Whatley, GOP-aligned super PACs canceled their ads and redirected spending to more promising states, even as Trump still campaigned for Whatley in North Carolina. Catch up quick: Cooper will succeed Republican Sen. Thom Tillis, who decided not to seek reelection after clashing with Trump over the "big, beautiful bill" and its associated Medicaid cuts. Trump had threatened to back a primary challenger against Tillis. On the trail: Cooper focused his campaign on affordability, blaming Republicans for high gas prices and tying GOP policies to inflation. Meanwhile, Whatley centered his platform on helping execute the Trump agenda, despite the president's historically low approval rating. Whatley attempted to paint Cooper as the "soft-on-crime candidate" and continued to recite a debunked claim that Cooper is responsible for freeing Decarlos Brown Jr. , the man accused of stabbing and killing a 23-year-old Ukrainian refugee on Charlotte's light rail. Trump alleged North Carolina had become "one of the most violent" states under Democratic leadership while campaigning for Whatley. What's next: Cooper will take office in January. He will be the first Democrat to represent North Carolina in the Senate in over a decade.

events.title: Democrats beat back GOP Senate challenge in N.H. with Pappas win
events.summary: Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas defeated former GOP Sen. John Sununu in the New Hampshire Senate race, AP projects, becoming the first openly gay man elected to the U.S. Senate. Why it matters: Pappas' victory keeps the seat in Democratic hands and could boost the party's chances of taking control of the Senate. Driving the news: Pappas led Sununu 61% to 38% with 20% of the votes counted. He'll succeed retiring Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.) in January. Catch up quick: Republicans saw New Hampshire as a top pickup opportunity, with Senate Majority Leader John Thune campaigning for Sununu in the competitive race, despite polls showing Pappas ahead. Most polls compiled by the New York Times in the weeks before Election Day showed the Democratic Pappas leading Sununu by 5 to 8 percentage points. Zoom in: Although President Trump endorsed him, Sununu has shown daylight with the president, criticizing his trade war with Canada and his so-called anti-weaponization fund — and he backed Trump's primary opponents in 2016 and 2024. Still, prominent New Hampshire Republicans — including Don Bolduc , the Trump -endorsed 2022 Senate nominee — endorsed Pappas in mid-October, accusing Sununu of being too beholden to the president. Between the lines: Republicans welcomed Sununu's entry into the race because of his family's long ties to New Hampshire politics. Sununu served in the Senate from 2003 to 2009 before losing to Shaheen in 2008. His brother Chris served as governor for eight years. Senate GOP Whip John Barrasso (R-Wyo.) posted on X in October 2025 that Sununu's decision to run catapulted New Hampshire to "a top-tier U.S. Senate race." The bottom line: Pappas' win reflects a preference New Hampshire voters expressed in pre-election polling : They wanted a check on Trump's power. events.title: All eyes on Florida as Dems win Senate seats in N.C. and Georgia
events.summary: Polls in multiple key states, including Michigan and Texas, closed at 8pm ET, but much of the current attention is on what's happening down in Florida . Why it matters: The results tonight will be the clearest national test of President Trump's second presidency , following war abroad, economic anxiety at home and sweeping changes in Washington. Trump has made himself the face of the Republican campaign for control. Data: AP; Chart: Erin Davis/Axios The latest: In a major win of the night, Democrat Jon Ossoff won reelection to U.S. Senate from Georgia, AP projects. Democrat Roy Cooper defeated Trump's handpicked candidate, Michael Whatley, flipping one of the Republican party's two U.S. Senate seats . Zoom in: Before the elections, Axios' Hans Nichols pointed out House races to watch in Florida that could be an indicator of the larger balance of power. Democratic Rep. Kathy Castor will win FL-14, AP projects, a sign that Republicans will see their House majority disappear. Democrat Rep. Jared Moskowitz will win FL-25, AP projects. Republicans need to keep it close in the district where Trump was +9 in 2024. It's also worth keeping an eye on Virginia, Nichols writes: Watch if Democrats are flipping VA-01, a Trump +5 seat in 2024. If they do, Democrats are in for a very good night. If they end up flipping VA-05, a Trump +12 seat, they're in for a great night. Similarly, VA-02 could tell us whether even a strong Republican incumbent like Rep. Jen Kiggans can survive a Democratic wave. Data: AP; Chart: Erin Davis/Axios What we're hearing: Voters are saying cost of living and government corruption are the two top issues in this year's election, according to exit polls from AP . Cost of living skyrocketed thanks to the Iran war and the president's tariff policies. Trump himself was deemed corrupt and dangerous in a poll of registered voters prior to the election. State of play: Throughout Tuesday, the Trump administration faced legal battles amid the White House crackdown on alleged voter fraud. Trump scored a victory Tuesday after a federal appeals court tossed a previous order blocking Trump officials from demanding election workers set aside the ballots of alleged non-citizen voters. The Department of Justice has sent more than a dozen target letters as part of its investigation into the Dan J. Sullivan campaign, which has been the subject of Trump's ire for several days. The legal battles come as the White House is circulating Election Day talking points across the administration, touting Trump's accomplishments. Voting machine glitches and hiccups popped up in various spots of the country Tuesday, including in the high-profile New York House race . What's at stake in the 2026 midterm races The big picture: Republicans have largely given Trump a free hand in Washington since his return to the White House. Democratic control of even one chamber of Congress would open the door to investigations, subpoenas and even more legislative gridlock. An unprecedented mobilization of election monitors and legal battles involving the Trump administration have raised concerns about potential disruptions and challenges to the results. Trump has said he'll respect the election results if "they're honest elections." What's at stake: Republicans enter Election Day defending narrow congressional majorities, with a number of battlegrounds and traditionally GOP districts and states shifting into toss-up territory during the campaigns' final weeks. The House: All 435 seats are on the ballot. Democrats need a net gain of three seats to reclaim the majority. Redistricting has reshaped the battlefield. The Senate: 35 seats are on the ballot. Republicans hold a 53-47 advantage, including two independents who caucus with Democrats. Democrats need a net gain of four seats. 3 scenarios for the 2026 midterms Some scenarios: Democrats flip the House: They gain greater investigative power, control of committees and leverage over spending — but Trump retains his veto and executive authority. Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) could become the first Black speaker of the House, or face an opponent from his left. Democrats take Congress: Democrats' oversight power expands, while Trump's agenda faces major obstacles. A third Trump impeachment could be on the table, although being convicted in a Senate trial would require a two-thirds vote. Republicans retain Congress: Trump and GOP leaders get another two years to advance his agenda, though narrow margins could complicate plans. Between the lines: Beyond control of Congress, the results will test whether Trump's gains among young, Black and Latino voters in 2024 have endured — or if those voters are moving back toward Democrats who are trying to rebuild a winning coalition for 2028. What we're watching: Whether close races, outstanding ballots and legal challenges delay a clear verdict.

events.title: Google responds to political backlash over removing search from schools that ban AI
events.summary: Politicians including Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont and New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani criticized Google following reports that the company would restrict search at schools that ban AI. Google responded to the outrage, saying that Gemini, Gemini Notebook and search will be turned off by default, and schools can choose to turn one or all of them back on. Chris Phillips, vice president for education at Google, told the New York Times that "Search and AI are deeply integrated." Google is playing defense on Tuesday after a political backlash to its new policy surrounding use of artificial intelligence in schools. In a blog post titled "Designing responsible AI for learning," Google said it's bringing AI into its Classroom offering with a product called Guided Learning. The New York Times published a story saying that the company will turn off search for schools that reject AI entirely. Following the Times' story, prominent left-leaning politicians, including Sen. Bernie Sanders from Vermont and New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani voiced their outrage on social media. "Google is trying to use its monopoly power to force AI into our public schools," Mamdani wrote on X. Sanders wrote that "Google is threatening schools," referring to the policy as "extortion." Google responded later in the day. In a post on X , the company said its new policy was meant to give schools more choice over how students interact with AI. Google said its Gemini chatbot, Gemini Notebook and search are turned off by default, and that "schools are in control," with the ability to turn them as they see fit. "We are also updating Search for schools to make it better for learning," Google wrote. "Specifically, AI Mode and AI Overviews will offer step-by-step guided learning through problems, so that students don't get quick answers to schoolwork." The company's post didn't explicitly respond to the claim that access to search requires use of AI. However, Chris Phillips, vice president for education at Google, told the Times that "Search and AI are deeply integrated." A Google spokesperson referred CNBC to the X post when asked for comment. Google's broader practices have come under fire in recent years, with the company losing antitrust cases over its search and advertising businesses. Former Federal Trade Commission Chair Lina Khan aggressively pursued Google and other tech giants, including Meta and Amazon . Khan said in a post on X on Tuesday that Google's new AI for learning policy highlights "the danger of allowing an unregulated monopolist to control an essential service." It's the latest controversy related to the impact of technology on children and the role leading internet companies are playing in delivering information. In August, Meta reached a landmark $16.7 billion settlement in its child safety trial after a number of state attorneys general accused the company of misrepresenting the extent of child mental health harms caused by apps like Facebook and Instagram . The same month, OpenAI launched ChatGPT for Teens after state attorneys general launched an investigation into the company's safety practices, with Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier, a Republican, filing a lawsuit in June. The nonprofit Common Sense Media recently gave Google's AI overviews an " unacceptable risk " rating. Last month, Sens. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., and Josh Hawley, R-Mo., launched an inquiry over Google's push of AI into classrooms. Google introduced AI overviews as a search function in May 2024 . — CNBC's MacKenzie Sigalos contributed to this report. WATCH: Meta settled its child safety lawsuit. Now comes the hard part.

events.title: UN elects five judges to International Court of Justice amid record cases
events.summary: The election, held at UN headquarters, required several rounds of voting to fill the fifth and final seat. The United Nations has elected five judges to the International Court of Justice (ICJ) for nine-year terms, as the court faces a record caseload, including South Africa’s genocide case against Israel over its war on Gaza. The vote was held on Tuesday at UN headquarters, with candidates requiring an absolute majority in both the General Assembly and the Security Council to win. list 1 of 4 From Morocco to South Africa, Israel election watched closely across Africa list 2 of 4 Why is the US sanctioning the International Criminal Court? list 3 of 4 Who is Navi Pillay, winner of the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize? list 4 of 4 UK-Mauritius Chagos sovereignty deal stalls amid fears of further delays Dapo Akande of the United Kingdom, Francois Alabrune of France, Mahmoud Daifallah Hmoud of Jordan, Rena Lee of Singapore and Phoebe Okowa of Kenya were elected to the 15-member panel. Their terms are set to begin on February 6, 2027. The two UN bodies initially agreed on four candidates but failed to select a fifth. The Security Council supported Ecuador’s Marcelo Vazquez-Bermudez, while the General Assembly backed Okowa, prompting further rounds of voting. Vazquez-Bermudez later withdrew from the race, and Okowa subsequently won the backing of the General Assembly and the Security Council. The votes were held by secret ballot concurrently, but separately. The ICJ is based in The Hague and has 15 judges, each from a different country. They serve nine-year terms and may be re-elected. To ensure a degree of continuity, a third of the bench is elected every three years. The election comes as the World Court faces a record workload. ICJ President Yuji Iwasawa told the General Assembly on October 29 that 24 contentious cases are pending, covering disputes over territory, human rights and the interpretation of international treaties. Among them is South Africa’s case accusing Israel of violating the Genocide Convention in its war on Gaza. The court has previously ordered provisional measures but has not issued a final ruling on whether genocide occurred. In October 2025, the court issued an advisory opinion outlining Israel’s obligations towards the UN and humanitarian organisations operating in the occupied Palestinian territory. Separately, the court announced on Tuesday that it would deliver a judgment on November 19 in The Gambia’s case accusing Myanmar of genocide against the Rohingya minority. Established in 1945, the ICJ is the UN’s principal judicial organ, responsible for settling disputes between states and providing advisory opinions on questions of international law.

events.title: Jon Ossoff wins Georgia Senate race, defeating Republican Mike Collins
events.summary: Ossoff is re-elected for a second term, winning a key seat for Democrats as the party tries to retake the Senate. Incumbent Democratic US Senator Jon Ossoff has won re-election in the state of Georgia, one of the midterm cycle’s marquee contests. He has defeated Republican Congressman Mike Collins, a staunch ally of President Donald Trump who faced intense scrutiny during the campaign regarding alleged ties to people espousing white supremacist ideology. Ossoff, who has served as a US senator since 2021, campaigned on affordability, healthcare, and government accountability. Collins, meanwhile, focused on the president’s agenda, immigration enforcement and reducing the size of the government. Republicans had hoped to defeat Ossoff, the first Jewish senator in a state that backed former President Joe Biden in 2020 before reversing course and narrowly supporting Trump four years later. Ossoff, seen by some as a possible contender for the 2028 Democratic presidential nomination, will rejoin his fellow Democrat in the Senate, Raphael Warnock, Georgia’s first Black senator, who is also rumoured to be considering a run for the presidency. Georgia’s US Senate seats were critical for building the Democratic Party’s power in Congress and in the South, a largely Republican stronghold. Ossoff was leading Collins 63 percent to 29 percent with 56 percent of votes counted, according to the Associated Press news agency. Trump won Georgia narrowly in 2024 after losing the state to Biden in the 2020 presidential election. In 2023, Trump and others were charged in Georgia with attempting to overturn the 2020 election loss by pressuring a senior state official to recalculate the results in his favour. The case was dismissed after Trump returned to office in 2025.

events.title: FBI arrests man for sending over 700 threatening letters to US officials
events.summary: The suspect, an Oklahoma City man, is accused of mailing hoax letters with white powder and treason warnings. A man from the Midwestern United States is facing federal charges after allegedly mailing hundreds of suspicious letters containing white powder and menacing warnings about treason ahead of the US midterm elections . On Tuesday, Robin Patrick Martin, a 67-year-old Oklahoma City man, appeared for the first time in a US district court after his arrest a day earlier. list 1 of 3 US midterm voting begins in high-stakes test of Trump’s presidency list 2 of 3 South Carolina shrimpers weigh costs, vote in crucial US midterms list 3 of 3 In Pictures: US midterm elections in 20 photos His charges include conveying false or misleading information or hoaxes, as well as mailing threatening communications. Prosecutors have accused Martin of sending more than 700 letters containing a white powder to hundreds of state and federal officials, including members of the US Congress and election pollsters. Initial testing showed the white powder was nonhazardous, consisting of yeast or flour, though not all the letters have been fully tested yet. In an affidavit, Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) agent David Cole described the letters as expressing grievances about election integrity. “The writer of the letter described perceived issues with the 2020 election, claimed that President Donald Trump won the 2020 election, and voiced concerns regarding some of the same issues recurring in the then-upcoming 2024 election,” said Cole. The letters reportedly warned their recipients that they could face arrest for treason “or worse”. “Stay on the right side of history! Your life may depend on it,” one letter read, in ink only visible through ultraviolet light, according to the FBI. Trump, a Republican, has repeatedly cited false claims of election rigging to argue that he — not Democrat Joe Biden — won the 2020 presidential election. Those false claims helped spur Trump’s supporters to storm the US Capitol on January 6, 2021, to disrupt the certification of the voting results. Since being re-elected in 2024, Trump has continued to use his platform to spread fears of election fraud, which is considered exceedingly rare in the US. The investigation that led to Martin’s arrest stretched back to 2024, when election officials in multiple states reported receiving mail containing a white substance. The letters included a return address for the fictional “United States Traitor Elimination Army”, in Takoma Park, Maryland. The FBI has said it gathered video footage of Martin visiting US Postal Service locations in Oklahoma City, Dallas and San Antonio, Texas, to send the mailings. It also claims it has his fingerprints on a letter addressed to FBI Director Kash Patel. The Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) reportedly participated in the investigation after a suspect the FBI believes to be Martin sent messages to the group’s mailing list. Those messages echoed the mailed letters, calling the DSA’s members traitors and accusing them of treason for voting in Tuesday’s midterm election.

events.title: Canva announces layoffs, job changes for about 22% of workforce
events.summary: Some 1,271 people, or 22% of Canva’s staff, will lose their jobs, change roles or relocate to central hubs, chief executive Melanie Perkins said. Canva will cut jobs and change roles for 1,271 staff, or 22% of its workforce, after growth slowed for the first time in 10 years. Chief executive Melanie Perkins said the company must become simpler, with smaller teams, fewer niche roles, and more work centred in Sydney. Perkins called it “the hardest moment in our 13-year history” as AI and wider software industry changes push firms to do more with fewer workers. SYDNEY – Canva announced job cuts and a sweeping overhaul that will impact more than one-fifth of the workforce, as artificial intelligence forces a structural reckoning at one of Australia’s highest-profile technology companies. Some 1,271 people, or 22% of Canva’s staff, will lose their jobs, change roles or relocate to central hubs, chief executive Melanie Perkins said in a note to employees that was posted on the firm’s website on Nov 4. The sweeping changes at Canva, an online design and publishing platform, mirror a broader upheaval across the software industry. Investors have wiped billions of dollars from the value of these firms amid concerns new technology like Anthropic PBC’s Claude will cannibalise their business. Artificial intelligence is allowing people to do more on their own without speciality programmes, while companies are using AI to operate with fewer workers. “New technology is transforming what people can create, how they create it, and what they expect from the products they use,” Perkins wrote in the note. “I’ve come to the difficult conclusion that small changes won’t be enough.” Perkins, who co-founded Canva with Cliff Obrecht and Cameron Adams, did not specify how many of those staff would lose their jobs. But after the Sydney-based firm’s growth slowed for the first time in a decade, Perkins said Canva needs to become a simpler business and return to running small, empowered teams. There will be fewer niche specialisations, she said. She described the reorganisation as “the hardest moment in our 13-year history”. Sydney will become the main base for more of Canva’s product teams. Perkins said more people will work face-to-face, and most hybrid staff will spend two to three days in the office a week from January. Canva has been preparing for a potential listing, and the overhaul leaves the company in a delicate financial balance. After hitting a US$40 billion (S$51.18 billion) high in 2021, Canva’s valuation tumbled to roughly US$26 billion a year later during a broad tech selloff. While Canva’s dollar worth subsequently rebounded, the effect of more recent tumult is not yet clear. While the AI era has led to widespread job losses, investors are also questioning when, or even if, the vast associated investments will deliver a financial dividend. events.title: Bomb threats disrupt flights across Europe, no explosive devices found
events.summary: At least seven flights and an Israel-bound cruise ship receive threats, but officials say searches found no explosives. All of the planes landed safely, and searches found no explosives. The airlines affected included Ryanair, Wizz Air, Scandinavian Airlines and the Polish carrier LOT. Ryanair, the Irish budget carrier, appeared to be the hardest hit, with four of its flights to different destinations being targeted. No one claimed responsibility, and officials did not attribute blame. The incidents came a day after a plane headed for Bulgaria was diverted to Hungary after receiving a similar bomb threat while in the air. In Poland, two Warsaw-bound flights were targeted. Scandinavian Airlines Flight SK751 from Copenhagen landed without incident at Warsaw Chopin Airport, which closed a runway while the plane was inspected. “The passengers disembarked, the plane landed normally; it was not an emergency landing,” Alexandra Lindgren Kaoukji, a spokesperson for the airline, told the Polish news agency PAP. She said the matter has been referred to the Polish police. A LOT Polish Airlines flight from London’s Heathrow, which was also due at Chopin, was diverted to the city’s second airport, Warsaw Modlin, which was closed after the alert. The plane, a Boeing 737 Max, landed safely. “Nothing was found,” said Adam Szablowski, a spokesman for Modlin. Airport officials said normal operations later resumed. In Italy, two Eurofighter jets escorted Ryanair Flight FR9611 from Dublin into Rome’s Fiumicino Airport, where it landed at 10:45am local time, the airport’s operator said. The Italian Air Force said it had responded immediately to “a report of a suspected threat aboard a civilian aircraft”. An earlier Ryanair flight from Lisbon that landed at Fiumicino at 9:40am was also subjected to anti-bomb procedures. Checks of passengers, luggage and the plane “were all negative and the alert was lifted,” the operator said. In Spain, Aena, the national airport operator, said it had activated an emergency protocol “due to a bomb alert” on a Ryanair flight from Manchester. The plane landed in Murcia at 10:30am without incident. In Bulgaria, a Wizz Air flight from Bergamo, Italy, was inspected after landing in the country’s capital, Sofia, a spokesperson for the Bulgarian Interior Ministry said. A Ryanair flight from Dublin to Sofia was also targeted, the country’s transport ministry said. No explosives were found on either plane. The threats followed a similar episode on Monday, exwhen a Wizz Air flight from London’s Luton Airport to Sofia received a bomb threat in midair and was diverted to Budapest. Hungarian Defence Minister Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi said on Facebook that NATO’s air-defence alert service had flagged the flight. He said Hungarian Gripen fighter jets “took to the air within minutes” and escorted it safely to the ground. In the United Kingdom, London’s Metropolitan Police said it had been made “aware of threats against … four aircraft due to depart from or arrive at Heathrow Airport”, one of Europe’s busiest hubs, on Tuesday. It also received a further warning involving a flight at Manchester Airport. After checks, police said “no security issues were identified,” without giving further details. Late on Tuesday, the Greek Coast Guard said a Panama-flagged cruise ship, the Crown Iris, had been evacuated while anchored off the island of Syros after a bomb threat. The ship was carrying about 1,500 passengers and crew and was bound for Haifa, Israel. No device was found, and the ship was expected to resume its voyage. While no country pointed fingers over the bomb threats, they came at a time when European officials have been blaming both Russia and Iran for what they describe as “hybrid attacks” and acts of sabotage. Moscow and Tehran both deny any such campaign. This week, unidentified hackers shut down fridges in supermarkets in several European countries. Some experts said hoax bomb threats could be part of a similar pattern of low-cost, deniable disruption efforts. Rhys Jones, analysis output manager at aviation risk advisory firm Osprey Flight Solutions, said that seven confirmed bomb threats in a single day affecting flights was exceptional.

events.summary: The Trump administration is doubling down on allegations that Democrats stood up a ‘spoiler’ candidate against Republicans. The administration of United States President Donald Trump has stepped up its investigation into a US Senate race in the state of Alaska, where it says the Democratic Party put up a sham candidate to confuse voters so the Republican candidate would lose. Federal prosecutors sent so-called “target” letters to a number of people on Tuesday, including attorney Marc Elias, who has represented the Democratic Party, warning them that it has gathered enough evidence linking them to a possible crime that it regards them as possible defendants in a future indictment. list 1 of 3 Alaska’s two ‘Dan Sullivans’: How common is ballot stacking, does it work? list 2 of 3 Sullivan vows to honour Alaska race outcome, US judge dismisses DOJ lawsuit list 3 of 3 Alaska Senate candidates trade accusations ahead of election In a statement on Tuesday, Elias said, “No one should be surprised that President Trump’s Department of Justice is targeting me and my law firm on Election Day.” “We will not be intimidated by a sham investigation,” the statement continued. “We are going to keep working around the clock to support our clients and make sure President Trump and his party enjoy a well-deserved beating at the ballot box.” Incumbent Republican Senator Dan Sullivan is facing a midterm elections challenge from a former Democratic congresswoman, Mary Peltola, for a seat that could prove pivotal in determining which party controls the Senate. But the Department of Justice, which unsuccessfully attempted to have a court block the certification of the election in the state if the incumbent Sullivan loses, has gone ahead with a sweeping investigation anyway. The AP reported that more than 100 subpoenas had been sent out so far as part of the investigation, according to an unnamed person briefed on the probe.

That missive, titled “An important update on our team,” doesn’t mention AI but does state “New technology is transforming what people can create, how they create it, and what they expect from the products they use.” Perkins observed that Canva’s rate of growth recently slowed for the first time in a decade and shared her view that continued success won’t happen without change. “After exploring a wide range of alternatives, I've come to the difficult conclusion that small changes won’t be enough,” she wrote. “To set ourselves up for the next decade, we need to refound Canva, getting back to our roots of small, empowered teams with the freedom to make decisions, take ownership and focus on what matters most for our community.” The CEO did not say how many jobs would go, but argued the changes are necessary because the company has become inefficient. The changes will therefore see Canva combine its product, growth and platform teams into a single “Product Org,” which Perkins says means “changing the way we work to provide clearer ownership, greater autonomy and flexibility to tackle our most important goals.” She characterized the changes as “simplifying layers, consolidating overlapping responsibilities, and ensuring teams have the right mix of skills and experience for the chapter ahead.” The CEO three times described herself as “deeply sorry” for the changes. Affected staff will receive a calendar invite for an optional individual meeting with a senior leader. Remaining staff get to attend two rounds of meetings next week – one company-wide affair and another with their reorganized teams. Another of Perkins’ decisions will see Canva move more of its product teams to its headquarters in Sydney, Australia. The company will ask some staff to relocate and has promised “comprehensive support” to make that happen. Departing staff can keep their company-issued MacBooks and will receive at least six months' pay, a year of health insurance, plus various forms of support to find a new gig including a one-year membership of LinkedIn Premium. Perkins’ post does not cite financial pressures as a reason for the layoffs. Canva is privately held and does not face the same financial disclosure requirements as a listed business, but last year revealed it had 260 million monthly users and revenue of $3.5 billion. Execs have previously claimed the company is profitable on a free-cash-flow basis. Canva and Atlassian are among Australia’s most successful and celebrated technology businesses. events.title: Canva announces major job cuts after 'our hardest year yet'
events.summary: Canva co-founder Melanie Perkins says this year has been "our hardest" yet Canva, one of Australia's best known start-ups, has announced a shake up of the business that will affect 22% of its workers, including job cuts. In what was "without doubt the hardest moment in our thirteen-year history" co-founder and CEO Melanie Perkins said 1,271 people would either lose their jobs, be asked to relocate or change roles. The firm's value has reportedly dropped in the past year over concerns about the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) on its business as well as the cost of incorporating the technology into its platforms. It had been "our hardest year yet, and as we shared earlier this year, our growth has slowed for the first time in a decade," Perkins wrote to staff. The "incredibly hard decision" meant "significant changes," Perkins said. "For some people, this will mean changes to their roles or being asked to relocate to centralised hubs. Sadly, it will also mean saying goodbye to teammates and friends who have helped build Canva into what it is today." The company, which has staff in 37 countries, said Sydney would become the "primary home" for more of its product teams and that as of next year hybrid workers would be expected to spend two to three days in the office. Earlier this year two of its backers, Blackbird Ventures and Airtree, reportedly downgraded its valuation from A$60bn ($41.8bn; £31.1bn) at the end of last year to about A$49bn. Canva also reportedly cut its own internal valuation amid soaring AI expenses related to the roll out of new products. "New technology is transforming what people can create, how they create it, and what they expect from the products they use," Perkins said in her note on Wednesday. Perkins, who left university at 19 to found her first venture, launched Canva in 2013. The company offers a variety of templates and tools to help users without technical skills or a design background to create a range of professional-looking graphics and presentations, from wedding invitations to business pitch decks. events.title: UOB’s Q3 net profit jumps 182% to $1.25b as bank sets aside less for bad loans
events.summary: UOB is the first bank to report its third quarter earnings on Nov 4, after all three banks saw shares fall on Nov 2. SINGAPORE - UOB’s third-quarter net profit jumped 182 per cent to $1.25 billion from $443 million a year earlier, largely due to a sharp drop in provisions for potential loan losses , the bank said on Nov 4. UOB set aside $258 million for credit and other losses in the three months ended Sept 30, down 81% from $1.36 billion a year earlier. Compared with the previous quarter , its net profit fell 15 % from $1.48 billion. It also missed the $1.38 billion forecast among six analysts polled by Bloomberg. Net interest income, which measures the difference between what a bank earns from lending and pays on deposits, rose 1% year on year to $2.28 billion. Net fee income in the third quarter hit a record $733 million, a 19% increase from the same period a year ago. It also marked a 10% increase over the previous quarter. This rise came on the back of strong growth in wealth, cards and loan-related activities, UOB noted. Customer-related treasury income also reached a new high, reflecting robust client engagement and demand for hedging solutions, it added. Meanwhile, assets under management grew by 3% over the same quarter last year to reach $204 billion. UOB chief executive officer and deputy chairman Wee Ee Cheong said: “The group continued to see healthy customer activity across our businesses this quarter, with strong growth in wealth management, healthy loan growth and record fees and customer-related treasury income.” For the first nine months of 2026, wealth income rose 13 % from a year ago, while card income was up 25% year on year. Wholesale banking loans grew 9% year on year, with trade loans recording a robust 31% growth. Transaction banking also remained an important driver of the franchise’s performance, UOB said. In the third quarter, net interest income remained stable at $2.3 billion, a 1% increase year on year, as sustained loan growth offset margin pressures. Total expenses fell to $1.6 billion, a 4% decrease over the previous quarter, in line with income moderation. Wee said this financial performance reflects the strength of the bank’s diversified franchise and customer relationships, with over 8 million customers in the region. “As connectivity across ASEAN strengthens, customers increasingly value banking partners that can support them across their business, personal and wealth needs,” he said. “We are broadening our wealth franchise and strengthening our wholesale banking capabilities to support our customers’ growth and capture cross-border opportunities.” He added that backed by a strong balance sheet, UOB will continue to invest for the long term. “We see significant opportunities ahead and are confident in the group’s long-term prospects. ” This strong performance comes as the shares of all three local banks - UOB, DBS and OCBC - fell on Nov 2 , as analysts projected that wealth management fees at Singapore banks could ease in the third quarter. This followed a strong showing in the three months before, even as pressure on net interest margins persisted. UOB shares closed at $40.46 on Nov 3. Analysts also said that investors are expected to scrutinise the banks’ exposure to artificial intelligence-related financing. They are also looking out for the impact of rising bond yields on investment portfolios and capital positions. Another issue that has come under the spotlight is the banks’ role in financing firms related to the haze that blanketed Singapore and the region in October. On Oct 28, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) said that banks should review their financing relationships with customers who are linked to activities contributing to transboundary haze. This includes limiting their exposure or cutting ties with those found to have clearly breached environmental laws. According to research by environmental coalition Forests & Finance, Singapore’s three local banks have provided billions of dollars in historical financing to major palm oil and forestry groups since 2010, including some that were named in recent probes into the sources of transboundary haze. The three banks said they uphold a zero-tolerance policy towards clients engaging in activities such as deforestation and open burning. MAS added that it supports the local banks’ clear stance against burning practices, and noted that the banks will take strong action where needed. Sue-Ann Tan is a business correspondent at The Straits Times, covering capital markets and sustainable finance.

events.title: Graduates are managing AI - but are they learning much else?
events.summary: Managing AI agents is a big part of Lotte Underwood's job Recent university graduate Lotte Underwood is a public relations executive with a twist - she spends more time using AI than actually doing PR. Underwood, 25, joined London-based PR agency Fight or Flight in November last year, in the new role of "AI associate" after completing a degree and then a masters in marketing. She's part of a recently established, dedicated AI team that has built around 30 AI agents. Specific tasks include industry research, client reporting, media interview preparation, helping clients create clearer briefs, and image generation. A big part of Underwood's job is to manage those agents, check their outputs and feed those to the team members who are dealing directly with clients and the media. Another key responsibility of hers is to monitor how clients appear in the responses from AI tools like ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and others. "A huge part is being in client meetings and calls to work out what is actually going to be most helpful from these agents," says Underwood. AI is seen as one of the main factors behind graduate job cuts , but companies are also creating dedicated AI-specific graduate roles like Underwood's. Dillan Patel, for example, joined engineering software company Stride 18 months ago as an intern. A business management graduate, he was put to work developing an internal chatbot designed to capture the knowledge of a senior staff member transitioning into retirement. Patel, 24, is now an AI automation analyst, tasked with developing further internal agents to provide specific information to individual teams, while also identifying which manual or repetitive tasks across the company could be done by AI. "My role focuses on finding practical ways to use technology, automation, data and AI to improve how we operate," says Coventry-based Patel. Debra Maxwell is looking for "AI disruptors" Such AI savvy graduates are also in demand from companies like ArvatoConnect, an outsourced contact centre company. CEO Debra Maxwell says the company's usual graduate intake is on hold this year, but she plans to resume it next year with a bigger focus on AI. "We would be looking for more AI-disruptor type roles, where you can challenge us as an organisation to think more holistically about where AI can be applied and where we could grow our business from," says London-based Maxwell. "We see our graduates as not filling administrative roles, but actually adding value to the organisation in a different way." Maxwell adds: "For example, one of our recent graduates is using AI to do deep dives on specific markets, and provide more information for when we're bidding [for new contracts]. It's basically giving him a more rounded role." If AI can make a graduate job bigger and more integral to the organisation, Maxwell argues that companies can create a more loyal, engaged workforce that is able to contribute more meaningfully, much earlier. Research from consultancy PwC found that some graduate roles are assuming more responsibilities because of AI, as it allows companies to demand more senior abilities from junior hires. For the consultancy's 2026 AI Jobs Barometer , external , it analysed 2.4 million entry-level jobs in the US. It found that the entry-level roles most influenced by AI are now seven times more likely to require traditionally senior-level skills. These include motivational leadership, strategic decision making and team building. Those entry-level roles with higher expectations have in fact grown 35% since 2019, PwC found, while other entry-level roles actually shrank by 10%. Cian Clinton uses around ten AI agents for work tasks Cian Clinton, who joined consultancy Valliance last September after graduating from a Bachelor of Science in 2024, says the incorporation of AI into his role makes him feel less like a graduate, and more like an equal team member. He uses around 10 AI agents daily for different tasks. "Your ideas and your creativity are a lot more valued because you actually get to implement those firsthand, and the responsibility you take on is a lot greater because of that," says London-based Clinton, 23. "I am now taking on responsibilities which would usually take me four or five years to get to." His career progression, he believes, will now be faster as a result. "AI is killing the 'pyramid' approach…progression is no longer based on your knowledge bank. Now it's more based on your critical thinking and understanding of the processes," says Clinton. There's no doubt Underwood, Patel and Clinton are developing valuable AI knowledge which can help them across their careers. But with their time at work so focused on AI, does it matter how much - or how little - time they're spending learning about the professional field they're supposed to be operating in?
