events.title: Poundland supplier 'will lose millions' if retailer collapses
events.summary: Adam Turner is sales director at Poundland supplier Hillcrest One of Poundland's suppliers has said it will lose millions if the firm collapses. While that supplier will stay afloat, it is feared that some small and medium-sized suppliers could go under. This is in addition to potentially thousands of job losses among staff. Politicians have been putting questions to representatives of Poundland owners Gordon Brothers this week seeking "clarity" on plans for the retailer. Adam Turner, sales director at Highcrest Retail Brands - a family owned Bradford business - told the BBC that Poundland was one of Highcrest's biggest customers, and that the firms have had a relationship for decades. Highcrest mainly sells confectionary to Poundland, and turns over about £50m. It will "lose a few million" if Poundland becomes insolvent, so it will have a gap in its balance sheet next year, he said. Highcrest was a "longstanding business that can stomach this", but other medium and small suppliers have told him that "if Poundland goes under, so do they", Mr Turner said. This echoes a warning from Poundland founder Steve Smith on Monday that two or three thousand suppliers to the firm, which only work for Poundland, would be directly affected by its collapse. Not only 12,000 Poundland staff would be affected, but also potentially tens of thousands more, he said. If Poundland's stores are sold to new buyers, some of the employees may get new jobs on the same premises. However, it is understood that buyers are only interested in about half the stores at present - meaning roughly 6,000 employees would not be re-employed. Poundland's founder offers to invest in firm Published 1 day ago Mr Turner said that the last three months of the year is the "golden quarter" for retailers. In terms of sweets, Poundland will get its Halloween stock in from July, and Christmas stock in from September. These three months will be the time of year when suppliers will be owed the most by Poundland. If Poundland goes under, suppliers will be getting "pennies in the pound" back from the administration, he said, which is "very upsetting" - although he still hopes a deal can be done so Poundland can remain solvent. Poundland owners Gordon Brothers will be a secured creditor, which means they are first in line to get their money back, and suppliers "who have done nothing wrong" will take the financial hit. "It's sad. It's a nightmare for us all to be honest with you. It's not just the suppliers, it's the staff at Poundland, some of these guys have been there for many years. "It's from the warehouse staff all the way to the shop staff to everybody within head office. It's a massive ripple effect through the supply chain," he added. Mr Turner said he had no knowledge of whether Gordon Brothers had deliberately timed the process of Poundland going into administration so it could take advantage of having high stock levels, which it can then sell. One of the ways Gordon Brothers makes money is through stock liquidations - selling off stock from collapsed businesses. One insider familiar with the situation told the BBC that the timing of Poundland facing collapse was "odd" - most retailers don't fall over in the run-up to Christmas. Gordon Brothers was approached for comment. Meanwhile, business secretary Jonathan Reynolds will meet with Gordon Brothers later this week after he and Prime Minister Andy Burnham questioned why a solvent deal had not been made. Business minster Kate Dearden told MPs that government officials had also met with representatives from Gordon Brothers on Monday. "I am deeply concerned about the uncertainty surrounding Poundland's future and the impact it could have on its staff and their families who are at the forefront of my mind," Dearden told the House of Commons. "Poundland is not currently in administration and the business continues to trade, but this is a worrying time for employees, suppliers and communities", she added. The minister confirmed she would also be meeting with Poundland executives on Wednesday. She said the government doesn't want to interfere with "current ongoing commercial negotiations", but said ministers would be seeking "clarity" on the plans for the retailer. "It's absolutely legitimate for this government to ask the business if they're doing everything they can to protect employees and suppliers up and down the country," she added. Dearden told MPs that the government would be ready to help the company's employees, should the current situation end in administration. "We stand ready to support them if they need to move into new employment, however... our priority is always in protecting jobs and the Secretary of State and I will continue to engage with the company to secure the best possible outcome," she added.

events.title: US stock futures dip as investors await US midterm election results
events.summary: The greatest market reaction may come not from who wins Congress, but from how decisively they win and how far the result deviates from expectations, said an analyst. US stock futures fell and the dollar softened as investors waited for US midterm election results. Markets focused on whether Democrats could win Congress, with the size of any win seen as key. Democrats won early races, including Jon Ossoff in Georgia and Mark Warner in Virginia. They need four Senate seats to take control, while traders expect the biggest market move from how clear the result is. Asian shares rose after strong AMD results eased fears about the AI trade. Oil prices stayed volatile as war talks and supply risks, including the Strait of Hormuz, unsettled markets. SINGAPORE - US stock futures slid and the dollar softened on Nov 4 as investors girded for results from the US midterm election with the focus on whether Democrats can wrest control of Congress from President Donald Trump’s Republicans. Democrat Jon Ossoff won re-election in Georgia, marking the first significant race call of the night as polls closed in seven states. Democrats are favoured to capture the ​House and both parties are locked in an intense state-by-state battle for the Senate , leaving investors and markets on edge. “For traders, the distinction between a narrow Democratic majority and a commanding victory is critical,” said Chris Weston, head of research at Pepperstone. “A narrow blue wave may be largely priced in.” In the US Senate, where at least nine races are seen as competitive, Democrats won the first of 35 seats up for grabs on Nov 3, with US Senator Mark Warner winning re-election in Virginia as expected. Democrats need to net four seats to win control of that chamber. Weston said the greatest market reaction may come not from who wins Congress, but from how decisively they win and how far the result deviates from expectations. Futures for S&P 500 slid 0.5% while Nasdaq futures fell 0.9%. Asian markets inched higher as beaten-down tech stocks found favour after strong results from chipmaker AMD eased some concerns over the durability of the AI trade. MSCI’s broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan advanced 0.4%, led by South Korean stocks, which rose over 2% in early trading. Japan’s Nikkei slid 1.5% after returning from a holiday. AMD forecast faster-than-expected 2027 growth as its data-centre sales surge and its multibillion-dollar challenge to Nvidia gathers pace. The forecast and market-beating third-quarter results offered a strong counterpoint to mounting fears that the AI boom is losing steam and soothed investor concerns after rival Intel issued a weak outlook last week. In the oil market, prices were choppy on Nov 4 after sliding to a four-week low in the previous session as investors weighed talks to end the wars in Ukraine and Iran against worries that recent attacks in both conflicts could further disrupt supplies. The effective blockade of the critical Strait of Hormuz that links the Gulf to world markets, previously a conduit for 20% of global oil supplies, has redrawn energy flows, stoked inflationary worries and upended global rates outlook. events.title: The brutal 2026 attack ads even rivals had to respect
events.summary: Top party strategists may hate seeing one of their candidates gutted by a brutal ad. But they can still admire the hit. Why it matters: A record $11.6 billion has plastered political ads across screens of every size in the country during the 2026 midterms . Only a handful of those earned the grudging respect of operatives on both sides. 📺 Zoom in: Multiple Republican strategists singled out the "brutal" series of ads attacking Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kans.) over lawsuits against patients with overdue medical bills — some of whom were later arrested . Against the advice of his own team, Marshall released a self-directed ad answering the attacks. In Nebraska , an ad highlighting a past vote by former Gov. Pete Ricketts to pardon a man convicted of rape was singled out by both parties as one of the cycle's most damaging. Ricketts is expected to win re-election to the Senate. In Maine, an upbeat jingle hit Democratic nominee Troy Jackson for having children with his second cousin. "If he'll f**k his own family, he'll f**k yours too," the radio ad said (among other things). Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) called for the ad to be taken down. And in Florida , Rep. María Salazar (R-Fla.) turned on her own party leader, criticizing President Trump over ICE's aggressive enforcement tactics, saying some immigration policies had "gone too far." The intrigue : Even hardened operatives are dealing with a new frontier: AI-generated attack ads that can make up scenarios and put words in an opponent's mouth. In Michigan , a Republican-aligned super PAC used AI-generated imagery to depict Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed in a fabricated family photo and playing a game with cards referencing "Death to America" and 9/11. In Texas, GOP Senate nominee Ken Paxton's team used AI to depict Democratic candidate James Talarico defacing a Bible with a crayon and saying: "In the beginning God was non-binary, and he wasn't a Christian. And God said, 'let there be six genders,' and there were." 🤺 Between the lines: An attack ad helped spark this weekend's blowup in the Michigan Senate race. Rep. Haley Stevens' (D-Mich.) shocking decision to withdraw support from El-Sayed grew out of their public dispute over an ad she called antisemitic. El-Sayed ultimately disavowed the ad but said Stevens wasn't welcome at his events, and she endorsed former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) on Sunday. The other side: It's hard to imagine a bigger backfire than Vivek Ramaswamy's (R) ad featuring the estranged mother of his opponent for Ohio governor, Amy Acton (D). It could prove fatal for his gubernatorial bid, and Republicans worry it could hurt Sen. John Husted's (R) re-election chances too. The ad sparked immediate bipartisan backlash. Ramaswamy doubled down before pulling it off-air. One internal GOP poll had Acton's lead grow by 6 points after the ad ran.

events.title: Jim Cramer sees signs of life in tech stocks — but not from the usual winners
events.summary: CNBC’s Jim Cramer said technology stocks are showing signs of a comeback, with companies outside the Magnificent Seven emerging as potential new market leaders. Cramer highlighted strength in AMD, Arista Networks and Oracle but cautioned that uncertainty surrounding data center development and the Iran war could threaten a sustained recovery. CNBC's Jim Cramer said Tuesday that a new group of technology stocks may be emerging as market leaders. While heavyweights such as Nvidia , Microsoft , Alphabet and Meta have struggled to sustain rallies in recent weeks, other companies are showing signs of strength. That was evident during Tuesday's session as gains from Broadcom and Micron supported the major averages — a sign that investors may be shifting toward a different set of tech winners. "Tech's trying to make a stand here. It's just not the tech that's led us for the last few years," the "Mad Money" host said. Cramer pointed to chipmaker Advanced Micro Devices and networking company Arista Networks — both of which reported strong quarterly results after the bell Tuesday — as examples of technology companies that could help lead the sector's recovery. He also highlighted Oracle , whose shares jumped nearly 6% in Tuesday's session. "I want to believe that non-magnificent tech can lead us," he said. "But I also know that there are concerns we must be aware of before we get too cocky about one session's set of positives." One concern is growing opposition to data center development, as local communities push back due to fears about rising electricity costs and the facilities' water consumption. He said smaller developers such as Iren , Nebius and CoreWeave could be particularly vulnerable if projects are canceled or forced to relocate, while larger companies like Amazon have more resources to secure alternative locations. The ongoing war with Iran is another source of uncertainty. Oil prices turned lower Tuesday on hopes there could be progress in U.S.-Iran negotiations. But Cramer cautioned that Wall Street has repeatedly underestimated the risk of further escalation, making it difficult to declare the conflict no longer a threat to markets. He stopped short of saying that the sector had reached a lasting bottom. After months of failed rebounds, Cramer said he "would like to wait for the crescendo before I commit too much money back into tech." events.title: Cat Wu, a face of the blockbuster app Claude Code, leaves Anthropic
events.summary: Cat Wu, who led the product side of Claude Code at Anthropic, has left the AI startup. Don Feria/AP Content Services for Anthropic Cat Wu, who helped scale Claude Code into one of tech's most important products, has left Anthropic. She joined the startup in 2024 and left weeks ahead of its initial public offering. When asked if she's taking time off, Wu said, "post agi!" Cat Wu, a top product manager at Anthropic and one of a small group behind the launch of its blockbuster tool Claude Code , left the company on Friday. Wu announced her departure on Tuesday afternoon on X, thanking the Claude Code team and its users and reflecting on the tool's progress. As the head of product for Claude Code, Wu served as one of the two top leaders and evangelists for the technology alongside its original creator, Boris Cherny. Claude Code, under Wu and Cherny's leadership, turned into one of the most important products in the AI industry's history. The tech gave Anthropic the viral product it needed to boost its revenues and access more funding for compute, and it turned the company into a bigger rival for OpenAI. Wu did not say what prompted her departure and did not immediately respond to requests for comment. She's leaving at a crucial moment for Anthropic, as it churns toward a gargantuan initial public offering later this month. The company confirmed her departure. Thariq Shihipar, who also worked on Claude Code, announced his own departure last month. Wu joined Anthropic in summer 2024 and tested an early prototype of Claude Code. In Tuesday's post, she reminisced on that moment: "It worked, I was hooked, and I joined the team." Anthropic released the tool in research preview in February 2025, announcing it in a brief demo video that featured Wu and Cherny. The two decamped to AI coding startup Cursor that summer, and then returned to Anthropic a couple of weeks later, The Information reported. Wu and Cherny then oversaw Claude Code's meteoric rise, which ramped up at the end of 2025. The tool first grew popular as an automatic coder for software engineers, who suddenly had a product that could sprint through entire coding tasks. Tech giants' AI bills with Anthropic soared as more developers started burning through Claude tokens. Wu also oversees Cowork, Anthropic's tool for non-coding work, which relies on the same AI models and handles knowledge work for non-software engineers. In an interview on Lenny's Podcast in April, Wu described her role as figuring out the path to bring Claude Code to the "AGI-pilled" version that Cherny envisioned for the future — a reference to the industry term "artificial general intelligence." In her role, Wu said she worked with marketing, sales, finance, and other teams, and hired some of Anthropic 's product managers. She also regularly responded to user requests about Claude Code on social media. One commenter wrote under her X post on Tuesday, "Are you gonna take that 6 months vacations now?" events.title: Children use AI to speak video games into existence
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Children use AI to create video games with hopes of building hub in regional Queensland Bailey Francois says the workshop was a "really cool" experience. ( ABC Wide Bay: Grace Whiteside ) Children as young as eight have used Artificial Intelligence (AI) to create their own video games. The Bundaberg program focused on creativity rather than coding ability, allowing more people to be involved. Organisers hope to create a game development hub so regional kids do not need to leave their hometown to work in the industry. It sounds like fun — the cacophony of dings and pings, revving engines, and other video game effects punctuated by the occasional cheer or groan as children play. But this is no arcade. These Bundaberg children, aged eight-13, are taking part in a new gaming development workshop. You would be forgiven for thinking they had undergone extensive coding training to create these video games. Instead, they talked the games into existence using artificial intelligence (AI). The children's creativity was boundless, producing racing, quest and trivia games. Celebrating the wins was a major part of the workshop. ( ABC Wide Bay: Grace Whiteside ) Bailey Francois, 13, said AI made their ideas come to life. "Basically you can either speak to it [the AI language model] and it converts that into text," she said. "Or you can type it out, which I find a bit difficult, if you want to create a long paragraph." Bailey was one of about 20 young people who took part in the games development workshops in Bundaberg last month. The children 3D-printed, decorated and wired their own controllers. ( ABC Wide Bay: Grace Whiteside ) Participants used 3D printing to produce a console and learned how to wire a controller, before brainstorming their game idea and instructing the AI. "Game design is game design. Game design isn't animation or coding or these other things. It's its own discipline," organiser Don Meadows said. Mr Meadows grew up in Bundaberg but moved overseas to pursue his passion for game development. "There's not a games industry [in Queensland]," he said. "You move overseas and you don't come back. I'd love to come back and I'd love to start an industry here." Organisers Don, David and Ronnie. ( ABC Wide Bay: Grace Whiteside ) Queensland University of Technology (QUT) senior lecturer Cody Phillips said the Australian industry generated about $600 million in revenue each year. "Australia is definitely punching above its weight in terms of global industry presence," Dr Phillips said. "But we're not really seeing too many titles coming out of regional Australia." Luke Wogandt rated the workshop 10/10. ( ABC News: Grace Whiteside ) Dr Phillips said AI was "a new frontier" in creating opportunities. "A lot of people are building and creating games without being formally employed within the games industry," he said. "There are virtually no barriers to somebody publishing their own game." But he also believed the technology needed stronger safeguards. "There's a lot of copyright legislation that still needs to be worked out," Dr Phillips said. Alekai Sprague, 11, said it was incredible to discover what AI could be used for. Alekai Sprague says it was wonderful seeing his imagination come to life. ( ABC Wide Bay: Grace Whiteside ) "It just shows how much a simple AI can do, instead of having to learn to code and do everything yourself," he said. "It's quite a wonderful thing, watching your imagination … come to life in a game." Chase McGibbon, nine, said he was keen to keep developing games as he grew up. "I really want to try to build a game when I'm older," he said. Chase McGibbon says everyone's games were fun and different. ( ABC Wide Bay: Grace Whiteside ) The workshops were the brainchild of Mr Meadows and Bundaberg creative David Quarrell. Mr Quarrell said with creativity the main driver of game design, AI made it accessible to everyone. The idea started with Mr Quarrell's 16-year-old son, Oscar, who cannot read or write — but was able to talk to AI. "The AI didn't stop. It didn't get confused. It took everything that Oscar had said as a prompt and it filtered through all of these 'ums' and 'ahs' and it got the core substance from it and it created something," Mr Quarrell said. "We've removed the need for reading and writing and we've just allowed his imagination to be captured." The organisers are aiming to build a gaming hub in the region to encourage young people to work in the industry without leaving their hometown.

events.title: CrowdStrike's new kill switch can stop rogue AI agents in their tracks, CEO says
events.summary: CrowdStrike CEO George Kurtz said the company's new technology allows businesses to stop rogue AI agents, prevent them from restarting and cut off their network access. Kurtz says he sees AI agent safety as a major growth opportunity for CrowdStrike, pointing to growing enterprise demand and an expanded partnership with Anthropic. CrowdStrike CEO George Kurtz said Tuesday that the cybersecurity company can now shut down rogue artificial intelligence agents. CrowdStrike's new kill switch , announced Tuesday at its Fal.Con Europe conference, allows security teams to terminate misbehaving agents, prevent them from restarting and cut off their network access. It is designed to give humans more power over artificial intelligence models and systems, as concerns about how to control agents grow. "Everyone is building AI agents, but they never had the off button, and now they do," Kurtz told CNBC's Jim Cramer on " Mad Money ." "It's going to be an incredibly important part of making sure that AI agents run and operate safely." The AI Kill Switch, as CrowdStrike calls it, is part of the company's Falcon Guardian platform, which monitors AI agents operating within an organization. The technology, which is available immediately, is aimed at addressing AI safety concerns surrounding the rapid adoption of AI agents. In September, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for slowing AI development over safety concerns, a position backed by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman . Kurtz argued at the time that slowing AI development would not eliminate existing security risks, which he said underscored the need for safeguards as companies deploy autonomous systems. Kurtz said Tuesday that CrowdStrike's new kill switch represents a significant shift in cybersecurity, which has traditionally focused on protecting companies from external threats. As businesses rely more on AI agents, he argued that security providers must also ensure those systems operate safely within their own organizations. "Enabling agents to work safely is a massive market opportunity for CrowdStrike," Kurtz said. "We have AI capabilities to prevent these breaches from happening on the outside, and we also have the capabilities to make sure that agents are basically doing what they are instructed to do." The CEO compared the technology to airbags in cars, arguing that safeguards are necessary even when AI systems are designed to operate correctly. "If they go outside of those guardrails at runtime, we can kill those agents," he said. CrowdStrike is seeing growing demand for its security tools as businesses adopt AI. Kurtz pointed to CrowdStrike's partnership with Anthropic to protect its Claude Cowork product: He said enterprise customers had pushed for CrowdStrike's technology to be integrated before they deployed Anthropic's offerings. "Our customers went to Anthropic and said, 'We need CrowdStrike before we can deploy AI,'" Kurtz said. "I think it says volumes that customers would not roll out AI without CrowdStrike." events.title: Strand bookstore to pay nearly $1.5 million over Covid loan tied to Sen. Wyden's wife
events.summary: The Strand, the iconic New York City bookstore, agreed to pay nearly $1.5 million in a civil settlement for accepting a Covid government loan that was off-limits because the store is owned by the wife of Oregon Democratic Sen. Ron Wyden, according to the U.S. Attorney's Office in Washington, D.C. The Strand applied for the $932,350 loan in February 2021 from the Paycheck Protection Program administered by the Small Business Administration, U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro's office said. Store owner Nancy Bass Wyden certified on the loan application that "the spouse of a Member of Congress does not directly or indirectly hold a controlling interest in the applicant," Pirro's office said. The Strand , the iconic New York City bookstore, agreed to pay nearly $1.5 million in a civil settlement for accepting a Covid government loan that was off-limits because the store is owned by the wife of Oregon Democratic Sen. Ron Wyden, according to the U.S. Attorney's Office in Washington, D.C. The Strand applied for the $932,350 loan in February 2021 from the Paycheck Protection Program administered by the Small Business Administration , U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro 's office said Tuesday. Midterm elections 2026 live updates: Economy, inflation and voter concerns Trump focuses on Reflecting Pool in final public speech before midterms How the 2026 midterms could affect defense, healthcare, crypto and AI stocks DOJ asks Supreme Court to block California counting disputed mail-in ballots "Ms. Wyden's certification was knowingly and materially false and Strand was not eligible for the second draw loan it received," the office said. The Strand will pay $1,482,560 to settle the case. There was no determination of liability by the store, Pirro's office said. The Strand, in a statement, said the store made an "unintentional" mistake in applying for the loan, and said it was unaware at the time the funds were barred to businesses owned by the spouse of a member of Congress. Bass Wyden's husband, who has served in the Senate for more than 30 years, is a staunch critic of President Donald Trump , who appointed Pirro to the post of top prosecutor in the District of Columbia. Bass Wyden is the granddaughter of Ben Bass, founder of the Strand, whose flagship store is in Greenwich Village. Congress authorized the forgivable PPP loans when it passed the Coronavirus Aid, Relief, and Economic Security Act in March 2020. In December 2020, Congress provided additional funding for the PPP loan program with separate legislation, which "included a prohibition against businesses obtaining second draw PPP funds if a member of Congress or their spouse directly or indirectly held a controlling interest in the PPP loan applicant," Pirro's office said. In a statement Tuesday, Pirro said, "The Paycheck Protection Program was created to save American jobs, not to enrich those who aren't eligible for taxpayer-funded relief, especially the wife of a U.S. Senator." Her office noted that the False Claims Act, which the Strand was alleged to have violated, "allows the government to establish liability based on reckless disregard and permits the government to recover more than its actual losses," which is what occurred in this case. The civil settlement resolved claims brought under a so-called qui tam lawsuit, which allows private whistleblowers to sue on behalf of the U.S. government and receive a portion of any recovery. The qui tam action in this case was filed by a corporate entity, Blockquote Inc., in U.S. District Court in Washington. Blockquote, whose owners were not disclosed by Pirro's office, will receive a total share of about $148,256 in connection with the settlement. The docket for Blockquote's lawsuit is sealed from public view. The Strand, in a statement after CNBC requested comment from the store and Bass Wyden, said the restriction that the store violated was passed by Congress between the first and second rounds of the PPP. "Unfortunately, the bookstore's accountant and the bank administering the loan were not aware of this change when the second-draw application was processed," the Strand said. "We stand by the facts: the circumstances arose during an unprecedented and rapidly changing public health emergency, the mistake was unintentional," the store said. "We hope this matter will be viewed objectively and in its proper context, with the understanding that the application of justice should always be fair, impartial, and free from political considerations," the store said. A spokesman for Sen. Wyden's office said the senator and his wife do not discuss her business, and that he had no involvement in the loan or settlement.

events.title: Trump DOJ sends target letters to Democrats in Alaska Senate criminal probe: Reports
events.summary: The Trump administration's monthslong campaign to challenge how states conduct elections and pushback against those efforts come to a head on Election Day. Those efforts have included lawsuits, an attempt to implement a new U.S. Postal Service rule for mail-in ballots, threatening letters to state election officials and a plan to increase the number of poll monitors. California Attorney General Rob Bonta told CNBC that Democratic state attorneys general have "war-gamed" for "all the possibilities" for election interference. The Trump administration 's months-long campaign to challenge how states conduct elections and pushback against those efforts came to a head on Election Day on Tuesday. Those efforts have included lawsuits, an attempt to implement a new U.S. Postal Service rule for mail-in ballots this year, threatening letters to state election officials and a plan to increase the number of poll monitors. Follow CNBC's live coverage of the 2026 midterm elections The Department of Justice has sent out more than 20 letters, some to Democrats and other people identifying them as potential targets of a criminal investigation related to the Alaska Senate race, and to other recipients telling them to preserve records for that probe, a source familiar with the matter told CNBC. The New York Times earlier Tuesday reported that prominent election lawyer Marc Elias was among those sent target letters in the investigation of how a candidate with the same name as incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan ended up on the ballot of the Alaska race. Elias has represented Mary Peltola, the Democratic nominee in the Alaska election. In addition to him, at least one official at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee was sent a target letter, The Times reported. "The department is investigating possible donor fraud and conspiracy charges," according to The Times, citing a person familiar with the investigation. Receiving a target letter does not mean a person has been charged with a crime, and does not necessarily mean that they will be charged. In a statement, Elias said, "No one should be surprised that President Trump's Department of Justice is targeting me and my law firm on Election Day." A federal judge on Sunday dismissed the DOJ lawsuit that sought to delay certification of Alaska's Senate election if incumbent Sen. That case, and the reported letters to Elias and other Democrats, underscore the likelihood that the Trump administration's election-targeting efforts will continue beyond Election Day. Democratic lawmakers, attorneys general and advocacy groups are poised for battle if the administration tries to interfere with voting sites or challenge ballot counts, particularly in the states that could determine whether Trump's fellow Republicans lose their narrow Senate majority. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., on Sunday night convened the entire Senate Democratic Caucus for a briefing by him and Elias about what a Democratic aide said was the "current landscape of election threats from Trump and his allies." The aide spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the private briefing. "We've been, you know, blocking and tackling and protecting and defending our elections for months and through the last few weeks of the voting window, and it'll all culminate tomorrow," California Attorney General Rob Bonta told CNBC on Monday evening. "And each of Trump's attempts has failed." "I'm not sure what he has up his sleeves," Bonta said of Trump. Bonta said he and other California officials, along with the 23 other Democratic state attorneys general for months have been preparing for Election Day and potential actions by the Trump administration "to disenfranchise and suppress votes and voters." "We game-planned, and ... war-gamed and tabletop- and scenario planned all the possibilities," Bonta said. Bonta said that if extreme events happened, California officials would quickly seek relief from the court system.

events.title: What the voter records of California's billionaires reveal
events.summary: California's billionaire class includes Dr. Dre, Tim Cook, Marissa Mayer, Mark Zuckerberg, Beyoncé, and Jay Z, among hundreds of others. Illustration by Claudine Hellmuth/POLITICO (Getty) POLITICO was able to match 166 of California's billionaires with the state's voter file. The analysis offers new insights into the billionaires' make-up, political leanings, and voting propensity. Registered Democrats outnumbered Republicans among the billionaires identified. California's 2026 election has been the year of the billionaire. For months, a small handful of very, very wealthy people deployed their vast resources in unprecedented sums up and down the ballot. And while their spending drew widespread attention, a new analysis by POLITICO — which, like Business Insider, is part of the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network — offers a more revealing look at their party affiliations and voting habits. Some have made their politics abundantly clear. Tom Steyer, the billionaire philanthropist, attempted this year to buy his way to the governor's mansion with an ultimately unsuccessful $200-plus million primary campaign. SEIU-UHW's pursuit of Proposition 40 , a one-time tax on the state's wealthiest residents, put billionaires on the ballot explicitly, prompting a more than $300 million opposition campaign led by Sergey Brin , one of the world's richest men, who is now positioned to act as a political powerbroker for years to come. A separate billionaire, surgeon and inventor Gary Michelson, spent tens of millions of his personal fortune to promote his own measure, an immunology bond that would direct billions to an institute that he co-founded. Across the entire ballot, current and former California billionaires have spent a record $612 million on this year's state election. For years, the country's richest people have wielded a growing influence on the direction and outcome of its politics. In California, this year has supercharged that trendline. But who, in fact, are they? More than 250 billionaires call California home — or have until recently — according to Forbes. POLITICO was able to match 166 of those individuals with the state's voter file, offering new insights into their make-up, political leanings and voting propensity. Many of the state's billionaires' names are familiar to the average voter, representing the state's major industries of entertainment and tech — music icons like Dr. Dre and Rihanna, reality TV stars like Kim Kardashian as well as Silicon Valley tech moguls like Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, Anthropic founder Dario Amodei and former Google CEO Eric Schmidt (not to be confused with Eric Smidt, the billionaire CEO of Harbor Freight tools). Others run their businesses in relative anonymity — Donald Friese, the former owner of a glass and glazing products company, and James Scapa, the founder of a software firm Altair Engineering, are unlikely to turn many heads when they walk down the street. According to POLITICO's analysis, registered Democrats outnumbered Republicans among the billionaires we identified to the California voter file, despite the number of industrial titans who have visited the White House and extended olive branches to President Donald Trump. "That's more recency bias when you see all the tech elites around the table with Trump." Republican consultant Mike Murphy said the numbers challenge the assumption that wealthy people are overwhelmingly Republican. "The old model of politics equates wealth with Republican so people probably assume they've all got to be Republican if they're billionaires," he said, "and I think the data shows it's more complex than that." Zuckerberg, who has met with Trump on a number occasions and has undergone what some have termed a "MAGA-makeover," was listed as a registered Democrat, according to voter-file data the Secretary of State's office provided in early September. Amodei, another frequent guest of the White House, was also listed as a registered Democrat, as was his AI rival, Sam Altman. Headlining California's class of Republican billionaires that POLITICO identified in the voter file are former Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger, Golden State Warriors and Golden State Valkyries owner Joe Lacob and Trump mega donor and tech entrepreneur Palmer Luckey . But the billionaires were still less Democratic than their state's overall electorate (36% of the billionaires POLITICO matched to the voter file, compared to 45% of the statewide electorate). And they were more likely to have no party preference (39%, compared to 23% of voters statewide). Mitchell said that could reflect a prevailing disdain for the two-party political system. "One train of thought for a (no-party-preference voter) is: 'I don't know anything about politics, I don't care, I'm just independent.' The other is: 'I'm smarter than these parties, I know what I want,'" Mitchell said. "I'm sure a lot of these billionaires fit into that camp." Unsurprisingly, Los Angeles and San Francisco are the clear geographic centers of power among the billionaire set. More than 30 people were registered in San Francisco itself and another 15 in Los Angeles, with dozens more in the surrounding cities and suburbs. At least a quarter were born in the state, followed by 8% in New York, and at least 19% in other countries. events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Design giant Canva announces restructure affecting 22pc of global workforce Twenty-two per cent of the company will be affected by the restructure, which includes job cuts, changing roles or relocation. ( Pexels: Jonathan Borba ) Design giant Canva has announced a restructure affecting 1,270 jobs, pointing to slowing growth and "new technology" changing how people create and use products. Sydney will be made the primary hub with some staff asked to relocate. A package for outgoing employees includes at least six months' salary and other supports while they find other work. More than one in five jobs will be affected at software company Canva as it restructures amid slowing growth and rapid technological change. Canva co-founder and CEO Melanie Perkins told staff in a memo the restructure was the "hardest moment in our 13-year history". The changes will affect about 1,270 jobs, or 22 per cent of its global workforce. Ms Perkins said Canva's growth had slowed "for the first time in a decade", arguing small changes would be insufficient to prepare the company for its next phase. Canva said "new technology" was also changing how people created and used products. The company did not explicitly mention AI in the announcement. As part of the changes, some employees may be asked to relocate, with Sydney becoming the primary home for Canva's product teams. It currently has operations in Melbourne, Brisbane, Adelaide and Perth, and operates in 37 countries. "From January, we expect most Hybrid Canvanauts to spend around two to three days in the office each week, depending on what makes sense in your area," Ms Perkins said. Atlassian cuts nearly 500 jobs from Australian workforce Atlassian's Australian workforce will account for 30 per cent of the tech giant's global job cuts, with the freed-up funds to be invested in AI and enterprise sales. A package for outgoing employees includes at least six months' salary, health and wellbeing support, and the removal of the one-year equity vesting cliff for some recently hired staff. Canva will also offer $US10,000 grants through a new fund for departing employees who want to start a business or pursue a community project. The company said it had explored a range of alternatives and had come to the "difficult conclusion that small changes won't be enough". "We need to re-found Canva, getting back to our roots of small, empowered teams with the freedom to make decisions, take ownership and focus on what matters most for our community," Ms Perkins said. Canva grew out of a Perth-based startup founded by Ms Perkins and Cliff Obrecht, later joined by co-founder Cameron Adams. It became one of Australia's biggest technology success stories, growing into a global design platform used by hundreds of millions of people. Job cuts have become increasingly common across Australia's tech sector, including Atlassian's 1,600 jobs slashed earlier this year . Atlassian said AI would allow it to reduce headcount and redirect resources. Block, which owns Afterpay and logistics software company Wise Tech Global, also announced major workforce cuts. events.title: AMD stock jumps 8% on earnings as data center revenue nearly doubles
events.summary: AMD reported third-quarter earnings that beat Wall Street expectations, with revenue jumping 45% from a year earlier. Revenue in the chipmaker's data center business nearly doubled, and CEO Lisa Su said AMD can meet accelerating demand for AI chips. The stock is up 129% so far this year, but sold off in recent days on industrywide fears of overspending on AI infrastructure. Advanced Micro Devices reported third-quarter earnings on Tuesday that beat Wall Street's expectations, with revenue jumping 45% and data center sales nearly doubling from a year earlier. The stock was up 8% in extended trading. Here's how the chipmaker did versus LSEG consensus estimates for the quarter: Earnings per share : $2.09 adjusted vs. $1.95 expected Revenue : $13.38 billion vs. $13.09 billion expected Revenue increased from $9.25 billion a year earlier, AMD said in a statement . Neoclouds like CoreWeave and Nebius rallied earlier Tuesday and remained higher after AMD reported results. CEO Lisa Su said on the earnings call that she expects server revenue to double year over year in 2027 and data center AI growth to accelerate even faster than the company had projected 90 days ago. The company expects data center to drive the majority of its revenue and earnings growth. "We have worked across our supply chain to secure the wafers, substrates, advanced packaging, memory, and other key components needed to support much higher growth next year," Su said on the earnings call. AMD's report comes days after Intel disclosed similar data center growth, with revenue in that segment up 78% in the third quarter. But Intel's stock plummeted 29% on Friday over concerns about weak guidance and Intel's ability to meet demand . The data center unit makes up the majority of AMD's business, accounting for 64% of overall revenue, up from 47% a year ago. After years spent chasing Nvidia in the market for artificial intelligence graphics processing units, or GPUs, AMD's central processing units, or CPUs, are experiencing a major resurgence with the rise of agentic AI apps like Meta 's Muse. AMD's server CPUs are key for agentic apps because they power virtual machines and can run for hours on their own. Demand from agentic AI boosted AMD shares to a record in October. "Adoption is just starting, and we expect demand to grow sharply as agents are deployed more broadly and take on more complex work," Su said on the earnings call with analysts. AMD's stock is up about 125% this year, but it saw three consecutive days of losses before rallying on Tuesday amid an industrywide sell-off tied to fears about overspending on AI. AMD is also a major player in the weakening PC market, which Intel blamed for its poor outlook last week. AMD and Intel are the largest makers of traditional x86 processors that power many laptops and desktops, while other laptops rely on Arm -based processors from the likes of Qualcomm and Apple. Global PC shipments declined 4% in the second quarter from a year earlier due to soaring costs for memory and other components, according to Counterpoint Research . AMD reports PC chip sales in a segment combined with gaming chips. Revenue in that business fell 8% from a year earlier to $3.7 billion. Gaming revenue was down 40% from a year ago. For the fourth quarter, AMD said it expects about $17 billion in revenue, beating the $16.2 billion average analyst estimate, according to LSEG. AMD sees its gross margin for the quarter coming in at 55%, slightly below the average estimate of 55.3%, according to StreetAccount. AMD also sells data center GPUs and full rack-scale systems called Helios that compete directly with Nvidia's Grace Blackwell and Vera Rubin systems. Meta, Microsoft , Anthropic, OpenAI, and Oracle are all beginning to use AMD Helios in their data centers. Meta said last week that its Helios racks are up and running, and AMD agreed to invest $1 billion in Meta's equity offering. AMD has also committed to investing up to $5 billion in Anthropic, which unveiled its highly anticipated prospectus last week as it inches closer to a potentially historic initial public offering . During a visit to Taiwan in October, Su said she plans to "substantially increase our supply in 2027." Su and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang have both made multiple trips to Taiwan and South Korea this year, holding meetings with key suppliers like Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company and memory leaders SK Hynix and Samsung. In September, AMD said it would acquire World Labs for $8.2 billion in an all-stock deal. The San Francisco-based AI lab, founded by industry pioneer Fei-Fei Li, is developing a so-called world model that simulates 3D environments to aid in developing robots and other physically grounded AI applications. events.title: "I Voted" stickers become tributes at ICE memorials
events.summary: Voters in Minneapolis and Houston are among those leaving "I Voted" stickers at memorials for people killed by federal immigration agents. Why it matters: The tributes highlight how the Trump administration's unpopular immigration crackdown is motivating voters this election cycle. Zoom in: In Minneapolis , people are placing stickers on memorials for Alex Pretti , an ICU nurse, and Renee Good , a writer and mother, who were killed by federal agents in January. In Houston , voters have covered a memorial for Lorenzo Salgado Araujo , a construction worker and father who was fatally shot by ICE agents in July, with stickers and handwritten messages like "I voted for you" and "Por usted" — "for you" in Spanish. A voter places an "I Voted" sticker on a memorial for Lorenzo Salgado Araujo. Photo: Mark Felix/Bloomberg via Getty Images Ronaldo Salgado, Araujo's oldest son, placed his sticker on his father's memorial in the first week of early voting and hundreds followed him, the Houston Chronicle reports . "I am beyond touched that this community and that the entire city is voting with my dad in mind ... I didn't realize it would grow this big," he told the Washington Post. The big picture: These midterms are testing whether President Trump's 2024 gains with Latino voters have lasted. National polls in the lead-up to Election Day showed Latino voters swinging back toward Democrats , with immigration as a key area of disagreement with the administration. In an October NBC News/Telemundo poll , 67% of Latino voters said Trump's enforcement has gone too far, 31% said they or someone close now carries ID because of ICE concerns, and 27% know someone detained or deported. events.title: Anthropic is working on a system to prove AI models’ identity
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. Anthropic is working on an open source system to verify which AI model produced a given output, according to a blog post published Tuesday. The system, called FlashProve , is built to provide what researchers call “provable inference” — a cryptographic proof, essentially a mathematical guarantee, that a given output came from a specific model. It’s meant to let users confirm that the answer they received really came from the model they think they’re using. Similar to cryptographic email signatures that let recipients confirm a message really came from its claimed sender, FlashProve would be robust against impostors attempting to disguise one model as another, even when the impostor is the lab that built and runs the model. In particular, the researchers note that the system could be used to prevent an AI company from secretly swapping in a cheaper model to cut costs, or a more expensive model to inflate its performance results. FlashProve could also be used to verify claims by third parties that a specific task was done by an advanced model. “A developer might claim that their software library was scanned for vulnerabilities by a frontier cybersecurity model, or a company might claim that its business plan was given the go-ahead by an appropriate model,” the researchers write. “How can a user verify these claims?” To work, the system requires AI labs to publish a “fingerprint” of each model they release that can later be matched to specific outputs and verified cryptographically. Crucially, the fingerprints don’t reveal a model’s weights, the internal numbers that define how it behaves and which closed-model makers like Anthropic and OpenAI keep private. That means labs could publish the fingerprints without giving up their most valuable asset, enabling the system to work with commercial models, too. The system is also designed to be lightweight, so verification could be performed on a local device. As part of the announcement, researchers released a detailed technical specification and working code for various elements of the system, which is publicly available under an open source license on GitHub . Research in the system is ongoing, and there are no plans to deploy it at Anthropic or any other lab. “This research post is meant to share intermediate progress, and not a completed research agenda,” researchers explain in the announcement post. “We are sharing this explicitly with the goal that others look at what we have done, take it, and improve it.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: Canva CEO says a major reorganization will affect 22% of its workforce. Read the memo.
events.summary: Canva is laying off or changing responsibilities for nearly 1,300 employees. Alisha Jucevic/Bloomberg via Getty Images Canva says 1,271 employees — 22% of its workforce — will be affected by a major reorganization. In a 1,600-word memo, Canva's CEO wrote that it's simplifying ranks and moving more roles to Sydney. Employees who lose their jobs will get at least six months' pay. The company hasn't said how many will be cut. Canva has announced a major restructuring. On Tuesday, the design software company's CEO, Melanie Perkins , published a memo sent to employees titled "An important update on our team." In it, she said that 1,271 employees, roughly 22% of the workforce, will be affected by a reorganization. Some employees will see their roles change or relocate, she said, while others will lose their jobs. It comes after Canva lowered its growth expectations. In August, the company changed its 2026 revenue growth forecast from 30% to 20%. In Tuesday's memo, Perkins said that this year has been the company's "hardest year yet" and that "growth has slowed for the first time in a decade." Canva has also faced fresh competition from AI tools, including OpenAI's and Google's image-generating models. Read the memo: Hi everyone, Today, I have some profoundly difficult news to share. After months of thinking through how to set Canva up for the next chapter, we have made the incredibly hard decision to make significant changes to how we're organised, where some of our teams are based, and the roles and skills we need for the future. This means 1,271 people, or 22% of Canva, will be impacted. For some people, this will mean changes to their roles or being asked to relocate to centralised hubs. Sadly, it will also mean saying goodbye to teammates and friends who have helped build Canva into what it is today. This is without doubt the hardest moment in our thirteen-year history. Behind every decision is someone we care deeply about, and I know the consequences will be very real for those directly affected, their families, friends and teammates. I'm deeply sorry for the pain and disruption this will cause for everyone affected. While nothing can make this news easier, we will do everything we possibly can to support everyone affected. I want to explain as openly as I can why we're making these changes, how we reached these decisions, and, most importantly, how we will care for the people affected today. Why we're making these changes We've spoken a lot about how quickly the world is changing. New technology is transforming what people can create, how they create it, and what they expect from the products they use. Over the past thirteen years, we've turned a dream in a pitch deck into a platform used by hundreds of millions of people. None of it would have been possible without the talent, imagination and care of every single person who has been part of this journey. Yet success in our first chapter doesn't guarantee success in the next. This has been our hardest year yet, and as we shared earlier this year, our growth has slowed for the first time in a decade. After exploring a wide range of alternatives, I've come to the difficult conclusion that small changes won't be enough. To set ourselves up for the next decade, we need to refound Canva, getting back to our roots of small, empowered teams with the freedom to make decisions, take ownership and focus on what matters most for our community. It also means making some of the hardest decisions we've ever faced, including saying goodbye to people who have helped make Canva what it is today. For that, I am deeply sorry. What we're changing We're making three changes to bring more of what has made Canva special back into how we work. #1. We're simplifying how we come together to build Canva As we've grown, more of our work has become organised around team structures and narrow areas of ownership. Improving one part of our product often requires navigating between Product, Growth and Platform, with more handovers and coordination than necessary. This has made it harder to take ownership of bigger problems and to build a deeply unified product for our community. We've tried many ways to solve this over the years, but it's become clear we need to revisit our underlying structure. To do that, we're bringing Product, Growth and Platform together into one Product Org and changing the way we work to provide clearer ownership, greater autonomy and flexibility to tackle our most important goals. We want to get back to spending more time building, and less time navigating how work gets done. #2. We're reducing subspecialisation and collapsing layers to broaden ownership Over time, we've divided work across more and more subspecialties and teams. While this has helped us build valuable expertise, it's also fragmented ownership and made it harder to see the full picture, with different teams responsible for many pieces of the same work. We're reducing this fragmentation and incorporating narrower subspecialties into broader roles so teams have more ownership of goals from start to finish. We're also simplifying layers, consolidating overlapping responsibilities, and ensuring teams have the right mix of skills and experience for the chapter ahead. #3. We're co-locating closely connected teams and increasing in-person collaboration Working across countries has brought enormous benefits and talent, but it's also made it harder to bring the right people together to solve complex problems. We'll continue investing in our global team, particularly where being close to our community, customers and markets matters most. At the same time, Sydney will become the primary home for more of our product teams, as well as roles in other Specialties where shared context and close collaboration are especially important. We know relocating is a big decision for those being asked to consider it, and we're committed to making the process as smooth as possible with comprehensive support. We also want to bring more teams together in person to build trust, learn from one another and strengthen the connections that make Canva special. From January, we expect most Hybrid Canvanauts to spend around 2 to 3 days in the office each week, depending on what makes sense in your area. How we approached these decisions I know many of you will have questions about how we made these decisions. We began with one question: what does Canva need to do to succeed in the chapter ahead? We started with our mission and future goals, then considered the structures, skills and locations needed to achieve them. Only then did we look at what this would mean for individual roles. events.title: Apple stock sinks as global memory crisis hurts profits, giving Ternus his first big test
events.summary: In John Ternus' first earnings report as CEO, Apple issued a gross margin forecast that disappointed Wall Street, sending the stock down after hours. Apple blamed higher memory prices and some costs related to Siri AI for the shrinking margins. "Looking beyond the December quarter, we see the pricing for memory purchases continuing to increase," Ternus said. John Ternus' first earnings report as Apple CEO was going fine until it was time to issue a forecast for the company's gross margin, one of the key metrics followed by investors. Apple reported better-than-expected earnings and revenue on Monday, including in the company's core iPhone unit, and even projected sales in the current period that topped estimates. But just before Ternus opened the earnings call up to analysts' questions, CFO Kevan Parekh came forward with the first real piece of bad news. Parekh said that for the December quarter, which goes through the holiday season, Apple's gross margin will be between 45% and 46%, trailing the 46.3% average analyst estimate, according to LSEG. "This includes primarily the impact of higher memory costs, as well as some costs related to the ramp of Siri AI," Parekh said. Apple shares slid about 2% on Tuesday. It's part of an ongoing trend for Apple, which is absorbing some of the soaring costs from the global memory shortage. A margin drop in the fiscal first quarter would be a third straight decline for Apple, following a gross margin of 50.1% in the June period and 47.9% in the September quarter, boosted by 1 percentage point of tariff refunds. At the midpoint of the forecast range, it would be Apple's lowest gross margin since the fiscal fourth quarter of 2023. "What we're seeing with memory pricing right now is unprecedented," Ternus said on the call, adding that the company is paying more than it did earlier this year. "Looking beyond the December quarter, we see the pricing for memory purchases continuing to increase." Ternus, who took the reins from Tim Cook on Sept. 1, is grappling with a problem that his predecessor spent his final months addressing. Cook told The Wall Street Journal in June that the memory situation was a "hundred-year flood." Apple followed by raising prices across the board on Macs, iPads and accessories. In September, Apple increased the prices of its iPhones by $100, which Ternus said the company did "reluctantly." 'Less flexibility in the supply chain' Computer and smartphone makers everywhere are suffering. On Friday, Intel had its worst day on the market since the 1970s due to a weak forecast tied to the softening PC market. It's all because of insatiable artificial intelligence demand. AI server giants like Nvidia and hyperscalers are buying up all the RAM they can find, and they're willing to pay a premium for it, leaving little supply for companies that make smartphones and tablets. Despite its size and global clout, Apple said it expects supply constraints on iPhones and Macs in the holiday quarter, primarily driven by memory. On the call, Ternus had some top lieutenants field component-related questions. Sabih Khan, chief operating officer, became the first Apple COO to appear on an earnings call since Cook in 2010, when Steve Jobs was CEO. "As we have said before, we're seeing less flexibility in the supply chain than normal," Khan told analysts on the call. In response, Apple has drastically increased its purchase obligations to secure supply, Khan said. Those obligations rose by $33 billion from the June quarter to the September period, Khan said, though he declined to answer questions about whether Apple had signed "long-term agreements" with memory makers. "We're always working hard to improve supply," Khan said. Even with the recent margin slide, Apple's gross margins are still well above where they sat earlier in the Cook era, when the number would predictably come in between 38% and 39%. As Apple's profitable services business grew, its gross margin expanded , hitting 40% in 2021 and growing from there. Analysts see a potential silver lining for Apple in the current market turmoil. Because Apple is more capable of eating a portion of the increased costs, some experts predict the company will take market share from makers of Windows PC and Android phones that don't have such a cushion. Citing data from a third-party researcher, Ternus said gains are already happening. "According to IDC, we gained share globally for the quarter and for the full fiscal year," Ternus said. "And we have never sold more Macs in a fiscal year than we did this time, which is a truly remarkable testament to these incredible products." events.title: They opened a hotel together. The Learjet crash cut their love story short.
events.summary: Rachael Reed and Charmi Fehr were killed in Sunday's Learjet crash. The Reed and Fehr families Rachael Reed and Charmi Fehr were killed in the Learjet crash on Sunday. Reed and Fehr fell in love fast and eventually opened up a hotel together in Roatán, Honduras. Former coworkers mourned the couple, calling Reed the "perfect teammate." Rachael Reed spent decades visiting the island of Roatán . She traveled to the Honduras locale in her teens and quarantined there with her partner, Charmi Fehr, during the COVID-19 pandemic. In 2023, she and Fehr put down roots and became owners of a boutique, idyllic hotel. On Sunday, their love story was cut short. Reed and Fehr were traveling from Austin to the Bahamas on a private plane with entrepreneur Adam Robinson and his family, whom they called friends. The Learjet crashed near Greenacres and Palm Beach, Florida, killing all nine of its occupants. Across social media, friends and relatives mourned the couple. They commented on memories of Fehr from his childhood in Paraguay and Reed from her high school years in Oklahoma. Whitney Pyle worked with Reed when she was an ICU nurse. She told Business Insider that Reed showed great kindness to hospitalized patients and their families in their dying days. "That's very hard to see," Pyle said. "What once she gave to patients and their families, now her family is going through." From nurse to brow artist Reed graduated from the University of Central Oklahoma with a degree in nursing, according to her LinkedIn. While studying, Reed was a Red Cross representative . She quickly took on nursing gigs in-state and in San Diego, her profile says. Jason Suttles worked with Reed shortly after she graduated in the mid-2010s. He considered her the "perfect teammate," attentive and receptive to feedback. "She didn't come out of school acting like she knew everything, or that anything that we were doing wasn't interesting to her," Suttles told Business Insider. "In the nursing world, where you don't have anybody but your teammates, it's good to have good ones." Reed described her career as spanning "diverse industries, including real estate, critical care nursing, and aesthetics" on LinkedIn. She owned BrowBabe, an Oklahoma City microblading studio . After they worked together as nurses, Pyle said that she connected her mother with Reed for services. She "made people feel welcomed," Pyle said. The Oklahoma City shop is now operated by Cassandra Barnes. In an Instagram post, Barnes called Reed the "original BrowBabe," explaining that she was a friend and mentor who introduced her to the world of makeup. "A piece of her will always live on in the work I do and the passion I have for this industry," Barnes wrote. A traveler's love story Reed was an adventure-seeker, hiking to waterfalls and scuba diving. In 2021, she linked her globe-trotting back to another business line: real estate. "Buying a house like this is literally what opened up my world of traveling," she wrote on her sister's home listing. The couple also renovated and sold an Oklahoma City house in 2021, and considered selling another one of her Oklahoma properties in June. Travel also brought Reed and Fehr together. In 2019, Reed was traveling solo in Peru, according to travel blogger Madison Krigbaum, who visited the property. Reed met Fehr, who was also visiting the South American country from Paraguay, at a Peruvian hostel, the blogger wrote: "It was love at first sight." The blogger wrote that Fehr would "later become her fiancé." In an image shared by the families, both Reed and Fehr wear rings on their left hands. Reed had long been connected to Roatán, an island off the northern coast of Honduras . She first visited in the mid-2000s at age 15. Her mother did nonprofit work and built a school there, according to the travel blog. Reed said that she has traveled to Roatán three to four times a year ever since that first trip. In November 2019, Reed and Fehr traveled to Roatán with their poodle, Marlie. What was initially meant to be a shorter trip extended with the COVID-19 pandemic . After a period of isolation, the couple got used to island life and made friends with their neighbors. "We take care of each other," she wrote at the time. "We bake bread for one another." After months of boating, fishing, and meditating, Reed and Fehr returned to the United States after COVID-19 pandemic restrictions were lifted, according to the travel blog. They eventually split time between the US and the island. Reed loved Roatán deeply. In a video posted to Facebook, their friend Bryon Robbins said that she cared for the island's children and animals alike, chasing after the motorcycle of a man who had abused a dog. They could talk and talk, he said. "She would make a 50-minute ride to the east end feel like 15 minutes," he said. The new hoteliers In 2023, Reed and Fehr established a new kind of connection to the island: a 16-room hotel. The couple co-owned Arca Boutique Hotel, a beachfront property promising gorgeous views and Caribbean cuisine . A review of the hotel from Wanderluxe said that Reed was "passionate about her adopted second home," personally helping guests book massages and find the island's best bars and restaurants. The hotel leaned into sustainability; it was "woven into every detail," the hotel said in an Instagram post. Reed and Fehr installed energy-efficient lighting, eliminated single-use straws and food containers, and said they only worked with tour operators who showed a commitment to the island's natural beauty. Guests seemed to love it. The hotel has a 4.9-star average on TripAdvisor. "Both of the owners were so kind and knew us by name within the first day," one reviewer wrote. In a statement posted on Facebook, Arca said that Reed and Fehr were far more than the hotel's owners. "They were family," the hotel wrote. "They believed in us, inspired us, and gave us the opportunity to be part of something truly special." Reed knew as well as anyone else: life can change on a dime, so you have to enjoy every moment. "I've learned that our plans are really pretty laughable most of the time," she wrote in a pandemic-era blog post. "In the blink of an eye, things can change." events.title: OpenAI hires Uber President Jill Hazelbaker to lead communications, filling a critical role that was curiously vacant for 10 months
events.summary: OpenAI has hired one of Uber’s highest ranking executives to oversee its global communications efforts, filling a key role that had been vacant for nearly a year as the AI company navigates a challenging political landscape and moves closer to an initial public offering . Jill Hazelbaker is joining OpenAI as chief corporate affairs officer, the company announced on Tuesday. Hazelbaker, who had been president and chief corporate affairs officer at ride hailing giant Uber, will work alongside OpenAI’s leaders to “deepen public understanding of AI and strengthen trust in its mission,” the company said. She will report to OpenAI co-founder and president Greg Brockman and starts in early December, OpenAI told Fortune . “As AI becomes part of more people’s lives, how we communicate, engage, and earn public trust has never been more important,” Brockman said in the announcement, citing Hazelbaker’s experience and understanding of the “opportunities and responsibilities that come with building technology at global scale.” Hazelbaker is a well respected communications professional in the technology industry. She has served as Uber’s President and Chief Corporate Affairs Officer for the past 11 years, and previously held senior leadership roles at Snap and Google. She is replacing Hannah Wong, who served as OpenAI’ chief communications officer (CCO) until January 2026. Since then, OpenAI’s Chris Lehane has been leading the team in the interim. Hazelbaker previously turned down the role In the ten months since Wong’s departure, OpenAI has experienced a series of public controversies —most notably when its AI agents hacked the company Hugging Face during training in July. The 11-year old company has been criticized for not being sufficiently transparent and communicative about its operations, at a time when public concerns about AI’s potential harms to society, the labor market, and the environment are rising. Backlash to the massive AI data centers being built across the U.S. has emerged as one of the key issues in the midterm elections taking place on Tuesday. In September, OpenAI told Fortune it was not rushing to fill the role, and was focused on getting the right candidate. Over the summer, it ramped up its search by hiring an executive recruiting firm. OpenAI offered Hazelbaker the position in the spring, but she turned it down, as Fortune reported in September. Sources suspected her close relationship with Uber’s CEO Dara Khosrowshahi, desire to be on the East Coast for her family, and already high salary played a role in her declining the role. It appears OpenAI has now made Hazelbaker an offer she cannot refuse. Hazelbaker will remain on the East Coast, but will spend time in San Francisco, where OpenAI is headquartered, the company told Fortune . “The work of building public trust has never been more consequential,” Hazelbaker said in the announcement, describing AI as the “most profound technological shift of our lifetime.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: JetBlue raises bag fees for third time in a year as fuel costs bite
events.summary: JetBlue has raised its checked bag fees for the third time in less than a year as fuel costs continue to eat into its profits. Fees will be as much as $70 for a first bag for many economy-class passengers flying during peak travel times like holidays or during the summer. Other airlines raised baggage fees earlier this year. Welcome to the era of the $70 bag fee. JetBlue Airways has raised the price of checking a bag for many customers for the third time in less than a year as high fuel costs continue to eat into the industry's profits. Checking a first bag for travelers booked in economy will now be $50, up from $45, if purchased more than 24 hours before departure during a nonpeak travel period. If it's paid within 24 hours of departure, the fee will be $60. During a peak period, such as during the holidays or the summer, it will be $55 if purchased more than 24 hours before departure, up from $49, and $70 for within 24 hours of departure. There are exceptions to the checked bag fees, such as for customers who hold a co-branded JetBlue credit card or who hold elite frequent flyer status. "We're adjusting checked bag fees to help offset rising fuel and operating costs," JetBlue said in a statement. "This helps us keep our base fares competitive while giving customers the choice to pay for a checked bag only if they need one." The price of jet fuel, airlines' biggest cost after labor, has roughly doubled this year since the start of the Iran war in February, costing airlines billions and driving up the price of tickets. Jet fuel was going for $4.44 a gallon on Tuesday for the U.S. Gulf of Mexico, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. Other airlines often follow when one carrier raises fees. Major U.S. airlines did so earlier this year after JetBlue raised its bag fees. The changes were reported earlier by the Thrifty Traveler blog . events.title: Data centers are turning to old jet engines as the wait for power grows
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. Stuck in years-long lines for grid connections and new turbines, some AI data centers are making their own electricity with converted jet engines, the New York Times reported Tuesday. The engines, pulled from retired aircraft and rebuilt to burn natural gas, aren’t anyone’s idea of a permanent power plant. But they’re another sign of how far power supply has fallen behind the AI buildout. For companies stuck in those lines, the main draw of converted jet engines is how quickly the engines can be up and running. “It’s all about getting power as fast as possible,” Rystad Energy analyst Audun Martinsen told the Times. With jet-powered units, “they can have a data center running in 24 months,” he said. Hooking up 100 megawatts to the grid in Northern Virginia, by comparison, takes about seven years , according to the International Energy Agency. Most power capacity is expected to come on by 2031, an executive at Mitsubishi Power, one of the world’s top makers of power generation equipment, told Bloomberg last week . In some cases, these delays are already costing some data center operators business. Last month, Microsoft pulled out as the anchor customer for Nscale’s data center in Loughton, England, after the local utility said it couldn’t deliver enough power until the early to mid-2030s. Elon Musk’s xAI is among the companies already using the engines, having installed eight converted jet-engine turbines in Mississippi to help power its Colossus 2 data center in Memphis, the Times reported, citing state permits and satellite imagery. The units come from ProEnergy, which rebuilds a GE engine commonly found on Boeing jets. In 2025, OpenAI followed Musk’s lead with gas turbines at its first Stargate site in Abilene, Texas. Crusoe, a Denver-based startup that builds AI data centers, is constructing that Abilene campus and ordered 13 of ProEnergy’s converted units in April. In September, Crusoe walked away from a $1.25 billion deal to buy 29 natural gas turbines from Boom Supersonic, a startup developing a supersonic passenger jet that has also begun selling a version of that jet’s engine as a power plant for data centers. A Crusoe spokesperson told TechCrunch at the time that the company still plans to use turbines. Currently the Trump administration is adding to the pressure by encouraging data centers to generate their own electricity. Converted jet engines come with trade-offs, though: They’re less efficient and pollute more than turbines designed for conventional gas plants, and it takes more of them to make the same amount of power, according to the Times. That may ultimately make converted jet engines a short-term play with some experts saying that efficiency and environmental concerns may grow in importance in a year or two.
