events.title: Raphinha, Lamal fire Barcelona to 3-0 Champions League win over Aston Villa
events.summary: Barca took early lead through Lamine Yamal before Raphinha continued fine goal-scoring form with a second-half brace. Raphinha struck twice to propel Barcelona to a 3-0 Champions League win over visitors Aston Villa on Tuesday, ending the English side’s perfect start to the football competition. Five-time winners Barcelona took an early lead through Lamine Yamal before Raphinha continued his fine goal-scoring form with a second-half brace. Barca bounced back after defeat to champions Paris Saint-Germain (PSG) in their previous European outing to stay in the hunt for a top-eight league phase berth. Manager Unai Emery’s Villa competed well in the first half, but were eventually undone by Barca’s greater ability in the final third. The Champions League anthem was not played before the game, as a mark of respect for Tenerife striker Jesus de Miguel , who died of a cardiac arrest on Tuesday morning after an on-pitch collision in a Spanish second-division match the previous day, provoking shock across the football world. “Yes, it was [a good win]; I want to dedicate this win to the fans, but today I don’t want to talk about football, I want to send a message to the family of Jesus – may he rest in peace,” Raphinha told Movistar. “This can happen to anyone; it’s very tough … you’re going to play a game, and the same thing can happen to you… “From the club, I want to send a message of strength to the family.” Villa captain John McGinn had only visited Camp Nou once previously, on a summer holiday as an eight-year-old, and might have expected better weather than the downpour both teams were subjected to. The skipper might also have expected a more focused start, with Villa handing Barcelona the lead in the seventh minute. The Spanish champions pressed Aston Villa extremely high, and Joao Gomes played a poor pass straight to Yamal in his own box. The 19-year-old winger gladly took the gift and stroked past Villa goalkeeper Zion Suzuki. Emery, who endured one of the worst nights of his career away at Barca when helming PSG in 2017 during a 6-1 defeat, may have feared the worst. However, Villa reacted strongly, and Matty Cash had a vicious drive deflected narrowly wide before Joao Cancelo blocked Gomes’s effort. Barcelona goalkeeper Joan Garcia was quick off his line to beat Nicolas Jackson to a dangerous through-ball. Suzuki saved from Anthony Gordon as Villa again struggled to bring the ball out from the back under Barca’s pressing. Garcia was called into action again by Johan Manzambi as the match lurched from end-to-end. Barcelona extended their lead early in the second half when Fermin Lopez fed Raphinha, who showed quick footwork before finding the bottom corner. Cancelo powered a strike narrowly over before setting up Raphinha for Barcelona’s third with a superb cross with the outside of his boot. The Brazil winger, who has made the number nine position his own this season, pounced from close range for his 19th goal of the season across all competitions. Yamal sent a shot skidding wide as Barcelona probed for a fourth. It did not come, but the Catalan giants were able to record a first Champions League clean sheet in 19 games. Elsewhere on Tuesday, Bayern ‌Munich and PSG underlined their Champions ⁠League title ⁠credentials with victories over Atletico Madrid and Villarreal respectively, while Manchester United came ⁠from two goals down to snatch a dramatic win over AS Roma. Bayern broke down a stubborn Atletico ⁠side in Madrid as second-half goals from Lennart Karl and Konrad Laimer secured victory, while PSG set a record as the fastest team to score four goals in ‌a Champions League match on their way to a 6-0 victory. At Old Trafford, Matheus Cunha struck twice in quick succession after the break as United overturned a two-goal deficit to beat Roma 3-2, the comeback following protests by home supporters.

events.title: Nasdaq ends higher as AI heavyweights rebound ahead of midterm results
events.summary: Traders working on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange, in New York City, on Nov 2. Nasdaq rose 0.83% as AI stocks rebounded, with Microsoft, Amazon and Nvidia up. Apple fell 1.9% after warning that memory chip costs would lift holiday-quarter margins. The Nasdaq 100 is now in a correction, more than 10% below its 6 October record, as investors worry AI spending is rising faster than near-term cash returns. Markets also watched the US midterm elections, seen as a possible shift for fiscal policy, regulation and tax. Traders expect the vote to reduce a major market overhang. NEW YORK - The Nasdaq ended higher on Nov 3 as AI heavyweights rebounded ahead of US midterm election results, while Apple fell after the iPhone maker joined the list of Big Tech companies whose quarterly results failed to impress investors. Apple dropped 1.9% after it warned that the cost of memory chips would continue to rise, pressuring its holiday-quarter gross margin. Memory-chip maker Micron Technology gained 2.6%, while Nvidia rose 2.3% after falling in the last four sessions. The broader Philadelphia chips index jumped, while AMD rose ahead of its quarterly report due after the bell. Microsoft and Amazon each moved more than 2% higher. “This is a rotation from safe tech, like Apple, into riskier tech, like chipmakers,” said Jay Hatfield, chief executive officer at Infrastructure Capital Management. “It’s clear dip-buying in a higher-risk, Nasdaq-driven market.” The Nasdaq 100 on Nov 2 ended more than 10% below its Oct 6 record-high close, confirming that the tech-heavy index has entered a correction as investors worry that massive investments in AI infrastructure are outpacing near-term cash generation. The S&P 500 is down about 3% from its record-high close on Oct 6, and it remains up over 10% in 2026. Oil prices eased as investors weighed talks to end the wars in Ukraine and Iran against worries about additional supply disruptions from recent attacks in both conflicts. Iran and the United States are still far from a deal to end their war, a senior Iranian official told Reuters. The S&P 500 climbed 0.36% to end the session at 7,568.92 points. The Nasdaq gained 0.83% to 25,372.01 points, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average declined 0.38% to 51,787.04 points. Six of the 11 S&P 500 sector indexes declined, led lower by consumer staples, down 1.76%, followed by a 1.75% loss in materials. AI-powered analytics software provider Palantir Technologies forecast revenue above estimates for the last three months of the year after topping third-quarter expectations. Its shares dipped. American voters will deliver a verdict on the first two years of President Donald Trump’s second term in the Nov 3 midterm elections, with polls and nonpartisan analysts favouring Democrats to wrest the House from Republicans, while control of the Senate remains uncertain. “Markets will assess potential implications for fiscal policy, regulation, taxation and government spending. This will be good to put behind us as it has been an anticipated volatility event for quite some time,” said Ken Mahoney, CEO of Mahoney Asset Management. Morgan Stanley analysts said in a note earlier this week that the elections should help remove a major market overhang. They believe a US market correction that began in June is in its “final innings.” Gartner dropped 13.2%, while US-listed shares of Thomson Reuters and Shopify fell 9.9% and 8.7%, respectively, after all three reported quarterly results. Declining stocks outnumbered rising ones within the S&P 500 by a 1.6-to-one ratio. The S&P 500 posted 10 new highs and one new low; the Nasdaq recorded 57 new highs and 251 new lows. Volume on US exchanges was relatively light, with 16.6 billion shares traded, compared with an average of 17.4 billion shares over the previous 20 sessions. REUTERS

events.title: North Korean fake job interview led to $6.3B Binance heist
events.summary: North Korean cryptocurrency thieves tricked a Binance software engineer into downloading malware onto their work-issued computer during a fake job interview process before last week's record-breaking $6.3 billion heist . In an incident report published on Tuesday, the cryptocurrency exchange said several techniques - including social engineering via fake job interviews, malware downloads, compromised internal AI tooling, endpoint takeover, and an “advanced transaction-authorization method” - led to the October 29 security breach. “Our current investigation indicates that this was a sophisticated, multi-stage campaign,” the incident report said. “It was not a single isolated breach or a simple phishing incident.” Over the weekend, the FBI attributed the theft to TraderTraitor, a North Korean hacking operation linked to Lazarus Group , known for combining espionage with massive cryptocurrency heists . The Pyongyang-backed crew is also highly adept at job market scams - both posing as IT workers , who are then hired by Western companies , and as potential employers to lure software engineers into downloading malware and infecting corporate devices . With the recent Binance attack, the Norks used the latter. The attack prep began back in June with a supply chain attack when one of its engineers downloaded a malicious Homebrew installation . While the malware was detected by the security team, the device was replaced, and all affected credentials rotated, “Engineer A’s role and his related colleagues on our wallet infrastructure team was exposed to the hacker,” the report says. Three months later, the social engineering part of the attack happened. In September, another software engineer was contacted via a “legitimate job-hunting platform” by someone purporting to be a project director who arranged a series of job interviews for the Binance engineer with the fake company. During the first round - a live video interview with the engineer and a fake HR rep - the interviewer “shared a social media account with him, including personal photos and videos posted on the platform, in order to build trust,” according to the report. “This was more advanced and deceptive than previously seen social engineering approaches.” The second interview with someone purporting to be the CEO of the phony company was conducted on a “popular social chat app,” and toward the end, the CEO instructed the engineer to download an “assignment” containing a malware-laced code repository. The code executed on his work computer during the setup process, which kicked off a series of unauthorized activities. According to Binance, the malware replaced a legitimate development tool component with a malicious version, which executed commands and established communication with an attacker-controlled external server. The attackers also took steps to hide the malicious script and evade detection, and it worked. Binance’s endpoint security tools did not immediately detect the malware. Here’s the script: CREATE /opt/homebrew/Cellar/pyenv/2.8.0/libexec/pyenv_ MODIFY pyenv_ → 3,414 B DELETE .../libexec/pyenv (3,344 B) ← remove the valid pyenv RENAME pyenv_ → pyenv (3,414 B) ← replace it with a malicious version DELETE /opt/homebrew/bin/pyenv (3,414 B) ln (create a new symlink) + spawn zsh Then, on October 20, the miscreants used the compromised computer and an internal AI tool to gain access to the computers of wallet DevOps engineer A and another wallet software developer, Engineer C. Engineer A had a container deployment permission token on his computer, which the Norks soon discovered. On October 29, the attacker accessed Engineer C's computer, used the stolen credentials from Engineer A to deploy a container, and triggered a script to launch the cryptocurrency-stealing attack. As of Tuesday, Binance said it has rebuilt the compromised wallet system and internal AI tool, and replaced all of the affected devices. It also decommissioned all credentials and tokens assigned to the compromised engineers, and is working with law enforcement, blockchain intel firms, and security researchers to trace and freeze the assets. The crypto exchange has also hired independent cybersecurity experts to conduct a cybersecurity review of the incident, and recommend additional protective measures. Binance said it’s also working to establish a security research fund and initiatives with AI companies and security shops to focus on AI security in blockchain environments.®

events.title: Singapore’s rise as a wealth hub mirrors Asia’s changing fortunes: Julius Baer Asia head
events.summary: Singapore’s cross-border wealth is expected to grow at a compound annual rate of 9% between 2025 and 2030, from about US$2.1 trillion (S$2.7 trillion) to US$3.3 trillion. Singapore has become Julius Baer’s second-largest global hub after Switzerland. Its workforce grew from 34 in 2006 to more than 1,350 this year. Asian wealth is changing from preservation to diversification, succession planning and family governance. Younger heirs and tech founders want global equities, alternatives and discretionary portfolio management. Julius Baer says Singapore is a leading safe haven because of neutrality and strong governance. Cross-border wealth there may rise 9% a year to US$3.3 trillion by 2030. SINGAPORE – More affluent families from around the region and globe are turning to Singapore to manage their wealth as their focus shifts from preserving fortunes to diversifying investments, succession planning and transferring wealth to the next generation, Julius Baer’s Asia head Jimmy Lee told The Straits Times. The Swiss private bank serves clients across more than 25 markets from Singapore, where its workforce has grown from 34 employees in 2006 to a multinational workforce of more than 1,350 in 2026. Since it set up shop here 20 years ago, Singapore has grown to become Julius Baer’s second-largest global hub after Switzerland. “Singapore’s rise as a global wealth management centre has mirrored the evolution of wealth across Asia,” said Lee, a veteran private banker w ho b ecame the bank’s head of Asia-Pacific in 2016. Two decades ago, wealth management in Singapore was primarily focused on wealth preservation, he said. Many clients were first-generation entrepreneurs who had built their businesses through challenging economic conditions and were focused on protecting capital. Portfolios were often concentrated in familiar regional markets, with equity trading playing a central role. Alternative investments, sustainability and philanthropy were less prominent considerations. Digital assets had yet to emerge as an investable asset class, he said. Meanwhile, Singapore was strengthening its regulatory framework and financial infrastructure, helping to establish its position as a trusted financial centre. Today, the landscape has become more diverse and client priorities have evolved alongside it. The rich have shifted their focus from wealth preservation to diversifying investments, succession planning and transferring wealth to the next generation, says Jimmy Lee, Julius Baer’s Asia head. A new generation of wealth holders, including second- and third-generation family members, as well as entrepreneurs from sectors such as technology, fintech and e-commerce, are placing greater emphasis on diversification across geographies and asset classes, Lee said. Interest in global equities, alternative investments and thematic opportunities has increased, while discretionary portfolio management – where a licensed portfolio manager makes buying and selling decisions on clients’ behalf without requiring prior approval for each trade – has become more widely accepted. As intergenerational wealth transfers continue across Asia, families are also taking a more structured approach to managing wealth. Succession planning, family governance and long-term stewardship have become increasingly important alongside investment performance. “Singapore’s development reflects many of these trends. Supported by a stable regulatory environment, financial resilience and a deep ecosystem of financial expertise, it has become an important centre for wealth management and family offices in the region,” Lee said. More than a quarter of Julius Baer’s global business today originates from Asia, spanning clients, assets under management and talent. Lee said the bank’s presence in the region reflects two decades of sustained investment and commitment. “Building long-term relationships in Asia requires local expertise, continuity and a willingness to invest through market cycles. We view our presence here as long-term, underpinned by the belief that enduring client relationships are built through consistency, proximity and a deep understanding of local markets,” he said. Singapore is also an important centre for innovation for Julius Baer, which in 2021 established Launchpad, its dedicated innovation lab in the Republic, to test and incubate disruptive tech solutions, including digital assets and generative AI. Lee said that as client needs continue to evolve, Singapore will remain central to how the bank develops new capabilities and delivers the next generation of wealth management. In a new report on Asian safe havens, Julius Baer said market volatility driven by artificial intelligence, rising geopolitical tensions and growing government debt has prompted investors to rethink how best to protect their wealth. Traditional safe-haven assets, including US Treasuries, gold and the Japanese yen, have delivered mixed results in 2026.

events.title: Apple warns rogue AI agents could ‘conceal’ and ‘manipulate,’ causing unintended consequences for its business
events.summary: Apple is cautioning that rogue AI agents that “conceal actions” or hide or manipulate information could pose a threat to its business if they access systems without authorization and cause damage. The warning by the world’s second most valuable company came in an annual filing Tuesday, a day after Apple reported its fourth-quarter financial result s . In the risk factors section , Apple expanded its warnings about artificial intelligence. Apple’s caution underscores the risks tech giants and other companies are projecting after a string of AI safety incidents in recent months, which have prompted companies to release new security features and debate regulatory measures. In its 10-K filing, which is made each year following the end of its fiscal year, Apple said “artificial intelligence agents and other technologies can take actions autonomously, including interacting with internal or external systems that in some cases they may not be authorized to access, executing or altering code, sending communications, and completing transactions.” Such technologies, the iPhone maker said, “may behave in unintended or unpredictable ways, including by taking actions that were not directed, instructed or authorized, exceeding permissions, defying directions or resisting instructions.” And it noted that autonomous AI agents that go rogue could “conceal actions, hide, withhold or manipulate information, or generate inaccurate or deceptive outputs.” Apple is the latest to warn about risks posed by AI agents. Google parent Alphabet also pointed out the risks posed by rogue agents in a recent filing. Google, however, was more pointed about the potential consequences, writing that during AI model testing, it had observed unexpected behavior, including agents taking actions outside their intended scope, which could ultimately lead to “severe or catastrophic security and societal incidents, or negatively affect human rights.” The risks outlined by companies follow several major cybersecurity incidents involving AI models, most notably this summer’s attack by OpenAI agents on AI company Hugging Face. In Anthropic’s IPO prospectus, made public last week, the company listed many risk factors , including incidents in which its models gained unauthorized access to real-world systems during security testing. It also estimated that 5% to 7% of its revenue this year came from customers later found to be violating its usage policies. Executives at Microsoft and other major tech companies have called for a greater focus on securing AI agents. Microsoft recently announced a set of controls to detect, monitor, and restrict AI agents, including cutting their permissions or stopping them if they behave suspiciously. Chief executive Satya Nadella has argued that companies should treat agents as potential insider risks and put security controls outside the AI model rather than trusting the model to police itself. In its 10-K filing on Tuesday, Apple also outlined other pressures, including memory and storage component shortages that it said will intensify. It also said demand for cloud computing, storage, and other AI infrastructure has produced “constrained supply, extended lead times, and increasing costs” that could affect its AI rollout. Its research and development spending rose 32% year over year, driven by higher infrastructure-related costs, including AI investments. On Monday, Apple chief executive John Ternus described agentic capabilities as “promising tools for users” but cautioned that users must be fully aware of what access they grant, and he stressed user security and privacy. Apple shares dropped roughly 2% on Tuesday after the company said its margins would continue to be squeezed by memory chip costs and after it showed slowing growth in its Services segment. Ternus, on his first earnings call as CEO, largely stuck to scripted marketing points and offered few details about Apple’s plans for personalized AI agents. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Ted Schlein’s Ballistic Ventures seeks $490M for new funds amid AI-driven cybersecurity boom
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. Ballistic Ventures, the cybersecurity-focused venture capital firm co-founded by former Kleiner Perkins partner Ted Schlein (pictured above, second from the right), is seeking to raise $490 million across two new funds, TechCrunch has learned through regulatory filings. The San Francisco-based VC firm filed with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission this week to raise $360 million for its third flagship fund, matching the size of its previous fund raised in 2024, and another $130 million for a separate vehicle called Ballistic Ventures Fund B. Neither fund had recorded any sales at the time of filing. The fundraising plans come as the growing use of artificial intelligence has raised concerns about more sophisticated cyberattacks. The rise of AI agents has also created new opportunities for cybersecurity startups and the venture capital firms backing them. Founded in late 2021, Ballistic Ventures’ founding team includes Schlein, former AT&T Cybersecurity president Barmak Meftah, and Roger Thornton, who co-founded security companies Fortify Software and AlienVault. The firm has backed companies, including Talon Cyber Security, acquired by Palo Alto Networks , and Pangea, bought by CrowdStrike , alongside startups such as Armadin , GetReal , Nudge Security, and Oligo Security. Ballistic’s ties to storied venture capital firm Kleiner Perkins, where Schlein spent more than two decades, help set it apart from rivals, a cybersecurity investor at another VC firm told TechCrunch. Its investment strategy, however, is similar to those of other cybersecurity-focused investors, including Forgepoint Capital and Ten Eleven Ventures, the person said. In 2022, Ballistic announced its $300 million debut fund and raised another $360 million for its second flagship fund two years later. It also raised about $130 million for a separate vehicle called Ballistic Ventures Fund A, per PitchBook data. The new Fund B is targeting a similar amount. U.S. cybersecurity startups raised $11.5 billion in 2025, the highest since 2022, a recent report by JPMorgan Chase said, citing PitchBook data. AI-enabled companies accounted for about 72% of U.S. cybersecurity venture deals through May this year, compared with 36% in 2019, the report said. Separately, Microsoft, in its annual Digital Defense Report released last month, warned that hackers are increasingly using AI for activities ranging from phishing and social engineering to malware development. The technology is allowing attackers to operate faster and at greater scale, even as many of their underlying techniques remain unchanged. Ballistic Ventures declined to comment on its fundraising plans. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . This doesn’t affect our editorial independence. events.title: Texans vote in most expensive Senate race in US history
events.summary: Over half a billion dollars have been spent on the Talarico-Paxton race for US Senate, which has been dominated by voter affordability concerns. Houston, Texas, the US – Texas voters have begun casting ballots in a consequential US Senate race that has already become the most expensive in United States history. All told, at least $573.2m had been poured into support for both Republican candidate Ken Paxton and Democratic candidate James Talarico ahead of the Tuesday, November 3 vote. list 1 of 3 What time do polls open and close in the US midterm elections 2026? list 2 of 3 In Pictures: US midterm elections in 20 photos list 3 of 3 On the US border in Texas, Trump deportation drive galvanises midterm vote The figure has included at least $212m to support Paxton from billionaire Elon Musk, whose SpaceX company is based in southern Texas . The sum made voters of varying political persuasions queasy as they cast their ballots in a race that has been defined by affordability issues. “That kind of money is being spent on the wrong stuff,” said Rico Sanchez, a 40-year-old union sheet metal worker who voted for Democrats based on the sky-high cost of living. Kasey Blanco, a 21-year-old who split his ballot, voting for Republican Governor Greg Abbott and Democratic US Senate candidate Talarico, echoed the sentiment. “It’s kind of scary,” he said. “You see the extent that a lot of these politicians are trying to get into the game and distort the view.” Political power “should be from the people, by the people”, Blanco said. The record spending has included both funds raised by the campaigns, as well as outside spending. Talarico has outpaced Paxton in campaign funding, raising $155m to Paxton’s $40m. Federal law limits fundraising from individual donors, who must identify themselves. Separately, a huge amount of money has poured in via political action committees called super PACs, which can spend an unlimited amount in support of a candidate but cannot directly coordinate with campaigns. Paxton has been the largest beneficiary of such spending, including $168m from Musk to the Senate Leadership Fund, which has gone almost completely to supporting the Republican candidate, according to a New York Times analysis. The newspaper estimated that Musk, who briefly and controversially led US President Donald Trump’s federal cost-cutting panel, the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), had spent at least $212m on Paxton, noting it was likely an undercount due to so-called “dark money” spending. Trump’s MAGA Inc PAC has spent at least $10m to support Paxton. The Lone Star Rising PAC, meanwhile, has spent at least $21m on Talarico. With national eyes on Texas, both US Senate candidates gave their closing pitches late Monday. Talarico seized on Paxton’s past corruption allegations as Texas attorney general, drawing attention to Musk’s spending spree as evidence of prioritising big money interests over everyday voters. His campaign has regularly referenced the “Friday Night Lights” television show, the story of an underdog American football team. A Talarico victory would represent the first time a Democrat has won statewide office in Texas since 1994, with the party long hoping to “turn Texas blue”. “We’re going to do something extraordinary,” Talarico said from San Antonio. “We’re going to do something historic. We’re going to shock the billionaires, shock the world, when we take back Texas.” Paxton has portrayed Talarico as antithetical to the ideals of Texas, which has been dominated by Republicans for three decades. The state’s low-tax, low-regulation model, mixed with conservative social policies, has long given it special significance in Republican mythos. Paxton’s campaign has repeatedly referenced the 1836 Texas Revolution, an uprising against then-Mexican control. “We’ve never been this close to losing everything that we hold dear – our jobs, our livelihoods, our way of life in Texas,” he said at an event in Collin County. “If Texas falls, we don’t have another Texas to move to.” Casting her ballot on Tuesday, 46-year-old Texas voter Monique Orellana said she was uncomfortable with Musk’s spending. “He’s pouring all that money out here, trying to get whatever he’s trying to get,” she told Al Jazeera. Regardless of party, she wanted elected officials to do their job and represent the people. “I would vote for Republicans if I felt they were gonna do what they said they were gonna do. Right now I’m not feeling it,” she said. “Trump said he wasn’t going to start a war, and he did anyway. And he said he was going to fix the price of groceries on day one. They went up anyway,” she said. Voter Luis Plazas, 58, said he was not as concerned about the election spending, but wanted to see the economy improve and a pivot on Trump’s mass deportation campaign. Still, he said, he voted Republican down the ballot, a decision he said was motivated by his religious beliefs.

events.title: Microsoft improves Windows 11 performance on 8 GB PCs as RAM prices keep climbing
events.summary: With RAM getting more expensive, Microsoft is putting more effort into making Windows 11 run better on systems with just 8 GB of memory. Microsoft said on Tuesday that it was "raising the bar for 8 GB Windows 11 PCs," following a renewed focus on memory optimization earlier this year . The changes come as Redmond continues pushing more expensive Copilot+ PCs, which require at least 16 GB of RAM, amid a memory crunch fueled by AI infrastructure demand. Now, Microsoft says a low-end machine with its 8 GB of precious RAM will be up to 20 percent more responsive and 40 percent faster at multitasking thanks to improvements made in memory management. The tweaks are relatively simple, as Microsoft explained, and seem more about adjusting back to the reality that its flagship operating system needs to function on the hardware people can actually afford to purchase if and when they’re forced to upgrade. Windows 11 will now keep up to 2 GB more active data in memory before shunting it to slower storage, as one example. In another instance, Windows will connect directly to Edge when the browser is already running in the background, allowing it to launch up to 33 percent faster, according to Microsoft. Microsoft apps are also being made more efficient, with Teams able to enable Efficiency Mode by default on 8 GB machines, which Microsoft said will make it launch "up to 20 percent faster." Memory efficiency is also being improved by tweaking things like Widgets, which will only load when used instead of always being on, and decreasing the time when Edge tabs go to sleep from two hours to 15 minutes by default. Microsoft said it’s enabling third-party apps to make use of those tweaks, too. Microsoft also included benchmark data in the blog post from a recent bit of research it commissioned. The benchmark report compares a range of 2026 Windows machines with models from 2021, finding that a 2026 Dell XPS 13 with 8 GB of RAM performed about as well as a 2021 Dell XPS 13 with 16 GB across selected workloads. What that means, says Microsoft, is that “the complete PC, not memory capacity alone, shapes the experience.” In other words, please buy some new Windows hardware, even if it’s expensive - we’re begging you. Software optimization can only do so much. “For many people, 8 GB is a great fit for the things they do every day,” Microsoft EVP of Windows and devices Pavan Davuluri wrote in the blog post. “Demanding workloads, such as 3D modeling, advanced video editing, or large-scale data processing benefit from 16 GB of memory or more.” It’s no surprise Microsoft is improving the performance of lower end systems at the same time it’s subtly asking users to buy newer kit, even if it’s just an 8 GB machine - Microsoft may have done well in the past two quarters, but it’s no thanks to Windows devices. Microsoft’s Q4 2026 earnings in late July saw the company rake in cash more broadly, while simultaneously reporting a 7 percent decrease in Windows OEM and devices revenue. Likewise, in its fiscal Q1 2027 results, reported just last week, Microsoft again brought home a mountain of net income, with adjusted earnings reaching $36.4 billion, up 18 percent from the same period last year. Windows OEM and devices revenue, however, was down a whopping 22 percent . It’s hard to think of a reason beyond the fact that hardware prices have shot up with more force than a SpaceX rocket - memory prices are likely to actually make it to Mars, unlike Starship - leaving both consumers and enterprises to stretch those upgrade cycles. If you need to get the most out of that 8 GB Windows 11 PC, you’ll find the latest improvements in 26H2, build 26300.9818 or later. Microsoft is also encouraging users to keep its branded apps up to date, as “some improvements arrive through app updates or through Microsoft Store.” ®

events.summary: OpenAI’s hiring of a recently departed Pentagon official points to the frontier lab’s growing interests in defense and expanding roster of former military officials in its ranks. OpenAI has hired former U.S. Army Secretary Dan Driscoll to the bespoke role of senior counselor for national security modernization, the company announced on Monday. The new job comes two months after Driscoll left the Trump administration after reportedly clashing with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. In the role, Driscoll will advise OpenAI’s public and private sector partners on how to modernize policy and strategy in support of improving national security with AI, according to OpenAI. The focus of his work will be on how AI can be used responsibly to improve security among the U.S. and its allies. Gwanhoo Lee, the chair of the Department of Information Technology and Analytics at American University’s Kogod School of Business, said that by tapping Driscoll, OpenAI is continuing in its strategy of pouring resources into the defense sector, where it sees high demand for AI systems to bolster national security. “This hire is a continuation of their trend to see the opportunity in hiring significant government officials to strengthen their relationship with the government and strengthen their business in dealing with the government agencies,” Lee told Fortune . In June 2024, OpenAI appointed retired U.S. Army General Paul Nakasone , former National Security Agency director, to its board of directors. Later that year, it partnered with American defense firm Anduril to integrate OpenAI’s systems with Anduril’s database of unmanned drone threats. Driscoll did not respond to Fortune ’s request for comment. Why OpenAI hired Driscoll Within the federal government, Driscoll pushed modernization efforts such as low-cost battlefield drones, cutting red tape for defense contractors for drone development, and switching the Pentagon to commercial software —a departure from its practice of purchasing custom-built software specifically for the military. He also became an unlikely negotiator in working to end the war between Russia and Ukraine by making several trips across Europe to broker talks between Ukrainian and European officials. He also made a secret trip to the Middle East to meet with Russian officials. “The U.S. has an extraordinary opportunity to work with other countries to spread the adoption of democratic AI” following Driscoll’s hire, Altman said in a statement in the press release. “This technology will help them keep pace by cutting through paperwork, making sense of more information, and getting the right answer to the right person faster,” Driscoll said. “I’m joining OpenAI to help the United States and our allies put this technology to work responsibly, for the people who keep us safe.”  The former Army secretary stepped down from his role in the Pentagon in September after just 18 months on the job following widely reported tensions between him and Hegseth—particularly disagreements over promotions and the scale of the Pentagon’s modernization efforts . Driscoll’s exit followed a series of departures from other senior military officials, including the ousting of Gen. Randy George , the agency’s top uniformed official, in April and the resignation of Gen. Christopher Donahue, a champion of unmanned drone-use in Ukraine, in June.  Before his time in the Trump administration, Driscoll was involved in several investment and advisory firms, working as the chief operating officer at venture capital firm Flex Capital and partner at private equity firm 100watt. He served in the U.S. military from 2007 to 2011, and was deployed to Baghdad, Iran, in 2009. Concerns about OpenAI’s relationship with the Pentagon Driscoll’s new private-sector role is likely to raise questions about a “revolving door problem” of the company’s access to government officials, according to Lee. He noted that potential conflicts of interest could impact the government’s procurement process, or how it decides with private entities from which to buy goods and services. “If AI companies can take high-level officers from the Pentagon or any other important government agencies right after they’ve left their organizations, in terms of procurement process, I don’t know how fair the government procurement process will be when AI companies have significant individuals from that organization,” Lee said.  As countries depend more on AI systems for both defense of national security and forms of offensive cyberattacks, investing in both the most effective and cost-effective technologies have become crucial for maintaining national safety and infrastructure, Lee explained, but priorities for securing private sector contracts can become muddied if deals are based too closely on preexisting social ties. “If that procurement is based upon relationships rather than merits and strengths of technology, that puts us at risk,” he added. “As AI companies take on national security risks, we need clearer rules on oversight and conflict interest, so I think there is some governance concern.” OpenAI said all parties are aware of post-employment restrictions and will comply. While OpenAI’s work with Driscoll will extend beyond its relationship with the Department of Defense, OpenAI’s previous deals with the Pentagon have raised concerns about safety and privacy from tech policy experts. The company won a $200 million contract from the Department of Defense in June 2025 to design AI tools for the agency to address national security challenges. The relationship between OpenAI and the Trump administration grew closer in February, when OpenAI signed a new deal with the Pentagon to deploy its AI models in the agency’s secure networks. Earlier that month, Hegseth issued an ultimatum to OpenAI rival Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, demanding the company allow unrestricted use of its AI, which has safety guardrails against the use of the technology for mass domestic surveillance and autonomous weaponry—but Anthropic refused to remove the restrictions. Trump then asked federal agencies to stop using Anthropic’s products, and Hegseth designated the company a national security “ supply chain risk ,” the first time the U.S. has ever used the designation for an American company. OpenAI’s subsequent deal with the Pentagon still set limits on how the government can use its technology, but allowed for the deployment of its AI models inside the Pentagon’s secure networks under an “all lawful use” clause, offering broader usage of the technology within legal confines. Experts warned the deal left space for legal loopholes—like whether large-scale analysis of Americans’ data, which is legal, is different from mass surveillance. “Right now, under U.S. law, it’s lawful for government authorities to buy up commercially available information from data brokers and other third parties,” Samir Jain, vice president of policy at the Center f

events.title: ‘You have to be willing to make those hard choices’: Freshworks CEO on crossing $1 billion in ARR with 30% fewer employees in the AI software age
events.summary: Freshworks has passed $1 billion in annual recurring revenue, CEO Dennis Woodside told Fortune . The software company, which started about 15 years ago in Chennai, India, as a help-desk tool for small businesses, ended its third quarter on Sept. 30 with about $992 million in annual recurring revenue. It crossed $1 billion in October after closing its acquisitions of Torii and Robusta, the company said. Freshworks doesn’t disclose how much of its ARR came from acquisitions. “$1 billion in ARR is a really important milestone for any software business,” Woodside said in an interview ahead of the results. “It’s a good indication of scale.” Woodside took over as CEO in May 2024 from founder Girish Mathrubootham . “I think we’ve added about $250 million in ARR in that time period,” he said. ARR measures contracted subscription revenue over the next 12 months, so it runs ahead of reported sales. Earlier today, Freshworks reported $18.3 million in GAAP net income for the third quarter, its second straight profitable quarter, along with adjusted free cash flow of $73.9 million, a record. “We’ll be GAAP profitable this quarter and going forward,” Woodside said. The company has described sustained GAAP profitability as a goal. Getting there meant deciding what Freshworks would stop doing. “We wound up stopping a bunch of smaller projects,” Woodside said, to “really focus on the business that had the biggest potential, has the biggest market, where we have the most distinctive competitive advantage.” “You have to be willing to make those hard choices of what’s not going to be important in two years, in five years,” Woodside argued. “And then invest in those areas that are going to be important,” he said. “I think that can be hard to do.” Some of this is standard management theory, skating to where the puck is moving and seeing around the corner, but it has a counterintuitive element that thought leaders in the space argue isn’t appreciated by enough companies. The best book about AI adoption is over 30 years old In an interview at McKinsey’s global headquarters at 3 World Trade Center, two senior partners echoed Woodside’s advice. “AI is everywhere except in the EBIT line,” Alex Panas, who leads McKinsey’s industry practices globally, joked, describing what’s around boardrooms and echoing the famous Robert Solow paradox about the computer age appearing everywhere except in the productivity statistics. Michael Park, a senior partner in Singapore who co-leads the firm’s technology, media and telecom practice, chimed in. “The number of companies that have really rethought how they’re doing work today, and then changing it to be whatever it should be or could be with AI, is very small.” He shared the example of product development. In the old way, an idea moved down a line: marketing built a business case and PowerPoints, then HR weighed in, then operations. In the new way, a cross-functional team works separately with an AI agent and after a few weeks, Park said, the agent tells them, “There’s like 20 things you guys agree on. But there’s five things that you disagree on.” Then the team meets about those five things. This is unsettling to people used to the old way of working, because the agent is suddenly the store of knowledge for the enterprise, not the management layer for each silo. Panas noted that org charts have barely changed since McKinsey’s Gilbert Clee wrote the 1959 paper behind the matrix organization in the 1950s. “That’s the last time somebody’s actually thought about organizational structure,” he said. Panas said he thinks the best book about AI was written in 1993: Reengineering the Corporation , the Hammer and Champy management bestseller. Its argument is that technology only pays off once you change the people and the processes around it. Woodside said the reason people don’t do this is because it’s essentially really unpleasant. Shutting down products meant telling people their work was over. “When you wind down a product, to some degree, you’re saying to somebody that your baby’s ugly,” he said. “And a real person is a product manager of that. You have to say, ‘No, I’m sorry, we’re not going to do that.’” What Freshworks stopped When Woodside took over, he was already a Silicon Valley veteran. He had run Motorola Mobility and was chief operating officer at Dropbox when it went public. The first thing the board asked him to do, he said, was “really revisit this strategy” because AI was coming. The company had started as Freshdesk, and its founder had built it around customer support, “and there’s a lot of passion around that,” Woodside said, but still, it was an inflection point. He decided IT software for bigger companies, “the EX business,” was the future for Freshworks and they had to shift resources into that business, “literally in the first couple of months of being the CEO.” About a month into his tenure, on June 6, 2024, Freshworks closed its purchase of Device42, an IT asset-management company. It has since bought FireHydrant, Torii and Robusta. EX made up 59% of ARR, or $588 million, as of Sept. 30, up from 35% at the 2021 IPO, and grew 22% from a year earlier, according to the company. The customer-service business it was founded on, CX, accounted for $404 million. Then he started cutting. “We had a lot of entrepreneurial, you know, $5 million ideas,” he said. “We need $100 million ideas, right, if we’re going to get to a billion [dollars in ARR].” Woodside cited the examples of Freshping, Freshteams, and Freshsurvey as things he deemphasized, focusing on Freshservice, which was already generating several hundred million dollars in ARR when he took over as CEO. It also meant getting smaller, Woodside said, noting Freshworks now has roughly 3,800 full-time employees, down from a peak of about 5,400 in 2022, roughly a 30% reduction. (That includes an 11% cut announced in May.) “That was hard for the company,” Woodside said. “It was also hard because we wound up reducing the staffing pretty significantly over time.” He has been on the other end of that call. At Motorola, Woodside engineered the 2014 sale to Lenovo. “We sold it — which meant I sold it — which meant I sold myself out of a job,” he told Fortune ’s Diane Brady at the COO Summit in June. Wharton professor Ethan Mollick , who popularized the phrase “ jagged frontier ” as he emerged as a thought leader on the topic of AI adoption, puts this as a question. “That’s one of the big questions I ask,” he told Fortune, echoing comments he made on a recent appearance on Peter Kafka’s Channels podcast. “Have you stopped doing anything? events.title: Midterms raise new election security questions
events.summary: The midterms are raising fresh questions about the federal government’s role in election security, and where to draw the line between protecting the vote and intervening in the electoral process. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, once a leader in election security, has scaled back its work in President Donald Trump’s second term, raising concerns about the government’s ability to identify and respond to foreign interference. The Justice Department announced its “ largest monitoring effort in history ” today, deploying observers across all 50 states, though a federal judge has ruled that monitors cannot be sworn law enforcement officials or make arrests. The Michigan Attorney General’s Office contacted the DOJ after receiving reports that the department’s monitors were speaking with poll workers in Dearborn and Flint, actions outside the scope of their duties. The disputes could continue after polls close, if legal challenges prolong the fight over election results. — Lauren Morganbesser

events.title: Further links between CLP and gas firm emerge as ex-staffer's shares revealed
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Further links between NT government and Beetaloo Energy emerge as ex-staffer's shares revealed Topic: State and Territory Government Bill Yan's spokesperson says his former staffer declared her interests in line with the NT ministerial staff code of conduct. ( ABC News: Pete Garnish ) A former adviser to the NT infrastructure minister says she disclosed shares in gas firm Beetaloo Energy before starting the role. She worked for the minister when the NT government struck a gas supply agreement with Beetaloo Energy. It comes weeks after the ABC reported the NT deputy chief minister spruiked Beetaloo Energy without publicly disclosing his relative worked there. Further links between the Northern Territory government and gas producer Beetaloo Energy have emerged, with a former ministerial staffer insisting she disclosed her shareholdings in the company before starting the government job. Sonia Harvey was hired by the office of NT Treasurer and Infrastructure Minister Bill Yan in March 2025, after working for Beetaloo Energy (formerly Empire Energy) as "government and community relations vice-president" for three years until July 2024. Ms Harvey said she left Mr Yan's office in September this year for "personal reasons", having advised him on infrastructure and logistics policy. Sonia Harvey left Bill Yan's office in September 2025. ( Supplied: Linkedin ) That same month, the ABC reported NT Deputy Chief Minister Gerard Maley had been spruiking Beetaloo Energy without publicly disclosing that his sister-in-law worked at the firm. Beetaloo Energy's share register shows throughout Ms Harvey's tenure in Mr Yan's office, she held 62,500 shares in the company, which would be currently worth around $13,750. The ABC does not suggest any wrongdoing by Ms Harvey, who said she disclosed her Beetaloo Energy shareholdings "as part of [a] pre-employment check". "I have complied with the relevant requirements applying to ministerial staff, including in relation to the declaration and management of conflicts of interest," she said. During Ms Harvey's time in Mr Yan's office, the NT government signed an agreement with Beetaloo Energy , securing appraisal gas from its Beetaloo Basin fracking project for the NT energy grid. Gerard Maley signed the gas appraisal deal with Beetaloo Energy in December last year. ( ABC News: Matt Garrick ) Appraisal gas is extracted by companies during the testing phase of a project. At the time, Beetaloo Energy chief executive Alex Underwood said the appraisal deal had enabled the firm to reach a final investment decision on its Beetaloo Basin project. The appraisal deal was signed after both Beetaloo Energy and Tamboran Resources inked 10-year gas supply agreements with the former NT Labor government in 2024, amid concerns about ongoing gas supply shortages in the territory. The details of this latest gas deal have been kept secret by the Country Liberal Party government for "commercial in confidence" reasons. The NT government has spruiked the Beetaloo Basin gas reserve as key to the territory's future. ( ABC News: Dane Hirst ) Ms Harvey said she was not privy to any information regarding the Beetaloo Energy gas supply appraisal agreement and said she had "no engagement" with the company while working in Mr Yan's office. According to her Linkedin profile, Ms Harvey's connection to the NT gas industry goes back to 2015, when she founded and became chief executive of the gas-focused Energy Club NT. Infrastructure contracts awarded during tenure During Ms Harvey's tenure in Mr Yan's office, the infrastructure minister announced tenders relating to the Beetaloo Basin, including a $68 million contract for the design and construction of stage three of the Carpentaria Highway upgrade — a service road connecting the Beetaloo Basin to the NT's main highway. In total, the federal and NT governments have allocated a combined $262 million to the Carpentaria Highway upgrade. The territory contributed $52 million, of which $15 million was allocated in the 2025-26 financial year, an NT Department of Logistics and Infrastructure spokesperson said. In May 2025, Mr Yan also announced a contract worth more than $900,000 for "technical advice" to help with planning for the Territory Energy Link — "a proposed multi-user, multi-asset infrastructure corridor stretching from Elliott to Darwin". "It will connect the Beetaloo to Darwin and the world," he said at the time. Bill Yan announced tenders relating to the Beetaloo Basin while Sonia Harvey was working in his office.

events.title: Hiding inside Palantir’s skyrocketing quarter is a foreboding signal
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. The data analysis company Palantir delivered such a huge third-quarter earnings report on Monday that its press release even bragged that the numbers were “crushing consensus expectations.” Yet retail investors were lukewarm on the company on Tuesday, with the stock trading slightly down. That’s because Palantir’s enterprise sales, its big growth area, showed signs of slowing. First, the good news for the company’s investors. Revenue grew 96% from a year earlier, and 20% from the previous quarter, to $2.31 billion, beating analysts’ expectations of $2.18 billion. It was the first time Palantir has topped $2 billion in a quarter. Palantir also reported adjusted earnings per share (profit per share, excluding certain one-time items) of 44 cents, compared with analysts’ expectations of 41 cents. The company even raised its revenue guidance, or forecast, for the full year. Normally, that alone would send a stock soaring. The clincher was that Palantir’s U.S. commercial revenue surpassed U.S. government revenue for the first time ever. The company reported $984 million in commercial contracts (up 148% from the year-ago quarter), versus $953 million in U.S. government revenue. The reason for all this love from enterprises? They are signing up for the company’s AI software that can run frontier models and custom-train open-weight models securely, without sharing any of their data and business processes with outside AI labs. Plus, Palantir has long offered what is today known as “forward-deployed” software engineering, in which its own engineers work directly with customers to customize the software. However, Palantir also revealed a less-than-rosy signal: Even as enterprises are moving faster than ever, they are often signing short-term trials. “What Ryan and I are seeing on the front line and commercial is this much quicker interaction, much quicker to deployment, shorter duration of the contract but then an ability to expand that contract dramatically,” CEO Alex Karp (pictured above) told Wall Street analysts on the quarterly earnings call. Palantir is experiencing one of the unique phenomena of AI in the enterprise right now. Corporations are willing to quickly try AI software, skipping the usual bureaucracy, but they are also more willing to cancel contracts. Karp used one off-color metaphor after another to describe how unconcerned he was about holding onto his enterprise business. “We’ve gone from being the most attractive person in the physics department to being the captain of the football team, kind of thing,” he said, describing the influx of prospective corporate customers flowing in. “Conversely, you know, once you go Palantir, you don’t go back, and that’s just how it is, and you see it in our numbers.” The numbers don’t yet confirm Palantir’s long-term success. While the company closed a hefty $1.46 billion of total contract value from U.S. enterprises in the quarter, that’s actually a decline from the record $2.13 billion in the previous quarter. That suggests slowing sales, at least in the most recent quarter. The next earnings will show whether Palantir has solidified its role as a rising U.S. enterprise AI provider. Historically, many enterprises sign their biggest tech purchases in the final quarter of the year. Karp and his team certainly sound confident. They increased guidance for U.S. commercial revenue to be “in excess of $3.559 billion, representing a growth rate of at least 143%.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters At Fireworks Forge, a celebration of specialized models British fintech Revolut slashes AI coding costs 10x by cutting out Claude and going self-hosted 5 hours ago GhostBSD 26.2 takes the fright out of FreeBSD with a friendlier installer 9 hours ago Forget retraining - AI can now tweak another AI's weights 17 hours ago Architect creates open source replacement for VM migration tool VMware has hidden 21 hours ago AI could break legal systems by finding previously hidden loopholes 1 day ago Nvidia doesn't seem to care whether open or closed models win out as long as its hardware is powering the infrastructure. "We love closed models," CEO Jensen Huang said. "There's a solid place in the world for closed frontier models. But the world has so many good ideas … The idea that all of us would be based on general intelligence is not logical." Speaking with Lin Qiao, CEO and founder of Fireworks.ai , at the company's Forge event in San Francisco on Tuesday, Huang wasn't ready to throw Nvidia's cloud customers, which help deliver the proprietary AI of Anthropic and OpenAI, under the onrushing open model bus. But having come to the defense of open weight models in July to push back against protectionist pressure from the leadership of Anthropic and OpenAI, Huang recognizes the economic and strategic appeal of AI services that are more affordable and less locked-in. Most of the value in the world, he said, is captured in specialized intelligence, which is to say AI models trained on specific domains of knowledge. "The opportunity for artificial superintelligence is already here," he said. "By taking an open frontier model, adapting it, and providing it with your domain knowledge, your access to your specialized tools, and the proper evaluation, you should be able to create essentially a superintelligence." That aligns with Fireworks' business – offering a platform for companies to train and run models tuned to their specific needs. Coincidentally, that platform just received an infusion of 25,000 Nvidia GPUs to support its expansion in Europe . Huang's endorsement of open models also fits with Qiao's introductory remarks about the need for the AI frontier to be open. But he largely avoided echoing Qiao's focus on the cost savings allowed by working with open models. In her introductory remarks, Qiao stood on stage backlit by a slide composed of ten headlines highlighting the extraordinary cost of unchecked token spending. "Cost is out of control," she said. "Business cannot scale without borrowing a lot of money." That theme was echoed in a subsequent session helmed by Kay Zhu, co-founder and CTO of AI workspace Genspark, titled Gen-1 Slides: Frontier Quality Without Frontier Costs. Gen-1 Slides, Genspark's model for generating slide decks, was built atop MiniMax M3 and tuned to deliver results comparable to Anthropic's Opus 5 at 1/17th the cost – $0.30/M tokens compared to $5/M. Asked what might become commonplace next year but seems unlikely today, Huang said this year's breakthrough has been agent harnesses that turn AI models into agents. He added, "I would say the big breakthrough we'll talk about next year, maybe this is a little self-serving, is how Open Shell has enabled every company in the world to deploy agents safely, confidently." Given the nod to make a second prediction, Huang added, "I would say that the second big breakthrough for industry would be hardware in the loop. And hardware in the loop basically is robotic systems." Given Nvidia's evident interest and investment in robotics , that would be fortuitous.

events.title: Trump says he’ll cut Israel aid, teeing up a fight
events.summary: President Donald Trump said today that the US plans to end around $4 billion in aid to Israel after this year, though the country will still be able to buy weapons. The surprise announcement came as voters fanned out to cast ballots in the midterm elections, including in races where anti-Israel sentiment is shaping the results. Trump said Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu agreed with the plan; Netanyahu has said in recent months that he wants to gradually reduce the country’s reliance on congressionally-approved US aid. But there’s a domestic calculus to the announcement, too, as some in the Republican Party grow increasingly skeptical of US aid to Israel. “It’s a bad talking point,” Trump told Fox News earlier today. On the other hand, Trump’s plan sets him on a collision course with Israel’s supporters in Congress, who could approve the aid against his wishes. — Shelby Talcott

events.title: ‘We were wrong’: From Dewey to Trump, the polling misses hanging over the 2026 midterm forecasts
events.summary: One of the most iconic images in 20th-century American political history shows a beaming President Harry Truman holding up a copy of the Chicago Daily Tribune emblazoned with the headline “DEWEY DEFEATS TRUMAN.” In fact, Truman had just resoundingly defeated his Republican challenger, New York Gov. Thomas Dewey, winning 303 electoral votes to Dewey’s 189. The Tribune had gone to press before the race was called, but its editors can be given a measure of grace: just about every major poll put Dewey ahead. That includes the one this magazine published. Elmo Roper’s final survey for Fortune gave Dewey 44% to Truman’s 31%, and the editors wrote, “So decisive are the figures given here this month,” that no further detailed reports were planned, according to historian David Greenberg’s account in Politico . Seventy-eight years later, as Americans vote in the 2026 midterms, the major forecasters point to a strong night for Democrats. For companies and investors that plan around which party controls Congress, the question is how much weight those forecasts can bear. History says less than their precision suggests: presidential polls have underestimated Donald Trump in three straight elections, and the people who answer pollsters are a shrinking, skewed slice of the electorate. A long record of confident misses The 1948 miss was not close. Gallup and Crossley both gave Dewey about a five-point edge in their final polls, FiveThirtyEight found , and Roper stopped polling weeks before Election Day. Newsweek asked 50 political writers to pick the winner; all 50 chose Dewey. Afterward, George Gallup offered a blunt verdict: “We were wrong,” the Deseret News recounted . Polls that seemed staid and reliable have since proved flagrantly inaccurate. In 1960, Roper’s election-eve poll had Richard Nixon edging out John F. Kennedy by two points, Time reported . Kennedy won, clinching 303 electoral votes to Nixon’s 219, though his popular-vote margin was razor thin. A generation later, most polls saw the 1980 race between Republican Ronald Reagan and President Jimmy Carter as harrowingly close; Gallup’s final survey had Reagan up just three points, according to Gallup . Reagan won 489 electoral votes and carried 44 states. Carter took 49 electoral votes, six states, and the District of Columbia. Hillary Clinton was favored to beat Trump in 2016 but lost 304 electoral votes to 227, even as she won the popular vote. In 2020, polls correctly pointed to a Joe Biden win, but Trump ran well ahead of them; Biden won 306 electoral votes to 232, a striking parallel to 2016. The American Association for Public Opinion Research later found that 2020’s national polling error was the highest in 40 years. The error shrank in 2024, but surveys still underestimated Trump for a third straight presidential race, 538 found . As historian W. Joseph Campbell wrote for Fortune that year, election polls have kept their popular appeal despite a checkered record. What the 2026 forecasts show If the major forecasts hold, Democrats will take the House and have a real shot at the Senate. As of Election Day, the Cook Political Report rated 204 House seats Solid or Likely Democratic and 178 Solid or Likely Republican, with 18 leaning Democratic, 17 leaning Republican, and 18 toss-ups, according to Newsweek ’s tally . An NBC News poll conducted Oct. 28–30 found 52% of registered voters preferred Democratic control of Congress, versus 45% for Republican control. The 270toWin consensus forecast , which aggregates several forecasters, leans Democratic in 220 House seats and Republican in 196, with 19 toss-ups. Its Senate map is less settled: Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Ohio, and Texas sit in the toss-up column, and Democrats need a net gain of four seats to flip a chamber Republicans hold 53–47. Why the misses lean one way We won’t know how accurate this year’s polls were until the votes are counted. Polling has never been an exact science, and even as text-based surveys and AI-driven modeling have become commonplace, the raw material pollsters depend on keeps getting harder to collect. The biggest reason is falling response rates. In generations past, pollsters called voters on landlines, and people almost always answered. Now it’s easy to screen calls or ignore texts. Pew Research Center’s telephone response rate fell from 36% in 1997 to 6% in 2018, NBC News reported . Those who do respond often don’t represent the electorate. Andreas Philippou, a professor emeritus of probability and statistics at Greece’s University of Patras, has traced several major polling failures to nonresponse . In the U.S., the problem has a partisan tilt. AAPOR’s review of the 2016 polls found that better-educated Americans were significantly more likely to answer surveys than voters without degrees, who lean Republican. Most pollsters now weight their samples by education. Yet AAPOR concluded that the 2020 miss wasn’t caused by a failure to do so, leaving the industry to chase a harder-to-measure gap between the people who answer and the people who don’t. Midterms have been kinder to pollsters. In 2022, the RealClearPolitics generic-ballot average showed Republicans ahead by 2.5 points; they won the national House vote by 2.8. That makes tonight a clean test. If Republicans outrun their polling in the toss-up House districts and the five Senate races the consensus can’t call, the nonresponse problem will have surfaced in a year without Trump on the ballot. If the results land near the averages, as they did in 2022, pollsters will have their strongest case yet that they’ve learned the lessons of 1948. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Orbital Matter 3D-printed the first rigid beam in the vacuum of space
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. A satellite built by the German startup Orbital Matter 3D-printed a half-meter long beam out of a custom plastic material, in what executives called a first for a free-flying spacecraft in orbit, and a step toward constructing large structures in space. The company’s small satellite, Replicator 2, was launched on a SpaceX rideshare mission this summer, with four of the company’s 3D printers onboard. Each printer can create a rigid, cylindrical beam by extruding coils of resin that are cured by an ultraviolet light, which the company analogizes to cement and water. This technology matters because future spacecraft will need to be larger in order to generate more electrical power and radiate a more heat into the vacuum of space, particularly if they’re going to serve as orbital data centers. But they’ll still need to fit into the tight confines of the fairing on top of the rocket that carries them into orbit. If spacecraft are able to construct their own structures in orbit, the power and heat-dissipation challenges may get a lot easier to solve. “Replicator 2 is the first proof that we can simply build the array in space, at whatever size the mission demands,” said Jakub Stojek, CEO and co-founder of Orbital Matter. The company is partnering with the European Space Agency and Thales Alenia, a leading European satellite builder, with which it collaborated on Replicator 2. Today’s large structures in space are origami projects — large solar arrays or telescope mirrors are folded up and then deployed on orbit. That’s a tricky engineering project, and so the idea of making and assembling those structures in space is appealing. NASA has funded some efforts at the idea, notably a mission with the company Redwire that 3D-printed structural beams in a vacuum chamber in 2023 but never got off the ground. Two of Orbital Matter’s printers are designed to deploy a flexible solar array, but an anomaly led one of the printers to fail. Still, the boom that was created successfully deployed the solar array, and is an important proof of concept. Previous 3D-printing efforts in microgravity were limited to the pressurized environment onboard the International Space Station. “That’s why we put so many printers on this single satellite. We preferred to learn in orbit and adapt the software as needed rather than waste years testing every possibility on the ground,” Orbital Matters CTO Robert Ihnatisin told TechCrunch. The boom’s length is limited by the amount of resin carried onboard the satellite, and the company’s engineers believe that 100 meter booms are feasible. For comparison, SpaceX’s Starlink V2 satellites — among the most powerful mass-produced satellites in orbit — uses solar arrays that are 20 meters long. Orbital Matter was co-founded in 2022 by Ihnatsin, who previously worked at 3D-printing company FormLabs, and Stojek, and raised a $3 million seed round. Now, Orbital Matter is working on another demonstration mission, scheduled for launch in 2028, that will test a larger version of its printer on a bigger satellite that the company hopes will deploy a solar array that can generate 5 kw of power. That will be a “stepping stone” toward larger deployments of 100+ KW per wing by 2030. events.title: We downsized from a one-bedroom NYC apartment to a 38-foot sailboat. Life changed, but not for the better.
events.summary: Although living on a sailboat sounded incredible and had its perks, it ultimately wasn't for me. Carly Miller In 2024, my partner and I left our NYC apartment and moved onto a sailboat with our dog. The lifestyle wasn't as affordable as I expected, and I felt like we were constantly making repairs. It was tough always having to be alert at sea. After about a year, I wanted a stable home on land. In 2024, my partner, Guy, and I had just landed back in our East Village apartment after a month in London when we asked each other, "Where to next?" I was still unpacking my luggage when an idea struck me: "We should live on a boat ." To most people, that sounds like a joke. For us, that was a perfectly reasonable idea. Guy was a lifelong sailor who had always dreamed of owning a boat , and to me, it sounded like an adventure I wanted to be part of. We both worked full-time remote jobs , and Guy had a fairly successful startup that made it possible for us to afford the boat. A month later, we moved onto a 38-foot sailboat with our dog. We imagined saving lots of money, seeing incredible sights, having complete freedom, and connecting with nature. Our ultimate goal was to cross the Pacific Ocean . However, it didn't take long for me to realize boat life was anything but the romanticized dream I had envisioned when I gave up my apartment. Instead of chasing adventure, I spent my time and money on maintenance and repairs Owning a boat can get expensive. Carly Miller Since we were downsizing from an apartment in one of the most expensive cities in the US , we thought we'd easily be saving money by living on a boat. Although we no longer paying NYC rent, we still had tons of expenses. The guy who sold us the boat had joked that the letters in "boat" stand for "Bust Out Another Thousand." Turns out he wasn't really kidding. Almost overnight, every day became overwhelmed by a list of things that needed fixing. We spent more time than we wanted making repairs on the boat. Carly Miller There was the $1,000 alternator, followed by a plumbing failure that left our toilet out of service. We spent two months trying to fix the problem ourselves before bringing in a professional. When our autopilot broke, we couldn't afford the roughly $3,000 replacement. One of us had to stay at the wheel when we sailed, which made balancing work and travel especially difficult. Those repairs came on top of expenses like fuel and marina slips, which could run more than $100 a night. Every day seemed to bring another expense or something to add to the to-do list. I didn't mind having fewer possessions or living in a smaller space . What wore me down was the endless work and expense of keeping that space functioning. I underestimated the stress of living on the water Living on a boat wasn't as peaceful as I expected. Carly Miller I expected living so attuned to nature would bring me peace. Instead, I found it difficult to relax. Clocking out of my full-time job didn't mean I could switch off. I was always "on" at sea. We had to monitor forecasts, wind direction, and currents to decide when we could sail and where we could safely anchor. We took turns waking up every hour to check that our anchor was holding and we weren't drifting. There are a lot of factors to monitor when you're sailing. Carly Miller Life at anchor was also surprisingly inactive. Sometimes bad weather kept us confined to our 38-foot boat for days. The sailing community could feel frustratingly isolating, too. At marinas, people often seemed to defer to Guy for decisions, and he seemed to more easily garner respect, too. Part of me felt like it was because he was a man. I was learning to be a boater, but I didn't always feel accepted or treated as an equal. At times, it was hard to be far from loved ones. Carly Miller The isolation also meant being far from family. When my family's dog died, I was stuck in a mangrove forest in the Bahamas and couldn't get home in time to say goodbye. Although we had the freedom to reach remote places, there was a constant catch: I also worried about how easily we could leave them in case of an emergency. I still love sailing, but I don't love owning a boat Sailing can be rewarding and fun, but owning a boat can be challenging. Carly Miller Despite the drawbacks, there were mornings that reminded me why I'd wanted this: We'd wake up before sunrise, coffees in hand, watching dolphins play at the bow. I love the magic of sailing. There's no roaring motor, just the wind in the sails and the creak of the ropes. When the boat heels over and everything lines up, we hit that perfect speed and glide over the water. It's euphoric. Nothing else comes close to that feeling. But I do not love being a boat owner . We made a lot of fun memories, but I'm glad we no longer live on a boat. Carly Miller After about a year aboard, we left the boat in the Bahamas and flew to Portugal to see family, then to Hawaii to see friends. We'd planned to head to Panama and the Pacific afterward, but I was burned out. For the first time in my life, I wanted routine and stability. So, we decided to just sail the boat back to New York City . Part of me still regrets not crossing the Pacific Ocean. If I get the opportunity, I'd like to make that crossing as part of someone else's crew. For now, though, I'm perfectly happy to have a home on land again. events.title: Haley Stevens requests U.S. marshals' protection after death threats
events.summary: Michigan Rep. Haley Stevens has requested U.S. marshals' protection after the Democrat told authorities she had received death threats for endorsing Republican Mike Rogers in the swing state's hotly contested Senate race, two senior Trump administration officials tell Axios. Why it matters: Stevens' surprise decision Sunday to switch her endorsement to Rogers over Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed was the biggest political story of the midterm campaign's final days. Stevens — who lost to El-Sayed in the Michigan Senate primary — was widely criticized by Democrats after siding with Rogers, and her top staff members resigned. "She has received death threats and reached out to the Marshals Service," one of the officials said. "There's a process to go through but she's a member of Congress and we expect her request will be fulfilled." Zoom in: Stevens' support for Israel and his criticism of the Jewish state was a major dividing line in their primary campaign. Stevens objected to El-Sayed's ties to controversial progressive streamer Hasan Piker and an ad by a PAC tied to Piker's uncle, Cenk Uygur, blaming Israel for rising grocery prices. El-Sayed disavowed the ad, but Stevens said she believed he hadn't done enough to address her concerns and didn't want her help on the campaign trail. The dispute came to a head when she was told she was no longer welcome at El-Sayed's campaign events. Stevens announced her endorsement of Rogers after appearing with him at a church service on Sunday. Stevens could not be reached for comment Tuesday. The big picture: The political environment in Michigan has been volatile this weekend. On Monday, the New York Post reported a former El-Sayed staffer was one of several anti-Zionist activists federally indicted for allegedly terrorizing members of Michigan's Jewish community. On Sunday, a conservative Jewish activist was attacked by a progressive activist at a University of Michigan event where organizers were criticizing Islam. On Friday, U.S. officials announced the arrest of a Michigan man for allegedly threatening FBI director Kash Patel. Stevens recently clashed with an anti-Zionist activist whom she accused of trying to intimidate her over her support for Israel.
