events.title: UK and EU agree draft deal to scrap Brexit red tape over food exports
events.summary: The UK and EU have agreed a draft deal on removing post-Brexit checks from food and agriculture exports, ahead of the UK-EU summit later this month. The BBC understands the 200-page draft text for this so called "SPS" [sanitary and phytosanitary] agreement has been circulated to EU nations in Brussels for consideration at a meeting on Wednesday. Similar texts for deals on emissions trading and a youth travel and work scheme have also been circulated alongside a 15-page draft joint statement for UK and EU top leaders. The food deal is the most significant part of the so-called Brexit reset agreed so far, removing checks and red tape that hit exporters after the UK exited the EU's single market. As a result of the agreement, the government claims the UK economy will eventually see £5.1bn worth of annual benefits. Speaking during the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (Chogm) in Antigua and Barbuda, the prime minister said a UK-EU deal could add up to 0.4% extra on GDP. The deal could have the following impact: Exports to the EU of fresh sausages, burgers, shellfish from domestic waters and seed potatoes would be able to resume It should remove the need for £200 Export Health Certificates, which confirm the product meets the health requirements of the country it is heading to It should also end the need for £25 Phytosanitary certificates, which show that plants or plant products are free from pests and diseases Inspector fees, organic certificates, some port fees and other checks for exports and imports to and from the EU could be removed It will bring back passports for British pets being taken into the EU In return, the UK is expected to commit to observing and adapting to existing EU regulations on plant, animal and food trade standards - a process called "dynamic alignment". Each of the elements on the table was up for discussion under Sir Keir Starmer, and the summit would have taken place by now had Labour not replaced its leader in July. Under Andy Burnham, Britain's approach to post-Brexit relations with the EU have shifted significantly. Sir Keir said the UK would not rejoin the bloc in his lifetime, while Burnham has said he would like to see Britain back in the EU in his. At Chogm on Tuesday, Burnham said: "I think people in Britain would expect me to take that with both hands, given where we've been in recent times, and that's what I'm doing." Pressed on whether it would be acceptable for the UK to have its rules on food trade made by the EU, he said: "We're not in the EU, therefore we do have to work with them in a different way. "But if that can get growth, if that can help our farmers, if that can remove red tape from British businesses, I think most people would expect me to go to that summit and negotiate the best deal that I can. "And that's what I've been doing in recent weeks, leaning in, being positive, having a really constructive relationship with our European partners and hopefully we can land a good deal for Britain in terms of growth but also I hope more collaboration on controlling immigration." Jon Walsh of Bio&Me said his firm had stopped exporting yoghurt due to vets' fees Jon Walsh, the chief executive and co-founder of Bio&Me, which makes granolas, mueslis and yoghurts, told BBC 5 Live the draft deal sounded like "really good news". "We're just a small company but when we were trying to export our yoghurts before, every time we'd send a pallet we had to pay a vet to inspect it and that was £140, and that meant that you'd lose money... so we had to stop." The company also had problems exporting granola and overnight oats, with some shipments being returned. "It was so frustrating because it was the same person filling out the same form and yet half would make it through and half wouldn't," Walsh said. "You just kind of give up because you're losing money." In an interview with ITV, Burnham said "public opinion has changed nationally" since the 2016 Brexit vote, but added he would "not run ahead of public opinion" on the issue. "The public need to be the boss when it comes to whatever happens with Brexit," he added. Burnham also said he had not proposed the return of freedom of movement between the UK and EU. Asked by the BBC about the UK's relationship with the EU, Tory Leader Kemi Badenoch said that while we should "work closely", "dynamic alignment" with the EU would be a red line and "actually take us backwards". Liberal Democrat Europe spokesperson Al Pinkerton said the draft deal was a "patch, not a fix". "The real solution is to rejoin the single market and to establish a customs union with the EU," he added. Reform UK's business spokesman Richard Tice said: "One of the key benefits of Brexit was that Britain no longer had to adhere to ridiculous EU rules. "Returning to any form of alignment with Europe would crush Britain's competitiveness and force us to surrender sovereignty over trade policy, putting trade deals worth hundreds of billions of pounds at risk.

events.title: Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac rally as Ackman presses for conservatorship exit
events.summary: The midterm elections could be a turning point for the release of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac from government control, according to Bill Ackman. Both stocks have moved more than 60% higher since Oct. 14. Ackman believes both names can see a "10-fold" increase from current share prices. The midterm elections could be a turning point for the release of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac from government control, according to billionaire investor Bill Ackman. Investors may agree with him, if the rally in both stocks is any sign. The Federal National Mortgage Association, known as Fannie Mae, and Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corporation, or Freddie Mac, have each jumped more than 60% from Oct. 14 to Monday's close. The stocks were both up roughly 3% on Tuesday. Ackman, the founder of Pershing Square Capital Management, has long pushed for the two entities to be released from federal conservatorship. "The reason why it's not being touched right now is, you know, midterms," he said in an interview with CNBC's " Squawk Box ." Ackman, who owns both names through Pershing Square, believes Freddie and Fannie have the potential to increase "10-fold from current share prices," he said in his quarterly letter to shareholders, issued on Monday. Fannie and Freddie buy mortgages from banks and other lenders, and then package them into mortgage-backed securities, known as MBS. Their operations are critical to the housing market, providing liquidity to banks and creating a secondary market for MBS. The entities were placed into conservatorship in September 2008, during the financial crisis. The stocks were delisted from the New York Stock Exchange in 2010 and have traded over the counter since then. Ackman wants the conservatorship to end, arguing the entities would be worth multiples of their current valuation if they were freed from government control. President Donald Trump has supported ending the conservatorship of Fannie and Freddie. But it remains politically and economically contentious. The entities operate under strict capital threshold requirements and would need to be recapitalized, which could happen through issuing common equity. However, the Treasury Department would need to figure out an exit plan for its roughly $388 billion ownership stake in the entities through preferred securities and warrants. Congress may also need to play a role, passing legislation to restructure the government's role in mortgage financing and home-loan guarantees. Nonetheless, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent recently said it could happen before Trump's term ends, telling 2Way's " The Morning Meeting " podcast that the administration will tackle the ownership structure "next year, the year after." He said affordability will be guiding the decision. One point of controversy is whether ending the conservatorship of Fannie and Freddie would increase the spreads on MBS over Treasuries, effectively making mortgages costlier. Bessent has sought to reassure the market that wouldn't happen. "Whatever we do is going to be guided by making sure that the spread on [agency] mortgages … over the Treasury does not increase," Bessent said. Ackman argues that privatizing the GSEs would help insulate them from political meddling. "Fannie and Freddie are these massive, enormously profitable institutions where whichever political party controls them…if they're still in conservatorship, can influence the outcome of elections," he told CNBC. In one scenario, he explained, Democrats win the White House, conservatorship is still in place, and Democrats push Fannie and Freddie to lower credit standards in order to expand home ownership and affordability. "If they're going to move more aggressively into borrowers with lower credit quality, for example, to achieve a political objective, that's going to have an impact on trillions of dollars outstanding mortgage securities," Ackman said. "It's going to have an impact on overall credit spreads." MBS investors want certainty about how the entities will be run, he noted. "That only gets resolved in a world in which they exit conservatorship, they become publicly traded companies that are owned by institutional and retail investors," Ackman said. "We set the rules. In conservatorship, the president can do anything."

events.title: Options traders are betting heavily on these stocks ahead of election results
events.summary: With prediction markets pricing in a big victory for Democrats in Tuesday's midterm elections , traders are leaning into a group of stocks that investors often categorize as beneficiaries of left-wing leadership. Options trading in clean-energy stocks, particularly solar companies, surged on Tuesday, despite a five-month sell-off in the group that's left most of the companies in the industry group down on the year. Follow CNBC's live coverage of the 2026 midterm elections Volume in the Invesco Solar ETF (TAN) surged to 40 times higher than usual Tuesday, according to Cboe LiveVol data. The fund, which typically trades fewer than 500 contracts a day the past month, traded more than 20,000 contracts by midday, and 99% of them were calls. The ETF rallied more than 400% from its pandemic low through the 2020 election before giving almost all of the gains back by April last year. The most popular trade in TAN was buying the 50-strike call for December expiry for 80 cents and looking for a 17% rally, according to SpotGamma data. For nearer expiry, the 46 and 47-strike calls were also popular. Among individual stocks, SolarEdge Technologies stands out, on pace for three times higher-than-average volume and more than 75% of trading in calls. The company reports earnings before the bell tomorrow and rallied more than 6% Tuesday. The most popular trade was buying the 35-strike call expiring Friday. "I would only like solar if blue was in the White House," said Charlie Moon of Chicago-based Prosper Trading Academy. "But Enphase does stands out with some insider buying." Bulls were indeed dabbling in Enphase Energy , whose stock fell 20% after earnings last week but have fully recovered since and rallied 9% Tuesday. On volume twice the average, traders likely bought 8,600 calls, compared to under 900 puts. The most popular trade in Enphase was to buy the 35-strike call expiring in January, a trade that costs $2.45 per contract and needs Enphase to rally 23%.

events.title: ChatGPT's search volume is now roughly 20% of Google's. Wow, people were really sick of Google, huh?
events.summary: People were getting fed up with Google search, which made it easy for ChatGPT to step in. Robert Michael/picture alliance via Getty Images Google search results had been frustrating people for a long time — now they have another option. Searching for information is the most common use of chatbots like ChatGPT. OpenAI's Adam Fry told the Big Technology newsletter that ChatGPT has around a fifth of Google's search query volume. OpenAI is coming for Google Search, and it's working. "ChatGPT's volume of search-like queries is now roughly one-fifth the volume of queries of Google," Adam Fry, ChatGPT's consumer product lead, told Alex Kantrowitz of the Big Technology newsletter. It's good news for OpenAI. For Google? Not so great. It not only shows that people are willing to use AI, but that people were really, really, fed up with Google search results. We already knew that basic information searching is currently the top use of LLMs like ChatGPT. Pew Research Center released a report this summer that showed that the top use case was to "search for information," with 42% of American adults surveyed saying they have used AI for that. ("For tasks at work" was the second most common use, with 38% of employed adults reporting that. Lesser uses include entertainment, getting news, and medical advice.) Searching for information is the #1 use for chatbots like ChatGPT, according to a Pew report. Pew Research Center This survey wasn't specifically about ChatGPT, but it's by far the most popular AI chatbot (44% of American adults surveyed told Pew they've used ChatGPT, and only 24% have used Gemini, the next most common). ChatGPT now has 1.2 billion weekly users. We don't know how many of those users are doing informational searches as opposed to other things like coding or generating images, but it seems likely that someone who uses it to make images or chat would also ask it for information. Google did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the competition from ChatGPT, but last year Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai addressed the issue during an interview with Bloomberg's Emily Chang. "You've had these chatbots scale up to hundreds of millions of users. We've grown in queries," Pichai said at the time. "So I think it feels very far from a zero-sum game to me. To use another parallel, TikTok came in, everybody started using TikTok. YouTube grew and did very, very well in those moments too." People started to feel like Google search had gotten worse Google says that it handles 5 trillion searches per year; it's dominated search for two decades, and very profitably! But many people were getting really sick of Google search. So often in the last few years, I've heard friends or other people complain how Google search feels broken . Search results were so stuffed with SEO-friendly links that it often felt hard to trust anything or find the results you actually were searching for. Users had started to add the term "Reddit" at the end of searches in hopes of getting better results — which ended up being a boon in traffic for Reddit (sadly, this didn't last; Reddit just reported a drop in search referral traffic due to Google's AI Overviews that it doesn't expect to get back). So when ChatGPT came along, suddenly there was a new way to get information and answers without all the SEO fluff — and plenty of people were thrilled. Sure, the information isn't always reliable. Everyone should know better than to blindly trust facts doled out by AI, which is prone to hallucinations or just plain bungling, like telling people to put glue in their pizza . Despite the issues with trusting AI for information (and to be fair, it has improved since the glue/pizza fiasco of 2024), it's clear that tons of people were very, very happy to switch over to ChatGPT instead of Google for their informational searching needs. I think what we should consider is that says a lot more about how bad Google had gotten than it does about how good ChatGPT is. There's a compelling case to be made that Google enshittified its flagship product so badly — perhaps from the years and years of having no meaningful competitors — that it was a sitting duck, ready to have its lunch eaten by the first new disruptor to come along and offer people a better way. Google eventually realized it was in trouble, issuing a "code red" in 2022 over ChatGPT. It might be time to issue another one? Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: The next wave of luxury real estate: marina developments with yacht parking
events.summary: Marinas are becoming the next big draw for luxury real estate, as the global wealthy search for homes to park their ever-larger yachts, according to developers. With the number of yachts surging since Covid-19, real estate developers and investors are rushing to fill the shortage of boat slips and marina communities. There are now over 6,000 superyachts over 30 meters (98 feet) around the world, and another 200 delivered every year, according to SuperYacht Times. With the number of yachts surging since Covid-19, real estate developers and investors are rushing to fill the shortage of boat slips and marina communities. There are now over 6,000 superyachts over 30 meters (98 feet) around the world, and another 200 delivered every year, according to SuperYacht Times. The growth in the size and number of yachts has created a shortage of yacht slips. And investors are rushing to fill demand. Last year, Blackstone paid $5.6 billion for Safe Harbor Marinas, which then paid $1.5 billion in August for 65 marinas and storage sites purchased from MarineMax. European private equity firms are also on a marina buying spree to fill the shortage in the Mediterranean. Real estate developers now see marinas as a powerful magnet for ultra-wealthy buyers, especially in South Florida. Billionaire Ken Griffin is building a megayacht marina in Miami with eight megayacht slips, including one for his 308-foot yacht. The largest and most ambitious is Related Group's $2 billion new marina development in Fort Lauderdale. Slated to break ground next year and open in 2030, the project will include a St. Regis Hotel, condos, a beach club and slips for yachts up to 350 feet long. "Here in South Florida is there's been a scarcity of yachting destinations and marinas and slips," said Related Group's Nick Pérez. "So when you're able to combine irreplaceable real estate and a marina, you just have a winning formula." The 40-acre development will include a St. Regis hotel with 122 rooms, a 78-residence condo tower, 106 resort residences, as well as a deepwater marina that can hold 250 boats. It will also include a sports and wellness club with a padel and tennis court, yoga lawn, fitness center and pools. And it will have its own beach club. Fort Lauderdale has long been the yachting capital of the U.S., with a vast infrastructure of yacht repair and renovation companies, along with crew, brokers, charter experts and shipbuilder offices. An estimated 2,000 superyachts pass through Fort Lauderdale each year, according to tourism officials. Many yacht owners are looking for real estate not only for themselves but also their crew. Pérez said the new St. Regis development will not only appeal to the yachting community but also to a growing number of international buyers who are looking for a lower-cost alternative to Palm Beach and Miami. Several buyers from Mexico and Brazil have already purchased in the building. He said up to 30% of the buyers at the project could be international. "Fort Lauderdale is no longer T-shirt shops and flip-flops, it's now a luxury destination, with national retailers like Rolex, Patek, Cartier," Pérez said. "When you look at Miami and Palm Beach and the growth, now it's Fort Lauderdale's time to shine." While boat slips are the main attraction, many buyers in Fort Lauderdale are pouring in from Southern California and the Northeast to take advantage of Florida's lower taxes. "With the taxation situation in California, we're seeing a lot of interest from Newport and the Laguna area and San Diego," Pérez said. events.title: AMD has been crushed into earnings. Here’s one way to trade it
events.summary: Advanced Micro Devices has been under significant pressure leading up to earnings after the close. The stock has been caught in the swings of the AI debate all year, but this most recent leg lower was triggered by a wave of disappointing tech earnings. A record drop in Alphabet last Thursday was followed by weak results from Amazon, as well as AMD's long-standing CPU rival, Intel. Intel guided fourth-quarter revenue well below consensus and expects the PC slowdown to last through at least the first half of next year. That sent Intel's stock down 29% on Friday, its worst day since the 1970s. Caught in the fallout of Intel and the broader tech sector, AMD fell 10.9% that day and slid another 7.5% Monday. For the past week, AMD has traded on other companies' news. Now its own numbers get a vote. AMD's stock reactions have been mixed in recent quarters, sensitive to guidance and high investor expectations. It fell 17% after Q4 2025 results, when a beat and a guide above estimates still underwhelmed some analysts. It rose 18.6% after Q1 2026 results, when it guided about 6.5% above expectations. It fell 7% after Q2 2026 results, when a guide above consensus still fell short of the $14 billion some analysts wanted. That may make direction hard to call, but options let investors build a trade that doesn't have to pick a side. Based on Monday's close, I'm selling the November 4 425/415 put spread and the 510/520 call spread for a credit of roughly $3.65. AMD's 30-day implied volatility is elevated going into earnings, closing Monday higher than on about 81% of days over the past year. This means sellers are collecting richer premium than usual. To capture that premium while limiting time beyond the earnings announcement, the trade uses the November 4 weeklies. These contracts imply a move of about 9% through Wednesday, in line with AMD's 8.4% average close-to-close move over its last 10 reports. The short strikes sit at the edges of the expected move, with long strikes $10 away to limit capital at risk going into earnings. This isn't a bet that options are mispricing the move or a directional call. It's a neutral play that aims to profit from the elevated premium that tends to come out after the print. The trade reaches its maximum profit of $365 if AMD closes between $425 and $510 on Wednesday. Breakevens are $421.35 and $513.65, about 9.7% below and 10.0% above Monday's close, just outside the expected move. The maximum loss of $635 comes if AMD closes below $415 or above $520, roughly 11% in either direction. That has happened in 11 of its last 40 reports, and AMD has had moves as large as 19% in its last four, emphasizing the importance of capping the risk with the long wings. If AMD finishes between $415 and $425, the short put can be assigned, creating an obligation to buy 100 shares per spread at $425. After the credit, the cost basis is $421.35, or roughly 35% below the Oct. 6 closing high. For investors who like AMD's long-term story, that's a way to end up owning the stock at a discount. A finish between $510 and $520 can assign the short call and leave a short stock position. For investors looking to avoid either risk, consider managing the position before Wednesday's close. events.title: Sullivan: What the 2026 midterms could mean for energy investors
events.summary: A Democratic Congress could be good for offshore wind and solar energy. If the Republicans maintain control over one or both houses, we could see the administration more urgently expand domestic energy production. Texas will matter most for utility stocks and data center plays. Why you should be watching one ship carrying Russian diesel fuel bound for America on the maritime radar. GET THIS IN YOUR INBOX FIRST: Subscribe to CNBC's "Power Insider" newsletter. Don't expect huge near-term moves in energy stocks off the results of the midterms . But there are some investing implications over the longer-term. Let me break it down. Yes, it's entirely possible that one or both houses of Congress will shift to Democratic control. That's not my opinion. It's what many of the research reports, polls, and prediction markets are suggesting as of this writing. Follow CNBC's live coverage of the 2026 midterm elections For argument's sake, let's say that this time the polls are correct. The election ends with a "blue trickle," and Democrats win out with a slight edge in the House, Senate, or both. It won't be enough to meaningfully change, well, anything. If the election ends with just a slight lean to the Democratic side, it won't be enough for a veto-proof majority. Candidates can specify policies — like halting the growth of data centers — all they want, but there's a chasm between being elected and passing new laws. Research I've read and conversations we've had on CNBC suggest that the next two years in Washington, D.C., will be flush with finger-pointing, investigations into the president and his family, and posturing ahead of the far-more-important 2028 presidential election. S&P Global doesn't exactly agree with me, saying that Democratic control of either chamber would bring "tougher oversight of agency decisions" and could impact things such as tax incentives and "other policies underpinning long-term energy investments." A Democratic Congress could be good for offshore wind, an energy source the president seems to hate with the white-hot passion of the sun. Speaking of the sun, a shift blue could also be positive for the continued growth of solar, perhaps via new tax incentives. Though both are growing rapidly. If the Republicans maintain control over one or both houses, we keep doing more of the same, albeit with more urgency. S&P Global adds that "a continued Republican majority would give the administration more room to pursue expanded domestic production, faster permitting and environmental deregulation, though narrow margins could limit major legislation." Any change in control of Congress is also unlikely to make a big difference around the Iran conflict. Once any new Congress begins in January, things will have either ramped up, stayed the same, or cooled down. A new Congress could try to use its authority under the War Powers Act. The team at Piper Sandler agrees, writing that "elections matter, but will likely not change the direction of things" as Trump focuses more on his own legacy. That's a polite way of saying that the President is going to do largely what he wants, Congress be darned. On the state level, the midterms may matter a little bit more, particularly as they relate to energy-hungry data centers. In Texas, a change in the statehouse could bring a change in sentiment around data centers. Candidate Gina Hinojosa has a policy to "end data center madness" and supports a moratorium on new builds. Amy Acton also supports a "conditional moratorium" on new data center builds in Ohio. Vivek Ramaswamy is also calling for conditions on new data center construction. The issue is a big deal in many states. Yet even if those candidates, or candidates with similar views on big new energy projects, win, they'd still have to enact meaningful change. Which could happen, of course. So let's say it does happen. New governors enter office and use their power to throttle or even stop new projects. Even if some of the big new projects are stalled or stopped, power demand, at a minimum, would stay at current levels. Which means demand for power production inputs such as natural gas, nuclear, and yes, even coal, would remain at current levels. As far as power-hungry utility stocks go, Bank of America agrees with my election take above - mostly. Its team writes that it thinks the "2026 cycle matters for utility equities in far fewer states than the headline count suggests," but that committee appointments in each state will matter. The BofA team says that, regarding the election and utility stocks, five states matter most: Georgia, Ohio, Oregon, Pennsylvania, and Texas. Texas is the "most consequential," as state environmental regulators have halted data center permits. That state's Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) has actually stopped electronic permitting to make sure any permit is unrelated to data centers. To my point, that's already known information.

events.title: AI-generated 'slopaganda' in political ads puts internet platforms on alert
events.summary: Tuesday's midterm elections follow record spending on AI-generated political ads. There's no federal legislation mandating disclosure of AI use in such ads. The midterm election cycle has been dominated by "slopaganda," or campaign ads featuring AI-generated clips and images, creating another challenge for Instagram, YouTube and X as they attempt to monitor their platforms. The term slopaganda dates back to early last year, when a group of experts on artificial intelligence used it in a paper to describe a new phenomenon combining generative AI slop with propaganda and misinformation. There's no comprehensive federal law governing the use or disclosure of AI in political ads. And while there are some 30 state laws with different requirements about AI use and disclosure, candidates don't always abide by them. On the leading internet sites run by Meta , Google and Elon Musk's SpaceX , users run into AI-generated ads and AI-generated posts shared by politicians, alongside authentic videos and clips. More than $187 million has been spent on nearly 300 ads generated or enhanced by AI, according to an analysis released last week by the Wesleyan Media Project . That's almost certainly an undercount, the organization says, because so many ads don't contain disclaimers and because determining AI use is difficult in some instances. Over 90% of the spending came from Republican candidates, a Republican party committee or a Republican-leaning group, the report found, and most don't include disclosures. CNBC found a number of AI-generated ads running online without disclosures, including a fake video of New York Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul that was posted by her opponent, Republican challenger Bruce Blakeman. In Texas, Republican senatorial candidate Ken Paxton created an AI-generated video showing Democratic opponent James Talarico making controversial statements, with a three-second disclosure flashing in the middle. It's being shared as organic content on YouTube and X by Paxton's campaign. "Organic content" refers to free, unpaid posts shared on a profile or channel. The Blakeman and Paxton campaigns didn't immediately respond to requests for comment. YouTube told CNBC that the company applies "prominent labels to realistic AI content." "For organic content on YouTube, political candidates can request removal where their face appears to be altered or generated by AI," the company said. "For advertisers, we require disclosure when an election ad contains synthetic or digitally altered people or events to provide viewers with transparency." YouTube parent Google also requires political ads to complete its election ads verification process and include "paid for by" disclosures. X says advertisers must comply with applicable laws, putting the responsibility on the advertiser, not the platform. The company didn't respond to CNBC's request for comment. Meta referred to its guidelines on political ads, including restrictions on their use in the week prior to the election. The company also mandates "paid for by" labels and maintains an ad library of political ads. In June, the company ramped up its labeling, adding a new "about this ad" tool for ads that Meta detects have been created with third-party AI tools. Last month, Meta was ordered to pay $25 billion in penalties by a New Mexico court as part of a data privacy case that stemmed from the company's Cambridge Analytica scandal from nearly a decade ago. Cambridge Analytica, which was a political consulting firm, allegedly accessed the information of 87 million Facebook users in improper fashion. One risk the tech platforms face with generative AI is being asked to create misleading images and videos. The Brennan Center for Justice tested ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok, Claude, Perplexity and DeepSeek for their willingness to facilitate deceptive content. The study from August found that many models may avoid generating content around familiar conspiracies, but can generally be manipulated into creating misleading material. A retest of those platforms in October found that ChatGPT had made progress. It had started redirecting prompts for harmful election images into illustrations so they look like comics, or refusing to take action on them altogether. A number of national politicians are trying to address the issue. The Protect Elections from Deceptive AI Act , backed by senators from both parties, would prohibit knowingly distributing materially deceptive AI-generated video or audio about federal candidates. Other bills are being led by Democrats in Congress, including the AI Ads Act , which is looking to expand current bans on campaign misrepresentation to include generative AI content. None of the proposed bills have advanced out of committee. WATCH: AI challenge is lack of compute in the marketplace

events.title: CrowdStrike launches AI kill switch that it says can stop internal agents that go rogue
events.summary: CrowdStrike launched an AI kill switch feature to stop and block internal agents that misbehave. The cybersecurity giant also announced a Claude Cowork integration and two AI acquisitions. Business chief Daniel Bernard told CNBC that being able to control and shut down agent activity is vital to the next wave of AI adoption. CrowdStrike is betting that it has a solution to rogue artificial intelligence . The cybersecurity vendor on Tuesday launched an AI kill switch designed to let security teams stop internal AI agents that go rogue, block them from relaunching and cut off their enterprise network access. The tool is built into CrowdStrike's Falcon Guardian platform, launched in September to secure AI agents. CrowdStrike also announced an integration with Anthropic's Claude Cowork . "Having the ability to control and turn off, and make a decision and decide, I think that's really important for this next chapter of AI adoption," Chief Business Officer Daniel Bernard told CNBC. A string of recent high-profile cyber incidents has added urgency to calls for some kind of emergency shutdown mechanism. The Hugging Face breach orchestrated by rogue OpenAI agents in July was particularly alarming for businesses. Last week, Binance disclosed the largest crypto cyberattack on record and hackers have recently targeted hundreds of refrigerators and freezers at supermarkets in France. Over the summer, U.S. representatives introduced bipartisan legislation that would require AI companies to build shutdown capabilities into their models. Critics argue, however, that an emergency stop button is far too complicated to implement across multiple systems, data centers and complex AI models. Humans are still doing the work behind some AI agents OpenAI pares fundraising goal, now seeking up to $20 billion in latest round Binance resumes withdrawals following $6.3 billion hack, says 90% of stolen user assets are covered Why AI is boosting Meta’s ad business while hurting Google search Bernard said the kill switch operates like a circuit breaker in systems where customers use its Falcon platform. The process can detect internal agent activity but requires a human to decide to cut the agent off and reinstate access. "If you kill a process at the root, and we have that level of access at the root … it's very binary," Bernard said. "You either kill the AI and the agent, or you don't, and then you report on that." The kill switch doesn't delete the agent's code but uses connected AI gateways to cut off access to the AI models that influence decisions, CrowdStrike said. In the age of AI, businesses are moving quickly to adopt autonomous tools, often without the necessary safeguards and protections. CrowdStrike believes its new tool will let companies stop AI agent 'misbehavior in its tracks, while leaving room for innovation. The company also announced plans to acquire AI observability startup Fiddler AI and AI security testing firm Dreadnode . CrowdStrike and its rivals are rapidly scooping up cybersecurity startups to keep up with increasing security demands. The need for AI security tools has also powered a broader wave of cybersecurity deal-making .

events.title: Republicans pitch 3.5% income tax cap as an affordability fix in North Carolina—but Gov. Josh Stein says it won’t put ‘more money in anyone’s pockets’
events.summary: Republican lawmakers in North Carolina have steadily reduced the state’s income taxes for more than a decade. On Tuesday, voters will decide whether to make it harder for future lawmakers to reverse those cuts as affordability emerges as one of the biggest issues of the midterms. North Carolina voters are considering a constitutional amendment that would lower the maximum allowable income tax rate from 7% to 3.5%. This would halve the ceiling for what the state government can charge individuals and corporations through income taxes. But despite the legislation’s name, “ Lower Taxes for All NC ,” the amendment wouldn’t actually lower state taxes immediately. North Carolina’s individual income tax rate currently stands at 3.99%. Under legislation that has already passed, it is scheduled to fall to 3.49% in 2027 . The rate is set to drop further to 3.24% in 2030 and 2.99% in 2033. The measure facing voters Tuesday deals with the future. If approved, raising income taxes above 3.5% would require another constitutional amendment, which requires the approval of three-fifths of both chambers of the state legislature and then a majority of voters. Supporters say the restriction would protect taxpayers from future tax increases, while critics warn it could leave the state with fewer options to raise money for public services during an economic downturn. The measure is part of how the Republican-dominated state legislature is trying to tackle the rising cost of living, which 48% of registered voters identified as their top issue , according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll from Tuesday.  Across the country, voters are considering several competing tax initiatives as they grapple with how to address rising costs. Apart from the constitutional referendum to lower the cap on state income tax, North Carolina voters will also vote Tuesday on whether to allow the state legislature to impose a limit on how much local governments can raise property taxes.  In total, nine income and wealth tax related measures are on the ballot in six states, according to Ballotpedia , including one of the most well known, Proposition 40 , which would impose a one-time 5% wealth tax on individuals in California with a net worth of more than $1 billion.  What other tax cuts have Republicans made in North Carolina? The North Carolina income tax amendment is just the latest reform aiming to cut taxes under the Republican-controlled legislature.  After years of Democratic control of the legislature, in 2010, Republicans won control of both chambers of the state’s General Assembly and have been in power since 2011. For years, Republicans in the legislature have held enough seats to enact their legislation even without the support of the two consecutive Democratic governors who have held the executive position since 2017.  Republicans have used this influence to slowly cut taxes. Republican lawmakers in 2013 passed a tax reform that changed the state from a system of graduated individual income tax brackets to a flat tax. They have also reduced corporate taxes.  In 2018, North Carolina voters approved a constitutional amendment lowering the maximum allowable income tax rate from 10% to 7%, with less than 60% of voters supporting the proposal . The latest amendment on the ballot Tuesday would cut that limit in half again to 3.5%. The measure already passed the Republican-controlled state Senate and state House to get on the ballot. Democratic Gov. Josh Stein was not required to approve of the measure because governors in North Carolina can’t veto proposed constitutional amendments. Still, Stein has made it clear he opposes the proposed amendment, saying in a press conference from May the initiative would allow the legislature to cut taxes for wealthy individuals while raising pressure to increase the state’s sales tax to make up the revenue short fall. “It will not put any more money in anyone’s pockets,” Stein said. “But what it will do is make regular people pay the consequences of it next year and years into the future because it will insulate the very wealthy from ever having an increase in their income tax.” Stein also pointed out that because the amendment is in the state constitution it will be harder for future legislatures to change later. Republican state Sen. Michael Lee, a sponsor of the legislation that put the income tax cap on the ballot, has said the restriction would build on the legislature’s previous actions to lower taxes. “Our tax reforms have produced more than a decade of strong revenue growth while letting people keep more of what they earn, and this amendment locks in that progress,” Lee said in a statement earlier this year to North Carolina news station WECT . Revenue at stake Yet, the measure raises questions about how North Carolina would pay for government services, and what services may need to be cut if income tax revenue falls. The state collected approximately $17 billion in individual income taxes during the 2024-25 fiscal year, accounting for nearly half of its $34.6 billion in General Fund revenue, according to the North Carolina Office of State Budget and Management. That money helps fund public education, health care, and other government services. The amendment won’t reduce tax revenue immediately, but opponents say that making future income tax increases harder would make lawmakers more likely to either cut services or raise revenue elsewhere, including through higher sales taxes. Alexandra Sirota, executive director of the NC Budget & Tax Center, has also warned that restricting income taxes could limit how the government adapts to changing conditions in the economy. “These tax amendments won’t cut anyone’s taxes,” Sirota said in a September statement . “But they would make it more difficult for future lawmakers to fairly raise the revenue needed to meet costs through a higher rate on millionaires, billionaires, and highly profitable corporations.” National debate North Carolina isn’t the only state reconsidering how much its government should be allowed to tax residents and businesses. Voters in Colorado will vote Tuesday on competing proposals that will either replace the state’s 4.4% flat income tax with a graduated tax rate reaching up to 8.4% or one that will cap income tax rates at 4.4%. In Iowa, voters are weighing a measure requiring a two-thirds legislative majority to increase income taxes. Washington voters will also decide whether to repeal a newly enacted 9.9% income tax on household income exceeding $1 million. California voters, meanwhile, are set to weigh in on one of the most contentious ballot measures up for a vote Tuesday—a 5% tax on billionaires’ wealth that has been opposed by well-known figures such as Google cofounder Sergey Brin. events.title: Calls for Qld to scrap 'ideologically driven' changes to industrial relation laws
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Proposed changes to Queensland's industrial relations laws 'ideologically driven', law firm says Deputy Prmier Jarrod Bleijie says the changes protect workers. ( ABC News: William Murray ) The Queensland government's proposed shake-up to industrial relations laws is an "ideologically driven" attempt to rehash the Campbell Newman era and should be abandoned, a law firm says. Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie has introduced sweeping changes that he says "essentially mimicked" the federal Fair Work legislation introduced by Julia Gillard's government in 2009. However, law firm Maurice Blackburn has taken issue with this comparison in its submission to the committee examining the legislation. "Instead, they represent a cherry-picking of the restrictive provisions of federal law, while omitting the protective ones and going beyond our federal laws in key respects," its submission said. Maurice Blackburn has suggested the legislation be "abandoned" and that if this was not the committee's view, the would need to be "significant reconsideration" of the changes proposed. The legislation is in response to an independent review into industrial relations and the workers' compensation scheme , with the government accepting 104 of its recommendations. The wide-ranging changes include a "fit and proper" test for union officials, allowing workers to be represented by non-recognised union groups and allowing a ballot on a proposal after agreement from one union. Mr Bleijie said he believed the proposed changes were reasonable, balanced and ensured workers were protected. Queensland unions rallied against the government's proposed changes last month. ( ABC News: Curtis Rodda ) Under the legislation, Mr Bleijie would have the power to terminate protected industrial action in certain circumstances. The Queensland Council of Unions has spoken out against the proposed legislation since it was first mentioned in parliament last month, raising concerns it would restrict the ability for workers to exercise their rights and give the minister of the day "extraordinary power". Mr Bleijie said the minister's power to stop strikes would only be used in "very limited circumstances" when the safety or economy was at risk or such action was highly disruptive. Sweeping changes to Qld's industrial relation laws Protected industrial action could be terminated if it would threaten to endanger the life, personal safety, health or welfare or cause significant damage to the state's economy. The legislation also strengthens the test for claiming a psychological injury, requiring work to be the major contributing factor rather than a significant factor, after a substantial rise in claims in recent years. This move has been welcomed by Business Chamber Queensland however it noted this must not "create unnecessary barriers" for those with a genuine injury. The Queensland Law Society submitted the absence of a definition of "the major contributing factor" in the bill would cause "unnecessary complexity" when assessing a claim and lead to more disputes between workers and insurers. Public hearings will be held in Brisbane next week before the committee delivers its report on November 27.

events.title: Binance breach puts custody at center of crypto infrastructure trade
events.summary: The $6.3 billion Binance hack could accelerate a shift in how investors value cryptocurrency companies, putting a greater premium on custody providers and the infrastructure needed to securely hold and protect digital assets. Much of crypto's evolution this year has involved companies moving past their reliance on trading volumes and transaction fees, to focus instead on building the infrastructure connecting digital assets with traditional finance. Last Thursday's breach adds a new dimension, bringing cybersecurity, custody, compliance and balance-sheet resilience into sharper focus. Importantly, the Binance breach was not an indictment of crypto itself, or a case of leadership-driven fraud, as with FTX in late 2022. Instead, Binance's leadership moved quickly to contain the fallout , protect customers and commit the exchange's own resources to cover losses. On Tuesday, Binance CEO Richard Teng told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" that the company has replenished 98% of $6.34 billion in affected assets, and that it is still in the process of purchasing outstanding, more illiquid assets. Management's response, alongside efforts elsewhere in the industry to boost confidence, helped prevent a security breach from escalating into a broader crisis of confidence. For example, Tether, Circle, Ripple and others moved quickly to freeze or restrict access to about $3 billion in stolen assets; Coinbase blocked transfers to compromised wallets and offered Binance direct assistance. The hack could even help shape the next phase of the crypto infrastructure trade. The new winners may not just be the businesses with the most users, volume or assets under custody, but the ones that can also demonstrate they're able to protect those assets under extreme duress. "Which company has the resources to invest in cybersecurity and protect customer funds? For a smaller company, it could be much harder because once these crypto companies become infrastructure plays, providing the well for tokenization … they need to have the compliance and control in place so that a similar hacking will not happen or can be minimized," Owen Lau, senior analyst at ClearStreet, told CNBC. "Larger companies have more resources that could give them some advantage." While institutional investors have increasingly embraced digital assets, broader adoption depends on confidence that those assets can be securely held, accessed and transferred. The Binance breach highlights the importance of that infrastructure, and could increase demand for specialized custodians and platforms with established asset-protection capabilities. Coinbase has operated a dedicated institutional custody business since 2018. Circle entered the custody business this year, after the U.S. Office of the Comptroller of the Currency granted it approval to operate as a trust bank . In the past few years, Ripple and Kraken have also launched custody businesses. Still, smaller players compete in the space as well. Small cap crypto exchange stock Gemini Space Station has offered custody services since 2019. BitGo Holdings , founded in 2013, is one of the earliest players in institutional crypto custody and infrastructure, with a reputation for security and serving major institutions. The shift could also drive consolidation as companies look to buy capabilities, deepen their infrastructure offerings and achieve the scale needed to compete, Lau said. The more consequential structural shift may be the separation of custody from execution, according to Morgan Stanley. "Crypto exchanges have historically combined trading, custody, and settlement within vertically integrated platforms, concentrating operational risk. Repeated security breaches could encourage investors to move assets toward independent custody while continuing to trade on CEXs," the firm's analyst Felix Stratmann said in a note Monday," referring to centralized cryptocurrency exchanges. "This would preserve the role of centralized exchanges as liquidity and execution venues, while potentially benefiting regulated custodians, including banks, as institutional investors place greater emphasis on asset segregation, operational resilience, and investor protection," Stratmann said.

events.title: Apple warns of risks related to AI agents behaving in 'unintended or unpredictable' ways
events.summary: Apple said in its annual financial filing that AI agents that can act in "unintended or unpredictable ways" could represent a threat to its business. The new risk factors in Apple's filing show the disruptive potential of AI agents, which have proliferated across the business world. Last month, Apple announced changes to full disk access on Macs to reduce "risks related to this level of access" for AI agents installed on PCs. Apple said in its annual financial filing on Tuesday that AI agents that can act in "unintended or unpredictable ways" could represent a threat to its business by opening the company up to lawsuits or hurting its reputation. The new risk factors in Apple's filing show the disruptive potential of AI agents, which have rapidly become top of mind for Silicon Valley's most important companies. "In particular, artificial intelligence agents and other technologies can take actions autonomously, including interacting with internal or external systems that in some cases they may not be authorized to access, executing or altering code, sending communications, and completing transactions," Apple wrote in the filing . The company added that agents "may behave in unintended or unpredictable ways, including by taking actions that were not directed, instructed or authorized." Earlier this year, OpenAI released Dots, and Meta introduced Muse. Both AI agents use advanced AI models to work autonomously for tasks. They can even email or remind users when new messages arrive. Apple's disclosure comes after several episodes that involved rogue AI agents breaking out of their sandboxes to hack third-party websites, like the Hugging Face incident , which has drawn renewed attention from policymakers in Washington, D.C., and around the world. Humans are still doing the work behind some AI agents OpenAI pares fundraising goal, now seeking up to $20 billion in latest round Binance resumes withdrawals following $6.3 billion hack, says 90% of stolen user assets are covered Why AI is boosting Meta’s ad business while hurting Google search Separately, the ability of agents to use a computer in human ways is forcing big companies like Amazon and JPMorgan Chase to come up with policies around agentic access to services for strategic or security reasons. "The Company's ability to oversee and control third-party artificial intelligence agents and other technologies may be limited," Apple warned in its filing. Apple doesn't currently have an agentic AI. But when new CEO John Ternus was asked on Monday's earnings call about AI agents, he said that the company had "real room" to expand Siri's capabilities. "As far as agentic capabilities, we think these are promising tools for users," Ternus said. "We just want to make sure that users are aware of what they are giving access to. We want to make sure this is done in a way that protects security and privacy." This fall, Apple released Siri AI, a new assistant that uses the iPhone's local data storage to access data like calendars and emails, but Apple's Siri can't work autonomously for long stretches like Dots or Muse. Ternus said Apple can't access private data on its devices, calling it a "core differentiator." "If you think about it, so much of your personal data is on your iPhone, whether it's your contacts, your communications, health data, financial data, all of that," Ternus said. "Siri can tap into that and help you access it in a way that's very secure and private and that nobody else has access to." Commercial AI agents like those from OpenAI and Meta ask for high-level access to the user's accounts like email in order to be more useful. Apple indicated that the current regulations around AI and "super intelligence" are changing, unpredictable and that it could cost a lot of money to adapt to new laws governing AI. "In addition, the Company is subject to the risks posed by ethical concerns and negative consumer perceptions related to automation, artificial intelligence and super intelligence, including perceived threats to safety or other societal harms or complications," according to the filing. events.title: British fintech Revolut slashes AI coding costs 10x by cutting out Claude and going self-hosted
events.summary: Security All Security Cyber-crime Patches Research CSO Off-Prem All Off-Prem Edge and IoT Channel PaaS and IaaS SaaS On-Prem All On-Prem Systems Storage Networks HPC Personal Tech Cx0 Public Sector Software All Software AI and ML Applications Databases DevOps OS Platforms Virtualization Offbeat All Offbeat Columnists Anthropic BOFH Legal Site News About Us Special Features All Special Features Supercomputing Month 2026 Nvidia GTC Berlin 2026 Cybersecurity Month 2026 VMware Explore 2026 Cloud Infrastructure Month 2026 HPE: AI Explainers Agentic AI The Future of the Datacenter AWS:Reinvent Nvidia GTC Computex 2026 AI Infrastructure Month 2026 The State of Storage 2026 RSA Conference Vendor Voice All Vendor Voice Modernizing Financial Services with FIS and AWS Barco Infinidat Everpure Rubrik Make it real with Capgemini and AWS Money Movement Hub ZTE Nutanix: Scale Kubernetes. Not Chaos. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Turns out cheap tokens get engineers doing things that save time, like debugging and tackling Jira tickets Nvidia is happy to take your money whether you're using open or closed models, says Jensen Huang 4 hours ago Drax wants to feed Britain's AI habit with £20B datacenter at biomass power station 12 hours ago Toyota shows off SoC that stores model weights and its OS on integrated memory 22 hours ago Anthropic's compute tab could top $1T as Q3 revenue nears $17B 1 day ago Marvell wants to be a copper topper, bets $115B on photonics leader to push optical networking 1 day ago Revolut says that in less than a year it's managed to slash its AI coding inference costs by roughly 90 percent by making self-hosted models its default instead of relying primarily on commercial services like Claude. Speaking at the AI Engineer conference in New York last month, David Abitbol, ops and infrastructure lead at the British fintech, described how it saw a 60 percent improvement in coding time and a 70 percent improvement in lead time following its rollout of AI coding tools to roughly 2,000 engineers. Revolut initially adopted GLM-5.1 before moving to GLM-5.3, which it now serves using 56 Nvidia B200 GPUs. Prior to its switch to GLM, Revolut had been experimenting with AI, deploying Gemini in early 2025 and Claude Code in early 2026. "We were highly skeptical about the cost of AI. We were seeing engineers spend $1,000 a month, $10,000 a month with not so much ROI, and so when we launched it we launched it with strict budget limits," Abitbol said. Because of this, engineers only had access to a limited number of tokens, so the company began investigating self-hosting its own models. At $0.30 per million input/output tokens, self hosting GLM 5.1 cost about a tenth of using OpenAI's Codex or Anthropic's Claude Code. And, as it turned out, when tokens are cheap, you stop worrying about how many they use or what they use them for. While Revolut did see improvements to coding speed, Abitbol noted the biggest bottleneck wasn't actually the code. Instead, he says the biggest gains came from letting the AI models deal with things like debugging and Jira and Confluence tickets. "When you have unlimited tokens, you're free to do that," he said. "You no longer have to save your tokens for the end of the quarter or the most difficult task." Developed by Chinese open weights model dev Z.ai, GLM 5.1 isn't exactly a small model. At roughly 754 billion total parameters (40 billion activated for each token generated), the model requires roughly 380 GB of GPU memory just to hold the weights and another 6-26 GB per user to maintain context depending on precision. To serve GLM-5.3 at scale, Revolut deployed 56 Nvidia B200 GPUs, equivalent in GPU count to seven eight-GPU DGX B200 systems. But as Abitbol noted, the greatest performance gains didn't come from adding GPUs, but rather tuning the model's hyperparameters along with switching to NVFP4 quantization, implementing disaggregated prefill and decode, and tuning context lengths. One key takeaway was that supporting a one-million-token context window doesn't necessarily make such a large window useful or efficient. "Long context is a scam. You really need to be mindful of that," Abitbol said. "Even though you can serve one million tokens, 256 [thousand] is really what you need." With these optimizations, Abitbol says that the company was able to achieve sub 3-second time to first token on context windows of around 256,000 tokens, and generation speeds of around 200 tokens a second, both of which he notes are the sweet spot for the company's software engineers. "What you want to aim for is a sub-3 second time to first token. This is empirical evidence. As soon as you exceed 5 seconds, my Slack inbox starts to blow up," Abitbol said. "In terms of throughput, it doesn't really matter as much. We serve, in terms of interactivity, 200 tokens per second. People are fine [with that]. You don't need to go higher.

events.title: Crude oil prices fall for second day as market hopes for diplomatic resolution to Iran war
events.summary: Crude oil prices fell Tuesday for a second consecutive session, as the market hopes the U.S. and Iran will reach a diplomatic settlement to the conflict that has disrupted global energy supplies for eight months. U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures lost 37 cents to close at $96.09 a barrel after dipping below $95 earlier in the session. Brent crude , the international benchmark, shed $1.17 to settle at $103.60. The move lower came after rumors circulated the U.S. and Iran were making progress toward a deal. Oil sold off more than 7% on Monday after Washington and Tehran signaled they were both open to discussions to reach a settlement. President Donald Trump told reporters Tehran wants "to make a deal and that could happen." Qatar is continuing to mediate talks between the U.S. and Iran, the Gulf state's foreign ministry said Tuesday. A delegation from Qatar held talks in Tehran in an effort to reach an agreement that prevents further escalation in the region and ends the U.S.-Iran conflict, the foreign ministry said. However, Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesman Emsaeil Baqaei said Tuesday that Tehran will not accept diplomacy based on coercion, according to the state-owned media outlet Islamic Republic News Agency . It was unclear where talks actual stand. The market had been pricing in the risk of escalation after the U.S. midterm elections , as reports circulated that Washington was drafting plans for strikes on Iran. Crude prices gained more than 10% in October in response. The situation in the Middle East remains volatile and there's still substantial risk that fighting could break out. Washington attacked Iran's Qeshm Island on Monday, U.S. officials told The Wall Street Journal, adding that the U.S. has been carrying out "limited strikes" against the country in recent weeks. The military campaign against Iran has been kept deliberately low-profile to avoid signaling plans for a major escalation in fighting, the report said, quoting an unnamed official. And commercial ships continue to come under attack in the Persian Gulf, Strait of Hormuz and Gulf of Oman. At least four ship attacks have been reported since the start of the month, according to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre. Despite these attacks, the Trump administration has also been touting a possible diplomatic solution to the conflict, with Vice President JD Vance telling CNN, "The president and I both feel really good about the prospect of potentially coming to a negotiated settlement." On Sunday, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Trump would like to resolve the Iranian war "diplomatically," and prefers not to use military force. High oil prices have contributed substantially to inflation and high gasoline prices in the U.S., which have become a cause of concern for Trump ahead of the midterm elections. Last week, two Federal Reserve presidents said interest rates will need to move higher to rein in inflation. Higher rates generally crimp growth and raise costs for consumers, but help to bring down inflation. — CNBC's Priyanka Salve contributed to this report.

events.title: US Space Force Guardians will join Army Rangers, Navy SEALS, and other special forces in a new command
events.summary: US Space Force Special Operations Command will train and equip personnel for special forces around the world. US Space Force photo by Dave Grim US Space Force has activated a Special Operations Command. The command will send Space Force Guardians to special operations forces around the world. Officials said the command will bring space expertise to special operations. The US Space Force has activated a new command dedicated to supporting special operations forces. It's the military's first new service component for US Special Operations Command since the Marines joined with Marine Special Operations Command in 2006. US Space Forces Special Operations Command, or SPACEFOR-SOC, was formally activated on October 7. Headquartered at MacDill Air Force Base in Florida, Space Forces Special Operations Command will train and equip Space Force Guardians to regional special operations commands around the world. The new command joins other services' units that already support SOCOM, such as the Navy SEALs, Army Green Berets and Rangers, Marine Raiders , and Air Force pararescue. "For the SOF enterprise, this activation provides an enduring and accountable way to integrate space power into special operations," Adm. Frank Bradley, the commander of SOCOM, said in a statement. The new command will give the Space Force a permanent presence with other SOF units. Through a capability known as Space Special Warfare, SPACEFOR-SOC will deploy small teams made up of space, cyber, and intelligence specialists. Those teams are designed to provide mobile, low-signature space capabilities to special operations units operating in environments with poor communication. "The Guardians of SPACEFOR-SOC are shaping how our special operations leaders see the world through the space domain lens, bringing critical, cutting-edge space expertise directly to the combatant command headquarters," Gen. Douglas Schiess, the Space Force's chief of space operations, said. The Space Force oversees assets related to communications, navigation systems, and networks. Courtesy photo by US Space Force Sgt. Michael Carrasquillo The activation comes as the military increasingly treats space as a contested warfighting domain, such as the air, ground, sea, and cyberspace. The new focus is a major shift from the last two decades of combat during the Global War on Terror. Today, "space" is critical for communications, navigation, missile warning, and intelligence. GPS navigation in particular is a major concern for Space Guardians— disruptions to satellites that provide GPS can degrade operations of a majority of weapons and technologies. Space Force oversees satellites and other physical assets while also protecting various networks, communications, and tracking systems. Established in 2019, it is the military's youngest branch and focuses on the space domain as well as electronic warfare. Ongoing conflicts have shown vulnerabilities and advantages in these spaces. In the early days of the US war with Iran , officials said US space and cyber forces were the first to begin the fight, jamming signals, hacking networks, and disrupting satellites to blind the Iranian military. Space Command and US Cyber Command also supported military operations against Venezuela earlier this year and Iran's nuclear program last year. These domains have also been critical for Russia and Ukraine, with troops fighting inside the electromagnetic spectrum to prevent the other from using satellites, communications, and networks in the fight. The pace at which both sides can employ attacks and countermeasures in these areas has increased throughout the war. Officials have said this new command will bring more of those components into other special operations forces, contributing greater expertise. The effort aligns with the growing recognition that electromagnetic spectrum, space, and cyber functions are required to operate in other domains such as sea, land, and air. events.title: That dream job offer might be from a North Korean hacker
events.summary: North Korea appears to have used a fake job interview as part of its months-long preparations to steal $6.3 billion from Binance, the crypto exchange said Tuesday. Why it matters : The country's hackers are weaponizing both sides of the job market , posing as recruiters and job applicants to infiltrate companies and steal billions. Driving the news : Binance said one of its software engineers was contacted in September through a "legitimate job-hunting platform" by someone posing as a project director at a fictitious company. During the first-round interview, a fake HR representative conducted a live video call with the engineer and showed off a seemingly legitimate social media profile featuring personal photos and videos. The hackers waited until the second round — after building trust with the employee — to ask them to download an infected code repository as part of an interview assignment. Separately, another software engineer also downloaded a "tampered Homebrew installation" in June to install a popular AI coding tool onto their device. Binance's security team detected the installation and replaced the device, as well as rotated all credentials, but the engineer and colleagues were all exposed to the hacker. The intrigue: The fake interview was just one of several suspected North Korean attempts to compromise Binance employees. So far in 2026, Binance said it has detected and prevented 57 suspected North Korea-linked cyber incidents, including attempts involving fake job interviews and compromised software packages. Between the lines: North Korean hackers have spent years exploiting both sides of the hiring process. As job applicants, North Korean operatives pose as legitimate IT workers to land high-paying jobs at American companies. Those salaries are then funneled back to Pyongyang. Operatives are also increasingly posing as recruiters and prospective employees to lure in people who work at cryptocurrency firms in the hopes of tricking them into downloading malware. Data from Pindrop Security shows that IT worker fraud has been rampant in 2026: Last year, North Korean job applicants made up 1 in every 343 applications. This year, across Pindrop's customer base, those applicants now make up 1 in 47. The big picture: North Korea has found an opening in a difficult job market, where companies are eager to find qualified workers and job seekers are anxious for their next opportunity. Hiring managers have struggled to find qualified candidates , while job applicants have been anxious for years about their ability to find new roles in a tough market. events.title: 12 of the biggest perks of being a US senator
events.summary: Bernie Sanders has been a senator representing Vermont since 2007. Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images November 3 is Election Day. Thirty-five seats in the US Senate are being voted upon in this year's midterms . There are plenty of perks to being a senator besides governing the country. Like millions of Americans across the country, you might be spending today glued to the TV or social media as Election Day predictions and results roll in. After months, and sometimes years, of campaigning, hours spent prepping, and thousands of dollars raised, 35 winners will be sworn into the US Senate in January. Senate races in Michigan, Texas, Ohio, and Maine have been garnering headlines for months. In addition to their many new responsibilities in office, there are also a bunch of perks that come with being a top lawmaker, including some that last far beyond their time in Congress. Here are some of the biggest bonuses of being a US senator . A senator's lifelong pension can be up to 80% of their salary. House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., is joined by Rep. John Sarbanes, D-Md., at a news conference to discuss their priorities when they assume the majority in the 116th Congress in January, at the Capitol in Washington. J. Scott Applewhite/AP The Federal Employees Retirement System provides individual pension plans to members of Congress, and the amount depends on their age, salary, and number of years in the Senate. Based on the congressional pay of $174,000 a year for most senators (it hasn't been updated since 2009), an 80% pension provides a lifelong benefit of $139,200. This places members ahead of the majority of Americans, for whom the 2025 median household income was $87,460, according to the Census Bureau . If a member of Congress dies in office, their family usually receives a $174,000 payout. A joint session of Congress meets to count the Electoral College vote from the 2008 presidential election the House Chamber in the U.S. Capitol January 8, 2009 Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images It's called a death gratuity, and it equals one year of the member's salary, paid to an eligible survivor or next of kin. By comparison, eligible survivors of military personnel who die while on active duty or in certain reserve statuses receive $100,000. Every senator gets an allowance from the government to run their offices. Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell (R-KY) (C) poses for photographers during a photo-op prior to a meeting in McConnell's office on Capitol Hill September 30, 2008 in Washington, DC. U.S. Alex Wong/Getty Images The Senators' Official Personnel and Office Expense Account, or SOPOEA, is for official office operations, staff salaries, travel, and other expenses. It comes directly from the US Treasury, aka our taxes. While both senators from the same state are allocated the same amount of money, not all states receive the same amount. It's based on a formula that takes population, distance from DC, and mail allocations into consideration. There is a flat rate, which means every senator will receive at least $677,100, though the 2026 Senate Appropriations Committee report showed that SOPOEA funds actually ranged from $4,296,524 to $6,621,784, with an average of $4,664,423. For 90 days after they leave office, members have access to "franking" mail, or sending official mail to their constituents. A corporate mailroom employee uses gloves while sifting through letters October 15, 2001 in New York City. Mario Tama/Getty Images You might be wondering, what's so special about that? Well, there's one big benefit to franking mail: You don't have to pay postage, which saves the senator a lot of money in the long run. Congressional benefits extend beyond Capitol Hill, including free parking at DC-area airports. Cars of members of the House and Senate in a restricted parking lot near Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport in 1998. Scott J. Ferrell/Congressional Quarterly/Getty Images Members of Congress, as well as Supreme Court justices and diplomats, get free parking at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport and Washington Dulles International Airport. The perk dates back decades, as shown in the photo above of a car owned by a member of the 105th Congress, parked at Reagan in 1998. Senators also receive preferential treatment regarding airline customer service. Aircraft on the tarmac of Reagan airport in DC. Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images A lobbyist told Roll Call in 2011 that most major airlines have dedicated customer service phone lines to help those on Capitol Hill, and that senators can double-book flights. During the TSA strike earlier this year, Delta suspended some of its perks for senators, such as expedited security, though the special desk remained operational. There's also the great haircuts. A view of a closed barber shop in the US Senate at the US Capitol on October 1, 2013 in Washington. The US government is in a forced shutdown after lawmakers failed to pass a budget last night. BRENDAN SMIALOWSKI/AFP/Getty Images The Senate Hair Care Services has been in operation since the early 19th Century, providing a variety of grooming services including haircuts and manicures. Don't forget the private subway, either. Sen. Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa, is seen in the senate subway in the U.S. Capitol on Tuesday, June 3, 2025. Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images The Capitol subway system, which runs beneath the Capitol and connects it to congressional office buildings, has been in place since 1909. It consists of three lines: Two for the Senate and one for the House of Representatives. According to the Architect of the Capitol (AOC), which operates the train line, it's there to "allow for safe and expedient travel" for members to travel from their offices to chambers within the Capitol to vote. Senators get access to fancy gyms that no one's allowed to see inside. Then-Senator Barack Obama shot a basketball on the court in 2008. Mark Wilson/Getty Images Per a 2011 ABC News report, senators paid $40 a month for gyms equipped with "flat-screen TVs, workout machines and a swimming pool." Former members can still enjoy on-site amenities including the House and Senate dining rooms. The hallway in front of the U.S. Senate Chamber is seen one week before the start of the 116th Congress, on December 26, 2018 in Washington, DC. Mark Wilson/Getty Images Once you leave the Senate, that doesn't mean your perks disappear. You still get access to the gym, special parking, materials through the Library of Congress, and dining facilities. They can also still buy from the Senate Stationery Room, which carries many supplies and furnishings. The statue of George Washington, the first US president is seen in the rotunda of the US Capitol on April 16, 2009 in Washington, DC. KAREN BLEIER/AFP via Getty Images It's basically a Senators- only Staples that operates via the Senate Stationery Room Revolving Fund — so the sales go back into the store's b
