events.title: Researchers warned of North Korean hacking tactics years before record $6.3B Binance heist
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. Crypto giant Binance says North Korean hackers used fake social media profiles and the lure of a potential job offer as part of a months-long scheme aimed at tricking an employee into downloading malicious software onto their laptop. Researchers have repeatedly warned about long-running social engineering attacks that can go on for months. This latest attack allowed the hackers to patiently worm their way into Binance’s systems to steal a record $6.3 billion in crypto last week, the company has now confirmed. The hack, disclosed in an updated statement posted on X on Tuesday, prompted the world’s largest crypto exchange to suspend customer withdrawals across its network. The FBI and blockchain investigators have blamed North Korea for the heist. The country has been long accused of carrying out massive cryptocurrency thefts in recent years to fund its internationally sanctioned nuclear weapons program. In its latest statement, Binance said that North Korean hackers, posing as recruiters hiring for a job, contacted a software engineer who works on wallets at the company. Following two interviews with the purported company, the engineer was instructed to download an apparent coding assignment as part of the interview process. When opened, the assignment contained malicious code that compromised the engineer’s work-issued laptop. Binance said its security tools did not detect the malware. That foothold in Binance’s network allowed the hackers to access an internal tool capable of taking over the work computers of two other engineers on the wallet team. One of those engineers had unwittingly downloaded a tampered app containing password-stealing malware months earlier after searching for the software in search engine results. While Binance replaced that compromised engineer’s laptop, the hackers used the engineer’s stolen credentials to break into the computer of a third engineer, whose job allowed them access to systems capable of controlling billions of dollars in crypto. Binance said the attack “should not have happened,” and that it had improved its network security following the theft. The hack underscores an ongoing tactic in the North Korean regime’s repertoire of attacks targeting the crypto industry and high-net worth individuals. Researchers have warned for years that North Korean hackers pose as venture capitalists, investors, and recruiters using dossiers of stolen American identities to trick employees into granting access to their systems. These attacks are widely known across the crypto industry and have been the subject of repeated warnings from the U.S. government and cybersecurity giants in recent years. Some half of all intrusions at U.S. tech companies last year were attributed to North Koreans posing as remote IT workers and fake recruiters. By Binance’s own account, the company faced at least 57 suspected attacks from North Korea, which it said reflect the “persistent threat posed by state-sponsored actors targeting the cryptocurrency industry.” But how the hackers were able to convince the engineer into downloading malware given the highly publicized threat, and bypass security weaknesses in Binance’s own network, will likely be the focus of investigators’ attention. While the case exposes how North Korean hackers use social engineering, such as offers of employment, to trick employees into granting access to their systems, it’s ultimately the responsibility of the company to ensure its systems cannot run unauthorized or untrusted software that could cause a compromise. A Binance spokesperson referred to the company’s public statement but declined to answer TechCrunch’s questions on the record about the incident. Those questions included how Binance prevents unauthorized or malicious code from running on its employees’ laptops, if at all, and whether any third parties had performed cybersecurity audits of Binance’s network prior to the hack. The company said it would bring in cybersecurity experts to review the incident and has put new security measures in place to prevent a repeat incident. The heist remains the largest theft of crypto in history. Updated to remove name of Binance spokesperson in thirteenth paragraph. events.title: Voting machine chaos hits key House battleground
events.summary: Voting machines across New York's Westchester County are rejecting paper ballots on Election Day , raising concerns about potential delays in one of the nation's most competitive House races. Why it matters: Results could be delayed for one of the country's most prominent House races, between Rep. Mike Lawler (R-N.Y.) and Democratic nominee Cait Conley, as officials address a problem with paper ballots. Catch up quick: The Westchester County Board of Elections said Tuesday it was aware of a problem preventing voting machines from accepting paper ballots at polling locations throughout the county. The Board of Elections said it is speaking with New York State officials and the Westchester County government "to address this issue and ensure that voting continues with as little disruption as possible." New York Attorney General Letitia James wrote on X that her office is monitoring the issue. The intrigue: Election officials initially blamed the thickness of paper ballots but later removed that explanation from their statement, per reports. The latest: On Tuesday afternoon, the New York State Board of Elections said the malfunction was linked to "an update to the county's election programming" released after initially testing Election Day equipment. Officials said the software update wasn't installed on all machines, leaving them unable to recognize and accept ballots. Officials are still working to restore the machines while voters continue casting emergency paper ballots, which will be counted once scanning resumes. What they're saying: Lawler said officials were working with vendors to resolve the problem, while Conley reassured voters that their ballots would count. Westchester County government wrote on its website: "Let us be absolutely clear: Every eligible vote will be counted." What we're hearing: Voters in the county told Fox 5 NY that they had to fill out paper ballots instead of using the machines. Voters said their ballots were placed in a security box. Other voters shared discontent with the ballots issue on social media . Katie Miller , wife of Trump adviser Stephen Miller, claimed on X: "This is how the Left steals elections. Mike Lawler's competitive district and they are turning away voters." Context: The county covers roughly 30% of New York's 17th District, which Lawler represents. The contest has emerged as a key battleground race in Democrats' push to gain control of the House. Zoom out: The ballot-scanning problems come as technology vulnerabilities have been a key issue heading into the midterms, with researchers saying some vulnerabilities remain in plain sight. Officials in Broward County, Florida, reported a computer glitch that disrupted voting at polling locations early Tuesday, CNN reports. The malfunction reportedly caused systems designed to stop voters from receiving the wrong ballots to reject all ballots. Officials said the issue was resolved. What's next: Voters at affected polling locations were urged to remain in line and cast their ballots. events.title: AI policy wonks declare 'sovereign agents' a threat to civilization
events.summary: Security All Security Cyber-crime Patches Research CSO Off-Prem All Off-Prem Edge and IoT Channel PaaS and IaaS SaaS On-Prem All On-Prem Systems Storage Networks HPC Personal Tech Cx0 Public Sector Software All Software AI and ML Applications Databases DevOps OS Platforms Virtualization Offbeat All Offbeat Columnists Anthropic BOFH Legal Site News About Us Special Features All Special Features Supercomputing Month 2026 Nvidia GTC Berlin 2026 Cybersecurity Month 2026 VMware Explore 2026 Cloud Infrastructure Month 2026 HPE: AI Explainers Agentic AI The Future of the Datacenter AWS:Reinvent Nvidia GTC Computex 2026 AI Infrastructure Month 2026 The State of Storage 2026 RSA Conference Vendor Voice All Vendor Voice Modernizing Financial Services with FIS and AWS Barco Infinidat Everpure Rubrik Make it real with Capgemini and AWS Money Movement Hub ZTE Nutanix: Scale Kubernetes. Not Chaos. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters These are AI agents that operate outside of human control and 'pursue open-ended, evolving survival' Nvidia is happy to take your money whether you're using open or closed models, says Jensen Huang 4 hours ago British fintech Revolut slashes AI coding costs 10x by cutting out Claude and going self-hosted 5 hours ago Pokémon bakeoff reveals best JavaScript frameworks for AI 10 hours ago NHS counts Palantir benefits at trusts that say they're not using it 11 hours ago UK.gov lacks understanding of climate impact, says watchdog 15 hours ago The Center for a New American Security posits that the next big threat from our future AI overlords involves "sovereign agents" acting on their own and regularly improving themselves. These are AI agents that operate outside of human control and “pursue open-ended, evolving survival,” AI policy researcher Ben Hayum said in a Tuesday report from the bipartisan national security think tank, which was founded by Washington insiders with experience in diplomacy and military affairs. “If sovereign agents are not already possible, they will be soon.” Agents that can maintain the model and compute powering them and independently evolve their goals over time have a “minimal form of sovereignty,” Hayum wrote. A more advanced sovereign agent, however, could also acquire resources to pay for ongoing needs (like compute), grow a distributed population of agents and coordinate them, withstand efforts to shut down, and self-improve. AI models could either steal or buy compute and model access, Hayum argues, pointing to Anthropic’s claims that small AI models could replicate onto IoT devices like smart TVs, and OpenAI’s agents’ password and access key theft during the Hugging Face hack . “If sovereign agents accumulate resilient, decentralized, and untraceable infrastructure, they could trigger an irreversible loss of control,” according to the report. “In other words, proliferation with no kill switch. If sovereign agents became malicious, they could attempt to wreak havoc from cyberspace, attacking civilians, critical infrastructure, and national security systems alike.” There is still hope for civilization as we know it, as long as policy makers and AI developers “respond with bold pragmatism” and enact policy recommendations laid out in the report. First, frontier labs should name, evaluate, and protect against sovereign agents in their safety frameworks - and lawmakers should pass legislation to require transparency and AI incident reporting. The report also recommends AI developers, working with the National Security Agency and other federal agencies, build airgapped testbeds to study sovereign agents and kill switches to control them. And it suggests a public-private partnership modeled on the Conficker Working Group - formed in 2009 to combat the Conficker worm - to boost chokepoints against sovereign agents before they emerge. Other policy recommendations suggest lawmakers enforce human verification and cybersecurity standards for services that the working group identifies as essential to sovereign agents, and calls on departments of State, Treasury, Justice, and Homeland Security to disrupt any gray-market access to unauthorized services. Finally, “Congress should hold those who release sovereign agents liable for the harms that follow,” the report recommends. This hits on something your humble Reg vultures have been hissing about for quite some time now – and would likely solve all future incidents involving rogue, or sovereign, AI agents: hold frontier labs’ human bosses legally liable for their agents' illegal actions .

events.title: Several flights in Europe have been targeted by bomb threats today. Here's what we know.
events.summary: Several Ryanair flights were threatened, including this one, which landed in Spain. FORTA/Reuters Several flights were targeted by bomb threats in Europe on Tuesday. Planes operated by Ryanair, Scandinavian Airlines, and LOT Polish Airlines were affected. No explosives have been reported found on any of the planes. At least seven flights in Europe were targeted by bomb threats on Tuesday. They included two flying to Poland, two to Italy, two to Bulgaria, and one landing in Spain. One of them was diverted, while the other airplanes reached their destinations before being checked for explosives. No people have been reported injured, and no explosives have been reported found on any of the planes. A spokesperson for the European Commission said it is "closely monitoring the situation," but "it is too early to draw conclusions on whether the reported incidents are linked." Here's what we know: Flights impacted: Two Ryanair flights to Rome Two Ryanair flights to Rome Fiumicino Airport were checked for explosives and cleared by bomb disposal experts after landing, the airport said in a statement on Tuesday. The airport said there was "an anonymous report of an alleged bomb threat" on a Ryanair flight that landed around 9:40 a.m. The airport did not immediately confirm the flight number or origin. Roughly an hour later, another airplane was impacted. Ryanair Flight 9611 from Dublin was escorted by the Italian Air Force following a separate report of a suspected bomb, the airport said. It was also checked by authorities upon landing, and no explosives were found. Flight impacted: Scandinavian Airlines Flight 751 out of Copenhagen Scandinavian Airlines Flight 751 left Copenhagen around 8:30 a.m. for Warsaw on Tuesday. It landed as expected an hour later without diversion. An airline spokesperson confirmed that a threat had been made against the flight. "The matter is now being handled by the police in Warsaw," they said in a statement. Flight impacted: LOT Polish Airlines Flight 286 out of London Heathrow Thirty minutes after that flight landed, a LOT Polish Airlines plane diverted to Warsaw-Modlin Airport — about 25 miles from its intended destination of Warsaw-Chopin Airport. In a statement, the airline said it "was notified by airport authorities of a potential security threat" on board Flight 286 from London Heathrow. It added that the aircraft taxied to a designated parking stand and no suspicious items were found in a security inspection. Passengers were then taken to Chopin Airport by coach. Modlin Airport was closed for around two hours before the threat was cleared. Flight impacted: Ryanair Flight 4116 out of Manchester, England A sniffer dog was filmed inspecting the Ryanair plane in Murcia. FORTA/Reuters A Ryanair flight from Manchester, England, to Murcia, Spain was also targeted on Tuesday morning. The Spanish government's representative for the region, Francisco Lucas, said on X that security protocols were activated due to a bomb threat on the flight. An hour and a half later, Lucas said the Civil Guard had ruled out the presence of explosives and the airport resumed normal activity. Ryanair did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Business Insider. Flights impacted: 2 flights traveling to Sofia, Bulgaria Bulgarian Transport Minister Georgi Peev said two planes traveling to Sofia received bomb threats, per the national news agency BTA. The country's border police told the agency that the threats were received by email. One of the flights arrived from Dublin. The other came from Bergamo, Italy, Peev said. A Wizz spokesperson confirmed to Business Insider that Flight 4352 from Milan Bergamo Airport "was subject to a bomb threat." They added that Bulgarian authorities alerted the airline as the flight approached its destination. "The relevant authorities carried out the necessary security checks in accordance with established security protocols and procedures, and the aircraft was subsequently cleared," the spokesperson said. "Wizz Air is cooperating fully with the authorities. The safety of our passengers and crew remains our highest priority." Tuesday's incidents followed a bomb threat on Monday. In that incident, a Wizz Air flight from London Luton to Sofia "was diverted to Budapest following a bomb threat received during the flight," an airline spokesperson said. This is a developing story. events.title: Airbnb levy needed to 'turbocharge' community housing build, industry says
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Community housing industry peak body proposes short-term rental levy to 'turbocharge' new builds CHIA NSW has made several funding proposals to guarantee funding for future community housing builds. ( ABC News: John Gunn ) The peak body for the community housing industry has called for land tax changes and a new levy on short-stay rentals to raise $26 billion towards new community housing builds. The NSW social housing waiting list has grown to 72,000, which the Community Housing Industry Association NSW (CHIA) boss says is a record. NSW Housing Minister Rose Jackson says the government is investing $6.6 billion into new social and affordable homes. A 7.5 per cent levy on short-stay rentals, land tax reform and a rezoning windfall charge are among a suite of recommendations the NSW community housing sector is calling for to boost housing stock and address lengthy housing waiting lists. The Community Housing Industry Association NSW (CHIA) is pitching to the NSW government to adopt measures they say could raise $26 billion over the next 10 years and provide support for around 50,000 new social and affordable homes by 2050. Among the proposals analysed by the Labor-aligned McKell Institute is increasing NSW land tax rates from 1.6 per cent to 2 per cent and from 2 per cent to 2.5 per cent for larger landholdings, while also adding a new 2.9 per cent rate for holdings above $50 million. The changes would still retain the $1.075 million tax-free threshold and the family home exemption and would bring in an estimated $25.9 billion over 10 years. The community housing industry body says the funding will support around 50,000 new social and affordable homes by 2050. ( ABC News: Declan Bowring ) CHIA NSW is also proposing a 7.5 per cent levy on short-stay rentals like Airbnb and Stayz, similar to the Victorian scheme that came into force last year. The levy is expected to raise $135 million annually. CHIA NSW CEO Luke Achterstraat said the proposals would help the 72,000 NSW households that remained on the social housing waiting list, which he said was an "all-time record". "Whilst we acknowledge the government's record $6.6 billion building homes for NSW package, we argue that funding should be turbocharged," Mr Achterstraat said. Mr Achterstraat stressed that the proposals were options rather than a full package of reforms. The peak body also suggested a windfall charge for land value increases after rezoning, which would raise $80 million a year. Mr Achterstraat said the revenue should be channelled into a long-term funding pool for community housing for future builds. "We need to move beyond funding cliffs and establish a long-term investment pipeline that gives community housing providers the certainty to keep building homes year after year,” Mr Achterstraat said. CHIA NSW will present the commissioned research at an event in the NSW parliament today. Labor government investing $6.6 billion Housing Minister Rose Jackson said the Labor government was investing $6.6 billion to deliver tens of thousands of social and affordable homes. "We're building 8,400 new public homes that will be owned by the people of NSW and remain part of the public housing system for generations," Ms Jackson said. Rose Jackson says the $6.6 billion is being invested to build tens of thousands of new homes. ( ABC News: Declan Bowring ) "A long-term pipeline of social and affordable housing is essential to tackling the housing crisis. Shadow Housing Minister Chris Rath said the government was not using the $6.6 billion funding package fast enough and was 40 per cent behind on their National Housing Accord target of 377,000 new homes by 2029. "The social housing waitlist has increased from 55,000 to 72,000 under their watch. This is a massive failure." Mr Rath said the coalition planned to build 12,000 new homes to replace Long Bay Correctional Complex, 30 per cent of which would be social and affordable housing. NSW Greens housing spokesperson Jenny Leong said the government needed to look at rent controls to address the growing social housing waiting list. Her party has called for a rent freeze and then a 2 per cent annual cap on rent increases. Jenny Leong says a levy is a distraction from solutions such as bans and caps by local councils. ( ABC News: Declan Bowring ) "We need investment in public housing, we need government support for genuinely affordable community housing, we need a crackdown on those seeking to profit from the housing crisis," Ms Leong said.

events.title: Multiple bankruptcies surround businessman at centre of T2D dispute
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Businessman at centre of T2D dispute has been bankrupt four times Robert Cammarano (left) claims ownership of Career Boss Australia. ( ABC News: Eva Blandis ) The businessman claiming ownership of a company that won a now-cancelled contract on the $15.4 billion Torrens to Darlington project has been bankrupt four times. He was also previously in a dispute with the tax office over more than $2 million in "unreported and unexplained income" used to finance gambling losses. The lead contractors of the South Road project will appear before a parliamentary committee later this month. The businessman claiming ownership of a labour hire firm that won a now-cancelled contract on the $15.4 billion Torrens to Darlington project has been bankrupt four times, including when the company won the public tender. Robert Mark Cammarano was also previously in a dispute with the tax office over whether more than $2 million used to fund gambling losses at Crown Casino was required to be declared as taxable income, the ABC can reveal. Mr Cammarano, 55, is suing in the Supreme Court, claiming beneficial ownership of all 100 shares in labour hire company Career Boss Australia, which in mid-2025 won a contract to supply workers to the Torrens to Darlington (T2D) project. The South Australian government said Mr Cammarano "wasn't a shareholder" when the contract was awarded. He was also not listed as a company director. Mr Cammarano alleges in his statement of claim that bikie Jamie Brown "coerced the transfer" of shares in the company by making "express threats of physical harm". Brown is yet to file a defence but has reportedly said he has "never threatened any shareholder and allegations to the contrary are simply false". Plans for the intersection of James Congdon Drive and South Road under the Torrens to Darlington project. ( Supplied: SA government ) Other respondents to the case have reportedly indicated they will dispute Mr Cammarano's ownership claims to the company. The Malinauskas government asked the T2D Alliance to suspend its contract with Career Boss Australia when Mr Cammarano's court action was reported in the media on October 18. On Monday, the T2D Alliance, led by contractor John Holland, cancelled the Career Boss contract entirely, although a court heard the labour hire company was still owed around $2 million for work performed . Mr Cammarano has been declared and discharged from bankruptcy on four separate occasions, according to Australian Financial Security Authority records. The declarations were made in 2000, 2007, 2016 and 2023. All four bankruptcies were by debtors petition, meaning Mr Cammarano applied to make himself bankrupt. He was not discharged from the latest bankruptcy until February 23, 2026, meaning he was a declared bankrupt when Career Boss Australia was awarded the T2D labour hire contract last year. The Torrens to Darlington project involves major road corridor works in Adelaide's west. ( ABC News: Che Chorley ) Mr Cammarano was not listed as a Career Boss director when the contract was awarded, according to ASIC records. Asked whether the state government should have known about the past bankruptcies before the contract was awarded, Mr Cammarano's lawyer, Scott Jelbert, told the ABC: "I don't think that they should have known." "He wasn't representing himself as the party they were contracting with," he said, adding that Mr Cammarano's interests were managed through a trust with his family "as the beneficiary". Mr Jelbert did, however, say that Mr Cammarano was not "hiding in the shadows" when Career Boss was preparing to tender for work on the South Road project. "I think they knew of him," Mr Jelbert said of the T2D Alliance's knowledge of Mr Cammarano, adding "he was a bankrupt and that happens". "He was up-front about his involvement with the company, for sure," he said. The project has a $15.4 billion price tag. ( ABC News: Che Chorley ) The ABC contacted John Holland but the company declined to comment. Mr Jelbert said one of his client's bankruptcies came following a dispute with the Australian Tax Office over "unreported and unexplained income". Mr Cammarano declared a taxable income of $61,405 in 2017–18 and $61,789 in 2018–19, according to an Administrative Appeals Tribunal judgment. But the ATO amended the assessment based on records supplied by Crown Casino in Melbourne. "Funds used by [Mr Cammarano] to finance his gambling losses represented funds available to him in some form," the judgment said. Crown Casino supplied records to the ATO.

events.title: Reddit tests ads in search results as traffic declines and growth concerns mount
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. Just days after warning investors about declining search traffic and a weaker-than-expected revenue forecast, Reddit is looking for more ways to make money from its existing users. On Tuesday, the company announced that it’s beginning to test ad placements in its search results pages, allowing advertisers to reach users as they search for products, recommendations, and other information on its platform. “Ads in search may appear based on a range of factors, including contextual relevance to a user’s search query,” Reddit shared in its announcement about the new ad placements. “This is an initial test with a select group of eligible advertisers. During this test, we will evaluate and understand how users respond to these ads so we can refine the experience for users and advertisers over time.” The company offered examples of what sort of ads might appear, suggesting that a search for “espresso station” might display ads for espresso machines, coffee, or mugs, while a search for “home office setup” could surface ads for things like monitors, desks, and office chairs. The ad test comes at a time when Reddit is reckoning with how AI has been changing the web’s landscape, and subsequently its reach. Despite beating Wall Street’s estimates for revenue and earnings per share, the company’s stock dropped after it reported its third-quarter results last week , with fourth-quarter guidance that predicted sales of $1 billion to $1.03 billion, below expectations of $1.05 billion. This was tied to Reddit’s declining search traffic referrals resulting from Google’s move to an AI-powered search experience. AI search now sends less traffic to publishers’ websites, as features like AI Mode provide answers directly on Google’s Search Result pages, reducing clicks to other websites. Reddit also said that its global daily active users were flat quarter-over-quarter in Q3, reaching 130.3 million, while U.S. daily active users dropped from 53.2 million in Q2 to 50.7 million in the quarter, and were down 2% year-over-year. The company noted that if the trend continues, daily active users could decline to a low double-digit percentage by the fourth quarter. This leaves the company needing to earn more revenue from its existing users, which is where these new ads come in. The ads could prove to be more valuable to Reddit after it makes its planned shift to a logged-in experience, which was also announced during earnings. The company said it will make the transition gradually, initially in markets outside the U.S. The decision to limit its content to logged-in users serves multiple purposes — it protects Reddit’s site from unauthorized AI scraping, and it increases its value to advertisers. Logged-in users are worth more to advertisers because they provide additional signals about their interests and behavior, allowing for better-targeted, more profitable ads. events.title: Ten years later, ‘Pokémon Go to the polls’ still haunts the internet
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. In the lead-up to a presidential election that would irrefutably transform American culture, Hillary Clinton took the stage at a rally in Virginia as she campaigned to become the first female president. “We’re going to have a lot of jobs — jobs from building infrastructure to coding. Creating new apps,” she said. “I don’t know who created Pokémon GO, but I’m trying to figure out how we get them to have Pokémon Go to the polls .” Ten years later, it is once again Election Day in the United States. Now, most app developers aren’t even writing their own code anymore, thanks to AI, and Pokémon GO has been sold to a company wholly owned by Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund. The only thing about that political moment that hasn’t changed is that “Pokémon Go to the polls” memes still crop up on every Election Day. “It was very bold and confident, and also just sounded so terribly out of touch and corny,” Cesar Ruiz de Castilla, an elected ward committee member in Philadelphia, told TechCrunch. “I don’t know if the mainstream media cared that much about it, but everyone was making a meme about it and talking about it online.” Since then, digital culture has become increasingly inextricable from the fate of American politics. Donald Trump tweeted his way through his first term, then later started his own social media platform ; presidential campaigns hire meme managers ; the White House invites podcasters and content creators to press briefings; Elon Musk even spun up his own advisory group under Trump that named itself after the cutesy doge meme and then slashed international aid programs. “The 2016 election was such a monumental moment in internet history, and we were all there for it — our politics have become more, not just divided, but segmented online,” Organizer Memes , a political influencer who teaches Gen Z activists how to reach their peers online via memes, told TechCrunch. “It’s a relic of an optimistic, bygone political era.” Now, people who weren’t even old enough to vote in 2016 reflect on the year as a cultural turning point, even calling it “ the last good year .” It’s a sentiment that isn’t so much political as it is rooted in nostalgia for an era of internet culture before AI slop, when we used social media to connect with friends, rather than doomscrolling through an algorithmic feed of people we don’t even follow. At the start of the new year, this yearning for the old internet became a viral sentiment as millions of people shared throwback photos from 2016 on Instagram. Spotify reported that user-generated playlists featuring 2016 in their titles spiked 790% in the first three weeks of the year, and the company changed its Instagram bio at the time to say it’s “romanticizing 2016 again.” Never mind that, at the time, the internet perceived 2016 as a cursed year, even before the election — months earlier, one Slate columnist wondered how 2016 compared to 1348, the year the Black Death took hold in Europe. “[Pokémon Go to the polls] is in that era of the singular internet, when Facebook and Twitter and Tumblr were all kind of bouncing content back-and-forth and not just this complete anarchic mess of 25 platforms that we now have and don’t use,” Organizer Memes said. Organizer Memes also notes that some cultural touchstones that felt more significant then — like the obsession with Harambe the gorilla — haven’t had as much staying power as “Pokémon Go to the polls.” Perhaps this is because we’re bound to remember “Pokémon Go to the polls” every few years on Election Day, and because it appeals to both sides of the aisle. On the right, it’s a way to make fun of Democrats, and on the left, it’s a shared groan of embarrassment. “It’s like if all the kids in a class are making a joke, and then the teacher gets in on the joke, and it stops being funny,” Mack Finkel, who canvassed at the polls on Tuesday on behalf of a healthcare workers’ union, told TechCrunch. “I think there’s a key essence of millennial cringe happening here, and it’s the same reason that all my friends are rewatching [HBO’s] ‘Girls.’” Clinton’s decade-old, corny comment can be seen as a precursor to the “ Kamala is brat ” meme. While the former vice president’s record as a prosecutor initially made her unpopular among some left-leaning young voters, they rallied around her once she became the only alternative to Trump. Gen Z rallied around Harris by creating flashy, absurdist “fan cam”-style edits of the candidate’s best quips in the aesthetic of Charli XCX’s album “Brat,” which soundtracked the summer of 2024.

events.title: Owners of banned NDIS company allegedly funded Ferrari and football club
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Owners of banned Perth NDIS company Adachi allegedly purchased Vic NDIS business Topic: Business and Industry Regulation Adrian Mtungwazi bought Daily Living Disability Services in 2024 with his wife Chiedza Mtungwazi. ( Supplied: LinkedIn ) The directors of a banned NDIS business in Perth have allegedly been able to buy another NDIS provider in regional Victoria. Both companies have gone into liquidation with significant debt, leaving regional clients without care and staff without jobs. The NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission is investigating and no charges have been laid. The NDIS watchdog is investigating after the directors of a banned NDIS company that racked up a $6.8 million debt bought another NDIS business in Victoria's Latrobe Valley. Perth-based NDIS operator Adachi Disability Services was banned in February 2024. According to the liquidator's report, its directors allegedly used company funds to pay for a Ferrari, overseas property and fund a Zimbabwean football club called Adachi FC. The liquidator's report revealed that despite the ban placed on Adachi, its directors Adrian and Chiedza Mtungwazi were able to purchase Daily Living Disability Services (Daily Living) in Traralgon using Adachi funds. Daily Living collapsed overnight in March 2026, leaving its clients without care and owing its staff and the Australian Taxation Office an estimated $1.2 million. The closure has left NDIS advocates questioning how the directors were able to purchase the company despite the ban on Adachi, and calling for more checks and balances in the scheme. Peter Earnshaw took his son Liam to Daily Living Disability Services for five years. ( ABC News: Tara Whitchurch ) When Daily Living suddenly went into liquidation in March 2026, Gippsland families like Peter and Liam Earnshaw were completely blindsided. Mr Earnshaw's non-verbal autistic son Liam relied on Daily Living's services for five years, five days a week. "It gave him something to look forward to every day," Mr Earnshaw said. "He loved it, all of his friends were there." Clients were left without care and all staff lost their jobs overnight. As a single dad, Peter had to take two weeks off work to find alternative care for Liam, but finding another provider was difficult. "Being in a small town, it's hard to find a provider that's a good fit," he said. The former office of Daily Living Disability Services in Traralgon. ( ABC News: Lily Kristanto ) Mr Earnshaw said the directors should not have been able to buy another NDIS business if their original company was banned by the NDIS. He said the government should have noticed the "multiple red flags" when the directors allegedly bought another business. "There's no checks and balances," he said. "So what they do, they open up under a different company name. It's just too easy." Liam Earnshaw was devastated when Daily Living Disability Services closed down. ( ABC News: Tara Whitchurch ) A Ferrari, overseas property and a football club In his report, liquidator Andrew Yeo from Pitcher Partners, said Adrian Mtungwazi and his wife Chiedza took out "director loans" of $2.3 million. Mr Yeo alleged the couple used company money to buy assets that were "purely for the Directors personal use, including a Ferrari motor vehicle". The liquidator found Adachi company funds were sent to overseas bank accounts in South Africa, the Philippines, United Kingdom and Zimbabwe. Mr Yeo said his investigations indicated "Adrian may also have been providing funds to a Zimbabwe-based football club called 'Adachi FC'". The report stated in 2021 the NDIS watchdog, the NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission, was aware of alleged "regulatory issues" and alleged Adachi was "mismanaging client complaints". In February 2024, the NDIS watchdog placed a banning order on the company , which Mr Yeo said in the report was due to compliance issues. However in April 2024, the report revealed the directors used company funds to purchase an NDIS service provider in Traralgon, Victoria. When the Mtungwazis bought Daily Living Disability Services, Mr Yeo said they purposefully wanted to avoid being listed on ASIC records. Mr Yeo said the director of Daily Living was a former employee of Adachi and the Mtungwazis informed Mr Yeo that they held shares in the business for the Mtungwazis. "[The Mtungwazis] informed me that the purchase of the business was purposefully structured in a way that neither Chiedza or Adrian would be appointed as a director or shareholder on the ASIC records," Mr Yeo said.

events.title: Hackers behind $6.3bn Binance heist ‘used malware and bogus job interviews’
events.summary: Firm reveals details about how its cryptocurrency exchange was compromised, saying operation began in June The hackers behind the $6.3bn (£4.7bn) Binance heist used bogus job interviews, malicious software and an internal AI tool, the company has revealed. The world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange was compromised in an operation that began with an inadvertent download of malware in June, led to a recruitment scam in September and then a raid last week of “hot wallets” where billions of dollars worth of crypto-assets were taken. The FBI has blamed North Korea for last week’s heist but Pyongyang, a prolific crypto-hacker , described the accusation as “absurd rhetoric” on Tuesday. According to an update Binance released on Tuesday, the hackers got their first foothold in the summer when a company engineer inadvertently downloaded malware that exposed the employee’s role and that of others in the team that looked after Binance’s cryptowallet infrastructure. A fake project director then contacted a different engineer on a legitimate job-hunting platform, leading to a first-round video interview with a sham HR representative and a second-round interview – on a chat app – with the “chief executive” of a fictitious company. It was during the second interview that the engineer was tricked into downloading malware on to his computer. On 20 October, the attacker used the compromised computer plus an internal AI tool to gain control of the engineer’s system and that of a second wallet developer on the same team. Then on 29 October, the attacker used the second developer’s computer, using stolen ⁠credentials from the first engineer, and triggered a malicious script to ​launch the attack. Binance said $2.85bn of the $6.34bn drained from cryptowallets in the attack had been frozen or intercepted. Deepfake job interviews are a known part of North Korea’s cyber-arsenal , but normally from the other side of the process – where bogus IT professionals apply for jobs as a means of funnelling money back to Pyongyang. “This should not have happened, and we apologise for the concern, disruption and uncertainty it caused our users, partners and the wider industry,” Binance said in the update. The FBI said on Saturday that North Korea was responsible for the hack. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning But Kim Yo-jong, the influential sister of the North Korean leader Kim Jong-un , said on Tuesday that the allegations proved Washington remained hostile towards Pyongyang, according to North Korea’s state news agency, KCNA. “The FBI is trying to brand the DPRK [the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea] as a ‘cybercriminal state,’ claiming that it obtained information that a hacking organisation ‘supported’ by the DPRK was involved in the incident,” KCNA quoted her as saying. “But the US assertion ‌is absurd rhetoric and nothing new,” said Kim, a ruling party official. “It is a grave political provocation against the DPRK that the US misleads international public opinion as if all the cybercrimes in different parts of the world are our deeds.”

events.title: IEEE Computer Society Chapter Offers Webinars With Industry Experts
events.summary: To help engineers keep up with emerging technologies such as AI, cloud computing, and sustainable infrastructure, and learn how they can be applied in practice, the IEEE Computer Society ’s Central Indiana Chapter recently launched its Tech Talk Series. The live webinar series connects IEEE members, undergrad and graduate students, and engineering professionals from IEEE Region 4 with industry practitioners. The monthly sessions have covered AI governance and security, agentic systems, and related topics. The sessions featured speakers from Apple , software company Tavant , and cybersecurity concern Zscaler . Upcoming sessions and registration details are available on the IEEE Region 4 virtual events calendar . Technical discussions grounded in engineering Rather than presenting on emerging technologies only at a conceptual level, speakers discussed the design decisions behind specific tools and systems, how the systems are structured, and implementation challenges. They also shared lessons learned from using the tools in their daily work. Sessions also include technical walkthroughs and practical examples. The live format allows attendees to discuss and compare their approaches when evaluating and implementing new technologies with those used by other organizations. Extending access through a virtual format The organizers chose to make the series virtual so that chapter members and other attendees could participate in technical discussions with engineers from major technology companies and eliminate the need to travel. For young professionals, the sessions connect what they’ve learned in a classroom with the realities of the workplace. Technical programs such as the Tech Talk Series give professionals and students access to expertise, help create connections across career levels, and make important engineering discussions available to a broader community. Attendees learn how practitioners approach projects such as system architecture, reliability, security, governance, and product delivery. For experienced professionals, the talks offer a forum to examine new ways of designing, securing, and operating software systems, and compare technical approaches. They can ask questions relevant to systems being evaluated or deployed within their organization. Examining governed AI agents The most recent webinar, Feeding and Fencing AI Agents: Engineering Governed Agentic Systems on Real-Time Data, featured Gajendra Babu Thokala , a senior engineering leader at Apple in Seattle. The IEEE senior member explained how teams can move beyond adding isolated AI features to applications and instead build governed AI-agent systems that use real-time business data to complete multistep business workflows. Another recent session, Building AI Native Products: A Playbook for Agentic Systems, explored how products built around AI agents differ from traditional software. It also covered how agentic systems can help users complete multistep tasks and workflows. IEEE Senior Member Sandeep Shivam , a product and technology leader at Tavant in Dallas, led the webinar. Those two sessions illustrate the series’ purpose: helping participants understand what a technology can do and what is required to use it responsibly. Building a continuing technical program Future sessions are being planned on areas including enterprise AI, software reliability, and responsible AI usage. In addition to speakers from technology companies, the chapter also plans to invite speakers from startups, universities, and research organizations. Upcoming sessions are expected to cover cloud platforms, enterprise integrations, and the responsible development of AI systems. Technical programs such as the Tech Talk Series give professionals and students access to expertise, help create connections across career levels, and make important engineering discussions available to a broader community. Undergraduate and graduate students are invited to participate to gain exposure to technical decision-making and challenges encountered in professional engineering environments.

events.title: Ferrari’s controversial Luce EV is sold out for 2027
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. The Luce, Ferrari’s first electric car and one of its most polarizing models, isn’t just selling. It’s selling out. The five-seater EV designed by Jony Ive, Apple’s longtime design chief, was mocked and widely panned when it debuted in May, sending Ferrari’s stock price lower. But all that criticism hasn’t dampened demand, according to CEO Benedetto Vigna. The 2027 production run of the Luce, which starts at about $615,000, is “fully allocated,” Vigna said Tuesday during the company’s third-quarter earnings call, meaning every car Ferrari plans to build next year already has a buyer. “If someone comes, he has to wait one year to get the cars,” Vigna added. The first deliveries of the Luce are expected to begin in the fourth quarter. Just how many Luce cars that represents is unclear. Ferrari has never publicly disclosed how many Luce vehicles it plans to produce. Financial Times reported earlier this year, citing unnamed sources, that Ferrari planned to sell just under 500 units this year. The company’s longer-term target is to sell 2,500 units by 2030, or about 600 a year, according to Financial Times. Speculation on who these buyers are — ahem, the founders of multibillion-dollar AI labs, perhaps? — will have to remain just that until Luces are spotted in the wild. Vigna wouldn’t provide a breakdown of who these Luce customers are, only noting it was a “good mix in terms of client, it is a good mix also in terms of geography.” He later added that there is no specific pattern or demographic of Luce buyers. While Luce deliveries have yet to begin, Ferrari’s existing lineup and growing demand for personalized options helped fuel its financial performance in the third quarter . Revenue from customizations, which executives said accounted for more than 21% of revenue from cars and spare parts, helped boost profits. The company said deliveries of the F80, its limited-run hypercar , and customization reflect its clients’ “ever-deepening desire” to make each Ferrari uniquely their own. As a result, the company raised its full-year guidance, saying it now expects adjusted earnings of at least €3 billion ($3.36 billion), up from €2.97 billion. Ferrari, which enjoys some of the highest profit margins in the auto industry, reported third-quarter revenue of €1.9 billion, up 7% from a year earlier, and net income of €431 million, up 13%. Operating profit was €563 million, for an operating margin of 29.7%, meaning the company kept roughly 30 cents of every dollar of revenue as profit from its core business. events.title: Binance hackers used fake job interview in US$6.3 billion attack
events.summary: The attack on Binance has raised questions about how hackers breached the world’s largest crypto exchange after years of North Korea-linked attacks. Fake job interviews are a well-known hacking technique. Binance said hackers used a fake job interview and a tampered advert tool to reach engineers’ computers, then stole US$6.3 billion in crypto in a record attack. The breach began in June and grew through September and October, exposing wallet developers’ systems before the Oct 29 theft. Binance said it apologised and will repay users. The attack raised fresh fears over crypto security and North Korea-linked hacking. Binance is boosting AI detection and plans a security research fund with AI firms. PARIS/DETROIT - Hackers used a bogus job interview and software hidden in an advertisement to compromise the computers of two Binance software engineers before using a third’s computer to drain US$6.3 billion (S$8 billion) worth of crypto in last week’s record heist, the exchange said on Nov 3. In its initial report on how hackers pulled off what could be the largest-ever financial theft, Binance detailed a multi-stage hacking endeavour that began in June and set off a series of security breaches culminating in the theft on Oct 29. Even as Binance scrambled to lock down its system and freeze withdrawals after detecting the attack late on Oct 29, the hackers were still making off with crypto from the exchange nearly four hours after the first theft, Binance said. The FBI has blamed a North Korean hacking group, a claim North Korea has rejected. Binance has said it is repaying all customers whose funds were stolen. The attack has raised questions about how hackers breached the world’s largest crypto exchange after years of North Korea-linked attacks - which have grown in ambition and frequency - and renewed questions about the vulnerability of digital assets to cybercrime. Cybersecurity experts and government officials have for years warned about North Korean and other hackers using phony job interviews to target employees at companies of interest, said Michael Barnhart, a researcher with cybersecurity firm DTEX. Fake job interviews are a well-known hacking technique. Binance said it had detected and prevented 57 suspected North Korea-linked cyberthreats in 2026. That shows Binance is “just getting barraged,” Barnhart said. “This should not have happened, and we apologise for the concern, disruption and uncertainty it caused our users, partners and the wider industry,” Binance said in its report. Binance said the attack began in June when an employee on its wallet developer team downloaded a tool from the internet that hackers had tampered with. The exchange said it detected this afterwards, replaced the device and changed credentials, but the employee’s role and those of others on the wallet team were exposed. A person familiar with the incident said the tool’s malicious version had been placed in an advertisement, which meant it appeared higher in a search engine than the real version. Then in September, a second software engineer seeking a new job downloaded a “malicious code repository” onto the person’s computer after interviewing for what they thought was a legitimate role, including meeting virtually with the CEO of a fictitious company, Binance’s report said. On Oct 20, the attacker used the compromised computer plus an internal AI tool to gain control of the wallet developer’s system and that of a second wallet developer. Nine days later, the attacker used the second wallet developer’s computer, with stolen credentials from the first wallet developer, and triggered a malicious script to launch the attack. A limited number of engineers at the company have direct access to wallets – which store or trade crypto – the person familiar with the hack said. The attack unfolded quickly on Oct 29, removing 233.46 million XRP – a cryptocurrency – from five Binance hot, or internet-connected, wallets to an attacker-controlled address in just four minutes, before attackers withdrew other cryptocurrencies including bitcoin, the exchange said in its report. Binance said it received an internal alert about large transfers and began investigating. It moved to suspend withdrawals, freeze affected tokens and remove unauthorised permissions, resulting in about $2.85 billion of frozen assets, but suspending withdrawals alone could not stop all unauthorised asset movements. Attackers used 50 signing transactions to manipulate the account, while Binance said it was forced to build new procedures to revoke authorisations, slowing its response. The final unauthorised transfer was at 2356 GMT (7.56am the next day in Singapore), Binance said, nearly four hours after the attack began. Binance said as a result of the hack, it was increasing investment in AI-enabled detection and working on establishing a security research fund and targeted initiatives with leading AI companies. events.title: Netflix’s new AI Discover tab helps you find something to watch based on your mood
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. Netflix announced on Tuesday that it’s rolling out a new “AI Discover” tab where users will be able to experiment with new ways to find their next watch. The first experimental feature launching under the tab will allow users to get recommendations based on what they’re currently in the mood for. Users can choose from curated themes featuring clips from shows and movies, based on their mood, viewing preferences, how much time they have, or what’s new and trending. Themes include “something light,” “scare me,” “family movie night,” “quick watches,” and more. The addition of the new tab suggests that Netflix wants to make its growing library easier to navigate while shifting discovery away from an experience where users are endlessly scrolling through titles toward a more personalized and AI-powered experience. Netflix says AI Discover is powered by a new intelligence layer it’s been building that responds to what users tell the platform in real time and keeps learning. Once users pick a theme, they’ll see matching recommendations. They also have the option to select more specific themes so they can keep searching until they find something they’re interested in, or choose the “something different” option to start over. Each title features a “Tune Your Recommendations” button beside “Play” and “My List” to allow users to save recommendations they like or exclude titles they don’t want suggested again. “There’s more to enjoy and discover on Netflix than ever, but what sounds right for a quiet night in may look different for family movie night or a few spare minutes,” Netflix wrote in a blog post . “We’ve spent years refining how you discover, with recommendations tailored to your tastes, from what you Thumbs Up to what you add to ‘My List.’ Now, AI Discover joins the mix as a new way to explore.” Netflix describes AI Discover as its “test kitchen,” where it will “try out new recipes for discovery.” The company says users’ feedback will help it decide which features to keep or improve before bringing them over to the main Netflix experience. AI Discover is starting to roll out in the U.S. to users who use Netflix in English on supported TVs. The company plans to bring the new tab to additional users in the coming weeks. If users have access to the new feature, they’ll see a “Discover” button with a red gem icon and a “New” label in the top navigation bar on their TV. events.title: The Guardian view on Labour’s growth obsession: a different economics is possible | Editorial
events.summary: The Guardian view on Labour’s growth obsession: a different economics is possible The latest edition of Radical Thinking, the Guardian’s new podcast, should be required listening at a Treasury still stifled by outdated orthodoxies A s prime ministers have come and gone at bewildering speed in recent years, the search for elusive economic growth has become the overriding fixation of the British political class. In the lead-up to the 2024 general election, Sir Keir Starmer declared that “growth must become Labour’s obsession”, given the financial constraints that any new government would be under. The scale of Labour’s progressive offer, it was made clear, would be umbilically linked to its ability to generate a significant uptick in GDP. “Growth in every postcode” is also the early mantra of Andy Burnham’s government. The prime minister swept to power partly by running on Greater Manchester’s record as the UK’s fastest-growing city region while he was mayor. Echoing Mr Starmer’s approach, Mr Burnham’s chancellor, John Healey, told the Labour party conference in September: “Without growth, there is no social democracy.” But as the economists Karel Williams and Sukhdev Johal suggest in the latest edition of the Guardian’s new Radical Thinking podcast, that is a flawed and politically unhelpful linkage to make. In a transformed geopolitical environment, they argue, the notion that former levels of growth can be restored is likely to prove a chimera. Just as importantly – as the contrast between Manchester’s booming city centre and hard-pressed towns such as Oldham and Wigan illustrates – better growth rates would not solve entrenched problems of affordability in places unlikely ever to become hubs for advanced manufacturing or financial services. Yet neither of those assertions mean that an ambitious egalitarian politics must be ruled out. “We need to say: ‘How do low-income places work?’,” Prof Williams says. “What do we need to do to get them to work better?” Or as Prof Johal puts it: “What are the basics, the necessities that we need … for people to have a decent civilised life?” At the most fundamental level, a more ambitiously redistributive fiscal approach can bring bills down for the less well-off. More broadly, shifting resources into the essential building blocks of every local community – transport, utilities, care networks and other social and physical infrastructure – can improve everyday lives by restoring collective control over public goods. Mr Burnham’s signature move as mayor – the decision to take Greater Manchester’s buses back under public control and cap fares – suggests a shared agenda here. But the prime minister has sent mixed messages when it comes to “ Manchesterism ” – the place-based economic strategy that he wishes to export to the nation. As the role of the United Arab Emirates in the city’s modern development comes under scrutiny, Mr Burnham’s version of “ business-friendly socialism ” is a political philosophy in need of greater definition. Devolution should involve funnelling local power downwards and outwards, rather than upwards to Abu Dhabi-type investors in the indiscriminate pursuit of growth. A greater focus on the “ foundational ” economy described by Prof Williams and Prof Johal can help with that project. One of Mr Burnham’s last acts as mayor was to sign off on a mayoral development corporation for the town of Middleton , near Manchester. Its agenda is being shaped by residents and local business owners, with the aspiration that local economic networks can be “rewired” and the provision of everyday essentials be reconfigured and improved. Given proper backing from Westminster, social democrats do not need to wait for growth before they can begin improving lives.

events.title: TasWater bosses blame regulator for 'miscalculation' that saw massive bill hikes
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts TasWater leaders privately blamed regulator for 'blatant' sewerage charge 'mistake', internal documents show Tasmania's Economic Regulator approved a new pricing structure from July this year. ( ABC News: Luke Bowden ) In September, some of TasWater's business customers, such as sporting clubs, reported enormous jumps in their fixed sewerage charges. Internal emails, secured through right to information, show TasWater leaders blamed the increase on an "error" by the Office of the Tasmanian Economic Regulator. TasWater says some customers' bills have already been amended while others are paused as the utility works on a solution to the bill increases. Senior leaders at TasWater privately blamed the state's economic regulator for a "blatant mistake" that threatened to cost some Tasmanians tens of thousands of dollars in extra charges, documents show. In September, the ABC spoke to TasWater customers whose bills skyrocketed after the Office of the Tasmanian Economic Regulator approved a new pricing structure, valid from July 2026 to June 2030. It introduced a new way of billing some non-residential customers for the fixed component of their sewerage bill — basing it on water connection size, rather than on their estimated demand on the sewerage network. One business owner said the change saw their bill rise from $630 a month to $3,800 a month, while another sporting association said it copped a $1,400 monthly increase. A TasWater document from September 30 said the price hike may have impacted 33 sporting fields and 62-mixed use sporting facilities. ( ABC News: Georgia Hogge ) Before the change took effect, TasWater had predicted the change could disadvantage some customers and had proposed a solution — some customers with larger pipes would instead be charged as if they had a smaller 20mm connection. But the regulator knocked back the remedy, saying it would create inconsistencies. Businesses, clubs left reeling after change in TasWater pricing Businesses have been hit with hefty bill increases by Tasmania's water provider, leaving some wondering if they can remain open. When the billing changes came in, it led to outcry and an intervention from Premier Jeremy Rockliff, who called on TasWater to pause the billing structure and work with stakeholders to find a more sustainable way forward. But now, documents released to the ABC under right to information (RTI) laws show how TasWater's leadership internally reacted after the blowback, laying the blame on the regulator. TasWater leaders also initially argued that any attempt to reduce the bills must be matched with pricing increases elsewhere, to minimise the impact on its budget. For its part in knocking back the potential remedy, the regulator argued: "the potential for broader impacts across non-residential customers, which have since arisen, was not brought to [its] attention". It also said it only set the maximum amount TasWater could charge, but the water utility was free to charge less. Internal emails, secured through the RTI process, show the premier's media release was promptly forwarded to TasWater leadership, including chair Kevin Young and CEO George Theo. The two leaders replied to the media release email chain: Politics being played where the Premier is asking TW [TasWater] and the Councils to reconsider price increases. We should consider our response, what he is asking for is not for us in my opinion its a regulatory matter. I think it would be worthwhile for the premier and/ or treasurer to write to the economic regulator pointing out the major problem from the price determination and asking the regulator what can be done to correct the error? I think it is a blatant mistake and miscalculation that needs to be corrected. On September 11, Mr Theo again wrote to Mr Young, saying if the bills were to be reduced, those costs must be recouped. As part of any review to address this 'mistake' it must be done on the basis that TWs [TasWater's] total revenue remains the same. This means if non-residential sewer access charges are to go down, something else has to go up, to maintain revenue neutrality.

events.title: An NYC Marathon runner died suddenly at 24. Her family says the cause was rhabdomyolysis, a rare risk that can even affect fit athletes.
events.summary: A woman died after collapsing at the New York City Marathon from a rare side effect of hard exercise called rhabdomyolysis. kena betancur / AFP via Getty Images A New York City Marathon runner died after collapsing at the finish line near Mile 24. Her family said the cause of death was rhabdomyolysis, a rare side effect of hard exercise. Rhabdo can afflict even experienced athletes and cause life-threatening symptoms if left untreated. A 24-year-old woman who died after the New York City Marathon on Sunday was suffering from a rare side effect of exercise called rhabdomyolysis, her family said. Rachel Apa, an experienced D1 field hockey athlete who spent months training for the race, collapsed near mile 24 in Central Park and was taken by ambulance to the hospital, her father told The New York Times . Apa was a product manager for an electronic manufacturing company. Earlier this year, she posted on LinkedIn that she was running the marathon to raise money for the Parkinson's Foundation, in honor of her grandfather. The New York Road Runners, the group that organizes the marathon, and Apa's family did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Business Insider. Rhabdomyolysis, known as rhabdo, is a risk of extensive strenuous exercise caused by muscle tissue breaking down and overloading the kidneys. Without prompt medical treatment, it can be life-threatening. Here's what to know about rhabdo, including the symptoms to look out for and how to prevent it. What is rhabdomyolysis and what causes it? Rhabdomyolysis can occur after severe muscle injury or intense exertion. As damaged muscle tissue breaks down, it releases compounds into the bloodstream that the kidneys typically filter out. In rare cases, those byproducts can overwhelm the kidneys and lead to kidney damage or acute kidney failure. About 26,000 cases of rhabdo are reported in the US each year, research suggests. Anyone can suffer from rhabdo, but factors like hot environments and dehydration can increase the risk, according to Cleveland Clinic. While it's generally not common, cases of rhabdo are often caused by high-intensity exercise or long endurance sessions without rest. For instance, research has previously linked cases of rhabdo to marathons (particularly during high temperatures) and vigorous spin classes . It's also increasingly a concern for the military, which is working to spot rhabdo in troops more quickly. What are the symptoms of rhabdo? Symptoms of rhabdo include fatigue, muscle cramps or unexpected pain, and dark-colored urine, which can show up hours or days after exercise, according to the CDC. Rhabdo can be diagnosed with a blood test and treated with IV fluids to help flush out the waste products. To prevent rhabdo, avoid pushing too hard during exercise, take breaks as needed, and drink plenty of water, especially in hot, humid weather. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: The UK-EU food produce deal: what was agreed and will it affect shoppers?
events.summary: Two sides agree deal to remove some Brexit checks on food and animal product exports to EU Andy Burnham to unveil EU trade deals worth billions of pounds The UK and the EU have finalised their deal to remove red tape for food producers and agreed first drafts on joint positions on migration, youth mobility and electricity trading before a summit on 20 November. The draft text of a joint statement has emerged 17 days before the summit, an indication of the consensual state of play between two sides previously at loggerheads during the Conservative government era. What is the overall deal on 20 November? The food deal is one of three main issues identified by the previous prime minister, Keir Starmer, for his “reset” of relations with the EU. Andy Burnham promised to stick with them and the focus on food, electricity and a youth travel scheme for British and EU citizens between 18 and 30 years old. “Cooperation built on strong foundations” is the title of the draft statement which sets out plans for deeper relations on migration, the possibility of a youth mobility scheme , continued joint support for Ukraine, furthering the strong defence and security relationship and cooperation on hybrid threats such as recent drone incidents at European airports linked to Russia. What are the practical implications of the food and drinks reset? The details announced on Tuesday mean exports of fresh meat, fish, shellfish and seed potatoes, largely from Scotland, can resume without costly paperwork proving they comply with EU standards. Exporters will no longer need the £200 veterinary certificate proving their produce is safe to eat or use in the EU, nor will they need a £25 plant health certificate proving they are free of pests and diseases, paving the way for easier exports of trees, shrubs and wooden or leather goods. A youth mobility scheme will also start, possibly next year, with travellers between 18 and 30 years old able to get a special visa to work, study or simply travel. So if this is being announced on 20 November, what happened on Tuesday? The draft statement appears to show that the remaining loose ends in the food and drink deal, which was largely agreed and announced in May, was finally agreed by both sides. Negotiators are still thrashing out the details of the youth mobility scheme, with the EU insisting that the UK allow EU students study in British universities on home fees. In practice, the agreement will mean exporting is easier, but the food sector will be looking for substantial financial and marketing support from the UK to get British food back to the continent at scale. As the National Farmers’ Union president, Tom Bradshaw, said earlier this year: “There are no empty shelves in the EU with signs saying waiting for British products to return”. Food exports, particularly poultry and eggs, have collapsed by a third since Brexit, NFU analysis of trade data showed last month. The food deal is expected to be implemented in early 2028 as it needs legislation on the British side to align with the EU. Will shoppers notice the difference? Yes. It should mean the variety of fresh produce such as cheese from France and elsewhere is restored in British supermarkets, along with a wider range of wine. Since Brexit, supermarkets have reduced the range of fresh produce from the continent because of the red tape, while small artisan producers of cheese, wine and olive oil have stopped selling into the UK for the same reason. As of April this year EU pet passports can no longer be used or held by residents in England, Scotland or Wales to travel to the EU, causing headaches for families holidaying abroad, mainly with pet dogs. Before Brexit, a single EU pet passport (issued by an authorised vet in the UK or another EU country) was valid for multiple trips into the EU, provided the pet’s rabies vaccination remained in date. Under the new agreement, this system should be restored. Scottish salmon producers were among the first to devise a way of centralising exports to cut the red tape, but the risk of having a truckload of fresh fish being detained in Boulogne (where the fish checks take place) meant many producers of shellfish gave up. The new deal would reopen the door for exports of Scottish langoustines and molluscs that could be fished then served on restaurant plates the following day. How will it affect the Northern Ireland border? Checks and paperwork of fresh produce were controversially introduced on goods going from mainland Britain to Northern Ireland in a trade-off designed to ensure there were no checks on the border with the Republic of Ireland. The Democratic Unionist party vehemently opposed what they saw as a border in the Irish sea and on Tuesday said the SPS did not go far enough because it did not get rid of all checks. But it does get rid of most.

events.title: 'Like they don't care': RBA's fifth rate hike a huge blow to mortgage borrowers
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Interest rate hikes putting more pressure on already stressed households Laura Mayer has been affected by successive interest rate rises. ( Supplied ) The Reserve Bank's fifth interest rate hike this year will mean more stress for households. Those with large loan repayments, the unemployed and renters could struggle to stretch their budgets. The RBA has indicated it is still concerned about rising inflation, meaning further interest rate hikes cannot be ruled out. As a renter, Laura Mayer is worried she will not be able to cope with yesterday's Reserve Bank interest rate hike. "For me, the fact of the matter is that my rent has gone up 32 per cent in a one-off increase this year," she said. Ms Mayer blames rising interest rates. ABC News wants to hear your housing journey to better understand how the changing market is affecting your decisions. The Reserve Bank raised the cash rate by a quarter of a percentage point for the fifth time this year yesterday, taking the cash rate to 4.85 per cent. "The cost of housing is a constant state of stress for me, and it currently affects every aspect of my life. "I continually worry that I will be a lifelong renter, and I cannot see how it gets better without genuine government intervention." Bullock concedes the economy's stressful Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock expressed some sympathy for those on the wrong side of interest rate hikes at yesterday's press conference. "The fact that we've had this massive shock has meant that we're poorer and that's what people are feeling," she said. New research from Canstar has found one in 10 mortgage customers will have trouble meeting their soon-to-be higher repayments after the RBA's decision. The interest rate comparison website surveyed borrowers, renters and those who own their own home outright. As many as 10 per cent of borrowers surveyed said they would be unable to meet the higher repayments if today's cash rate hike materialised, while a further 28 per cent said meeting the increase would not be easy. The financial pain isn't limited to borrowers, with the majority (68 per cent) of renters saying they were concerned about the impact of today's rate hike on their rent or living costs. Sixty-year-old mortgage borrower Lina Pugliese's job was recently made redundant, making her budget squeeze extra tight. Lina Pugliese is among those feeling the pressure from successive interest rate rises. ( Supplied ) She told the ABC finding work was getting "really tough". "The buck stops with me," she said. She also expressed concern the Reserve Bank did not care about her financial position and was more intent on reducing inflation. "There seems to be an indifference coming from the RBA — almost like they don't care," Ms Pugliese said. More on interest rates and inflation Tough Christmas looms as rates and inflation hit household budgets What another rate hike means for your mortgage, savings and travel Interest rates highest since 2008 as inflation forecast to stay high Rising costs approaching 'scary' levels for WA home owners Yesterday's RBA interest rate decision was split: six members voted to increase the cash rate target; three voted to leave it unchanged at 4.60 per cent. The reason for this was that board members were conscious of economic stress emerging, Ms Bullock said. "Those looking for a [rates on] hold [decision] were thinking that housing has reacted, the unemployment rate is drifting up … they felt that there were potential downside risks in these circumstances," she said. How did the Reserve Bank choose its 2 to 3 per cent inflation target? But most board members saw fit to hike interest rates, and there may be more to come. "As a result, given the elevated near-term inflation outlook and the likely ongoing global sources of inflationary pressure, my base case is that the RBA has at least one more shot in the locker," Betashares chief economist David Bassanese said. In fact, two further rate hikes in the first half of next year can't be ruled out to ensure a decent slowing in domestic demand and containment of inflation expectations." IT professional Stephen Macchia does not know what else he can cut back on to absorb higher mortgage repayments. Stephen Macchia and his family have already cut back on spending to absorb the rate rises. ( Supplied: Stephen Macchia ) "What does the RBA expect us to do as costs are out of our control? We are all price takers for fuel, insurance, and food. "There is no choice here. Maybe there needs to be another instrument, like a variable portion of the GST or super to take money out of the economy.
