events.title: Gas policy consultants worked for industry and government at same time
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Consultancy ACIL Allen advised on government gas policy while working undisclosed for gas industry The Future Gas Strategy committed to expanding Australia's investment in gas. ( ABC News: Chris Lewis ) Consulting firm ACIL Allen helped to develop the government's Future Gas Strategy while also doing undisclosed work for the gas industry. Climate Integrity said its investigation had revealed conflicts of interest that the consultancy should have disclosed to the energy department. Greens senator Steph Hodgins-May says the government and energy department must explain why perceived conflicts of interest were missed. A consulting firm hired by the federal government to help develop its Future Gas Strategy was simultaneously doing paid work for the gas industry and did not disclose that conflict of interest to the energy department. An investigation by advocacy group Climate Integrity found ACIL Allen did not disclose that while it was working on two reports for the government, it was also undertaking work for Gas Energy Australia, the Australian Pipelines and Gas Association and the Business Council of Australia, which represents several gas giants as members. Consultancy ACIL Allen was commissioned to assess proposed reforms to the east coast gas market in late 2023, at the same time it was working for three gas industry groups to produce reports about the benefit of gas to the economy and its role in Australia's transition to net zero emissions by 2050. Months later, ACIL Allen was hired by the government again to provide advice on Australia's gas needs, to be fed into the government's landmark Future Gas Strategy — the policy plan for how Australia will transition away from gas towards net zero emissions. "This will inform an understanding of energy security, whether other sources of firming can perform this role and whether government action is needed," a department official wrote about the ACIL Allen contract, in emails released under freedom of information (FOI) laws. Tender records and documents obtained under FOI show ACIL Allen's work for government and industry over 2023 and 2024 directly overlapped. Madeleine King delivered the Future Gas Strategy in 2024. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts ) The ABC attempted to reach ACIL Allen, including in questions sent by email. When the ABC spoke to an unidentified ACIL Allen representative by phone, he responded, "Yeah, no, I don't want to talk to you, thank you," before hanging up. ACIL Allen also did not respond to questions put by Climate Integrity several months ago. Future Gas Strategy promised plan for gas beyond 2050 The Future Gas Strategy delivered by Resources Minister Madeleine King in 2024 concluded that "the analytical findings are clear … natural gas is needed through to 2050 and beyond", with the policy committing to expand Australia's gas investment. Labor backbench 'blindsided' by Albanese gas strategy Labor backbenchers say they were caught off guard by the government's new gas policy, which the resources minister says will keep the fossil fuel in Australia's energy mix until 2050 "and beyond". It prompted a revolt on Labor's back bench, with several MPs at the time telling the ABC they had been blindsided by the policy , and its focus on expanding gas and continuing it beyond 2050. Climate Integrity executive director Claire Snyder said the gas industry had obvious financial interests in shaping the Future Gas Strategy, and ACIL Allen should have been clear it was also doing work for them. "The gas industry clients of ACIL Allen have a direct financial interest in the outcomes of the Future Gas Strategy and of the gas policies that ACIL Allen is working on for the government. So to us that is a clear conflict of interest," executive director Claire Snyder said. "What we have is a consultancy with undeclared ties to the gas industry advising the government on consequential gas policy. "Our analysis has also shown that the body of work produced by ACIL Allen over that period of time consistently overstated the cost of zero emissions alternatives to gas, and it entirely omitted the climate cost of developing new gas supplies. The result of this is it advantaged the case for gas." As an example, Climate Integrity pointed to modelling based on up-front capital costs of energy projects, rather than system costs comparing expense over a project's lifetime, as a methodology that advantaged gas. Greens deputy leader Steph Hodgins-May said the non-disclosure called into question the government's Future Gas Strategy. "It has no integrity.

events.title: Primark lacks fizz as it approaches its go-it-alone moment
events.summary: After a profits dip, the chain’s demerger from its sister food company still makes sense but is unlikely to reveal tons of value Primark brings forward home deliveries plan by two years as profits slide T he business logic for demerging Primark from Associated British Foods’ greater Ovaltine-to-Twinings empire – an event due to happen by the end of next year – is impeccable. Read this year’s results statement and you wonder why the controlling Weston family took 20 years to get behind the idea. One paragraph can be about a yeast plant in India or the impact of high gas prices on sugar-refining margins; the next can jump to Primark’s new “digital flywheel” or the progress of the “By Coleen” collection. Even by conglomerate standards, food staples and discount fashion has always been an odd mix. Separating into two FTSE 100 companies, with stand-alone governance, makes sense. But it would be hard to say the rejig will reveal tons of value, another reason conglomerates often give for doing the splits. Primark obviously isn’t a hidden jewel because it already makes two-thirds of the group profit – and it isn’t currently on sparkling form either. Or, at least, it’s not in continental Europe. A like-for-like sales decline there of 4.7% for the financial year is jarring even in the context of “weak” consumer sentiment. The way ABF tells it, the continental operation is simply a year or so behind the refresh treatment that has been administered on the UK stores. We’re talking sharper digital marketing campaigns, a rejig of ranges, the introduction of click & collect and so on. The trouble is, the same explanation was given in January, when the gap between the home performance and that on the continent became apparent. Ten months later, the story remains largely the same. The UK and Ireland are in positive like-for-like sales territory (of 0.5%) but the continent is still miles off. Market conditions in Germany, Italy and Spain were all described as “very challenging”. Since Britain is now the priority for a home delivery service to capture “incremental” shoppers, one can imagine the gap will remain wide for some time yet. Perhaps online-only operators such as Shein, Temu and Zalando are simply more of a headache on the continent. None of which alters the underlying strength of the Primark machine. Never mind the U-turn on the economics of home delivery, there are still physical stores being opened, including in the US. This is still a formidable operation with almost £10bn of annual turnover. But the potential for profit growth tends to be a metric would-be new investors in newly liberated companies look at. On operating profits, Primark stayed above £1bn (just) for the year, but the number was 11% down on a year ago. For this year, the forecast is for a same-again profit margin of 10%-ish. There is a sense, even while opening new stores, of working hard to go roughly sideways. No new money will be raised in next year’s demerger, so timing is irrelevant in one sense. Shareholders will get what they already own, just in two parts; there will be no real need for investment banking hype. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning All the same, the overall ABF, as currently constituted, is forecasting a second year in a row of lower earnings because the food ingredients side, especially sugar, is still sticky. Meanwhile, the £1.9bn of share buy-backs over the past four years have come to an end as the group is in long-term investment mode. There could be another 12 months until the big split, which allows time for things to perk up. But in current “macroeconomic headwinds” conditions, ABF is travelling slowly to the historic separation. It’s still the right thing to do – just don’t expect fireworks.

events.title: CrowdStrike to shell out nearly $500M for 2 AI security startups as the market for securing agents takes off
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. Cybersecurity giant CrowdStrike is buying two AI security companies that expand its products to more broadly monitor, test, and cover AI models and agents, as companies across industries start rolling out AI agents and models wholesale. CrowdStrike said it will buy Fiddler AI , which makes observability software for monitoring AI agents inside enterprises, and Dreadnode , which helps companies automate security testing specifically aimed at detecting flaws in AI models, apps, and agents before they are set live. The company is paying around $400 million for Fiddler AI, and about $95 million for Dreadnode, according to The Wall Street Journal . The deals are happening at a time of significant upheaval in the cybersecurity space, especially as companies’ policies and processes lag behind AI adoption within their walls. Teams and individual employees alike are experimenting with AI tools, automating workflows, vibe-coding custom apps, and deploying armies of AI agents to do their bidding, which is understandably causing headaches for security teams. CrowdStrike, whose products are used widely across enterprises and governments, is clearly trying to leverage its already significant heft and presence to capture a share of this quickly burgeoning market . It’s not alone, of course, as we’ve already seen several startups and cybersecurity vendors raising dozens of millions in funding to solve issues for companies, though most of these approaches are essentially based on the conviction that existing security software isn’t enough to monitor and control AI tools, connectors, or usage. The company has itself been building detection and response controls , dubbed Falcon Guardian, to help companies see and understand what agents are doing on their devices, and these acquisitions seem to further flesh out its offerings. Fiddler AI is going to be part of CrowdStrike’s Falcon platform as Falcon Observe, where it’ll ostensibly help the company’s clients evaluate agents before they’re deployed, understand their actions, and monitor what they do, and feed that information as telemetry into the broader platform. Dreadnode, meanwhile, will be integrated into the Falcon Guardian product , to which the startup’s software will feed its testing results as security policy recommendations. Founded in 2018, Fiddler AI has raised a total of about $99 million to date, according to PitchBook. Dreadnode, founded in 2023, has raised $14 million so far. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Mobile comms body wants a joined-up approach from governments and regulators to mitigate downtime Virgin Media O2 outlines plans to lay off thousands as revenue falls 12 hours ago UK finance watchdog wants firms to report AI failures and close calls 14 days ago London’s mobile networks fall to bottom of Europe’s capital league 14 days ago Singapore’s central bank wants all FinTech AI use cases subject to independent review 27 days ago Three becomes one as Vodafone buys out merger partner July 31, 2026 The GSMA wants governments and regulators to work more closely with mobile operators to help protect networks against growing risks from extreme weather. As the global body representing the mobile network industry, the GSMA claims that severe storms and floods already cost operators $1.7 billion annually to repair damage to cell radio sites, and it believes that figure could nearly double to more than $3 billion a year by 2050, under the climate conditions expected then. The GSMA sets out its findings in a six-part research series, Futureproofing Connectivity: Climate Risk and Resilience in Telecommunications , alongside a separate document outlining its Policy Principles for Mobile Network Resilience . The report identifies weather-related risks that can affect telecoms networks, along with the associated restoration costs. Towers, masts, and rooftop sites are particularly exposed to wind and storms or lightning, for example, while ground-level equipment at mobile sites can be inundated in flooding incidents. High temperatures can cause radio equipment to overheat, while heavy rain can degrade wireless signal strength, and infrastructure in coastal locations may be exposed to storm surges. However, the report fingers the electricity supply as the biggest vulnerability. If that gets knocked out, the network could go offline once any backup power is exhausted, which may take anywhere from a few hours to considerably longer, depending on the site. Under current climate conditions, the cost of damage to cell sites is estimated at $1 billion associated with severe storms, while river and coastal floods account for $577 million and $124 million, respectively. Based on projected mid-century climate conditions, the GSMA expects costs due to severe storms to rise significantly to about $2.37 billion, accounting for three-quarters of all damage. The report asserts that cell network resilience requires a whole ecosystem approach, pointing out that if severe weather impacts power networks, then that also affects the telecoms infrastructure. The GSMA says that network firms have traditionally managed the operational risks that may affect network availability, but claims they face barriers in conducting full assessments of those associated with climate change. Some of these barriers are internal, such as lack of shared information between departments. Other barriers are in the different regulatory reporting frameworks, with infrastructure rules tending to focus on service continuity, while climate disclosure frameworks focus on governance, financial exposure, and reporting for investors and other stakeholders. The report lists separate recommendations for network firms and for policymakers and regulators. Operators are advised to embed resilience by design, using modeled projections for severe weather and future risk scenarios. They are also told to plan and test resilience across the wider ecosystem, engaging with others such as public authorities. When it comes to policymakers and regulators, the report asks for resilience frameworks to be developed through consultation with the operators. It also advises coordination among mobile operators, electricity and fuel providers, and emergency services to help maintain vital communications during major disruptions. And as if that isn't enough to chew over, the separate policy document sets out five principles for governments and regulators.

events.title: States take steps to secure vote after federal pullback
events.summary: State officials have largely taken securing the 2026 midterm elections into their own hands after nearly two years of federal program and funding cuts during the second Trump administration. Why it matters: The reduction in federal support has come as AI tools threaten to make it easier for hackers to uncover software vulnerabilities, launch cyberattacks, and spread disinformation that undermines trust in election results. Reality check: Just because a security flaw exists doesn't mean hackers can exploit it to manipulate election results. Nearly all U.S. elections maintain paper records that can be used to verify electronic tallies. Threat level: Election officials are preparing for everything from cyberattacks and AI-generated disinformation to physical threats, logistical disruptions and legal challenges. The big picture: State election officials relied on homeland security agencies, fusion centers, police, National Guard units and private cybersecurity firms to prepare for the midterms, John Milhofer, a spokesperson for the National Association of Secretaries of State, told Axios. That group and the National Association of State Election Directors are helping states exchange threat intelligence and connect with federal agencies and private sector experts. Catch up quick: State resources have become more important after the Trump administration scaled back federal election security assistance. CISA cut election security personnel and services in 2025, while federal funding for the Elections Infrastructure Information Sharing and Analysis Center, a key information-sharing network for election officials, ended that year. Election officials are receiving fewer election-specific threat briefings and less direct technical assistance, even after CISA outlined plans to restore some services in September. Zoom in: Michael Moore, chief information security officer for the Arizona secretary of state's office, told Axios that the state has been without a dedicated CISA cybersecurity adviser since March 2025. The Arizona Department of Homeland Security has helped fill the gap, providing security tools and monitoring services to smaller counties. On Election Day, Arizona is bringing together its state cybersecurity team, National Guard, the FBI and a representative from CISA's Region 9 office to coordinate responses to potential threats, Moore said. Moore's team has spent years conducting tabletop exercises covering cyberattacks, AI-generated impersonations of election officials, suspicious packages and other disruptions. Between the lines: Arizona is also getting threat intelligence from former CISA personnel who work in the space, election security nonprofits and officials in other states. Moore said his relationship with New Jersey's election security officials is particularly useful because his East Coast counterparts can warn him about threats hours before they might emerge in Arizona. What they're saying: A CISA spokesperson said in a statement that the agency will provide state and local government officials, including election officials and election vendors, "no-cost voluntary services" like vulnerability scanning and technical expertise, when they request it. "We are committed to supporting state and local elections officials to protect election infrastructure and safeguard our democracy," the spokesperson added. Yes, but: Moore said he still wants CISA to return to its 2024 staffing levels — and then double them. "If we are literally experiencing a cyberattack from a nation-state, it shouldn't be Arizona versus that nation-state," Moore said. "We're the United States of America. It should be a unified response." David Becker, executive director and founder of the Center for Election Innovation and Research, told reporters during a briefing Thursday that states have hired vendors and built their own networks to compensate for the federal retreat. "They might not be able to replace everything," Becker said. "They're not going to get the same bird's-eye national-level view of potential disinformation or potential cyber events." The bottom line: Election officials said they're prepared for disruptions, even if they can't prevent every attack. "The goal is prevent as much as we can, detect and recover," Moore said. "We're going to have some amount of disruption.... We're going to recover."

What surprised us was how much,' says Sandia physicist Nathan Moore Google's AI satellite sends a very expensive haiku to Earth 3 days ago Voyager 1 gives controllers the silent treatment 4 days ago NASA ponders a Hubble servicing mission or a controlled deorbit 4 days ago Boffin's software found a possible dwarf planet - a result so rare he thought it must be a bug 5 days ago China's spaceplane bears striking resemblance to America's X-37B 6 days ago Researchers at Sandia National Laboratories have developed a method to make asteroid deflection modeling faster and more detailed. Their simulations also demonstrated just how much asteroid shape and orientation can complicate efforts to deflect a threatening space rock. Sandia researchers, led by staff physicist Nathan Moore, were looking for a way to better model how X-rays from a nuclear detonation near an asteroid can change its trajectory, as explained in a recently published research paper . “Before, the calculations were so time-consuming, one could not do very many of them,” Moore told The Register . “So it was very difficult to explore different scenarios, different asteroids, or different mission concepts.” The complexity of those calculations forced earlier researchers to make compromises, often modeling asteroids as spheres or simplifying the physics involved. Perfectly spherical asteroids are rare, and their irregular shapes present an additional challenge for those keeping an eye on the skies to avert a potential asteroid apocalypse. To overcome the computational problem and enable better modeling of irregular asteroid shapes, Moore and his team combined two high-fidelity simulation codes already in use at Sandia: ALEGRA, which models radiation heating and high-energy material dynamics, and SPARTA, which simulates the behavior of low-density gases. As Moore explained to us in an email, both codes are good at one particular part of asteroid impact modeling, but bad at the other. “ALEGRA … can very accurately simulate the vaporization of the rocky surface, but the calculation becomes more inefficient for matter at low densities,” Moore told us. “This is a problem for asteroid deflection simulations, because as the gas expands around the asteroid, the calculation time goes up.” Earlier asteroid simulations using ALEGRA typically modeled asteroids as spheres to reduce calculation times. “SPARTA is more efficient at low gas densities,” Moore said. “The problem is, conversely, SPARTA gets more difficult to run at high gas densities. So the key here was using both codes.” In Moore’s model, ALEGRA handles regions of high gas density, while SPARTA tackles the more dilute regions of an irregular shape. The result is two codes handling the parts of the problem they're best suited to solve, reducing the overall computational burden. The combined approach is more than 1,600 times faster than earlier methods, Moore said in a Sandia press release , while retaining sufficient accuracy to predict deflection in irregularly shaped asteroids. The improved simulations reveal just how much asteroid shape and orientation can complicate attempts to calculate the outcome of a nuclear deflection. “We expected aim to matter,” Moore said. “What surprised us was how much.” Deflection simulations using detailed models of three well-studied asteroids – Golevka, Bennu, and Itokawa – found that irradiating different sides of the same asteroid with X-rays from a nearby nuclear detonation could produce as much as a fivefold difference in the resulting velocity change. Bennu, the most symmetrical of the three, still showed nearly twofold differences in deflection velocity depending on which side faced the blast. In other words, we need to be incredibly precise about where we detonate a nuclear device near an asteroid, or we risk giving it a much smaller shove than intended.

events.title: A New York Giants co-owner says the NFL can reach new fans in 2 key ways
events.summary: Carolyn Tisch Blodgett is bullish on flag football and international expansion for the NFL. Carl Timpone / BFA New York Giants co-owner Carolyn Tisch Blodgett sees room for the NFL to grow. International games are crucial, Tisch Blodgett said, since there "isn't enough room to continue to grow in the US only." The sports investor is also optimistic that flag football will bring in new fans. The NFL is America's favorite league, and a New York Giants co-owner says there are ways to keep it growing. Carolyn Tisch Blodgett , whose family owns a 45% stake in the Giants, said flag football and international games are the two biggest avenues for the NFL to build on its massive audience. "There just isn't enough room to continue to grow in the US only. You have to be thinking about international growth too," Tisch Blodgett said at Business Insider's The Long Play event. Tisch Blodgett, who runs sports-focused venture capital firm Next 3 and Gotham FC in the National Women's Soccer League, said that playing games abroad is crucial to the league's long-term success, as it helps build a younger, more diverse audience. "A sports fan today in 2026 looks different than a sports fan did maybe 100 years ago," Tisch Blodgett said. NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell has made international contests a key cornerstone of his tenure for the last two decades. The league has played games abroad every year since 2007 (except for 2020), going from one game a year in London to nine this season across the globe in places like Melbourne, Rio de Janeiro, Paris, Madrid, Munich, and Mexico City. Tisch Blodgett has seen championship-caliber teams with Gotham FC and the New York Giants. Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images Flag football, which will be an Olympic sport in 2028, is another way for the NFL to connect with new fans abroad and in the US, Tisch Blodgett said. That includes girls who may not have the opportunity to play tackle football. Playing a sport is correlated with fandom, Tisch Blodgett said. She's bullish that kids who try flag football will develop a lifelong affinity for the NFL. "If we know we need people to be playing to be a fan, we're going to invest in flag so that we continue to grow that fandom," Tisch Blodgett said. Flag football participation among high school girls surged 49% last year to over 100,000 — making it one of the 10 most popular sports for that demographic, according to a recent survey by the National Federation of State High School Associations. The NFHS said that four years ago, fewer than 16,000 high school girls played flag football, making it the fastest-growing high school sport in the years since. Tackle-free football leagues are also open to boys whose parents may not want them to risk getting concussions, which have been an area of focus for the NFL in the last decade. The NFL is investing in flag football, and its efforts include launching Premier Flag — a new pro flag football league that will start next summer. "As tackle football has declined, they didn't just sit back," Tisch Blodgett said of the NFL. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Protect Poundland from predatory capitalism, MPs tell government
events.summary: Budget retailer and 12,000 jobs at risk after US owner fails to accept buyout offers MPs have called on the government to protect Poundland and other high street stores from “predatory capitalism” and asset-stripping. The fate of the retail chain and its 12,000 staff remains uncertain after it filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators at the high court last Thursday. The board of Poundland has lined up the advisory company AlixPartners to run the process after the owner, US restructuring specialist Gordon Brothers, ceased providing funding. In an urgent question in the House of Commons on Tuesday, Gareth Snell, Labour MP for Stoke-on-Trent Central , asked the government what could be done to “send a message to Gordon Brothers that the predatory capitalism that they are putting into this company will not be tolerated, because we in this country will always stand with people before profit”. Another Labour MP, Antonia Bance, asked what measures the government would use to “hold Gordon Brothers to account”, and if it would “establish an urgent review of whether our corporate governance and insolvency frameworks give sufficient protection against asset stripping and short term financial engineering, at the cost of jobs and our high streets?” The Green party MP Hannah Spencer said the “scandal” of Poundland “exposes a very serious problem, that our economy is vulnerable to private equity vultures who swoop in and prey on our high street brands by loading them with debt and then trying to ditch them for a profit”. Kate Dearden, the minister for the future of work, told parliament that government officials had held talks with Gordon Brothers on Monday night and she would meet Poundland’s management team along with Usdaw, the shop workers’ union, on Wednesday. She said Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, would meet Gordon Brothers again later this week as political pressure mounts on the company to accept a solvent bid for Poundland. Liam Byrne, the chair of business select committee, has also asked Gordon Brothers to answer its questions about Poundland on Wednesday next week. Dearden said the government could not involve itself in the “commercial negotiations” with potential buyers or comment on individual bids. However, she said the government was “taking a responsible approach not to sit by and do nothing” and was putting pressure on Gordon Brothers to accept it had “responsibilities as well as rights” over Poundland and its employees. Gordon Brothers is understood to remain in talks with at least two potential buyers for the whole company, including a fully funded offer from Northern Ireland’s Martin Property Group. Another offer from Innovest, an investment group understood to be advised by former Reform election candidate Charles Bunker, is believed to have partial funding in place. The chance of Poundland avoiding mass store closures and job losses is shrinking by the day because suppliers have held back on deliveries, hurting its ability to trade . Gordon Brothers is believed to be unwilling to accept Martin Property’s offer of about £15m, only half of which would be paid immediately, because it falls short of repaying a £30m shareholder loan. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning The prime minister’s spokesperson said: “We continue to stay close to what’s an extremely worrying situation for Poundland staff, their families and communities. “Gordon Brothers need to explain why they haven’t accepted any offer to keep the company going. That’s the case. It appears they’re not acting in the best interests of their loyal UK staff and stores.” In a letter to the government, reported by Sky News, Gordon Brothers executive Mark Newton-Jones defended its approach, saying it had “supported Poundland with £85m of additional financing” since acquiring it for £1 last year and the chain had returned to underlying profit. However, the letter added: “Like other high street retailers, the company faces multiple economic challenges, including rising inflation, increasing staffing costs and shrinkage from severe levels of shoplifting, which means it is still not cash-generative at a sustainable level despite the turnaround efforts.” Dozens of MPs from around the UK have called on the government to reassure their constituents that action would be taken to stop Poundland’s collapse. Bradley Thomas, the Conservative party business spokesperson, blamed the government for Poundland’s demise. He said: “The current economic landscape is hostile to British business.” Earlier on Tuesday, the founder of Poundland, Steve Smith, told the Guardian that staff at the chain could be out of work for years if it collapsed. Gordon Brothers was approached for comment.

events.title: Food suppliers in UK hit by cyber-attacks after freezers targeted in Europe
events.summary: Cybersecurity experts say national impact ‘minimal’ but incidents may represent the ‘foothills’ of a wider threat Food suppliers in the UK have been hit by cyber-attacks after hackers raised the temperatures of supermarket freezers across Europe . The UK’s National Cyber Security Centre (NSCS) said it was working with the affected companies but the national impact was minimal. Speaking at the launch of the NCSC’s annual review on Tuesday , its director of operations, Paul Chichester, said: “We’re aware of those incidents in the UK, and obviously we’re working with the affected organisations. We’ll keep monitoring that. At the moment, the impact is minimal.” Cybersecurity experts meanwhile reported that attacks on “dummy” fridge controls – deliberately placed online to lure would-be hackers – displayed characteristics similar to malicious operations linked to Russia. Retailers in Belgium, Estonia, Finland, Ireland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Sweden reported problems with their refrigeration systems on Monday – with some rising to as high as 50C (122F) – and several companies confirming they had been hacked. Similar incidents were reported in France last month . It has emerged that the cyber-attack on French supermarket fridges involved legacy technology connected to the internet with default passwords. No UK grocery chain has been directly affected so far. Chichester said the NCSC, part of the GCHQ spy agency, was working with organisations to identify loopholes in their technology and close them before hackers exploited them. He said the NCSC was not able to comment on who might have carried out the attacks, but that they were not AI-enabled and had used vulnerabilities that had been “out there for a long period of time”. The NCSC’s chief executive, Richard Horne, said the fridge attacks represented the “foothills” of an enlarged cyberthreat that companies and the public faced as AI systems highlighted flaws in IT networks that owners were not aware of or had neglected to patch. “There are so many vulnerabilities out there that … you could say are waiting to be exploited,” he added. The agency’s chief technology officer, Ollie Whitehouse, said everyday domestic devices connected to the internet would be susceptible to hackers in certain situations. He said manufacturers needed to be encouraged to make their technology safer, and consumers needed to accept paying more for safer equipment. The British Association of Independent Meat Suppliers said some of its more than 300 members had been affected after becoming “collateral” in the hack. Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters The industry body said no meat had been lost in the refrigeration hacks but the incidents were a “reminder to all in the food industry at whatever point in the supply chain they are that their businesses may be seen by some as targets”. One meat supply company saw its cold units rise to up to 100C while another two reported their units had started to defrost. The association said the affected units were empty at the time. A fruit and vegetable wholesaler in London was also affected but prevented the attack from escalating by pulling the internet connection to its cold storage units out at the wall. Alex Pearce, managing director of Langridge Organic, said the hackers had changed the parameters on a number of units, setting them to defrost for more than four hours at 150C. However, Pearce and his staff intervened before any stock could be damaged. “It clearly must have been easy to get in [to the system] because the simple solution was to unplug ourselves from the internet,” he said. Pearce said Langridge uses the same fridge control system, developed by a US software company called Copeland, that was involved in the French supermarket incidents. The Grocer news website first reported the Langridge incident. Copeland said it is talking to affected customers and has recommended software fixes. Cybersecurity researchers said attacks on dummy Danfoss fridge controls – whose systems were also targeted by the hackers in mainland Europe – were similar to recent operations linked to Russia . Xavier Bellekens, the chief executive of the cyberdefence firm Lupovis, said it had recorded 256 attempted attacks from 91 different sources between 20 October and 30 October after setting up online “honeypot” traps that are indistinguishable to attackers from real Danfoss fridge controllers. The attackers attempting to take over the dummy controls remained anonymous, but most of the authentication attempts used the manufacturer’s publicly documented factory-default username and password credentials. They also used what Bellekens called “bulletproof” hosting, which means using internet service providers that are particularly tolerant of malicious activity, often ignore abuse complaints or make it difficult for authorities to disrupt their customers’ operations.

events.title: I tried Ina Garten's easy chicken chili. It's a delicious, hearty dinner that's perfect for chilly temperatures.
events.summary: I made Ina Garten's chicken chili, and it was easy, healthy, and so comforting. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider I tried Ina Garten's chicken chili recipe. Garten came up with the recipe while running her Barefoot Contessa store in the Hamptons. She swapped beef for chicken, and it became even more popular than the original. Ina Garten served traditional chili to her customers for 20 years while running her Barefoot Contessa store in the Hamptons. One day, Garten decided to tweak the recipe and swap the beef for chicken. It became even more popular than the original dish. The Barefoot Contessa store is long gone, but Garten's chicken chili recipe still lives on — and it's perfect for fall . Ina Garten's chicken chili features plenty of spices. Ina Garten appears on Sunday TODAY with Willie Geist in October 2018. Mike Smith/NBCU Photo Bank/NBCUniversal via Getty Images via Getty Images To make Garten's chicken chili for six, you'll need: 4 split chicken breasts, bone-in, skin on 2 (28-ounce) cans of whole-peeled plum tomatoes in puree, undrained 4 cups of chopped yellow onions 2 red bell peppers, cored, seeded, and large-diced 2 yellow bell peppers, cored, seeded, and large-diced ¼ cup of minced fresh basil leaves ⅛ cup of good olive oil, plus extra for chicken ⅛ cup of minced garlic 2 teaspoons of kosher salt, plus more for chicken 1 teaspoon of chili powder 1 teaspoon of ground cumin ¼ teaspoon of dried red pepper flakes, or to taste ¼ teaspoon of cayenne pepper, or to taste Freshly ground black pepper Chopped green onions, for serving Corn chips, for serving Grated cheddar cheese, for serving Sour cream, for serving While these are Garten's recommended measurements, I should note that I doubled some of the seasoning and added 2 teaspoons of chili powder, 2 teaspoons of ground cumin, ½ teaspoon of dried red pepper flakes, and ½ teaspoon of cayenne pepper. I wanted the chicken chili to pack a punch, and doubling these spices turned up the flavor without making things too hot. I prepped my ingredients and preheated the oven to 350 degrees Fahrenheit. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider I chopped my onions and bell peppers and minced the garlic. I misread Garten's recipe and cut my bell peppers a bit smaller than she recommended, but their shape still held up well in the chili. I think larger pieces might actually be too chunky for this dish because there's so much chicken in the chili, so I recommend going with a smaller dice for the bell peppers instead. I cooked the onions in olive oil for 15 minutes, then added the garlic. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider "You want to cook the garlic for just a minute so it doesn't get really bitter," Garten explained in a "Barefoot Contessa" episode while demonstrating the recipe. I added the bell peppers and seasoning. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider I threw in the chili powder, cumin, red pepper flakes, cayenne, and salt, and cooked everything for one minute. Then it was time to add the tomatoes. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider "I always make this with canned tomatoes; life's too short to peel a tomato," Garten said in the episode. According to the recipe, you can crush the tomatoes by hand or throw them in a food processor. If you opt for the latter, Garten recommends adding them in batches and pulsing the processor six to eight times. I don't have a food processor, so I crushed the tomatoes by hand. I also threw the leftover juice into the pot. After adding basil, I brought my chili to a boil and then reduced the heat to a simmer. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider Garten's recipe is designed so the chicken and chili are ready at the same time, so she recommends cooking the chili for 30 minutes. I had some extra time on my hands, so I allowed the chili to simmer for a little longer to give the flavors more time to develop. While my chili simmered, I roasted the chicken. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider During the "Barefoot Contessa" episode, Garten said she cooks the chicken with the skin on because she found it "really keeps it moist." She also noted that she roasts the chicken instead of boiling it because it makes the meat taste better. I rubbed my chicken breasts with olive oil and generously seasoned them with salt and pepper before throwing them into the oven for 35 minutes. Garten said the chicken breasts should be "just cooked" when you take them out of the oven. Once my chicken had slightly cooled, I separated the meat from the bone and started chopping. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider "Tear off the bone with your hands; it's the best way to do it," Garten said in the "Barefoot Contessa" episode. Garten then recommended cutting the chicken into ¾-inch chunks so the meat can be "really delicious and chunky." I added the chicken to the chili and continued simmering it uncovered. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider Garten's recipe calls for the chili to simmer with the chicken for 20 minutes. While the chili was simmering with the chicken, I prepped my toppings. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider Since I bought pre-grated cheese, all I needed to do was chop my green onions. Garten's chicken chili made for a fantastic dinner. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider Garten's chicken chili is so hearty and comforting. The rich tomatoes paired really well with the tender, juicy chicken, which soaked up so much delicious flavor, and the bell peppers and green onions added great texture. I also enjoyed the extra hit of acidity and creaminess from the sour cream. I made this chili for my friend Kayla, who was also a huge fan. "This chili is reminiscent of a chicken tortilla soup, but it's so much heartier!" she added. "It makes you feel so warm and cozy." As temperatures continue to drop, Garten's comforting recipe will definitely satisfy your chili cravings. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: AI isn't on the ballot, but it's still being tested
events.summary: Stephen Maturen/Getty Images This post originally appeared in the Business Insider Today newsletter. You can sign up for Business Insider's daily newsletter here . Americans are casting their votes in an election cycle that could reshape Washington's power structure. The GOP's control of both the House and Senate seems likely to break, according to most forecasts. Democrats are favored to win the House, with a shot at the Senate if they can net four seats while defending their own. BI's Brent D. Griffiths and Madison Hoff broke down everything you need to know — from the key topics to the closest races — for the 2026 midterm elections . Throughout the day and into the evening, we'll also have updates on the tightest races and the business world's reaction, so keep checking our homepage . Today's results could serve as a litmus test for AI on multiple fronts. Affordability remains a top concern for most voters . But one aspect of AI turned into a hot topic on the campaign trail. Data centers were a major talking point for politicians . The vast majority of Americans previously said they don't want them built where they live . Politicians responded with everything from outright moratoriums to calls for additional safeguards to address data centers' impact on water supply and electricity costs. Midterm results could offer more color on the public's appetite for AI infrastructure, shaping how tech companies try to appeal to voters going forward. OpenAI is already thinking about the next major election cycle. A memo from its top lobbyist, obtained by Politico, shows it pitching 2028 hopefuls on how to talk about AI . Others aren't waiting to make an impact. Elon Musk has donated nearly half a billion dollars, the largest amount for a non-candidate to spend in a single election cycle, according to the New York Times . A good chunk of that money is supporting Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton's Senate campaign, a key race for the GOP. AI's unofficial home state could also face a shake-up thanks to one proposal on the ballot. California's proposed billionaire tax has already sent some AI-focused billionaires packing, with many relocating to Florida . Meta's Mark Zuckerberg considered leaving the state over the tax before the tech giant stepped in to ease his concerns (and his potential tax bill). The proposal is a one-time 5% tax on current billionaires, but its approval could prompt hopeful billionaires to reconsider staying in the state. When we asked founders if they'd remain in California under a wealth tax, we got mixed responses . Read the original article on Business Insider

events.summary: Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Technical Papers Home '; AI/ML/DL Architectures Automotive/ Aerospace Communication/Data Movement Design & Verification Lithography Manufacturing Materials Memory Optoelectronics / Photonics Packaging Power & Performance Quantum Security Test, Measurement, Analytics tech papers Transistors Z-End Applications Videos & Research Videos Industry Research Newsletters & Store Newsletters Store MENU Home Special Reports Systems & Design Low Power-High Performance Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Test, Measurement & Analytics Auto, Security and AI Knowledge Center Videos Startup Corner Business & Startups Jobs Technical Papers Events Webinars Industry Research Newsletters Store Special Reports Seoul National University -led researchers published “Resolving the Kay–Dunn limit and the speed–endurance dilemma in ferroelectric Hf 0.5 Zr 0.5 O 2 for DRAM-class sub-volt capacitors.” “Ferroelectric hafnium zirconium oxide can increase charge density in scaled capacitors, but its high coercive field limits the low-voltage, high endurance switching required for dynamic random-access memory and embedded ferroelectric memories. Here we show that plasma-engineered (111)-textured TiN electrodes with N-rich, oxidation-resistant surfaces suppress interfacial oxidation and enable robust switching in 5 nm Hf 0.5 Zr 0.5 O 2 capacitors. The devices exhibit saturated hysteresis at 0.6 V, with 2 P r = 31.5 μC cm −2 and E c = 0.62 MV cm −1 , and no hard electrical breakdown through 10 12 bipolar cycles. Their nucleation-limited switching kinetics extrapolate to sub-nanosecond polarisation reversal at DRAM-relevant capacitor areas. At 1.1 V, circuit simulations of a common plate 1T–1 C cell yield short- and long-term stand-by sensing margins of 482 and 201 mV under a 20 fF bit line load. Electrode texture and interface engineering therefore enable low-voltage, high speed switching without compromising endurance, mitigating the practical Kay–Dunn scaling penalty and the speed–endurance dilemma.” Find the technical paper here . events.title: The NYC Marathon costs more than $300 to enter. Here's what it's like to run it.
events.summary: The 2026 TCS New York City Marathon took place on November 1. David Schwartz Nearly 60,000 runners participated in the 2026 NYC Marathon, starting from Staten Island. Entry to the NYC Marathon is tough, with a 1% chance in the general drawing. Business Insider reporters who participated in 2026 take you inside the iconic race. On Sunday, November 1, nearly 60,000 runners took part in the 2026 NYC Marathon, starting in Staten Island and crossing the finish line 26.2 miles later in Central Park. It's not easy — or cheap — to get in. The odds of gaining entry through the general drawing are about 1%. New Yorkers can secure a spot through the "9+1" program, which requires completing nine NYRR races and volunteering at one. Charity bibs are another option, often requiring runners to raise thousands of dollars, and a select few can earn a spot with a qualifying time. If you're lucky enough to get your hands on a bib, registration will still cost upward of $300. In 2026, the fee was $333.11 . It is also a major feat of preparation and training in the months leading up to the event. My colleague Noah Sheidlower and I were among the runners who took on the five-borough race this year. Here's what it was like. The TCS New York City Marathon begins in Staten Island. Courtesy of Noah Sheidlower Transit to the start begins as early as 5 a.m. The race falls on the first Sunday of every November, coinciding with the end of daylight saving time. The extra hour of sleep makes a difference when your alarm is set to go off in the 3s or 4s. Noah and I take a bus from Midtown. The lines are long, but organized. Runners board the Midtown Manhattan bus before the sun comes up. Noah Sheidlower There's also a bus from MetLife Stadium, and many runners take the Staten Island Ferry. The ferry ride, while cold, offers an epic flyby of the Statue of Liberty. After arriving in Staten Island and going through security, we have a few hours to kill before the gun goes off. This year, temps are in the low 40s at the start. Runners bring blankets and wear layers they can shed at the start line. Runners bundle up to stay warm in the starting village. Volunteers may even lend you a pair of gloves if you ask. Kathleen Elkins There's coffee and bagels in the starting village — and bathroom lines that can last half an hour. The sun rises over the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge, which runners cross during the first mile of the NYC Marathon. Noah Sheidlower There are five start waves, with Wave 1 beginning at 9:10 a.m. and Wave 5 at 11:30 a.m. Runners head to their assigned corrals about 30 minutes before their wave begins. Runners wait inside the starting corrals before walking to the start line. Noah Sheidlower As we approach the start line, the vibes are immaculate. Music plays as runners make final preparations, take photos, dance, and high-five one another. Just before the starting cannon fires, the soundtrack shifts to Frank Sinatra's "Theme From New York, New York." This is my seventh time running the race, and that exact moment — as soon as I hear, "Start spreading the news" — still sends goosebumps down my arms. The first mile takes you over the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge, from Staten Island to Brooklyn. It's the steepest part of the course — and one of the most picturesque, with lower Manhattan in the distance. Runners cross the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge, the steepest climb of the whole course. Noah Sheidlower After climbing for about a mile, we're rewarded with a downhill that spits us out in Brooklyn. We spend the next 11 miles running through New York's most populous borough. Lafayette Avenue, through Clinton Hill and Fort Greene, is particularly rambunctious, with block parties and live music. Passing through Williamsburg also feels like crashing a house party. From Brooklyn, we cross the Pulaski Bridge into Queens around the halfway mark. We then run through Long Island City before approaching the dreaded Queensboro Bridge. It's steep, silent, and soul-crushing — the only part of the course where spectators aren't allowed. But once we reach the apex and begin descending, we start to hear what's known as the "wall of sound": spectators waiting with open arms — and beer cans — at mile 16. Their energy is contagious, making it easy to forget that you still have a lot of running ahead. The author, absolutely leaning into the Mile 17 crowd. Summer Conner The crowd carries us up First Avenue and into the Bronx, where we're greeted with hip-hop music and some tricky hills. If your name hasn't yet fallen off your shirt — as happened to one of the authors — strangers cheer for you personally. That can help if you hit the infamous mile-20 wall, when your legs start to feel like lead. We reenter Manhattan around mile 21, and prepare to face the 5th Avenue hill starting around 23. It's brutal. As NYC Marathon veteran Casey Neistat described the course, it's "not the hardest, it's the meanest." View this post on Instagram A post shared by Travel + Leisure (@travelandleisure) The final three miles are the toughest, but the crowds are thick. They make sure you reach the finish line. Runners cross the NYC Marathon finish line in Central Park. Noah Sheidlower Crossing the finish line is emotional. Happy tears at the finish line are inevitable. Kathleen Elkins Almost as iconic as the finisher medal is the bright orange poncho volunteers wrap you up in. It keeps you warm — and guarantees enough "Congrats!" from strangers for the rest of the day that you can't help but wonder if this is what it feels like to be Jalen Brunson. Noah Sheidlower Despite the stiff legs and lost toenails, most runners — including yours truly — already can't wait for next year. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Photos from the 2026 NYC Marathon, from celebrity sightings to record-setting finishes
events.summary: More than 240,000 people applied for this year's drawing, and about 1% received a spot. Reuben Ingber/Business Insider The New York City Marathon, the world's largest marathon, took place on November 1. Over 60,000 runners finished the 26.2-mile-long race that weaves through all five boroughs. Several celebrities joined in on the race, including Casey Neistat, Jennifer Connelly, and more. New York City traded Halloween costumes and candy for running shoes and bibs as the five boroughs transformed into a racetrack for the city's annual marathon. The 26.2-mile race, which drew over 2 million spectators on November 1, is the world's biggest marathon. There are a handful of ways to get in, but probably the best-known is the lottery system. Runners apply in one of three pools: those who live within 60 miles of the city, US residents outside the metro area, and international applicants. The application opens in February, and the drawing takes place in early March. Of the 240,000 people who applied this year, only about 1% received a spot — yet it saw more finishers than ever before. Beyond the lottery, runners can get in by raising money for charity, meeting qualifying time standards, participating in New York Road Runners programs, or booking through an approved international travel operator. NYRR is the nonprofit that organizes the race. From Halloween costumes and celebrity sightings to record-setting runs and emotional finishes, here are some of the best photos from the 2026 New York City Marathon. The New York City Marathon celebrated 50 years of its five-borough course in 2026. Participants enter a hall to pick up their bibs at the marathon expo in New York City, United States, on October 30, 2026. (Photo by Michael Yanow/NurPhoto via Getty Images) Michael Yanow/NurPhoto via Getty Images While the first New York City Marathon began in 1970, the first marathon to weave through all five boroughs took place 50 years ago in 1976. Runners pay between $255 and $358 to race, depending on where they live and if they're an NYRR member. The race starts in Staten Island and ends in Central Park. NEW YORK, NEW YORK - NOVEMBER 1: An aerial view as runners cross the Verrazzano–Narrows Bridge during the 2026 TCS New York City Marathon on November 1, 2026 in New York City. (Photo by Paul Seibert/Back Left Media/New York Road Runners via Getty Images) Paul Seibert/Back Left Media/New York Road Runners via Getty Images Runners start at Fort Wadsworth on Staten Island, cross the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge into Brooklyn, then continue through Queens, Manhattan, and the Bronx before finishing in Central Park. With the earliest start time at 8 a.m., racers braved the cold morning air as they arrived. Reuben Ingber/Business Insider The professional wheelchair, women's professional, and men's professional divisions began between 8 and 9:05 a.m. The general public waves followed, starting at 9:10 a.m. and continuing through 11:30 a.m. The temperatures at the start were in the low 50s. By the afternoon, temperatures reached the mid-60s under sunny skies. Exactly 61,529 people started the race, and 61,146 finished — the most ever in any marathon. Runners pass through Central Park as they compete in the 2026 TCS New York City Marathon. Kena Betancur / AFP via Getty Images The 2026 New York City Marathon set a world record for the most finishers for the third straight year, and became the first marathon to see more than 60,000 people complete the race. The second-largest marathon is the Paris Marathon , which attracts between 50,000 and 60,000 runners each year. Runners from all walks and stages of life completed the race — the youngest participant was 18, and the oldest was 90. Runners celebrate after competing in the 2026 TCS New York City Marathon in New York City on November 1, 2026. The 26.2-mile race passes through all five boroughs, beginning in Staten Island and finishing in Central Park. (Photo by TIMOTHY A. CLARY / AFP via Getty Images) TIMOTHY A. CLARY / AFP via Getty Images The oldest finisher was Danil Farkash, 90, from the US, with a race time of 11:24:18. The youngest was Lucy Weld, 18, from the US, who turned 18 on race day. Her race time was 4:12:06. The runners represented 153 countries. Italy had the highest number of non-US finishers this year, followed by France. Celebrities, including Jennifer Connelly and Casey Neistat, ran among the participants. Reuben Ingber/Business Insider Neistat, a famous YouTuber, completed his 10th New York City Marathon—and his 30th marathon overall — on Sunday. He's called the city's marathon " the meanest " of all marathon courses because of its hills and hard surfaces. Spectators across all five boroughs showed their support with signs and cheers. Reuben Ingber/Business Insider Signs ranged from supportive slogans to funny messages. Taking place on the day after Halloween, several racers chose to run in costumes. Reuben Ingber/Business Insider Other costumes included runners dressed up as bananas, slices of pizza, and a Trojan War-era soldier. Tracy Morgan was the marathon's official Grand Marshal. Grand Marshals Tracy Morgan and Estee Stimler participate in the 2026 TCS New York City Marathon. Bryan Bedder/New York Road Runners via Getty Images As Grand Marshal, the " 30 Rock " star joined spectators in cheering runners at the finish. Sheila Chepkirui won the women's race, crossing the finish line at 2:24:36. Kenya's Sheila Chepkirui crosses the finish line to win the women's race at the 2026 TCS New York City Marathon in New York City on November 1, 2026. The 26.2-mile race passes through all five boroughs, beginning in Staten Island and finishing in Central Park. (Photo by TIMOTHY A. CLARY / AFP via Getty Images) TIMOTHY A. CLARY / AFP via Getty Images Her time translates to a pace of roughly 5:30 per mile. The women's professional field also included Julia Paternain, who holds Uruguay's women's marathon national record, among others. Andreas Almgren won the men's race, crossing the finish line at 2:06:01. Sweden's Andreas Almgren crosses the finish line to win the men's race at the 2026 TCS New York City Marathon in New York City on November 1, 2026. The 26.2-mile race passes through all five boroughs, beginning in Staten Island and finishing in Central Park. (Photo by TIMOTHY A. CLARY / AFP via Getty Images) TIMOTHY A. CLARY / AFP via Getty Images His time translates to a 4:48-per-mile pace. The men's professional field also included Edward Cheserek, who holds one of the world's fastest mile times, and Joe Klecker, a professional runner for On. Catherine Debrunner and Marcel Hug won the wheelchair division race, respectively. NEW YORK, NEW YORK - NOVEMBER 01: Catherine Debrunner of Switzerland and and Marcel Hug of Switzerland pose for a photo after finishing first in the wheelchair division of 2026 TCS New York City Marathon on November 01, 2026 in New York City. events.title: Anthropic is still grappling with the economics of compute
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. There’s a lot of mystery around the finances of major AI labs, and as Anthropic inches towards it IPO, we’re starting to get some answers. In particular, the company is finally disclosing more about the economics of compute, and how much of Anthropic’s skyrocketing revenue is being lost to compute costs. In a new filing on Monday , Anthropic released data that showed those margins on compute actually getting worse. The filing was an update to the S-1 released last week — but where that filing’s financial disclosures only covered through June 30 of this year, the new data extended to disclose results through an extra quarter, to September 30. Broadly, Anthropic had a good quarter: revenue reached $17 billion, up from $11.5 billion in the previous quarter, suggesting durable growth. But the operating loss grew at the same time, thanks in large part to growing compute costs. Looking at the compute margins makes the picture even worse. In the new quarter, compute took up 58% of the company’s revenue, up from 48% the quarter before. At a moment when the company could win over IPO investors by showing margins improving, they’re getting worse. A chart in the filing shows this even more clearly, tracking the company’s revenue for every dollar spent on compute. Since the start of 2025, it’s been steadily growing, peaking at just over 2x this past quarter, then falling back down to 1.72x. Many indications imply that this shift in compute margins is more of a blip than a long-term problem, but it still tells us important things about the business of running a major lab. Trying to keep up with demand, Anthropic’s compute bill shot up to $10 billion for the quarter, including, as the filing notes, “$5.0 billion of compute under short-term commitments, which currently costs significantly more than comparable compute procured under our multi-year commitments.” Basically, demand was growing so fast that Anthropic had to scramble for compute, which meant paying higher rates. Some of those deals have already played out in public. Anthropic has been paying SpaceX $1.25 billion a month for compute, alongside multibillion-dollar deals with Nscale , Akamai , and Volta . In the parlance of the industry, these are neoclouds rather than hyperscalers — smaller outfits that offer more flexible compute deals at higher rates. Anthropic’s margins got worse in Q3 because of deals like these, and there’s no sign they’ll be able to do without them anytime soon. As the new filing puts it, “We expect compute and infrastructure expenses to increase in absolute dollars and remain our largest operating expense for the foreseeable future as additional committed compute becomes available to us under multi-year arrangements with CSPs, and as we continue to invest in additional compute.” Anthropic is still trying to lower its compute costs. In particular, the company talks quite a bit about its efforts to build its own compute base under a project it calls “Anthropic Direct.” But with demand growing so fast, those efforts aren’t going to be able to keep pace, and the neoclouds will continue to be the best option they have. In a sense, these are champagne problems. As long as revenue is growing at nearly 50% a quarter, few investors will worry about high compute costs — and the moment demand slows down, investors may be comforted by a compute picture that has gotten a lot sunnier. But it’s a reminder of how much AI labs still depend on the trillion-dollar infrastructure buildout — and how vulnerable they are to hiccups in that process. It’s easy to imagine the data center buildout slowing down over the next year if bond markets get skittish or local opposition gets more intense. There’s not much Anthropic can do to address either of those risks, and either one would make a messy compute picture a whole lot messier. In the meantime, the future of Anthropic and other labs will be at the mercy of compute prices. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . This doesn’t affect our editorial independence.

events.title: 'Super energy efficient' washer-dryer one of the worst products of 2026
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Shonky Awards handed to ticketing giants, Virgin, Sony and a 25-hour washer-dryer Choice has handed out its 2026 Shonky Awards to the worst products and services. ( ABC News: Eric Hao Zheng ) Consumer group Choice has handed out the 2026 Shonky Awards to the worst products and services. Ticketek and Ticketmaster were named for "fleecing fans with tricky ticket tactics", while Virgin claimed its first Shonky for pocketing $75 million worth of expired flight credits. Protein chips, a pet insurer, Sony and a washer-dryer that takes 25 hours also made this year's list. Two ticketing companies, an airline and a washer-dryer that takes 25 hours are among the recipients of the one award no business wants. Consumer group Choice has released the winners of its 21st annual Shonky Awards, handed to the worst products and services of 2026. Ticketek and Ticketmaster have been awarded their second Shonky. ( Supplied: Choice ) Ticketek and Ticketmaster have won their second Shonky, this time for "fleecing fans with tricky ticket tactics", called out for using dynamic pricing and "in demand" tickets. Tickets sold by Ticketek this year for a John Farnham Tribute concert were priced up to $1,650. NRL fans purchasing through Ticketmaster were asked to pay $50 more for "in demand" seats, even when they were just one row or bay apart from regular seats. A Ticketek spokesperson said variable pricing was used on fewer than 7 per cent of tickets for the John Farnham Tribute and did not apply to the $1,650 tickets. "Where it is used, fans are notified about potential price changes before they enter the on-sale," they said. Ticketmaster has been called out for the use of "in-demand" tickets. ( AP: Phelan M Ebenhack ) Changes to Australian Consumer Law from July 2027 ban dynamic pricing under certain circumstances where it unreasonably manipulates customers or distorts their decision-making. Choice editorial director Mark Serrels said there was heightened awareness around ticket prices. "I think it was really exacerbated by these big events like the Oasis reunion," he said. A Ticketmaster spokesperson said it did not use surge pricing and "for in-demand tickets" and that "event organisers set the prices of sought-after seats closer to market value and may review these over the sales period." This year, Choice gave Qantas a break and awarded Virgin Australia its first Shonky for pocketing $75 million worth of expired flight credits. The airline cancelled several flights between April 2020 and July 2022, at the height of the COVID pandemic, holding about $93 million in unused flight credits as of February this year. Virgin Australia has earned its first Shonky Award. ( ABC News: John Gunn ) Customers were forced to book trips by June 30 this year, with a deadline to fly by May 27, 2027. Virgin notes in its 2025/26 annual report that $75 million worth of expired COVID-19 credits "impacted" its underlying net profit of $404 million. A Virgin Australia spokesperson said more than 93 per cent of COVID credits were redeemed. "We regularly communicated the expiry date and later extended the fly-by date to 27 May 2027, giving guests almost another year to travel," they said. Hisense earned its first Shonky for releasing an 8-star energy-rated "super energy efficient" washer-dryer. The catch? That rating is tied to the machine's eco settings, which take 12 hours to wash and 13 hours to dry — 25 hours for a load of laundry. Mark Serrels says Hisense's 25-hour washer-dryer cycle could be "greenwashing", pun intended. ( Supplied: Choice ) Mr Serrels said the energy rating system was due for an overhaul, with almost all white goods manufacturers exploiting it. Also claiming a Shonky are Quest Nacho Cheese Protein Chips, priced at more than $20 per 100g — 886 per cent more than a pack of Doritos without the protein label. Quest Protein Chips will help get you ripped (off). ( Supplied: Choice ) Mr Serrels said this was a difficult decision with an influx of added-protein goods hitting store shelves, noting some goods were ultra-processed with very little additional protein and a much higher ticket price. While the entire pet insurance industry has won a Shonky, with insurers not covering pre-existing conditions the main issue, this year Petcover has earned its own for taking things further. One of its policies requires customers to enter a new policy every 12 months, which classifies all conditions the pet has previously experienced as pre-existing, therefore excluding them from cover.

events.title: Chipotle's COO says he looks for this problem-solving skill in future leaders
events.summary: Chipotle's COO looks for problem-solving skills in the workers he promotes. Chipotle, Ana Altchek; Alyssa Powell/BI Today's tip to get better at work: Get better at showing you have leadership potential. Chipotle's chief operating officer, Jason Kidd, said he looks to promote workers who solve problems. Instead of coming to your boss with what went wrong, go into conversations with a solution. Get better at: Showing leadership potential Today's move If you want to get promoted, don't just bring your boss problems — come to them with possible solutions when something goes wrong. Jason Kidd , the chief operating officer at Chipotle, visits roughly a dozen restaurants every week and he uses team dinners in every location as a way to scout talent for promotions. He said he looks for four qualities in the people he promotes, including how they respond when things go wrong. Why it works At any company, including a fast-moving restaurant like Chipotle, problems are bound to arise. Kidd looks for leaders who can anticipate issues, take ownership, and find a solution. Those employees show they aren't waiting around for problems to land in their lap. They're actively taking initiative to improve the workplace. Try it today The next time an issue comes up at work, take a few minutes to brainstorm possible solutions. When you approach your manager, tell them what went wrong, a couple of possible solutions, and your recommendation for what to do next. That demonstrates leadership and initiative. The bottom line You aren't directly responsible for every problem that comes up at work. However, by showing your boss that you're actively working to avoid adding another task to their to-do list, you're helping make their job easier and showing them that you can handle more responsibility. Source This insight is based on Business Insider's reporting about how Chipotle's COO Jason Kidd promotes workers, and the qualities he looks for. events.title: Datacentres are deeply unpopular – so the geniuses at OpenAI are rebranding them | Arwa Mahdawi
events.summary: Datacentres are deeply unpopular – so the geniuses at OpenAI are rebranding them These resource-guzzling centres drive up utility bills and are hated across the political spectrum. Cue a clunky, but potentially influential, new name for them J esus may have turned water into wine, but Donald Trump has done one better: he turned Lake Ontario into Lake America and the Gulf of Mexico into the Gulf of America. And then, for his next trick, he insisted we all stop talking about artificial intelligence (AI) and call it superintelligence (SI) instead. Those, of course, are only a few of the name changes the president has ushered in. When he’s not golfing or commenting on senators’ buttocks , president Trump loves a rebranding project. Which makes sense: coming up with a new name is far easier than making meaningful improvements to people’s lives. Trump isn’t alone in thinking a rebrand can distract from bigger issues. The tech industry seems to be on a mission to pepper every inch of the earth with datacentres that will facilitate our glorious AI-powered future. One slight problem: the hoi polloi are not quite so enthusiastic. People around the world are increasingly nervous about AI. Meanwhile, a majority of Americans across the political spectrum hate datacentres with a passion; so much so that they have become one of the biggest talking points of the midterms. There are various reasons for this anger, but the big one is that a lot of people blame the resource-guzzling centres for driving up the cost of utility bills. And so, with Trumpian logic, the great minds at OpenAI have come up with a brilliant solution to their very bad image problem. They will rename datacentres … wait for it … compute campuses. Did a consultant (or ChatGPT) land on this new alliterative formulation because it sounded a smidgen warmer, a bit more human, than datacentres? I presume that is the case, but the official explanation is somewhat more convoluted. “Compute campuses better describes the scale and role of the infrastructure we’re building for AI,” an OpenAI spokesperson told Business Insider on Sunday. “These are long-term investments in computing, energy infrastructure and skilled work.” As someone once said, nobody ever went broke by underestimating the intelligence of the American people, but do the geniuses at OpenAI really think the public is stupid enough to be swayed by a few new buzzwords? I won’t speculate as to what these people think, but I will concede that names do matter. The Affordable Care Act (ACA), the major US healthcare reform passed in Barack Obama’s first term, is one obvious example. When the ACA was being debated, Republicans started calling it “ Obamacare ” to try to make it seem as if it was a self-serving power grab by the president. This wasn’t an entirely successful ploy, but it did cause a lot of confusion. A 2017 Morning Consult study found that a third of Americans had no idea that the ACA and Obamacare were the same things. About 80% of Republicans strongly disapproved of Obamacare while only about 60% strongly disapproved of the ACA. “Very slight variations in how you describe something can change people’s minds,” the co-founder of Morning Consult noted at the time. That said, I’m fairly certain that a new name for datacentres isn’t going to win hearts and change minds. But that’s OK: the tech industry has other tricks up its sleeve and a number of helpful partners in crime. Fox News, for example, seems to be going out of its way to do PR for the industry. According to a new analysis by Media Matters for America, the volume of pro-datacentre claims made by Fox News personalities and guests increased 420% after 18 August. That’s not a random date; it’s when the National Republican Senatorial Committee sent out a memo warning that animosity towards the industry could hurt pro-datacentre Republican candidates in the midterms. As the propaganda proliferates, I don’t think it’s a stretch to say that we’re simultaneously seeing the gradual criminalisation of opposition to AI. In June, the Intercept reported that Philadelphia police were scanning “social media looking for posts opposing AI datacentres” because of a supposed risk from “domestic violent extremists”. Meanwhile, in August, Futurism counted at least 37 arrests from protests related to datacentres so far this year, many for petty infractions . Since that analysis, there have been a number of other reported arrests . It seems the powers that be think that if people can’t be brainwashed into loving the “compute campus” next door, they can always be scared into shutting up.
