events.title: Rivian spinout Also was working on an e-moto project in Kenya — until it walked away
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. Also, the micromobility startup spun out of Rivian in 2025, quietly started and then walked away from an electric two-wheeler pilot project in Kenya earlier this year, as it sought to focus its resources on its consumer e-bike and autonomous vehicle ambitions, TechCrunch has learned. The project received grant funding from the Shell Foundation, an independent charity established by the British oil and gas giant Shell plc. A section of the Shell Foundation’s website that has since been removed said the project’s goal was to “enable and de-risk global OEM entry into Africa’s EV market by piloting a locally integrated electric two-wheeler platform in Kenya, with potential to scale across East Africa.” According to the deleted section, Also was expected to work on modular battery designs and distributed EV charging, and planned on “developing a purpose-built electric motorcycle for African riders.” The opportunity for electric motorcycles seems ripe on the continent, which has a massive two-wheeler market. African mobility company Spiro recently said it has more than 130,000 electric motorcycles operating across seven countries, along with 2,500 battery-swapping stations. This boom has drawn interest from Chinese mobility companies and investors, which are pouring resources into the space . In a September email, Also told TechCrunch that it had “explored this project” with an unnamed partner, but ultimately “decided to focus on its core roadmap” after completing only “some early-stage work.” Also said the grant funding it received from the Shell Foundation “will follow the project to support its ongoing development,” but declined to offer specifics. The Shell Foundation told TechCrunch in an email that the project was “intended to generate evidence on driver income uplift potential, operational performance and commercial viability to deepen the company’s understanding of the market opportunity.” But when TechCrunch asked for more specifics, the Shell Foundation declined, citing a nondisclosure agreement with Also. Days later, the project disappeared from the Shell Foundation’s website. During an interview last month at TechCrunch Disrupt, Also co-founder and president Chris Yu said the Kenya pilot project initially made sense given Also’s mission to build small, purpose-built vehicles that are “first and foremost cost-optimized to do the job that needs to be done in a particular market.” But other projects took precedence, Yu said, especially the development of small autonomous vehicles — which Also is working on as part of a partnership with DoorDash . “We piloted and ultimately decided, largely because of just urgency and pace around autonomy, frankly, that our attention would be best, in the near term, served fully focused” on that, he said, adding that he thinks there’s a “high chance that autonomy will show up first, and at a broader scale in these types of purpose-built smaller vehicles than at scale in passenger vehicles.” Also walked away from the Africa project during a somewhat rocky first year of independence. Supply chain problems forced the company to repeatedly delay deliveries of its first product, a premium e-bike called the TM-B, frustrating customers who had reserved one. What made matters worse was Also’s relative silence. The company said little for much of 2026 about when the bikes would arrive — a communication failure its leadership now acknowledges was a mistake. “I think we did a pretty poor job communicating to our reservation holders through the summer when they were all waiting, and we got called out for that,” Yu said in the interview. “But I think it’s actually great. It’s really hard to earn the opportunity for people to care, and to tell us what they think, and to help us improve.” Getting its first product launch back on track is crucial for Also, which has ambitions far beyond e-bikes. The company plans to sell commercial cargo bikes to companies like Amazon , including four-wheeled models, and has the partnership with DoorDash. These products are next in the company’s pipeline, Yu said, and represent bigger revenue opportunities. But the TM-B comes first. It’s Also’s most visible product to consumers, and its striking design has drawn plenty of curiosity. Yu said no single problem was responsible for delaying the bikes, which finally started shipping to customers in early October. Instead, Also spent much of the year playing supply chain Whac-A-Mole, a particularly difficult challenge given the TM-B’s complexity. Yu described the bike as “kind of a computer on wheels.” At one point, Also found itself competing for the same raw materials used to make printed circuit boards for AI data centers. At other times, the company struggled to navigate certification requirements with different government agencies.

events.title: Keeping mortgage interest relief approved
events.summary: The States agreed to phase the tax relief out in 2015, but it was frozen between 2024 - 2026 A move to keep tax relief on interest paid on mortgage payments has been approved. Deputy Aidan Matthews, who brought the amendment to the Budget in Guernsey, said it was currently the "worst possible time" to consider phasing out the tax relief. It also meant that the phased withdrawal of the relief, which was agreed in 2015, would also stop, it was confirmed. The relief allows homeowners to apply for tax relief on any interest paid on the mortgage of their principle residence of up to £3,500 a year. Speaking against the move, Deputy Neil Inder said that, while the idea was right in isolation, if all amendments were approved, it would add "£20m to the budget". Listen to the latest news for Guernsey Alderney representative Alex Snowdon said the timing of the amendment was "important". He said: "There is a lot of Guernsey and Alderney people will be working two to three jobs that are really struggling to try and support the mortgage and their families. "I think this sends a strong message that we are trying to do a little bit to try and help people who are going through a very difficult time. "Some might say [these are] normal interest rates, but we've had money so cheap for so long that we are getting back to more difficult interest rates because house prices are going up so much people are borrowing so much more money." Deputy Jayne Ozanne said in the debate that she was "very split" on the amendment because it was an "unfair advantage" to homeowners over renters. "This will not solve the crisis of people leaving the island," she said. "They can not afford to save for a deposit for a mortgage because they are paying such high rents," she said. "Their monthly outgoings does not allow them to create the capital egg that they need to put a deposit down. This will not help that; it may help them once they've got a mortgage to decide to stay. "I'm wrestling because I feel there is an inequality here... the average rent in the island is over £2,000 per month while the average mortgage, I believe, is £1,000. "But two wrongs don't make a right. I recognise that families are feeling squeezed." Follow BBC Guernsey on X , external , Facebook , external and Instagram , external . events.title: Primark brings forward home deliveries plan by two years as profits slide
events.summary: Retailer acquires robot-assisted warehouse and intends to have UK service up and running before end of 2027 Primark is to begin making home deliveries by the end of next year as it aims to win new shoppers after a slide in profits. George Weston, the boss of the cut-price fashion chain’s owner Associated British Foods (ABF), said it had brought forward the launch of Primark’s home delivery plans by about two years. The company was able to speed up the process by snapping up a robot-assisted warehouse in Sheffield from Debenhams, the owner of Boohoo, PrettyLittle Thing and Karen Millen. Primark will take over the warehouse by the middle of next year and is working on preparing its suppliers to provide stock suitable for sending out to individual shoppers as well as the usual bulk orders for stores. Primark already offers a click and collect service in the UK which it has gradually rolled out since 2022 . The service is not available to its stores in mainland Europe. The chain, which has 511 stores across 21 countries, will launch home deliveries in the UK by December next year. It intends to offer the service in mainland Europe after that, but has not set out a timeframe. Primark has previously said it could not make money by selling fashion for home delivery, but Weston said the economics had changed with delivery and returns charges that could cover most of the logistical costs now common across the industry. He added that the group’s research had shown it could attract new customers, rather than just substituting a sale in store for a less profitable one online. “We now know there’s a group of shoppers who don’t reject Primark but just don’t use us very often as they are too far away from a store or prefer to shop online,” he said. The move comes as Primark faces tough competition from the rise of cut-price online specialists such as Shein as well as the supermarkets’ clothing ranges and the likes of H&M and Zara, all of which sell online and in stores. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Weston insisted that Shein was not grabbing more than a “little bit” of market share from Primark, and that there was more competition from those who could mix online and stores. Sales at Primark rose 4% to £9.8bn in the year to 12 September led by new store openings. Sales at established UK stores rose just 0.5% and sales at established stores in mainland Europe slumped 4.7% and in the US were down 2.6% as shoppers reined in spending on clothing amid higher energy and fuel bills. Primark said performance in the UK had been helped by improved ranges, action to cut prices and more marketing, tactics that are now being rolled out across Europe. However, that action saw profits drop 10% to £1bn. ABF intends to spin off Primark in December 2027, separating it from its sugar and food business that includes brands such as Twinings teas, Blue Dragon flavourings and Jordans cereals.

Google announced on Tuesday that it plans to disable AI tools for K-12 students next year unless school administrators explicitly turn them on. The tech giant says the change follows consultations with schools, teachers, leading researchers, and policymakers. As a result, Google is revising its approach across Gemini, NotebookLM, Gemini in Classroom, and Google Search. The decision means that schools choosing to restrict AI altogether will no longer be able to access Google Search, as AI features are now integrated into the search engine. Chris Phillips, vice president for education at Google, told The New York Times that “Search and AI are deeply integrated,” which means that if a school chooses to restrict AI altogether, students “will not have access to search, and they’ll see a message from their school that indicates it’s not available.” The change raises an issue for schools. Although teachers may not want students to use AI Overviews in Google Search to conduct research or complete assignments, they likely still want them to be able to have access to the search engine to find sources and other learning materials. However, Google Search and its AI features are now inseparable. Given the dominance of Google’s suite of apps in classrooms and the widespread use of Chromebooks, the decision underscores the company’s influence over the education sector. Schools that want to continue to have access to Google Search will have to accept its AI features. “We’ll share more specifics with schools in the coming months ahead of the changes rolling out so they have time to prepare and enable a smooth transition,” Phillips wrote in a blog post . “Our goal is simple: provide school leaders the control and confidence to use AI products in classrooms as they see fit.” Google announced the upcoming change alongside the launch of Guided Learning in schools. The tool, which was unveiled earlier this year, sort of functions like an AI tutor, as it’s designed to help users build a deep understanding instead of just getting answers. events.title: How political candidates charter jets to travel across battleground states during election cycles
events.summary: Philippe Reines, Hillary Clinton's 2016 presidential campaign advisor, speaks to members of the traveling press aboard the campaign plane. Justin Sullivan/Getty Images Campaign travel is a niche corner of aviation that moves political candidates across the country. DC-based firm Advanced Aviation Team served Susan Collins' and Hakeem Jeffries' campaigns in 2026. Each trip involves carefully coordinating aircraft, crews, press, and — sometimes — armed security. It's been a busy year for campaign travel as state and federal lawmakers — and their challengers — crisscross the country for rallies and fundraisers for the 2026 midterm elections. But moving candidates and their staff, donors, press, and, in some cases, armed security, from one stop to the next isn't as simple as booking a commercial flight. Political travel has become a niche of its own within aviation. One pro in that realm is Gregg Brunson-Pitts, the founder and CEO of Advanced Aviation Team. Founded in 2015, the Washington, DC-based firm arranges VIP travel for ultrawealthy families, celebrities, and corporate C-suites, with a particular specialty in campaign travel. Gregg Brunson-Pitts founded Advanced Aviation Team after working for former President George W. Bush. Courtesy of Gregg Brunson-Pitts Brunson-Pitts' company manages every step of political travel — from scheduling flights and sourcing crews to branding planes, coordinating security, and adapting to rapidly changing itineraries. Advanced Aviation handles hundreds of thousands of dollars in contracts over a single election cycle and describes itself as nonpartisan. This year, Federal Election Commission (FEC) filings show it received roughly $58,000 from Sen. Susan Collins' leadership PAC and $66,000 from Rep. Hakeem Jeffries' campaign committee for 2026 travel, among others. All 435 House seats, 35 Senate seats (including two special elections), 36 governorships, three territorial governorships, numerous state offices, and thousands of state legislative seats nationwide will be on Tuesday's ballot. "We are hyper-focused on client satisfaction, which means seeing around corners, being problem solvers, and being solutions-oriented," Brunson-Pitts told Business Insider in early 2026. "We're seeing organizations plan earlier and lock in travel support sooner, because once the calendar tightens, capacity disappears quickly." A firm run by former White House travel directors Brunson-Pitts previously ran the White House Travel Office for eight years under former President George W. Bush. He said a charter jet carrying the White House press corps, Secret Service personnel, and other staff would almost always fly in tandem with Air Force One . President George W. Bush and first lady Laura Bush board Air Force One in June 2004 PETER MUHLY/AFP via Getty Images That experience — blending chartered aircraft, armed security, and government protocols — helped him build a specialty focused on the logistical demands of modern campaigns: "Our approach allows us to support clients affiliated with any party," he said. Unlike charter operators or fractional owners such as NetJets or Flexjet , which operate and maintain their own planes, Advanced Aviation Team functions as a broker with access to contracted aircraft. "We can source smaller private jets, but we can also do group travel for 100 or more people and customize an airliner," he said. "Not a lot of brokers can do that; that's what sets us apart." Brunson-Pitts said he built a team drawing from inside and outside the aviation industry, bringing together experience in politics, campaign travel, logistics, and private aviation chartering , brokerage, and sales. For example, Peter Newell, the former director of the White House travel office under President Barack Obama, joined as company president in March. Meanwhile, before joining Advanced Aviation, company vice president Jonathan Tasler organized the McDonnell Douglas MD-83 chartered by Mitt Romney's 2012 presidential campaign. The MD-83 campaign plane that Republican candidate Mitt Romney chartered in 2012. Justin Sullivan/Getty Images This logistical expertise is imperative to a successful campaign, as winning can come down to how fast, cheaply, and visibly candidates can move across battleground states. "The campaign plane is an important tool to help candidates safely meet with voters and get out their message. Down the homestretch, it becomes a working office and a home away from home," Brunson-Pitts told Business Insider ahead of the midterms. "Our team works behind the scenes coordinating crews, airports, ground transportation, security and last-minute changes so the candidate can keep moving ." Campaigns can rent smaller jets and full-sized airliners Brunson-Pitts' client list spans two decades of election cycles and includes officials from both parties. Beyond Sen. Collins and Rep. Jeffries, 2026 FEC filings show the campaigns of Arkansas Sen. Tom Cotton and West Virginia Sen. Jim Justice also paid AAT for air travel. In 2024, the firm worked with Doug Emhoff, the husband of former Vice President Kamala Harris, and Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz, Harris' 2024 running mate. He has also handled contracts for politicians such as former President Joe Biden, Hillary Clinton, John Kerry, Sen. Bernie Sanders, Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, and "many more." Brunson-Pitts said AAT arranges flights on aircraft ranging from regional jets to full-size airliners: Emhoff traveled on a Bombardier CRJ-200, and Walz used a Boeing 757 in 2024. Biden used a Boeing 737 during his 2020 campaign. The Harris-Walz 2024 campaign plane was a Boeing 757 that had previously flown for the now-defunct New Pacific Airlines. Aimee Dilger/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images The team may modify aircraft inside and out — from changing seat layouts to adding campaign logos — in coordination with design teams and third-party vendors. Branding can range from simple decals to fully repainted liveries . "From Labor Day to Election Day, the travel gets really intense," he said. "So we try to make it a home away from home with WiFi, power, and catering; maybe their favorite food or a meal from their favorite local restaurant." Comfort, however, is only part of the challenge. Security is often the most complex variable. Brunson-Pitts said sitting members of Congress sometimes receive Capitol Police protection, while governors may rely on state details. Most first-time House or Senate candidates, however, hire private security. Democratic presidential candidate Sen. John Edwards (D-NC) chartered a Boeing 737 jet for his campaign in 2004. Shaun Heasley/Getty Images A smaller group of high-profile candidates receives Secret Service protection due to national prominence or credible threats. That can dictate everything from airport choice to how close an aircraft can park to a terminal. events.title: Montana voters take on Citizens United with a ballot initiative to strip corporations and nonprofits of their political spending power
events.summary: Sixteen years ago, the Supreme Court decided in the Citizens United case that corporations have a First Amendment right to spend money to influence elections. On Tuesday, Montana voters will decide whether their state can take that power away.  Initiative 194, also known as the Montana Plan , would strip corporations, trade associations, nonprofits, and other organizations of the legal power to spend money supporting or opposing a political candidate or ballot initiative in Montana. Backers say they’ve found a way around Citizens United, while critics argue the semantics of the ballot initiative still violate the 2010 Supreme Court ruling.  Rather than ban corporate political donations outright, I-194 would change the powers Montana grants to corporations and other entities it refers to as “artificial persons,” limiting them to only those powers that are “necessary and convenient.”  The measure would apply to entities that do business or hold property in Montana, but exempts political action committees (PACs), news and editorial content, and individuals. Organizations that violate this would forfeit the privileges Montana grants them to do business in the state, including limited liability, which protects owners from personal responsibility for business debts. A way around Citizens United At first glance, the language of the ballot initiative looks like it contradicts what Citizens United established—that corporations can spend money on elections. But Tom Moore, a former chief of staff to FEC Commissioner Ellen Weintraub and now senior fellow at the Center for American Progress (who also devised the legal theory behind the Montana Plan), told Fortune that states have authority over what corporations can do through corporate law. “When the state creates a corporation, it is starting from nothing and deciding what to give the corporation, and no case has ever held that they have to give local spending power to a corporation,” Moore said. He said I-194 would no longer grant corporations and nonprofits the ability to spend money on elections, which is different from banning them from exercising an existing right. “It’s not regulation; it’s redefinition,” Moore said.  He said he believes the measure would shut down dark money spending by preventing wealthy donors from hiding behind organizations that don’t disclose their contributors. For instance, a donor can give money to a nonprofit that then funnels it to a PAC, which would report the nonprofit as the donor rather than identifying the person. Moore said I-194 would cut off that route by preventing corporations, nonprofits, and trade associations from political giving, though individuals can still donate. “This is not going to stop Elon Musk from writing a big fat check to some election in Montana,” Moore said. “What it will stop them from doing is laundering the money through a dark money group.” But opponents of the ballot measure say the distinction between banning corporations from political giving and exercising their political rights is blurry. Bradley Smith, a former FEC chairman and professor at Capital University Law School, told Fortune states can’t sidestep the First Amendment by calling political spending a corporate power instead of a right. “The Supreme Court isn’t engaged in a semantic game,” he said.  Smith said states can set rules for corporations, but they can’t make them surrender constitutional protections in exchange for the benefits of incorporation.  “The core centerpiece undoubtedly is we’re going to deny all corporations in the state the right to speak about political affairs and about political candidates, and that’s just going to fail,” he said. Montana’s century-old fight against corporate interests Montana has tried curbing corporate influence in elections before. In 1912, Montanans passed the Corrupt Practices Act by initiative with 76% of the vote , angry at the political power of mining giant Amalgamated Copper, years after the state’s mining magnates, known as the Copper Kings , had bribed state legislators.  The law barred corporations from spending money to influence elections, but the Supreme Court struck down the restriction in American Tradition Partnership v. Bullock in 2012 , ruling that it conflicted with Citizens United.  Montana also isn’t the only state trying to limit corporate influence over elections. Hawaii enacted a law similar to I-194, called Act 11 , in May. It’s now facing two federal lawsuits: one from the U.S. Chamber of Commerce and another from the Grassroot Institute of Hawaii , which the Institute for Free Speech, an organization Smith founded, represents. The cases could help decide whether states can use corporate law to restrict political spending despite Citizens United. Moore expects the issue to go up to the Supreme Court, whether through I-194 or the Hawaii lawsuits. If voters approve I-194, it would take effect Jan. 1, 2027, unless a court blocks it.  This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: A promising new drug could turn the tide against HIV
events.summary: Fla. Governor Projected winner Byron Donalds • R 1 minute ago Wyo. Governor Projected winner Eric Barlow • R 10 minutes ago Election 2026 live results: Democrat Roy Cooper projected to win NC Senate race, flipping seat blue Experts say that a promising drug that offers complete protection against HIV and requires only two shots a year isn't getting to enough people MBARARA, Uganda -- In the red light district in Mbarara, a city in western Uganda known in part for sex tourism, a sex worker named Lisa Mutoni insists on using condoms when men enter her room, to protect her against HIV and other infections. The problem: Some try to remove or tear the condom while having sex. She takes HIV-prevention medication called PrEP, or preexposure prophylaxis, which can come in the form of daily pills or periodic injections. But there’s a new option for her and millions like her — if they could only get it . It’s a drug called lenacapavir that studies have shown can offer nearly complete protection from HIV with just two shots a year. Mutoni said access to lenacapavir would benefit sex workers who sometimes shift elsewhere for months at a time. “If you know that you have that injection for six months, you feel like you are safe,” she said. “And then it is very good, nice because sometimes you can also forget, if it is the pill, you can forget to swallow.” But Mutoni says every time she tries to get what is commonly referred to as “lena,” it's not available. “They tell me that it is finished,” she said. Such is the promise and the frustration with lenacapavir, a drug developed by Gilead Sciences. Other PrEP options, including pills and an every-other-month shot of the drug cabotegravir, are very effective and widely available. But health experts say lenacapavir has the power not just to protect individuals but potentially even turn the tide of the HIV epidemic globally because of its long-lasting effects. But there are not nearly enough doses, in this East African country or the rest of the world. “The rate of growth (of lenacapavir rollout) isn’t fast enough. We need to be getting to the millions pretty soon,” said Andrew Hill, an expert in HIV treatment who is a senior visiting research fellow at the University of Liverpool in northwest England. That may start to change in the coming months. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has just tentatively approved a generic version of lenacapavir that could help speed the production and distribution of the drug to 120 low-income countries at a price of roughly $40 a year, far below the U.S. list price of $28,218. The approval was announced Monday. The hope, according to the Global Fund, is to get it to 3 million people by the end of 2028. Some, including Doctors Without Borders, known by its French initials MSF, say this isn't nearly enough. The group is calling on Gilead to make cheap doses available to more countries and to sell it directly to MSF so it can help protect more people faster. “Gilead says it wants to end the HIV epidemic ‘for everyone, everywhere,’ but its actions say otherwise,” said Melissa Barber, MSF USA global health advocacy and policy adviser, in a recent statement. For now, people in Mbarara, where an estimated 10% of the adult population has HIV — double the rate of Uganda as a whole — have to settle for inferior choices. Julius Bampe, a polygamous man, was alarmed earlier this year when testing confirmed his younger wife had HIV. She was immediately given drugs to suppress her infection, while Bampe sought lenacapavir. Learjet with 9 aboard crashes in Palm Beach County, Florida: FAA Captain identified after deadly Florida Learjet crash 2 college students found dead after going missing while hiking, police say But when Bampe, an itinerant builder, went to get his injection, he found that there were no doses left. “When I got here, they said that is what they would have given me, but they said they didn’t have enough doses for everyone,” he said. The facility that Bampe goes to received 40 lenacapavir doses in April, with instructions to focus only on pregnant mothers at risk of acquiring HIV. The guidelines were later changed to include couples like Bampe and his wife, sex workers and others. That batch was quickly administered and another 70 doses sent in June were used up within 10 days, said Tarsisio Biryeija, a nursing officer working as a counselor at Mbarara Health Centre IV. Uganda has slashed its HIV rate over the past three decades, and it's far below that of some southern African countries. But like in many nations, health authorities in Uganda say infections are driven largely by transactional sexual encounters like those in Mbarara — and the type of transmission that lenacapavir could be so effective at stopping. Mutoni, the sex worker in Mbarara, gets counseling and other support, including condoms, from Immaculate Nyamwija, founder of a Mbarara-based organization known as Action for Improved Health and Wealth.

events.title: I spent years trying to make family vacations perfect. Giving up made them fun again.
events.summary: The author said she always loved traveling and assumed not much would change when she had kids. She now admits she was wrong about one thing. Courtesy of Annabel Lee. I love traveling and was looking forward to bringing my kids along with me when I became a parent. But what we want in a vacation differs, and I spent years feeling exhausted by our family trips. I've changed my expectations for what family vacations should look like, and we're all much happier For years, when people have asked me how my family vacations were, I'd smile and say something along the lines of, "Great, but I need another one to recover." The truth was, while I'd been away to relax and have fun, I usually felt exhausted by the time I got home, thanks to conflicting expectations about what we all wanted to do. My husband, our kids (now 7 and 9), and I have tried trips to hotels in Cornwall, holiday parks in France, and cottages in Wales , but none were what I would describe as restful. Our trip wish lists are very different I adore traveling, and when I had children, I thought I would just bring them along and have similar experiences with them. My favorite trips involved beautiful hotels , European cities, sightseeing, lying on the beach, and long lunches at sidewalk cafes. When I had one baby, this was still fairly easy to accomplish. After all, babies are amenable and don't have strong views on where you go for dinner. We went to Italy and on road trips around the UK, and he wasn't too difficult to travel with. But as he grew into a toddler and we had another child, I realized family vacations would no longer be the same as my pre-children vacations. Our individual needs and ideas of what constitutes a good time differ greatly. While heaven for me is a late dinner and an Aperol spritz while sitting on a Roman street, my kids want pizza at 6 p.m., followed by cartoons back in the hotel room. I'd love a day looking around Pompeii or lying on the Amalfi Coast while they'd prefer to be engaged in soft play somewhere or splashing around in a family-friendly swimming pool. I want architectural arcades; they want arcade games. Vacations became more of an endurance test than a rest I spent years fighting our competing ideas, trying to make my kids fit my ideals of family vacations. They didn't love it. When we were on trips, they didn't want to pose for family photos or sit through pasta dinners at sunset. The author said she would prefer to linger streetside sipping on a cocktail, while her kids want a familiar meal of pizza while on vacation. Courtesy of Annabel Lee. I'd end up stressed out and annoyed that my ideas about what our trips should be like weren't coming to life. They'd be frustrated at having to do things they didn't want to do, like museum trips and sightseeing. None of us were getting what we wanted. This turned family trips into a challenge for all of us, and the experience felt more like an endurance test than a break, with me constantly trying to make things go according to plan I had formed and convince my kids to go along with my ideas. I returned home from our adventures frazzled and feeling like I needed a rest more than when I started. Changing my expectations became the secret to happy family vacations After many years of struggling with this, I have now realized the secret to enjoying my family trip: lowering my expectations. I'm no longer bothered by trying to do it all when we go away or making my kids fit into my ideas of what a trip away should be like. We now prioritize a child-led approach to plans and destinations. I'm happy to book less beautiful hotels and stay in places with pools, early dining options, and family-friendly activities. While I miss the aesthetics, I know that there will be time for gorgeous city breaks when they are older. For now, I'm prioritizing peace, ease, and comfort. This strategy has transformed how we travel, and it means that, for the first time, family trips feel like fun again. They aren't like they were before, but knowing my kids are safe, happy, and having a great time is worth it. I've learned a 6 p.m. pizza and Aperol Spritz can be a little slice of heaven, too. events.title: Binance says fake job interviews used as part of $6.3bn crypto hack
events.summary: Hackers who stole a record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) from Binance used fake job interviews and a compromised internal AI tool, the firm has revealed. Initial findings published by the company, which operates the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, said hackers gained access to its systems through "sophisticated, multi-stage campaign". It said they used a range of techniques such as malicious software downloads to compromise the computers of Binance engineers and gain control over tools to drain its wallet of billions of dollars worth of crypto. Binance called it a "serious and highly sophisticated security incident" and apologised, saying "this should not have happened". In a post on X , external , Binance said hackers targeted its engineers using social engineering techniques. These see hackers use approaches such as phishing to trick people into parting with sensitive or personal details, that can then be used to try and access their accounts. Binance said as part of the hack, one of its engineers was contacted through a legitimate job-hunting platform and invited to bogus job interviews with fake company representatives. It said the perpetrators used "more advanced and deceptive" methods to build trust with him, such as sharing social media accounts that contained personal images. The engineer in question was instructed to download malware masquerading as an "assignment" during a second interview, that deployed malicious code with "obfuscation techniques" evading detection. Binance said hackers then leveraged the engineer's compromised computer and a compromised internal AI tool in October to gain control over two other engineers' laptops, and execute the next steps of the attack. The incident led Binance to suspend withdrawals for customers globally, meaning users could not get their cryptocurrency out of the platform until the service was restored on Sunday. Customers withdrew billions of dollars worth of assets after it reopened . "We apologise for the concern, disruption and uncertainty it caused our users, partners and the wider industry," it said. The company added it had taken a range of steps following the incident, including working with law enforcement to trace and freeze affected assets. It said it had also set aside more than 100% of the funds needed to cover the loss, noting 98% of the token assets impacted had been "replenished" as of Saturday. The record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) attack is thought to be the largest crypto hack to date . What we know about the $6.3bn Binance hack US crime agencies, including the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and Secret Service, have been assisting Binance in tracing the crypto taken from the platform's own wallets. The agencies, along with a range of cyber analysts, said that the hack - like similar breaches before it - bore the signs of having been orchestrated by North Korea. Pyongyang hit back at the claims on Tuesday , denying it was behind the hack. Kim Yo Jong, a top Democratic People's Republic of Korea official and the sister of leader Kim Jong Un, said on the accusations were another "sinister attempt" by the US to damage North Korea's public image. The country has consistently denied being behind a number of major cyber attacks it has been blamed for in recent years. The TraderTraitor unit, which is also known as the Lazarus Group, was blamed for a then-record $1.5bn hack of crypto exchange Bybit in 2025 . Binance had previously not responded to the BBC's queries about North Korea's alleged involvement in the hack. But on Tuesday, the company wrote in its post on X , external : "The latest information released by the Federal Bureau of Investigation indicates that the Democratic People's Republic of Korea is responsible for this incident." As part of its security efforts following the attack, Binance said it would also increase investment in AI tools that can detect security threats, as well as engage third-party cyber experts to carry out a full-scale review of the incident. It also said that it would seek to stablish a security research fund and work with leading AI and security firms on targeted initiatives. events.title: America's tech elite are holding their breath as they await California's billionaire tax vote
events.summary: Californians are voting on a proposal that could send a one-time, huge tax bill to the state's billionaires. Lester Cohen/Getty Images Californians are debating how to tax their ultra-rich neighbors. Silicon Valley is sweating it. It could bring in $100 billion to plug a coming Medicare hole — or lose billions in tax revenue. The debate has created fresh political and tech exec divides. Tune in to the latest episode of "How to Tax a Billionaire: California Edition" — it's filled with drama, tech celebrities, and there's a big pot of money at stake! Today, Californians are heading to the polls, where they'll be asked to answer "Yes" or "No" to Proposition 40, which would impose a one-time "5% tax on certain taxpayers with assets over $1 billion." The vote has started a showdown that's been shaking up Silicon Valley executives for months. Google cofounder Sergey Brin , former Google CEO Eric Schmidt, Affirm CEO Max Levchin, Stripe CEO Patrick Collison, DoorDash CEO Tony Xu, Kleiner Perkins Chairman John Doerr, and angel investor Chris Larsen have collectively poured millions into an opposition campaign . Brin himself has donated more than $100 million to the "No" team, per Cal Matters. State campaign-finance filings show committees opposing Prop. 40 had reported about $130 million in contributions through October 22, versus about $33 million for its supporters. Meanwhile, other tech executives are preparing, just in case they have to pay up. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg weighed moving out of the state. In October, the company created a new class of shares that would give Zuckerberg $20 billion in "immediate liquidity" if the vote passes — potentially allowing him to pay the tax without giving up some of his voting power. "I've got to tell you, I have not even thought about it once," Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia, said during a January spot on Bloomberg TV. "We chose to live in Silicon Valley, and whatever taxes they would like to apply, so be it. I'm perfectly fine with it." The vote has also split some regular political alliances. Progressive Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders has backed the billionaire tax, while California's Democratic governor, Gavin Newsom, opposes the measure. There are multiple paths to "No" If a majority of voters fill in the "Yes" bubble on Prop 40, roughly 200 people who were California residents on January 1, 2026, could face the one-time tax. That vote has two lurking trap doors — propositions 41 and 42 could ruin the "Yes" team's finale. Both countermeasures were designed to undercut Prop. 40 by imposing new auditor reviews and prohibiting taxes on certain assets. If either measure receives more yes votes than Prop. 40, the billionaire tax could be stopped from taking effect, even if a majority of Californians vote for it. What California's billionaires could owe In broad terms, the measure would tax billionaires based on more than their salary. Taxable wealth would include ownership stakes in businesses, securities, investment accounts, art, collectibles, and intellectual property, among other assets. Real estate, pensions, and retirement accounts would generally be excluded. If the billionaire tax passes, it'll be due in 2027 — though taxpayers could spread out their payments across five years at a higher cost. Supporters say the measure could raise tens of billions of dollars over several years. A majority of the proceeds would go toward healthcare, with the remainder allocated to education, food assistance, and the operation of the tax program. The campaign has pitched the measure as a way to help backfill looming federal cuts to Medi-Cal. Overall, Prop. 40 backers have said the tax event would raise over $100 billion for the state. A National Bureau of Economic Research working paper from Stanford economists, published in October, warned that the results could be much less rosy . The initial tax event could bring in around $30 billion before prompting high-earning executives to leave the state, the paper said. That could lose California $38.9 billion over time, the paper warned. Read the original article on Business Insider

AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Customers left wondering what's been compromised after vendor advises resetting passwords, 2FA and passkeys 'Password1' and a forgotten test account land Welsh outfits in hot water 14 days ago '123456' password linked to Denmark data breach affecting 8.8M people 21 days ago UK.gov begins killing off passwords for 23 million users September 14, 2026 IT department put sticky notes on the laptops to help employees log in August 6, 2026 Law firm insisted on one password to rule them all July 16, 2026 Password manager mSecure has warned customers to change their passwords, reset two-factor authentication, and potentially remove their passkeys after detecting suspicious activity, but it has not explained what happened or whether anyone's secrets were exposed. In an email sent to customers on November 3, seen by The Register , US-based developer mSeven Software said it launched an investigation after discovering something amiss with its password management application. "mSeven Software ('mSeven') recently learned of suspicious activity associated with the mSecure password management application," the company wrote. "In response, mSeven quickly launched an investigation, took steps to mitigate the issue, and engaged external cybersecurity experts to assist." The company has yet to answer what the suspicious activity involved, when it occurred, or whether attackers accessed customer information. Its advice to customers, however, suggests that they should take this seriously. "Given the potential security implications, mSeven recommends that you immediately take steps to protect all confidential information stored within the mSecure password management application," the email continued. "This may include changing passwords, resetting or re-enrolling two-factor authentication methods, or removing existing passkeys." For anyone with hundreds of passwords stored in mSecure, that's potentially hours of work. And without knowing what happened, customers have no way of telling which credentials they actually need to replace. The warning has understandably gone down poorly with customers, who have taken to mSecure's support forum demanding answers. "Please provide more context to your email below advising there has been a security breach," one customer wrote. "It is not acceptable to offer the vague advice 'take steps'. Please state what remedial action is required, and what data was compromised." Others are wondering whether they're expected to spend the next several days changing every password they've ever saved. "I have over 800 passwords in mSecure, is the email saying I need to change all of them!" another customer asked. A separate user, who said they had more than 500 passwords stored in the application, questioned whether the warning applied to every two-factor authentication method and passkey associated with their accounts, or just those used to access mSecure itself. The confusion has also spilled onto Reddit , where customers have shared copies of the vague notification and questioned what might have happened. mSeven has yet to respond to The Register 's questions, leaving customers to guess whether their data has actually been compromised or the company is simply being cautious. That's not exactly reassuring from a business whose entire purpose is keeping other people's secrets safe. The company's email concludes: "We regret any inconvenience that this may cause." For customers contemplating hundreds of password resets, "inconvenience" may be putting it mildly.

events.title: UEFI bootkit infected fully patched Windows machines. Is Microsoft to blame?
events.summary: In 2023, malware tracked as BlackLotus became the first publicly documented in-the-wild UEFI bootkit capable of bypassing Secure Boot on fully updated Windows 11 systems. With the industry-wide chain-of-trust mechanism subverted, the malware was able to run malicious code before Windows was fully loaded and many security defenses were operational. Microsoft had already patched the vulnerability that BlackLotus exploited in 2022. In 2023 and 2024, Microsoft issued additional updates. The first added a new certificate that no longer trusted the vulnerable boot managers. The second provided the means to revoke trust in the digital certificate used to sign older vulnerable Windows boot managers. The organizations infected by the new bootkit, which is tracked under the name BlackX, had installed all of these patches. So how did they fall victim? UEFI bootkit refresher Before discussing the incident further, a brief review of BlackLotus and UEFI malware is in order. Short for Unified Extensible Firmware Interface , UEFI is firmware that runs immediately after a computer is turned on. One of its main jobs is to load system configuration settings, identify and initialize hardware components, and prepare the computer to start its OS. Read full article Comments

Yet voters are headed to the polls Tuesday largely gloomy over an economy beset by higher prices . U.S. job openings jumped to 7.5 million from a revised 7.19 million in August, the Labor Department reported Tuesday . It is the largest number of openings since May and up from a recent low of 6.9 million in March. The department’s Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey (JOLTS) also showed that gross hiring — job gains before subtracting people who quit or lost jobs — rose and layoffs fell in September. The increases are a hopeful sign that hiring could improve, but the trend would have to continue for several months to suggest real improvement. Hiring has been sluggish for nearly three years, though layoffs have also been historically low, a sign of meager “churn” in the labor market. Low churn means those who are employed are enjoying relatively high levels of job security, but it is much harder than normal for those looking for work to find a job. The government will issue the October jobs report on Friday, which is forecast to show that employers added 65,000 positions last month, according to data provider FactSet. That would be an improvement from 29,000 in September. The unemployment rate is expected to stay at a low 4.2%. events.title: GhostBSD 26.2 takes the fright out of FreeBSD with a friendlier installer
events.summary: GhostBSD, the easiest-to-install flavor of FreeBSD for the daemon-curious desktop dabbler, is back with a fresh update. GhostBSD 26.2-R15.1p6 , to give it its slightly unwieldy full version number, is based on FreeBSD 15.1. It brings a new installer, full-disk encryption support, a smaller installation image, and fixes across its desktop tools. FreeBSD 15.1 was released back in June , and at the time of writing, it's the most recent point release of FreeBSD. The original plan was that FreeBSD 15.1 would include the option of installing KDE Plasma directly from the setup program, so that the OS would have a graphical desktop from its very first boot. However, this feature isn't ready just yet. That gap inspired Daemonarchy, which we covered late last month . But its Omarchy-derived, keyboard-driven tiling desktop can feel unfamiliar even to experienced Linux users accustomed to conventional desktops. GhostBSD has different goals. It brings Linux-like desktop convenience to FreeBSD: a live graphical environment to explore before installation, a graphical installer, and tools for managing software and updates. These conveniences are familiar to desktop Linux users, but a standard FreeBSD installation takes more work. Its text-mode installer leaves users to install and configure a graphical desktop themselves, if they want one. This is just how the BSD family does things, and most BSD users we've talked to regard it as standard operating procedure and see nothing wrong with it. For Linux users who are curious about how things are on the other side of the FOSS Unix fence, though, those extra steps can form formidable barriers. GhostBSD is an attempt to lay down a welcome mat. The standard edition of GhostBSD installs the MATE desktop, and the downloads page also offers a community-maintained version with Xfce instead. As the project said it would back in February, this release uses the XLibre fork of the X.org X11 server. That's one fewer desktop than when we last tried GhostBSD in August 2025 . That release also offered the Mac OS X-like Gershwin environment. There are practical hardware fixes too. The release notes list improvements for Intel AX200 Wi-Fi cards, open networks, password alerts, and non-ASCII network names, while USB HID support is enabled by default. Where has Gershwin gone? Gershwin remains in active development , so we asked project lead Joe Maloney why it wasn't included. "It has been difficult to find time to package for GhostBSD. It's the only distro I have ever packaged for," Maloney said. He added that rapid contributions from AppImage creator Simon Peter, known as probono, had made packaging increasingly difficult. He also pointed to the fact that GhostBSD project lead Eric Turgeon is developing his own environment too: the Mocka desktop . Mocka is still in its very early stages – alpha version 0.0.2 appeared early last month – but the plan is that when it's ready, it will become GhostBSD's default desktop. For now, the only available module is a dock for the MATE desktop, but the curious can follow its development on the GitHub project page . There may be no Gershwin included, but GhostBSD 26.2 offers MATE 1.28, and there's also a community-supported version with Xfce 4.20 instead. We tried the default MATE edition, and it works as well as ever. It defaults to a dark theme and the classic two-panel GNOME 2 desktop layout. The System menu in the top panel has an Administration submenu with a few of the project's own apps that aren't from upstream FreeBSD: "BE Station" for managing system boot environments, "Software Station" for browsing and installing applications, and "Update Station" for updates. We regularly hear from users growing tired of the Linux vendors' headlong rush into Rust, Wayland, systemd, containerized app formats, and so on. Some are curious about whether FreeBSD offers a usable alternative. GhostBSD is the easiest way to get a complete, ready-to-use graphical FreeBSD desktop. There is a price to pay for switching to FreeBSD: for a start, most proprietary Linux apps, from Chrome to Slack, are not available here. Hardware compatibility needs more checking than on mainstream Linux, especially with recent GPUs and Wi-Fi adapters. If Windows gaming is a priority, this isn't the obvious choice. But if you can live without those proprietary apps and find suitable open source replacements, FreeBSD is a viable alternative – and GhostBSD takes much of the setup work out of trying it. ®

events.title: AI Is Changing How Semiconductor Fabs Work — and Engineers Are Moving Faster Because of It
events.summary: Your browser doesn't support HTML5 video. Here is a link to the video instead. Demand for advanced chips is rising. The processes to build them are getting more complex. And the margin for error is shrinking. For engineers, understanding how a process change will behave, how a material will interact with a new step, how a defect maps back to a root cause are critical, challenging steps in semiconductor manufacturing — and these analyses can take days. Physical experiments on a fab line are slow and expensive. A wrong call on yield or process quality has real consequences. AI is transforming semiconductor manufacturing, impacting what engineers can do — and how fast. Accelerated computing shortens simulation time, allowing engineers to evaluate more alternatives before committing to physical trials. Physics-based AI helps engineers predict process behavior without running a full simulation every time. AI agents handle sequences of engineering tasks that once consumed hours. And digital twins let teams test changes in a virtual environment before committing to physical trials. Together, these capabilities describe an AI-defined fab: a semiconductor manufacturing factory where AI helps engineers optimize processes, catch problems earlier and make better decisions across the full manufacturing chip lifecycle. Engineers direct the work and make decisions based on their expertise while spending less time waiting for answers. Shorter Simulation Cycles Change What Engineers Can Explore Accelerated computing doesn’t just speed up individual calculations — it changes how many alternatives engineers can test before committing. Multiphysics simulations model interactions among physical effects, such as heat transfer, electrical behavior and mechanical stress. Using the NVIDIA cuDSS library, multiphysics software provider COMSOL is accelerating such simulations for semiconductor manufacturing by up to 10x. This helps engineers optimize equipment and processes, compare alternatives and decide which changes to test physically. Applied Materials and NVIDIA are collaborating to accelerate atomic-scale materials discovery and process development. By integrating NVIDIA cuDSS, Applied’s Ginestra simulation platform runs up to 10x faster than CPU-only approaches. And with NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo, Applied’s ACE+ multiphysics platform delivers topography simulations up to 35x faster. In some cases, acceleration doesn’t just shorten the calculation — it enables it altogether. Computational lithography — which defines how circuit patterns are printed onto silicon — involves calculations too intensive to complete on CPU at production scale. Siemens is integrating NVIDIA cuLitho into its Calibre lithography software, delivering up to 17x acceleration on key simulation workloads. That expands what engineers can verify before a wafer goes to print. As such, faster calculations can help researchers explore material behavior and reaction pathways that influence next-generation semiconductor processes. Predicting Process Behavior Without Running Every Simulation In addition to accelerating simulations, AI trained on physics can predict how materials and processes will behave — without running a full simulation each time. The payoff is most visible in complex calculations that are expensive even on accelerated hardware. Plasma — the electrically charged gas used in semiconductor etch processes — is one example. Modeling plasma behavior requires solving equations that capture how electrical, chemical and thermal processes interact, making repeated simulation costly. Lam Research demonstrated that the NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo framework can predict plasma behavior in milliseconds, compared with days for a full simulation — giving engineers a faster way to explore process conditions without rerunning the full model each time. Agents Handle the Steps Between Decisions Engineers turn analyses into decisions — revising a design, investigating a test failure, adjusting a production process and more. AI agents can help carry out the steps between those decisions. Evaluating which AI model to apply to a given task is one example: a sequential, manual process that can consume hours on the test floor. Advantest is using NVIDIA NeMo Switchyard AI agents to automate that selection, reducing response times from hours to minutes. Testing Factory Changes Before They Reach the Line Digital twins let teams simulate equipment configurations, layouts and process changes in a virtual environment before committing to physical trials. This reduces experimentation costs, especially as fabs become more complex and the stakes of a wrong change get higher. Applied Materials uses NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to build physically accurate digital twins of entire fabs. Teams can simulate material movement, identify bottlenecks and evaluate layouts and operating strategies — extending virtual experimentation beyond individual processes to how the factory works as a whole. The future of semiconductor manufacturing lies in connecting these capabilities: using production data to inform models and models to evaluate changes, then bringing those findings back to the engineers making production decisions. That’s the promise of the AI-defined fab: where AI helps people learn from each production cycle and act on that knowledge sooner. events.title: What's happening to UK interest rates and what does it mean for mortgages?
events.summary: Policymakers at the Bank of England are expected to raise UK interest rates for the first time in more than three years at their next meeting. Most analysts believe the Bank rate will go up from 3.75% to 4%, following holds at the previous six meetings. Before the US and Israel launched strikes against Iran in February, rates had been expected to fall this year, but the economic fallout from the conflict has pushed up inflation across the globe. Interest rates affect mortgage, credit card and savings rates for millions of people. What are interest rates and why do they change? An interest rate tells you how much it costs to borrow money, or the reward for saving it. The Bank of England's base rate is what it charges other banks and building societies to borrow money, which influences what they charge their own customers for mortgages as well as the interest rate they pay on savings. The Bank moves its base rate up and down in order to keep UK inflation — the rate at which prices are increasing — at or near 2%. When inflation is above that target, the Bank typically puts rates up. The idea is to encourage people to spend less, reducing demand for goods and services and limiting price rises. What is happening to UK interest rates and inflation? The Bank of England's base rate rose to 5.25% in August 2023. It remained at that level until August 2024, when the Bank started cutting. Five cuts brought rates down to 4%, before the Bank held rates at its meetings in September and November 2025. It then cut in December 2025 before holding rates steady in January, March, April, June, July and September 2026. Meanwhile, the main UK inflation measure, CPI, has fallen significantly since the October 2022 high of 11.1%, which was caused by Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. However, the rate has been heading back up and is expected to go higher. It was 3.5% in the year to September 2026 , up from 3.1% the previous month and well above the central bank's 2% target. The Office for National Statistics (ONS), which tracks UK inflation, blamed the acceleration on sharp rises in petrol and diesel prices. The US-Israel war with Iran has put up energy and fuel costs around the world, which has increased the pace of price rises more generally. What is happening to UK prices? Published 21 October What is expected to happen to UK interest rates? At the start of the year, the Bank had been expected to cut interest rates twice in 2026, with the first drop predicted to come in March or April. However, the increase in fuel prices and inflation after the outbreak of the conflict has upended all of this. Oil prices initially rose sharply as a result of disruption to supplies in the region, but dropped back when various ceasefires were agreed. Oil prices rose again when the US and Iran resumed attacks in the Strait of Hormuz in July. UK household energy bills rose after the increases in the price cap in July and October, while global oil prices have risen again recently. Given the uncertainty, many analysts think UK interest rates will rise at the November meeting and again early next year. What will the energy cap changes mean for my bills? Published 28 September Why are UK fuel prices rising again? Published 2 October How do interest rate changes affect mortgages, loans and savings rates? Just under a third of households have a mortgage, according to the government's English Housing Survey , external . About 500,000 homeowners have a mortgage that "tracks" the Bank of England's rate. Any rise in the Bank rate means an increase in the monthly repayments on their outstanding loan. For a typical loan, the cost would go up by about £31 a month if the Bank raises the base rate by 0.25 percentage points, but it depends on the size of people's loans. An additional 500,000 homeowners on standard variable rates (SVRs) would wait to see if their lender chose to pass on any Bank rate rise. Typically, this would mean a £14 increase per month in repayments for a 0.25 percentage points rates rise. But the vast majority of mortgage customers - some 87% - have fixed-rate deals. While their monthly payments aren't immediately affected by a rate change, their future deals are. Most lenders have already priced in a rise in the Bank rate in November, so this is already reflected in the rates being offered. As of 3 November, the average two-year fixed residential mortgage rate was at 5.97%, while the average five-year rate stood at 5.99%, according to financial information service Moneyfacts. The average two-year tracker rate was 4.67%. About 800,000 fixed-rate mortgages with an interest rate of 3% or below are expected to expire every year, on average, until the end of 2027. Borrowing costs for customers coming off those deals are likely to rise sharply. You can see how your mortgage may be affected by future interest rate changes by using our calculator: How much could my mortgage payments change?

The Ivy League institution first confirmed the attack, later claimed by ShinyHunters, in November 2025, although HIBP gave the first indication about how many people may have been affected by the breach for the first time today. Run by venerable infoseccer Troy Hunt, HIBP ingested all the files and revealed that the types of data stolen from the university extended beyond the personal and donation information it referenced in its initial disclosure. According to HIBP, the 850,000+ figure pertains to unique email addresses found in the data dump. The following data points may not have been collected about each and every individual, but are included in the stolen files: Harvard did not immediately respond to our requests for more information. Its disclosure at the time described the attack as an instance of "phone-based phishing" that targeted its Alumni Affairs and Development department, leading to unauthorized access to its systems. It did not specify the attacker by name, although ShinyHunters claimed responsibility for the intrusion on the same day it listed the University of Pennsylvania on its leak site. The group claimed to have stolen more than 1 million records from Harvard and 1.2 million from Penn. In Penn's case, HIBP pegged the total number of affected individuals at around 623,800, based on unique email addresses, although additional data types such as donations, personally identifiable information, religions, and more were affected. ShinyHunters' raid on Harvard systems came around a month after the university probed a separate attack by Cl0p , which at the time was on a tear exploiting a zero-day in Oracle’s E-Business Suite. The impact from that attack was limited to a small amount of data at a small administrative unit, however. Earlier this year, Harvard was also affected by ShinyHunters for the second time in the space of a few months after the cybercriminals attacked Instructure, the EdTech vendor behind learning platform Canvas. events.title: Apple restricts dating apps and AI companions to users 18 and up
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. Apple is adjusting its App Store policies to make it more difficult for minors to use online dating apps or AI companions that engage in “sexual or romantic content,” the tech giant shared in an announcement to developers on Monday. The new rules follow other changes the company has made to better protect minors, which include the rollout of its age assurance technology globally and more parental controls and child safety features . While most major dating services typically restrict their platform to adults, Apple’s new policy will require all apps offering dating or romantic relationship features to carry an 18+ rating. Starting November 16, developers will be required to include new content descriptors to ensure their app’s age ratings reflect its features, the company said. It’s perhaps more interesting how this rule could impact AI companion apps, or those where such functionality is one of many features. Often targeted at younger people, Character.AI, Replika, and other AI apps let people create AI companions, including friends, lovers, boyfriends and girlfriends, and other fantasy characters. xAI last year also launched 3D animated AI companions that allowed users to unlock NSFW capabilities . As of last summer, top AI companion apps across the Apple App Store and Google Play had been downloaded 220 million times globally . In addition to “dating and relationships,” apps will also need to indicate if they are sharing the real-world locations of a user with another person or group as part of their functionality. Any app doing so raises obvious privacy concerns, especially if the user wasn’t aware that their location was being shared. The company noted that in Brazil, apps that provide location-sharing features for families can request an official rating from the government’s Ministry of Justice and Public Security (MJSP/Ministério da Justiça e Segurança Pública), instead of being required to list them with the A16 rating, as the local law requires. events.title: Prediction markets have a lot riding on the blue wave
events.summary: Prediction markets like Kalshi and Polymarket officially don't care which side of a bet wins. There is no "house." They get their cut either way. It's a business model that's attracted billions of VC dollars. Yes, but: Kalshi and Polymarket should be pulling hard for Democrats in today's midterm elections. Even if that feels counterintuitive. Catch up quick: Prediction markets burst into the public consciousness two years ago, when their users correctly "picked" Donald Trump to beat Kamala Harris. It bestowed credibility at a time when public trust in traditional polling had cratered. Fast forward: More recently, however, they had electoral misses in Brazil and Israel. Three would be a trend. Both platforms currently have markets on Democrats sweeping Congress, with "yes" at around 75%. If that's how today plays out, it would further cement prediction market legitimacy. A Republican win in either chamber, however, would dump them into the same pot as pollsters — even if 75% probability includes a sizable improbability. Zoom in: Democrats are often more hostile to prediction markets than are Republicans, but companies like Kalshi and Polymarket don't have too much to fear from a Democrat-controlled Congress. Yes, there would probably be an uncomfortable hearing or two. But neither chamber would have veto-proof majorities, and the Trump administration has been very sympathetic to the industry. The real constraints, if any, are more likely to come via the Supreme Court. The bottom line: Political predictions generate much less revenue for Kalshi and Polymarket than do sports predictions, but they have a much longer tail.

events.title: Binance says fake job interviews and internal AI tool used in $6.3bn heist
events.summary: Cryptocurrency platform Binance has said fake job interviews and an internal artificial intelligence tool were used for the massive $6.3 billion breach it reported last week. The culprit leveraged the compromised computer of one of its engineers and used an AI tool to gain control of the wallets of two other engineers, Binance said in a post on Tuesday. That was “used as a springboard” on October 20, as “the attackers combined a range of techniques, including social engineering by fake recruitment interviews, malicious software downloads, compromised internal AI tooling, endpoint compromise and an advanced transaction-authorisation method”, the company said. Preparations for the theft stretched as far back as June, traced to a supply chain attack in which an engineer downloaded a tampered Homebrew installation to install a popular AI coding tool after finding it on a search engine, Binance said. Homebrew is software that allows users to easily install apps, particularly for Apple's macOS and Linux. Binance did not identify the AI coding tool and the search engine that were used. https://t.co/sU9dUqLQDH — Binance (@binance) November 3, 2026 By September, Binance had determined a social engineering attack – one in which someone is deceived into revealing sensitive information – hit one of its engineers through a legitimate job-hunting platform, with someone posing as a project director. It culminated in instructing the engineer to download an “assignment” that contained a malicious code, Binance said. Binance also said it has taken measures to protect its systems, including rebuilding the affected wallet system in a new environment and internal AI tools and access controls. It has also replaced affected devices and decommissioned credentials and tokens related to the affected engineers, and continues to work with law enforcement, blockchain intelligence companies and industry partners to trace and freeze the affected assets. Further action includes independent cybersecurity reviews with independent third-party experts to study the incident, expanded investment in AI security and prevention, and working on a security research fund and other industry initiatives to protect against such attacks. “We will continue to strengthen our measures as the investigation progresses,” Binance said. “There are a number of security measures we have implemented and are implementing that will remain private to prevent malicious actors from compromising our security.” Binance lost an estimated $6.3 billion to hackers last Friday, in what has been described as the single biggest theft of crypto on record, exceeding the $1.5 billion stolen from Bybit in February 2025 . The company, founded by Changpeng Zhao, previously said it would absorb the financial impact of the stolen funds rather than passing the losses on to customers. It resumed withdrawals on Sunday as investigations were under way. The FBI on Saturday attributed the attack to TraderTraitor , a North Korean state-sponsored hacking unit. Members of the group were observed by law enforcement converting the stolen assets into ether, the FBI said in a statement, adding that it expected further laundering through related technology.

events.title: Energy companies brace for new Iran tension as cost of resilience mounts
events.summary: Energy companies operating in the Middle East are preparing for another potential escalation in the Iran war, with executives warning that keeping businesses running through conflict comes at a growing financial cost. Speaking to The National at Adipec in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday, industry leaders said they are now better prepared after months of adapting to disrupted supply chains. They have stockpiled critical supplies, shifted transportation routes and reduced workforces to withstand further disruption. Several executives said that resilience comes at a cost. Their comments came after the US struck Iran's Qeshm Island on Monday night, targeting a missile launcher after an American drone was brought down near the Strait of Hormuz. The attack raised new concerns about renewed regional fighting , as Americans headed to the polls for midterm elections that could influence Washington's next moves in the conflict. For energy companies, the question is no longer simply whether another escalation will occur but how long they can sustain operations if it does. Sherif Foda, chief executive of energy services firm NESR, said his company had continued operating throughout the conflict by relying on domestic employees and maintaining sufficient supplies to withstand prolonged logistical disruption. “We will be able to continue to operate as long as our clients are operating,” he said. “We are not going to evacuate. We are staying.” Mr Foda said the company had adopted a 30, 60 and 90-day contingency strategy, stockpiling spare parts, chemicals and other essential materials inside countries where it operates. The strategy allowed NESR to maintain operations even when international supply routes became unreliable. “I am insisting on having a local workforce,” Mr Foda said. “You have to really look at the localisation as a must, not as a nice to have.” Cost of survival While some businesses have maintained operations, others have been forced to make difficult financial decisions. Youssou Jules Diop, executive director of Senegalese engineering and procurement company Helix SEN, said the conflict had already forced his company to cut 30 per cent of its management team. The company maintains its treasury, board and key decision-making functions in the UAE, which Mr Diop described as an important hub for African businesses. “The ABC of business is trust and confidence,” he said. The financial pressure extends across the energy industry, particularly for companies dependent on maritime transport through the Strait of Hormuz . Bruno Placha, a senior quality and regulatory professional, said the initial disruption had severely affected operations as vessels stopped entering the region. “If we don't have vessels, we don't have work,” he said. The threat to shipping remains acute. The International Maritime Organisation said on Monday that at least 125 vessels had been attacked in and around the Strait of Hormuz since the war began, including 34 in October, the highest monthly figure so far. Companies have since adapted by using alternative ports and moving more materials by road than by sea, Mr Placha said. The adjustments have also involved workforce reductions and a greater focus on longer-term projects, allowing businesses to operate with less dependence on regular shipping movements. George Alexopoulos, deputy chief executive of Greece's HELLENiQ Energy Holdings, said maintaining alternative supply arrangements had become essential, even when they were expensive. After the conflict disrupted crude shipments from Basra in Iraq, the company turned to the North Sea, the US and West Africa for replacement supplies. “Optionality has a cost and especially at times of crisis,” Mr Alexopoulos said. He cited tanker charter rates on Gulf routes to China reaching $1 million a day as an example of the extraordinary expenses companies face. “What is the alternative? Shut down your operations, so you have to go on.” His comments echo concerns raised at Adipec on Monday , when Minister of Industry and Advanced Technology and Adnoc managing director and group chief executive, Dr Sultan Al Jaber, called for stronger energy infrastructure and diversified supply routes as shipping costs surged. Prepared but vulnerable Despite the industry adjustments, executives warn that another prolonged escalation could expose vulnerabilities that cannot be resolved quickly. Robin Mills, chief executive of Qamar Energy, said companies had made significant progress in rerouting logistics, expanding port capacity, and using road and rail networks. But it is not enough for long-term resilience. “There's a limit to what can be done in the space of eight months,” he said. Major infrastructure projects can take years to complete, leaving energy facilities and shipping routes exposed to further attacks. Nevertheless, he said energy companies remained active, with growing demand for maintenance, repairs, security and infrastructure development. That resilience comes as the UAE continues to emphasise the importance of avoiding another round of conflict, while remaining prepared for further escalation . For Mr Alexopoulos, even an immediate end to hostilities would not bring an immediate return to normal business conditions. He warned that damaged infrastructure, refinery disruptions and shipping shortages could take several weeks to begin normalising, while a full recovery could take years. His biggest lesson for companies navigating an increasingly unpredictable energy market was straightforward. “Keep options. Develop and maintain options. Options have a cost, but in this environment you have to pay the 'option premium' in order to be able to handle this and the next and the next crisis,” he said. Salma Arafa contributed to this report.
