events.title: Listing review process to come fully under SGX RegCo in move to speed up listings
events.summary: From Jan 4, 2027, SGX RegCo will review the listing documents submitted by prospective issuers seeking to list on the mainboard and Global Listing Board. SGX RegCo will take over listing document reviews from Jan 4, 2027, aiming to approve complete applications within six to eight weeks and make Singapore listings faster. Issuers will submit prospectus and listing applications through one portal. MAS keeps exemption powers, while SGX RegCo handles the main review. The change follows consultation support from law firms and issue managers. SGX RegCo says it will keep improving the process and seek more market feedback. SINGAPORE – Singapore’s stock market exchange regulator will take over the review of the listing process, and commits to processing complete applications within six to eight weeks. The move, announced on Nov 3, follows a month-long consultation that ended on Nov 29, 2025, as well as a review group’s recommendations to simplify the listing process and encourage more companies to go public in Singapore. From Jan 4, 2027, Singapore Exchange Regulation (SGX RegCo) will review the listing documents submitted by prospective issuers seeking to list on the mainboard and Global Listing Board (GLB). The GLB lets eligible companies valued at $2 billion or more list on SGX and NASDAQ at the same time, using a single set of offering documents. Previously, prospective issuers had to engage SGX RegCo on their suitability to list and separately submit their listing documents to the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) for review under a much longer process. Issuers will now submit both the prospectus and listing application to SGX RegCo via the regulator’s electronic submissions portal, which will serve as a central interface for reviews, document tracking and regulatory correspondence. Having a single touchpoint is expected to streamline the review process for applications while maintaining review quality, said SGX Re gCo. MAS will retain the power to determine and grant exemptions from prospectus disclosure requirements and will continue to oversee the regulatory responsibilities performed by SGX RegCo. Steps have been taken to ensure SGX RegCo is equipped and adequately resourced for its expanded responsibilities. These include broadening the range of qualified individuals who may be appointed as SGX RegCo directors, thereby incorporating a more diverse range of industry perspectives and insights at the board level. “Ensuring appropriate safeguards to maintain the independence of SGX RegCo board’s judgment will remain our priority,” SGX RegCo said. The regulator will also disband the Listings Advisory Committee (LAC). The LAC predates SGX RegCo, which was etablished to carry out the exchange’s regulatory duties independently of its commercial operations. SGX RegCo chief executive Tan Boon Gin said the changes will enable greater regulatory certainty for companies seeking to list on the SGX. “Singapore investors have become more sophisticated, and they have access to more information of higher quality. Equity investing has also become much more global in nature. This requires an evolution of our philosophies and roles,” he said in a statement. He added that under the exchange’s new disclosure-based approach, SGX RegCo will focus on ensuring that companies give investors the information they need to assess for themselves the merits of investing in a stock. Respondents to the consultation – comprising law firms and issue managers – were supportive of the changes, citing a more streamlined listing process, reduced regulatory touchpoints for issuers and improved market efficiency and competitiveness. At the same time, many highlighted the need for continual process improvements driven by ongoing market engagement, and the importance of accessing practitioner expertise in SGX RegCo’s work. SGX RegCo will therefore be solicit ing feedback from market participants as the changes are made and will assess the need for further enhancements. Robson Lee, director at Kennedys Law, noted that while having a consolidated gateway to review and process listing applications will expedite the process and shorten the time to market , “whether more and better issuers will be attracted to list on the Singapore bourse will primarily depend on valuations and liquidity, post-IPO”. Lee welcomed the regulator’s assurance that faster reviews would preserve listing standards and the requirement for full and accurate disclosures so investors can make informed decisions. Tan Kian Tiong, chief operating officer at SAC Capital, said the streamlining of initial public offering listing reviews under SGX RegCo is a “positive and practical step towards making Singapore’s capital markets more accessible and efficient”. He added that a more efficient review process will allow companies to better plan their fund-raising strategies and respond to market opportunities.

events.summary: Security All Security Cyber-crime Patches Research CSO Off-Prem All Off-Prem Edge and IoT Channel PaaS and IaaS SaaS On-Prem All On-Prem Systems Storage Networks HPC Personal Tech Cx0 Public Sector Software All Software AI and ML Applications Databases DevOps OS Platforms Virtualization Offbeat All Offbeat Columnists Anthropic BOFH Legal Site News About Us Special Features All Special Features Supercomputing Month 2026 Nvidia GTC Berlin 2026 Cybersecurity Month 2026 VMware Explore 2026 Cloud Infrastructure Month 2026 HPE: AI Explainers Agentic AI The Future of the Datacenter AWS:Reinvent Nvidia GTC Computex 2026 AI Infrastructure Month 2026 The State of Storage 2026 RSA Conference Vendor Voice All Vendor Voice Modernizing Financial Services with FIS and AWS Barco Infinidat Everpure Rubrik Make it real with Capgemini and AWS Money Movement Hub ZTE Nutanix: Scale Kubernetes. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Memory crunch pushes 16GB Pi 5 to $385, more than triple its launch price, just a month after the last round of hikes Microsoft improves Windows 11 performance on 8 GB PCs as RAM prices keep climbing 3 hours ago Apple's Mac business is booming, but the memory market has other plans 12 hours ago PC chip plunge wipes out a quarter of Intel’s value 4 days ago Traces of new Pi hardware spotted in GitHub 5 days ago SK Hynix says memory shortages to persist until 2030 6 days ago Raspberry Pi has announced yet another round of price hikes, this time adding $80 to the cost of its 16GB Pi 5, which now sells for more than three times its original launch price. The latest bump, announced by Raspberry Pi boss Eben Upton, takes the 16GB Pi 5 to a whopping $385. The 16GB Compute Module 5 variants are also getting $40 more expensive, although the Raspberry Pi 500+, which packs the same amount of RAM, has escaped this particular round. Upton blamed a familiar culprit: soaring memory costs, worsened by a lack of alternative suppliers for 16GB DRAM and ongoing shortages of other components. "Unfortunately, a lack of alternative supply for 16GB DRAM, compounded by other ongoing component shortages, means we now need to make further price increases on some of our highest-density products," Upton wrote. It's becoming an expensive habit for Raspberry Pi customers. The 16GB Pi 5 cost $120 when it launched in January 2025, which seems almost reasonable now. Raspberry Pi added $25 in December, another $60 in February, and a further $100 in April . With today's $80 increase, buyers are being asked to cough up $265 more than they were less than two years ago, a price hike of 221 percent. And it's barely been a month since Raspberry Pi raised prices on its 2GB Pi 4 and Pi 5 models by $12.50 apiece, taking them to $67.50 and $77.50 respectively. The repeated markups come despite Raspberry Pi reporting record first-half results in September. Revenue jumped 90 percent to $256.9 million, while gross profit rose 79 percent to $59.4 million. Gross profit per board climbed 53 percent to $12.20, helped partly by memory purchased before prices went through the roof. That stockpile advantage has since largely disappeared. For customers unwilling to pay nearly $400 for a single-board computer, Upton advises buying something with less RAM, using an older Pi, or optimizing applications to make do with less memory. He also warned that some sellers are exploiting the shortages by charging inflated prices or offering products that aren't what they appear to be, urging customers to stick to approved resellers. “We’re aware that a few bad actors have been taking advantage of the current memory supply circumstances to sell Raspberry Pi products at inflated prices or shift products that aren’t what they seem,” he said. There is, apparently, some good news, as Raspberry Pi continues to insist the increases are temporary. "As we've said from the beginning, the current memory landscape is difficult but ultimately temporary, and we look forward to rolling back our price increases when memory costs fall once again," Upton wrote. That could be a long wait. Micron has previously warned that memory shortages could drag on into 2028 or beyond, so anyone hoping to see a $120 Pi 5 again probably shouldn't hold their breath.

events.title: UK and EU agree deal to remove Brexit checks on food and animal products
events.summary: Agreement to ease rules on food imports and exports is expected to come into force in first quarter of 2028 The EU and the UK have completed their deal to remove Brexit checks on imports and exports of food and animal products ranging from sausages and cheese to leather goods and flowers. A wider series of mini-deals expected to be sealed at a UK-EU summit on 20 November would also result in Britain once again contributing to the EU budget as the price of rejoining a single electricity market. It will prove a boon for British food exporters and will also mean smaller retailers in the UK such as delicatessens can return to buying smaller batches of cheese and wines, something that became impossible because of the cost of Brexit checks introduced in 2022. But sources say the sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) deal, largely agreed in May, will not be implemented until the first quarter of 2028 after the change in UK prime minister caused a six-month delay to the second EU-UK summit, now due to be held on 20 November. Last month the National Farmers’ Union said exports of British food to the EU had collapsed by a third since Brexit, with eggs, chicken and potato products worst hit. Sources said a 200-page text on post-Brexit food exports had “been settled and there will no further negotiation”. A draft of a joint statement to be issued by the British prime minister, Andy Burnham, and EU leaders on 20 November is to be discussed by EU ambassadors at a meeting in Brussels on Wednesday. It states the SPS deal would allow “the vast majority of movements of animals, animal products, plants and plant products between Great Britain and the crown dependencies and the EU to take place without the certificates or controls that are currently required”. It adds that the UK goods would also be exempt from a carbon pollution tax, known as the carbon border adjustment mechanism, as the bloc and Britain are already aligned on emmissions. Rejoining the EU’s single electricity market is designed to help stabilise supplies but will allow UK energy companies to sell into continental grids again. The draft joint text says: “We agree that the UK’s participation in parts of the EU’s internal market requires an appropriate level of financial contribution towards reducing economic and social disparities between the regions of the EU that reflects the degree of the UK’s participation in the EU’s internal market”. The deal has divided opinion among unionists in Northern Ireland, with Gavin Robinson, the leader of the Democratic Unionist party, saying it does not go far enough and reflects what he sees as a “lack of ambition” by the government. The DUP, which is in turmoil after the MP Carla Lockhart’s decision to quit the party on Monday, supported Brexit but not the Windsor framework part of the withdrawal agreement because it cemented SPS checks on goods sold into Northern Ireland from Great Britain. Steve Aiken, the Windsor framework spokesperson for the rival Ulster Unionist party, gave a cautious welcome to the deal. “If the agreement goes ahead, checks on most agricultural goods coming from the rest of our nation will be significantly, but not completely, reduced,” he said. The SPS deal will be presented to EU ambassadors at a meeting on Wednesday that will discuss the first iteration of a joint statement to be issued by Andy Burnham and EU leaders on 20 November. The “zero text” of a joint statement, as it is known, also includes chapters on a widely expected youth experience scheme, but this is still being negotiated, and ambassadors are also due to discuss an 11th-hour proposal from the UK over tuition fees for young Europeans to break a deadlock in talks. Two weeks ago the European Commission was so concerned that the UK would not budge on its insistence that EU students should pay full international fees that the ambassadors discussed “decoupling” the issue and agreeing instead to negotiate on it separately for another six months. The SPS deal was largely agreed in May and published by the government to allow food producers time to prepare for the change. At the time, the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs said it expected the deal to be implemented in May next year. Defra has now briefed industry leaders that it may not be implemented until 2028, with a further six-month transition period for a handful of key products such as grains grown this year with fungicides not yet approved in the EU. The delay is caused by the UK’s need to “dynamically align” British food standards legislation with the EU’s. Although the UK has largely followed EU rules, it has diversified in some areas such as fungicides used to help crops grow in British wet weather. The legislation is expected to renew controversy over whether the UK is a “rule taker” rather than a “rule maker”, a key issue in Brexit.

events.title: ChatGPT creator OpenAI loses bid to block Singapore start-up’s GemGPT trademark
events.summary: OpenAI argued that the name “GemGPT” conflicted with its earlier registered trademarks, including ChatGPT and numbered GPT marks like “GPT-3”. OpenAI lost its bid to stop Singapore start-up Porolis Technologies from registering “GemGPT”. The tribunal said sharing “GPT” was not enough to prove confusion or bad faith. The Intellectual Property Office of Singapore ruled on Oct 28 that “GemGPT” should be seen as a whole name. It found the public would view it as a gemstone AI product, not an OpenAI service. Porolis, part of the B.P. de Silva group, won $10,000 in costs. The ruling said OpenAI may still prove “GPT” is distinctive in a future case with different evidence. SINGAPORE – ChatGPT maker OpenAI has failed to stop a Singapore start-up from registering the name “GemGPT”, after an intellectual property tribunal found that sharing the letters “GPT” was not enough to establish its case. Por olis Te chnologies, which uses artificial intelligence to assess gemstones , can proceed with registering the trademark following the decision by the Intellectual Property Office of Singapore (IPOS) on O ct 2 8. The start-up, part of the B.P. de Silva group , was also awarded $10 ,000 in costs, including disbursements. OpenAI’s five objections to the trademark application were all rejected. At the heart of the dispute was whether people in Singapore would see “GPT” as a part of OpenAI’s products and services, or simply a type of AI technology. Porolis had applied to register GemGPT for its AI-powered gemstone authentication and related software services. Principal assistant registrar Gab riel O ng found that, as at May 2 2, 20 23, when Porolis applied to register GemGPT, OpenAI had not established that the three letters alone identified its business. The assessment turned on public perception at that date, less than six months after ChatGPT’s launch on Nov 30, 2022. Porolis, found ed in 2022, develops technology to help determine the grade, authenticity and treatment of gemstones, using images and optical data. Its parent group has its core business in gemstones and jewellery. According to the decision, Porolis said it chose “Gem” to refer to gemstones and “GPT” to describe its use of generative AI models. GPT stands for “Generative Pre-trained Transformer”, a term referring to a type of AI model. Its service is neither built on nor powered by OpenAI’s models. Porolis said it developed its systems using data that it owns or licenses, including samples labelled by gemmologists. Why OpenAI lost the GemGPT trademark bid OpenAI argued that the name GemGPT conflicted with its earlier registered trademarks, including ChatGPT and numbered GPT marks such as GPT-3 and GPT-4. Its objections included the likelihood of public confusion, harm to its well-known logos and an allegation that Porolis had applied for the name in bad faith. But Ong found that ChatGPT and GemGPT had to be considered as whole names, rather than giving disproportionate weight to the letters they shared. Although some of the companies’ services overlapped, this did not outweigh the other factors pointing against a likelihood of confusion. “The ultimate impression given is that ‘GemGPT’ concerns an unrelated AI or technology product or service for gemstones,” he said. The public would not be likely to mistake GemGPT for OpenAI’s marks or assume that they came from the same or related businesses, simply because both contained “GPT”, he found. OpenAI also failed to establish that GemGPT would weaken ChatGPT’s distinctiveness by causing consumers to associate the two. “In my view, blurring does not arise simply because both marks contain ‘GPT’,” Ong said. Comparing with Gmail: ‘Mail’ non-distinctive element Ong drew a comparison with Gmail: the fact that it is well-known would not, by itself, prevent another business from using the non-distinctive element “mail” for e-mail or traditional mail services. On the bad-faith allegation, OpenAI argued that Porolis had sought to ride on OpenAI’s reputation. It pointed to the application being filed less than six months after ChatGPT’s launch. Porolis countered that knowing about ChatGPT was insufficient to establish bad faith, and that GPT described a type of technology used by others in the industry. Ong accepted that Porolis knew or must have known of OpenAI and ChatGPT. But this did not mean its conduct fell below acceptable commercial standards. “Against this backdrop, the mere fact that the Application Mark contains the letter string ‘GPT’ does not, without more, justify a finding of bad faith,” he said. He also stressed that the ruling did not mean OpenAI could never establish that GPT was distinctive. “At a future relevant date, based on some other evidence, it could be possible,” he said.

events.title: Oil prices fluctuate after US strikes on Iran’s Qeshm Island
events.summary: Oil prices dropped on Tuesday evening following a sharp rise in the morning after reports of a US strike on Iran’s Qeshm Island revived concerns about an escalation of the conflict and further disruption at the Strait of Hormuz . Brent, the benchmark for two thirds of the world’s oil , was trading 1.72 per cent lower at $102.97 a barrel at 6:16pm UAE time. West Texas Intermediate, the gauge that tracks US crude, was down 1.03 per cent to 95.47 a barrel. Both benchmarks rose sharply earlier in the day, with Brent reaching nearly $107 a barrel. The gains followed a sharp slide on Monday, when both Brent and WTI plunged more than 7 per cent. US forces struck Iran ’s Qeshm Island on Monday night, The Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday. The WSJ cited US officials, who described the attacks as defensive measures aimed at preventing Iran from targeting commercial vessels in the strait. Iranian state media said there were several explosions on the island, which is at the mouth of Hormuz. It was the ​latest in a series of limited attacks carried out by the US in recent weeks, the WSJ report said. Smaller scale strikes have been carried out and kept secret to avoid indicating any US intent to resume its major military campaign against Iran , the report added. “Overnight US strikes renewed uncertainty, leaving crude near $105 per barrel this morning and the diplomatic opening vulnerable,” said Daniel Richards, senior economist at Emirates NBD. The latest military action comes as the US goes to the polls on Tuesday for midterm elections. It also puts the focus back on the risk of supply disruption, a day after US President Donald Trump reportedly said he wanted to give diplomacy with Iran more time before considering renewed military strikes. “For oil, the decisive question will be whether the midterm elections can align the political pieces to pave the way for more normal supply conditions – or push that prospect further away,” said Ipek Ozkardeskaya, senior analyst at Swissquote. “The clearest downside scenario for crude is credible de-escalation of geopolitical tensions followed by improving supply flows. The clearest upside scenario is renewed disruption while inventories continue absorbing the shortfall.” While the US midterms could change expectations rapidly, “they cannot, by themselves, reopen shipping routes, repair damaged infrastructure or reverse the AI impact on broader economies”, she added. The Strait of Hormuz, a vital shipping route connecting the Gulf to global markets, carried about a fifth of the world's crude oil and natural gas supplies before the conflict began in late February. Oil prices hit a six-month high at the end of October on Hormuz strikes and the probability of the conflict escalating again after the midterm elections. "Energy prices have been at lofty levels for a while, at least from our perspective. Oil trading above $100 and European natural gas above €90 is difficult to reconcile with current market realities," said Norbert Rucker, head of economics and next generation research at Julius Baer. "We are in an extraordinarily noisy week due to the midterms, and in a phase where the complex energy supply chains are normalising. Given this setting, today’s exceptional market fever and wild price swings should not come as a surprise. We maintain our cautious view on oil."

events.title: Apple warns of ‘unprecedented’ rise in memory chip prices
events.summary: iPhone maker says decision to raise prices has offset some of impact, as revenues are stronger than expected Apple has warned of an “unprecedented” rise in memory chip prices, as it battles with datacentres to lay its hands on supplies. The iPhone maker’s shares fell in after-hours trading after it told investors that the higher prices will eat into its profit margins. “What we’re seeing with memory pricing right now is unprecedented,” John Ternus, Apple’s new chief executive, told a conference call on Monday, predicting that memory costs in the fourth quarter of this year would be even higher than in the previous three months. The tech industry has been gripped by “RAMageddon” for months , as demand for memory chips from AI datacentres has surged, driving up prices. Ternus said Apple’s decision to raise iPad and MacBook prices in June, followed by iPhone prices in September, had “provided some offset” for the company. Ben Barringer, the head of technology research at Quilter Cheviot, said Apple’s results were “OK, if on the disappointing side”. “Revenues were up 12%, driven primarily by iPhone sales and strong sales of Mac Mini, which users can use to apply agentic AI. China growth was robust which is pleasing to see, while iPad and wearables disappointed with services growing but lower than the group average at 10%,” he added. “There appears to be a lot of interest in the iPhone Duo, but it is early days yet with the product not yet on full release, but it is hoped that can help drive the next leg of Apple’s product innovation.” Apple’s shares were down 2.75% in after-hours trading on Wall Street. Apple posted stronger-than-expected revenue in the fiscal third quarter, giving Ternus an upbeat start to his tenure, which began in September. The solid results bucked a downward trend for tech companies this quarter, as companies including Alphabet, Amazon and Intel had disappointing quarterly results. Jacob Bourne, an Emarketer analyst, said record iPhone revenue and strong growth in China demonstrated the resilience of Apple’s business. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Apple earned $30.71bn (£22.89bn), or $2.10 a share, in the July-September period, up 12% from $27.47bn, or $1.85 a share, in the equivalent period a year earlier. Apple said its earnings included five cents a share from tariff refunds. Revenue rose 12% to $114.5bn from $102.5bn. Analysts, on average, were expecting earnings of $1.99 a share on revenue of $113.4bn, according to a poll by FactSet. While its rivals are facing investor uncertainty over huge investments in artificial intelligence, Bourne said Apple’s “tepid approach” to AI infrastructure spending had helped preserve its cashflow – while partnerships with companies such as Alphabet could help the iPhone maker strengthen its AI capabilities without taking on the same financial risks as its peers.

events.title: FCA sets expectations for firms making car finance settlement offers
events.summary: Research shows consumers want the choice, rather than wait for the legal challenges to conclude. Almost 9 out of 10 (89%) car finance customers who have complained or are considering doing so want the choice of an offer of compensation now, rather than waiting for the legal challenges to the FCA's compensation scheme to conclude. 86% would be comfortable making the decision, and 61% say they’d accept an offer in line with the scheme. Timing matters for many: 77% say receiving compensation sooner would make a great deal or fair amount of difference to their financial situation.The survey findings are being released today alongside the FCA's expectations for lenders who want to make settlement offers to those owed compensation under its scheme, while legal challenges continue. This comes as Barclays Partner Finance confirms it will make settlement offers to some of its customers owed compensation.The regulator supports lenders making settlement offers, as long as customers are offered no less than they would receive through the scheme.Lenders will need to be clear with people about what accepting any offer means. This includes that they will keep any money received, even if the outcome of the legal challenges means they would have received less. However, they also wouldn’t be able to claim more later if the outcome of the legal challenge means they would have been paid more. As consumers can reject an offer and leave their claim to be dealt with under the scheme, these offers can’t be referred to the Financial Ombudsman Service for review.Stephen Braviner Roman, the FCA’s general counsel and co-lead on the motor finance project, said:'Fair settlement offers could result in some people getting money sooner. And it’s clear they want the choice.'Anyone who wants to wait can, and there’s no obligation to agree to the offer. We’ll closely monitor firms making offers and expect them to be clear what accepting an offer means.'To help consumers make informed decisions, the FCA has published a factsheet (PDF) that lenders must share with customers when making settlement offers. Not all lenders are likely to make offers, and those that do may only make them to some customers owed compensation. The FCA will regularly update its website with lenders making settlement offers to help consumers check whether an offer is genuine. Firms are expected to notify the FCA if they plan to make offers.Payouts under the motor finance compensation scheme were due to start this year. The scheme is currently partially suspended, pending the outcome of legal challenges due to be heard between 16 February and 3 March 2027. Under the partial suspension, firms must keep preparing for the scheme and continue progressing complaints as far as possible, but do not need to calculate or pay compensation under the scheme until the legal process concludes.Anyone who is concerned about their car finance deal and has not yet complained should complain directly to their lender. There is information on the FCA website on how to complain for free. There is no need to use a law firm or claims management company, which may charge up to 36% of any compensation, including VAT.Notes to editorsResearch conducted by Kantar, surveying 1,000 motor finance customers online between 25 and 28 June 2026. Findings cited are based on a subset of 590 respondents who said they had made or were considering making a motor finance complaint.Barclays press release.Statement confirming motor finance legal challenge to be heard in February 2027.Statement on the partial suspension of the motor finance scheme and what it means for firms and consumers.

events.title: Final_FINAL_v7.docx is not a version control strategy
events.summary: The Register and LucidLink are hosting a dinner for senior technology, infrastructure and data leaders at the Covent Garden Hotel on Tuesday 24 November. Joe Fay of The Register is in the chair. The subject is one most of them will know from their own shop, where the same file lives in several places at once and nobody is quite sure which copy is current. Most organisations have a folder that proves it. There's a file called final, another called final2, and then the one people are actually using, which somebody emailed to a contractor last Thursday. It's mildly funny until two people spend a week editing different copies and one of them loses the argument. Meanwhile the storage bill picks up another copy of everything, and each team that builds its own way round the problem gives IT another place it can't see into. Alan Marshall, Strategic Director, EMEA at LucidLink, joins a small group of peers at the table, and nobody is there to give a presentation. Because the evening is held under the Chatham House Rule, people tend to say what really happened, like the team that quietly built its own sync service because the approved one was too slow, or the leaver who could still open a file share months after going. From there the conversation widens out to unstructured data that won't stop growing, the duplicate storage piling up, the security risk of access scattered across all those copies, and how to modernise without binning the storage and governance the business has already paid for. Drinks start at 6.30pm, then it's dinner around one table until 9pm. Places are limited. Request your place at the November 24 dinner Places go by invitation and each one is confirmed personally. events.title: Australian central bank chief signals pause after split decision on latest rate hike
events.summary: The Reserve Bank of Australia’s governor Michele Bullock says “we’re basically preserving our options” on whether to raise interest rates again next year. The Reserve Bank of Australia raised rates to 4.85%, an 18-year high, in a 6-3 split vote. Governor Michele Bullock said, “We’re basically preserving our options.” Bullock signalled a pause, saying the latest hikes have not yet fully impacted the economy. The RBA still worries inflation may stay above 3% and expectations could become “embedded”. The tougher policy is slowing demand, lifting unemployment and hitting housing. Home values in major cities fell 1.4% in October, and recovery may not come until rate cuts in late 2027. Australia’s central bank governor Michele Bullock signalled a wait-and-see approach to further tightening after policymakers lifted the benchmark rate to an 18-year high, in a split vote that sent the currency lower. At a press conference on Nov 3 in Sydney, the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) chief highlighted that the tightening to date in 2026 has yet to feed through to the economy, while reiterating the ongoing inflation challenge . Her comments came after the nine-member policy board raised the cash rate by a quarter-percentage point to 4.85%, extending the most aggressive tightening among developed economies. The RBA board voted 6-3 in favour of raising the key rate for a fifth time this year. It omitted a reference that it was willing to hike further if needed, a line that has been included in each statement since June. “I’d not be interpreting this as saying we’re not going up. I wouldn’t be interpreting it as saying we definitely are going up,” Bullock said in response to a question on why that wasn’t kept. “We’re basically preserving our options.” Emphasising that the impact of the latest rate increases have yet to be felt, Bullock said “the last couple haven’t even started to flow through yet”. She added tighter policy was already weighing on demand, which is starting “to slow relative to supply, and ultimately it’s going to come back into balance”. Markets and economists read the governor’s remarks as dovish. The currency fell against the greenback as traders pared to about 30% the odds of the RBA raising the cash rate to 5.1% in 2027, compared with an almost 50% chance it would do so by next May before the announcement. Australia’s move comes in a week when Sweden’s Riksbank may also hike and the Bank of England is expected to increase borrowing costs for the first time in three years, as economies struggle with the energy-driven inflation shock. While Bullock talked tough on inflation, she noted that the three dissenters on the board had put greater emphasis on the downside risks in the economy. “We think the RBA will remain on edge as we enter 2027 but keep rates on hold,” said Belinda Allen at Commonwealth Bank of Australia. “The slowdown in the economy through next year, led by the consumer and the resultant lift in the unemployment rate should see inflation moderate from here and return closer to target in late 2027.” Consumer prices have shown little sign of easing back to the central bank’s 2-3% target band. RBA officials worry that inflation expectations may be starting to untether, with deputy governor Andrew Hauser noting that a growing share of firms think 3-3.5% inflation is “a new normal”, a scenario he described as “the central bank’s nightmare”. “Inflation is now expected to remain above 3% for the coming year and there is an increasing risk that higher inflation expectations will become embedded,” the RBA’s board said in its decision statement. “The board is conscious of the period in which inflation has been too high.” The central bank also on Nov 3 released its quarterly update of forecasts in the statement on monetary policy. It showed underlying inflation will come back inside the RBA’s target band about six months later than assumed in August, with the economy seen slowing next year and unemployment tracking higher. The RBA now judges financial conditions to be “restrictive” and said labour market conditions “remain a little tight”, despite a rise in unemployment. Sally Auld, chief economist at National Australia Bank, warned the RBA left itself little room for error given the forecasts imply a “Goldilocks” disinflation. This is “especially considering the RBA’s hawkish description of the inflation challenge at present,” she said. “While we are not forecasting further policy tightening from here, there is little doubt the RBA will be sensitive, and responsive, to any upside surprise in inflation in coming months.” In addition to the impact of surging fuel prices, Australia has become more inflation-prone due to very weak productivity. That’s forced officials to scale back the potential growth rate, the level of expansion the economy can sustain before it generates inflationary pressures. The RBA has failed to hit the 2.5% midpoint of its inflation target band since late 2021.

events.title: North Korea denies being behind record $6.3bn Binance hack
events.summary: Kim Yo Jong, the sister of North Korea's leader Kim Jong Un North Korea has denied claims that it was behind the record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) hack of cryptocurrency exchange Binance , calling the allegations "absurd rhetoric". Kim Yo Jong, a top Democratic People's Republic of Korea official and the sister of leader Kim Jong Un , said on Tuesday that the accusations are another "sinister attempt" by the US to damage Pyongyang's public image. The US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), the Secret Service and cyber analysts have said North Korea orchestrated the hack, which has been described as the largest in history. This is the latest hack to be linked to North Korea, which has been accused of relying on cyber-crime to help finance its sanctioned economy. Blockchain analysts and the FBI have said the attack was led by state-backed hacking group TraderTraitor. The FBI has called on industry partners to help block transactions involving cryptocurrency accounts linked to the group. "The US has made a trite provocation of linking it with the Democratic People's Republic of Korea again," Kim Yo-jong, the director of North Korea's General Affairs Department, said in a statement. "It is a grave political provocation against the DPRK that the US misleads the international public opinion as if all the cyber crimes in different parts of the world are our deeds," she said. Why North Korea's 'elite' hackers are the prime suspect in major Binance hack Published 3 days ago Who could be behind the Binance hack and what we know so far Published 4 days ago But Pyongyang has been blamed for a number of major cyber attacks in recent years - accusations that it has denied. The TraderTraitor unit, which is also known as the Lazarus Group, was blamed for a then-record $1.5bn hack of crypto exchange Bybit in 2025. Pyongyang has systematically built its cyber operations, recruiting promising students from universities and sending them to hacker units overseen by North Korea's intelligence agency, research groups like the S Rajaratnam School of International Studies think tank have said. The country has consistently denied such claims. Kim Yo Jong said "it is the consistent policy stand of the DPRK government to resolutely oppose all sorts of malicious acts in cyberspace". Kim Yo-jong: North Korea's heir apparent? Published 16 June 2020 Who is Kim Yo-jong? Video, 00:02:32 Who is Kim Yo-jong? Published 16 June 2020 Binance did not respond to the BBC's queries about North Korea's alleged involvement in the hack. Since the incident, the crypto giant has largely focused its public statements on the technical nature of the breach and its response to protect users. The company's spokesperson said that a net $4.72bn has been withdrawn from the exchange since transactions resumed on Sunday. The net outflow represents a "relatively limited portion" of Binance's total assets, which stand at approximately $157bn, the spokesperson told the BBC on Tuesday. That figure reflects the impact of the hack, subsequent withdrawals and market price changes. "Withdrawal levels are stabilising to what we would consider normal and expected on-chain activity," she added. The company said last week that initial checks indicated that an engineer's laptop had been compromised, enabling an attacker to make unauthorised withdrawals. Trading in major cryptocurrencies on Binance has since resumed after the exchange worked with issuers to freeze assets impacted by the hack. The company has repeatedly said it would cover all of the losses linked to the attack and that it has so far covered around 95% of the assets stolen in the breach. events.title: Forget retraining - AI can now tweak another AI's weights
events.summary: The outputs of AI models are the result of a complex interplay between neurons, weights, training, and inference, and are therefore difficult to follow. But in some ways they're starting to look more like open books. Recent work by Anthropic safety fellow Joshua Fonseca Rivera has revealed how certain neurons in a neural network can be associated with a specific persona . Now, computer scientists from MIT's Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL) have found that frontier AI models like OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra can rewrite the weights of another model directly, as opposed to indirectly through training, and alter their behavior. "We find early signs that frontier LLMs are surprisingly good at natively reading, writing, and reasoning about neural network weights," said Rikiya Takehi, a PhD student at MIT CSAIL, in a social media post . "Instead of training, models may treat raw weights like readable, editable code: diagnosing failures and patching them directly." To demonstrate that, Takehi and colleagues Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang, and Omar Khattab asked GPT-6 Astra to edit Qwen3.5-0.8B weights to make it better at math. Astra changed only 0.016 percent of the model's weights, reducing its reasoning loops and improving its math performance by as much as sixfold on the MATH-500 benchmark, while boosting its instruction-following score on the IFEval benchmark roughly threefold. There was no training using gradient descent ; Astra just revised the numerical values that constitute Qwen's weights. "All of this is possible without allowing Astra to write training loops," the researchers wrote in a blog post . "It uses its reasoning to figure out what each part of a neural network computes, or should compute, and changes the weights accordingly. We call this Weight-Space Programming. "Throughout the history of deep learning, we encoded our simplistic inductive biases into tiny symbolic optimizers like Adam or Muon. This is changing: our neural network weights will soon be natively optimized by LLMs that deliberately reason about their weights." Astra's ability to program weights extends to being able to write a neural network from scratch, zero-shot. The researchers told Astra: "write, from scratch, the weights of a policy network that plays [Breakout] as well as possible." And it did so. Takehi suggests this technique shows promise for improving models without the consequences of catastrophic forgetting , which can occur when a model is revised to include new knowledge. More generally, the authors expect Weight-Space Programming will open the door to new ways to understand models and optimize them, and to implement recursive self-improvement. The technique may also prove useful for reducing model sycophancy and improving interpretability and alignment. The next step, the authors say, involves building a benchmark and a harness for carrying out Weight-Space Programming on LLMs. "We believe this will provide a standardized evaluation to measure and accelerate progress in Weight-Space Programming, turning what currently seems like black magic into a rigorous, reproducible engineering discipline," they say. ®

events.title: John Lewis Christmas ad stars Kristin Scott Thomas as glamorous granny on a gift hunt
events.summary: Company tugs at heartstrings with Pickles the talking toy dog as it celebrates 20 years of blockbuster festive ads Review: Kristin Scott Thomas v Pickles the evil AI overlord puppy John Lewis has turned to a celebrity best known for playing aristocrats to put a playful but rather upmarket spin on the countdown to Christmas with this year’s festive ad, which features a toy dog called Pickles and a glamorous granny. Kristin Scott Thomas, known for playing upper-crust characters in films such as Four Weddings and a Funeral and the Apple TV show Slow Horses, is cast as Gloria, a grandmother searching for gift inspiration, with the tagline “don’t give up on giving”. In the 20th version of its blockbuster Christmas ad, the department store kickstarts the official countdown to Christmas by tugging at the heartstrings, with Pickles, voiced by the comedian Paul Whitehouse, challenging Gloria to “do better than cash” when choosing a gift for her grandchildren. Pickles drags Gloria out of the house on a last-minute mission to find gifts, and after rejecting options in other shops, she sets off on a magical tuk-tuk ride to John Lewis, where she snaps up some disco balls and fairy lights to create a “gran cave” to hang out with her grandchildren, Freddie and Maggie. Rosie Hanley, the marketing director of John Lewis, said the retailer had increased its spend on this year’s festive ad as the cost of production had risen and it wanted to “push the boat out” for its 20th year. However, she said the company was confident it would see “a really strong return on our investment” as it tries to grab shoppers’ attention before the Black Friday discount period later this month. She said the company had wanted the ad “to be more joyful” this year because “things are tough for lots of families”. Despite concerns among British households about higher energy bills and housing costs, Hanley said spending on Christmas-related gear at John Lewis was already up on last year. The ad, set to a Sam Fender version of the Rolling Stones song You Can’t Always Get What You Want, features a range of John Lewis products in different price brackets, including the £12.99 Fisher-Price pull-along toy dog and a £255 Weekend Max Mara top and matching £290 skirt worn by Gloria. The three-minute ad will launch on social media on Tuesday morning, including Facebook, Instagram, TikTok and YouTube, before a 60-second version airs for the first time on TV in the ad breaks for ITV’s Coronation Street and Channel 4’s The Great British Bake Off on Tuesday evening. John Lewis will also erect a giant Christmas tree outside its store on London’s Oxford Street to mark the recent pedestrianisation of the road . The company said the numbers of visitors to its store on the street last week were up by more than a fifth on the same week last year. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning This year’s ad, created by the Saatchi & Saatchi agency, returns to a formula of using a cute character – such as Monty the penguin in 2014 and Buster the boxer in 2016 – after two years foregrounding other family relationships. However, it has the twist of focusing on the relationship between Pickles and a grandmother rather than centring on cute children. Hanley said the ad was inspired by research which had revealed that 52% of grandparents give cash as presents because they are not sure what youngsters really want. “People want to give thoughtful gifts but can often lack confidence, so resort to giving cash,” she said. Now considered a national moment which invites social media comment and skits, the first big-budget John Lewis festive TV ad launched in 2007, soundtracked by a piece of music by Prokofiev. Previous John Lewis Christmas TV ads have been soundtracked by covers including the Smiths song Please, Please, Please, Let Me Get What I Want and Together in Electric Dreams by Giorgio Moroder and Philip Oakey. Last year’s ad included the 1990s club classic Where Love Lives by Alison Limerick. This year’s track, which features the choir from the John Spence community high school, which Fender previously attended, and the Easington Colliery Band, will be released on vinyl later this month, with proceeds going to Action For Children. Pickles the dog is based on an existing Fisher-Price pull-along toy called Little Snoopy that is celebrating its 60th year. The John Lewis ad launch comes hot on the heels of other festive ads for most of the big supermarkets that kicked off last weekend. Total ad spending across the festive period is set to reach £14bn, up 8.2% year-on-year according to the annual review by the Advertising Association and research group WARC. That growth is led by an 18.5% year-on-year surge in social media spend, while total TV spending is expected to be up by 1.6%.

events.title: Yvonne Bajela is bringing $17M in fresh capital to Europe’s startup scene
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. Yvonne Bajela knew it was time to launch her own fund. She spent more than a decade as a VC, most recently at LocalGlobe and Impact X Capital Partners, where she made bets on now-unicorn companies like the fintech Wise, the insurance company Marshmallow, and robotaxi Mooves. On Tuesday, she announced that her own fund, Evertrue Capital , officially closed an oversubscribed $17 million Fund I. “After more than a decade backing founders who bet everything on their ideas, it felt like time to make a bet of my own,” she said. “I wanted the independence to act on those convictions and build something that reflected my own approach to investing.” The firm, which has already backed seven companies, will focus on early-stage investing across the U.K. and Europe. The average check size will be around £350,000, she said, with plans to back at least 20 companies over the next three years. Perhaps unsurprisingly, she said this AI boom helped her realize that this was the right time to launch her own fund. Not only has it changed the economics of launching a company, she said, but it has created new opportunities for early-stage investors like herself. “The ability to build has been democratized,” she said. “But the ability to build something enduring remains rare.” As TechCrunch has previously reported, the U.K.’s startup scene is having a moment. King’s Cross, for example, is one of the world’s top AI hubs, while companies like Revolut, Synthesia, ElevenLabs, and the Bezos-backed CuspAI are redefining what it means to scale and attract success in the U.K. market. For someone like Bajela, this moment means there is an opportunity to snap up investments in the next generation of top British talent early. “I think more globally significant businesses will emerge from a wider range of starting points,” she said. However, this is also a tough market for emerging fund managers. In the U.S., it has been described as a barbell market where capital is concentrated at the top and among firms led by those who already have solid track records. Things may be slightly rosier in the U.K., as PitchBook data through the end of September shows that emerging fund managers in this region raised $7.4 billion, already surpassing the $6.2 billion they raised in all of 2025. Still, Bajela said fundraising was a grind. The hardest rejections weren’t necessarily the outright nos. “They were the ones that came after months of conversations and significant time invested, only for the answer to ultimately be no,” she said. “Time is one of the most valuable resources a founder has, and a prolonged process without clarity has a real cost.” Still, she said the fund nabbed five institutional backers, including the British Business Bank and Basecamp, the fund-of-funds of the investment firm Phoenix Court, which is also home to LocalGlobe. Evertrue was part of the £400 million British Business Bank’s Investor Pathways capital initiative, which saw it distribute £90 million to 10 first-time fund managers. Bajela said Evertrue wanted to raise around $13 million but saw a lot of investor interest. She decided to turn down additional investors rather than expand the fund size. “Fund size is a strategic decision, not a measure of success in itself,” she said. “I wanted enough capital to build meaningful positions in my highest-conviction investments without creating pressure to deploy capital simply because it was available.” Around 80% of Evertrue’s LPs are U.K. based, with the rest scattered across Europe, Asia, and the U.S. She said her international LP base represents the relationships she’s built “over more than a decade investing across markets.” It also reflects the fund’s global ambition, she said, especially since so many British founders keep their eyes on a U.S. expansion; more than half her portfolio already operates in the U.S. Evertrue will invest mainly across AI and fintech, she said, adding that she’s “particularly interested in people with a unique insight into a problem, an unusual ability to execute, and the ambition to build something much bigger than their initial product.” “I also pay attention to the distance a founder has traveled, what they’ve overcome, and how that has shaped their perspective,” she continued. She’s lived in Japan as a senior investment manager at Mitsui and started her career as an analyst at Goldman Sachs. Throughout her career, she said she’s seen how “widely distributed ambition and talent are.” “I want Evertrue to be known for the quality of the founders I back and the businesses they go on to build.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . This doesn’t affect our editorial independence. Dominic-Madori Davis is a senior venture capital and startup reporter at TechCrunch.

events.title: From scooters to shampoo - the people saving hundreds from dumpster diving
events.summary: 'I've always looked in bins for clothes' Darryl Baker was shocked to see piles of clothes dumped beside the recycling bins outside her local supermarket. On several trips to the dumpsters she has also found a host of other items, such as "a perfectly decent" Ikea picture frame and children's scooters. Always on the lookout for ways to save money and appalled by the waste, the thrifty mother-of-two from north London asked supermarket staff if she could take some of it. Permission granted, "I got my children entire new wardrobes," says Darryl, 39, adding that she's stuff put away for years to come. During a six-month stint this year, "I have probably saved hundreds of pounds," says the freelance journalist. Darryl reels off the names of brands she has salvaged - Ralph Lauren, Nike and The North Face, among others. "My mind was blown," she says. "This stuff is just strewn all over the floor." Darryl Baker takes the clothes for herself and her children, and to sell In addition to finding clothing for her children and her nephews and nieces, she keeps some for herself. Others she donates or sells, including recently getting £30 for a men's Barbour jacket. Darryl has joined the ranks of so-called dumpster divers – people who rummage through commercial bins for treasures. Motivations include saving money, giving items to charity and disgust at how often perfectly usable items are being consigned to waste - or a combination of all three. Texan Jeff Ferrell has been rooting around in trash for more than 50 years. "I still dumpster dive every day by bicycle," says the 72-year old, who lives in Fort Worth, and has written books on the topic. "I still enjoy it as much, or more, than ever." Jeff considers himself a "bit of Robin Hood mixed with anarchist direct action", only scrounging in more affluent neighbourhoods and giving away many of his finds. "Almost everything in our home is scrounged, and I never buy, for example, soap or toiletries or medical supplies, or shoes and clothes and tools and garden supplies," he says. Jeff Ferrell sells some of what he finds, and gives away other items Jeff looks for discarded metal to sell at a scrapyard which, he says, earns him around $150 (£110) every two weeks. His wife sells his other finds, such as "an antique or piece of jewellery", on eBay. Through savings and selling the more valuable items, he estimates his finds are worth "tens of thousands of dollars a year". 'If something catches my eye, I'll grab it' While dumpster diving may have been considered taboo in the past, it's now something many people are proud to do and post about online. Millie Diamond, a London-based stylist, posts videos on Instagram of her rummaging through bins. But she has a very specific aim - to unearth fabrics and clothing that she can salvage and refashion into new items, some of which she then sells. Millie Diamond turns dumped textiles and clothes into new outfits She estimates that one dress she found was worth £600. "I'm a bit of a magpie. I like collecting things off the street or anywhere that there's a freebie. If I see something that catches my eye, then I'll grab it." Millie, 36, began bin diving after spotting some fabrics discarded by a business that had shut down. "I literally clambered into the bin. It turned out it was loads of vintage clothes." 'I haven't bought shampoo for years' For Charlotte Bayford in Essex it's all about timing. Her best finds come when students at Essex University head home for the summer and ditch anything they don't want to take with them. This includes half-filled toiletries. "I haven't bought shampoo for eight years," says the 44-year-old sales assistant. "I'd say that has saved me some money." Like other dumpster divers, Charlotte gives a lot of her finds to charity. But she has also filled her house with salvaged objects, and sells on some valuable items. Food, as long as it remains sealed, is fair game too. "I've found tins of Heinz baked beans, perfectly fine. I'm quite happy to eat those," Charlotte says. Charlotte Bayford gives some of her finds to charity But is taking things out of bins and keeping them acceptable in the eyes of the law? Jeff, who is professor emeritus of sociology at Texas Christian University, says many US cities have made the practice illegal, including New York, Cleveland and Wichita. "Dumpster diving is considered illegal [in such places] because that which is thrown away now belongs to the city... or to the private company that provided trash services," he explains. Any dumpster diver also risks trespass charges. In Fort Worth, where Jeff lives, items can only be removed from bins if they are on public land , external . In the UK, Sunjay Versani of Duncan Lewis Solicitors says it depends on the circumstances. "In many cases involving genuinely discarded goods, prosecution is unlikely," he says. "But there is no general rule that something is free to take simply because it has been put in a skip or bin.

events.title: China’s ‘Lipstick King’ touts AI tokens in first for Singles’ Day festival
events.summary: Li Jiaqi, also known as Austin Li, hosting a live stream at the headquarters of MeiONE in Shanghai on Sept 7. Li sold 100,000 monthly memberships of Alibaba’s QwenWork office AI service within half an hour during a Taobao Live broadcast on Nov 2. China’s Singles’ Day added AI token packages as a major new product, moving beyond cosmetics and home appliances. It is the first time such AI credits were sold widely in the festival. Alibaba’s Austin Li sold 100,000 monthly memberships of QwenWork in 30 minutes. The stream also sold AI laptops and workplace devices, with Alibaba and JD.com launching AI token centres. AI token sales rose 450% from the previous month, and AI laptop sales jumped more than 300% in the first hour. Analysts said users may stock up, but fast AI change could make prepaid plans risky. BEIJING - The Singles’ Day shopping extravaganza in China unveiled a new attraction for 2026 as it graduates beyond a long association with cut-price cosmetics and home appliances: computing credits used to access artificial intelligence tools. The launch is the first time AI token packages have been offered as a significant consumer product category during Singles’ Day, the world’s largest shopping festival originally held on Nov 11 each year. Top live-streamer Austin Li sold 100,000 monthly memberships of Alibaba’s QwenWork office AI service within half an hour during a Taobao Live broadcast on Nov 2, the company said. That is equivalent to about two trillion AI tokens, or units of text processed by AI models. “Chinese consumers are now very accustomed to using AI productivity tools,” said Lian Jye Su, chief analyst at tech research firm Omdia. Frequent users can run short of credits, he added, which makes extensive purchases during a sales period “a very reasonable action”. It was unclear how much the token plans were discounted from normal prices, however. First sale of AI products for ‘Lipstick King’ The live stream marked the first sale of AI products by Li, who earned the “Lipstick King” moniker for amassing a huge following while selling vast volumes of lipstick online. It showcased QwenWork token plans, AI-enabled laptops and workplace devices. Chen Yusen, an Alibaba Group vice-president and chief executive of QwenWork, also made an appearance. Li asked Chen if AI could be used to build a digital avatar of himself to chat with fans around the clock. While AI could not replace Li, Chen responded, he hoped it could handle everyday tasks for users, freeing them to spend time with their families. Alibaba’s Tmall has launched an AI Token Center for the Singles Day festival, offering consumer token packages from Alibaba Cloud, MiniMax, Moonshot AI and Z.AI. Alibaba’s Tmall has launched an AI Token Center for the festival, offering consumer token packages from Alibaba Cloud, MiniMax, Moonshot AI and Z.AI, the e-commerce giant said. JD.com has also introduced an AI token section bringing together services from companies including DeepSeek, Z.AI and ByteDance’s Volcano Engine. Sales of AI token plans from Oct 1 to Oct 20 soared 450% from the previous month, Alibaba said, while sales of AI personal-computer laptops surged more than 300% year on year in the first hour of the Nov 11 checkout period. Su said the tokens’ relatively long expiry periods could spur users to stock up, but warned that rapid changes in AI products may make consumers wary of prepaying for services at risk of being replaced or retired. Singles’ Day, which has run since 2009 in an effort to spur consumer spending, earned total revenue of 1.70 trillion yuan (S$327.3 billion) across platforms in 2025, according to third party data provider Syntun. events.title: China regulator tells banks to pause IPOs: Report
events.summary: The move follows a sharp selloff that saw the blue-chip CSI300 Index slumping 8.5% in October, its worst monthly performance in more than a decade. China’s securities regulator told banks to pause IPOs and large share sales, The Financial Times reported, citing three sources. The China Securities Regulatory Commission gave informal “window guidance” after meetings with investment banks, Reuters could not verify the report. The move follows an 8.5% October fall in the CSI300, while regulators also launched market support steps on Nov 2 to stabilise shares. BEIJING – China’s securities regulator has told investment banks to pause initial public offerings and has suspended large share sales by existing shareholders until markets recover, The Financial Times reported on Nov 3, citing three sources with knowledge of the discussions. The China Securities Regulatory Commission held meetings with investment banks and gave informal “window guidance” over the past few days, the report added. Large sales by existing shareholders have also been temporarily suspended until the markets have recovered, according to the report. Reuters could not immediately verify the report. Chinese financial regulators did not immediately reply to a Reuters request for comments. Persistent weakness in the world’s second-largest economy, weighed down by frail consumption, a prolonged property debt crisis and a steep tech stock selloff, has sapped investor confidence. Chinese regulators rolled out a handful of measures on Nov 2, from conducting swap operations to upgrading a lending facility for stock buybacks by listed companies, as part of efforts to stabilise struggling capital markets. The effort to steady its sliding stock market struggled for traction on Nov 3, with AI-related shares leading declines as investors judged the financial support measures insufficient. China’s blue-chip CSI300 Index and the benchmark Shanghai Composite Index both dropped more than 1% in early trade, before paring losses to 0.1% and 0.7%, respectively, by midday. REUTERS

events.title: RBA interest rates: Bullock says ‘pain now’ will prevent worse later as Reserve Bank hikes rates for fifth time
events.summary: Reserve Bank of Australia increases official cash rate to 4.85%, bringing it to highest level since 2008 Get our daily political email , free app or daily news podcast The Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock has said that “some pain now will prevent even worse pain down the track”, after lifting official interest rates to an 18-year high of 4.85% in a bid to combat persistent inflation. The RBA’s decision to hit mortgage holders for a fifth time in 2026 will intensify pressure on indebted households, but there were signs that the central bank will at least now wait through summer to gauge the impact of higher interest rates on the economy. The decision split the monetary policy board, as six members voted for a hike, while three were in favour of a steady cash rate. Financial markets halved the probability of another rate rise before Christmas to 12%, but continued to price in a roughly 30% chance of a sixth hike by May. Speaking to journalists shortly after the rate decision, Bullock said: “I know this is not the news that many Australians want to hear, but it is what’s needed to get inflation down.” “Inflation is too high, and our forecast suggests it will stay higher for longer. Some pain now will prevent even worse pain down the track,” she said. The back-to-back hikes will heap more pain on over 3.3m households with home loans and turn the screws on a federal government under pressure for its economic management. The latest rate rise will lift the monthly interest payment on a $700,000 home loan by $107, according to Canstar, bringing the total rise in repayments over this year’s five hikes to $532. Jim Chalmers, the treasurer, said higher fuel prices due to the Middle East conflict were the “primary driver” for the recent inflationary surge. “Our budgets are not what’s putting upward pressure on inflation. But we can play a helpful role and that’s what we intend to do,” Chalmers said. With surveys showing Australians are increasingly inclined to blame the Albanese government for ongoing high cost of living, Angus Taylor, the opposition leader, said voters “deserved to hear the truth”. “Labor’s spending spree is driving up inflation, it’s driving up interest rates, and Australians are paying the price,” Taylor said. The RBA’s post-meeting statement removed an explicit reference to the need for further hikes – an omission that economists at UBS interpreted as “clearly dovish”. And with the cash rate now at its highest level since 2008, Cherelle Murphy, the chief economist at EY, said the RBA “is likely to take a wait-and-see approach over summer”, even as she said higher interest rates could not be ruled out. The RBA’s latest set of forecasts in its Statement on Monetary Policy (SOMP) showed a difficult period ahead for the economy. The forecasts suggested the country’s cost of living crisis would extend for another year, even as Australia struggles with below trend economic growth and climbing unemployment. Inflation will push higher through the final months of 2026 to about 4.5% and only return below 3% – within the bank’s 2% to 3% target range – by the end of next year, or nine months later than hoped. Global oil prices would ease over the coming 18 months, but still remain relatively elevated, according to the forecasts, suggesting limited relief from high fuel costs for motorists and ongoing high costs for businesses. “We view the risks to the inflation outlook as still skewed to the upside,” the report said. Alongside persistent cost of living pressures, the RBA also predicted weak economic growth through to the end of 2028. The economy would grow by 1.6% this year and by 1.3% in 2027. That would be well below an estimated potential growth rate of about 2%, but better than recent forecasts by bank analysts. And despite the risks associated with a housing downturn that “is one of the steepest over the past 50 years”, the central banks’ economists saw no evidence that the country was headed towards recession over the coming two years. Unemployment, now at 4.7%, would end next year at about 4.9%, before creeping over 5% in 2028.

events.summary: XRG , the international energy investment unit of Adnoc, has agreed to acquire Shell’s stake in an Australian natural gas project for $1.5 billion, as the company seeks to diversify its portfolio amid disruption to global energy markets caused by the Iran war. Abu Dhabi-based XRG will buy the stake in Australia's North West Shelf LNG project, marking its first investment in the country's gas sector and opening up greater access to customers in the Asia-Pacific region, the company said on Tuesday. The deal, which is subject to regulatory approval, will give XRG access to one of the world's largest integrated LNG developments, with liquefaction capacity of 14.3 million tonnes per year and 4.4 trillion cubic feet equivalent of remaining resources. XRG has been actively increasing its portfolio of investments globally and plans to double its asset value over the next decade. Launched in 2024 as an international lower-carbon energy and chemicals investment company, with an enterprise value exceeding $80 billion, it has acquired stakes in several global gas projects. The latest acquisition strengthens XRG's position in the Asia-Pacific region. The North West Shelf project has been operating for more than four decades and plays a key role in the country's domestic gas supply and energy exports. The asset has supported domestic energy supply, jobs, international trade, and Australia’s emergence as a leading global energy exporter, XRG said. “This investment advances XRG’s strategy to build a leading international gas business serving growing demand across Asia-Pacific. The North West Shelf combines immediate production, strategic infrastructure, and future upstream development opportunities, making it a strong fit with our long-term ambitions,” said Mohamed Al Aryani, president of international gas at XRG. “XRG understands the importance of balancing export success with local energy needs. We believe continued investment in the North West Shelf can help sustain domestic gas supply, support regional energy security, create jobs, and deliver lasting economic benefits for Australia.” XRG said the project offers a combination of existing production, strategic infrastructure and opportunities for future upstream development. The company, which is wholly owned by Adnoc , has an enterprise value of more than $150 billion and invests across natural gas, chemicals and energy solutions.

events.title: Aged over 50, experienced and looking for work. Will employers bite?
events.summary: Even as older workers are encouraged to remain in the workforce for longer, the question is whether employers are willing to hire them. Singapore will raise retirement age to 65 and re-employment age to 70 from Jan 1, 2029, as the Government backs plans to help older workers stay in work. Older jobseekers like Raj Bharij, Gurmit Singh Kullar and Jason say they face instant rejections, overqualification fears and long job searches after retrenchment or resignation. Data shows weaker hiring for older workers: 42% in their 50s and 39% over 60 found jobs within six months, versus 61% in their 40s; employers may still value contract roles and transferable skills. SINGAPORE – Raj Bharij lost his job in 2026 when his employer, a global bank, restructured. “I’m 50 years old,” he recalls thinking, when told of the retrenchment in April. “Is anyone going to actually hire me now?” Six months on and more than 100 applications later, the former transformation director is still searching for his next job. He has received “instant” rejections, within seconds, from some firms’ automated systems and radio silence from others. An artificial intelligence chatbot tasked with helping to refine his resume suggested he take five years off his age. Bharij and other mature job seekers whom The Straits Times spoke to believe that being older and more experienced has somehow made their job search harder. Their experiences highlight a question facing Singapore: Even as older workers are encouraged to remain in the workforce for longer, will employers be willing to hire them? Singapore will raise its retirement age to 65 and re-employment age to 70 from Jan 1, 2029 – one year ahead of an earlier target. This was announced on Oct 26, 2026, when the Government accepted recommendations from the Tripartite Workgroup on Senior Employment aimed at helping older workers remain in meaningful employment for longer. The move comes as the Republic’s population ages . The share of workers aged 50 and above in the workforce grew from 34% in 2015 to 40% in 2025, and is expected to rise further, a report by the workgroup said. Gurmit Singh Kullar, 52, left his job as a marketing director in July 2024 after experiencing burnout. Re-entering the workforce after a six-month break has proven an uphill task. Many marketing roles these days, he found, merge what would previously have been three jobs into one, effectively denting the value of his past experience. He applied to more than 200 openings in less than two years. When he did not hear back from prospective employers, he widened his search to include more junior or mid-level roles that paid just half of what he had been earning. Still, they did not bite. Hiring managers sometimes commented he had too much experience. “Isn’t it better for you to have someone more qualified?” he wondered. He attended career counselling and a handful of courses to learn new skills, where he encountered other mature job seekers in a similar situation. “Have you heard this line from people, that you’re overqualified?” he was asked by a man who had been retrenched from the insurance industry. Older workers are taking longer than others to find new work after losing their jobs, data from the Ministry of Manpower shows. In the second quarter of 2026, 42% of people in their 50s and 39% of those over 60 found new jobs six months after a layoff, compared with 61% for those in their 40s. A study by researchers, including Lee Zeewan from the National University of Singapore, found that 47% of employers surveyed were likely to hire workers in their 50s, compared with 35% who were neutral and 18% who were unlikely to do so. That number fell to 33% for workers aged 60 and above, they said, in a paper published earlier in 2026. Kirsty Poltock, a country manager for Singapore at recruitment firm Robert Walters, notes that the difficulties which older job seekers describe come as the market grows tougher for candidates in general, and firms’ hiring slows. She surmises that the labour market has become “less forgiving about a mismatch” between job seekers’ existing experience and the skills which firms are looking for, but believes there are still opportunities for workers in their 50s, having regularly placed such candidates in new roles. Contract work is one area that could play to senior workers’ strengths, she said, as more companies hire for non-permanent roles on a one- or two-year horizon as the economic outlook weakens. People who can articulate how their experience can help firms transform their human resources or finance operations, for instance, are seen as valuable hires, Poltock added. As their search for new work continues, Bharij and Gurmit are also having to deal with the emotional toll that being unemployed later in life brings, after having grown accustomed to the rhythm of work over decades. “The loss of identity is massive,” said Bharij, who used to describe himself as someone who worked at a bank.
