events.title: Cities Worldwide Build and Scale AI Services With NVIDIA Physical and Agentic AI
events.summary: Cities generate enormous amounts of data from cameras, sensors and operational systems, but turning it into useful action — for planning, maintenance and public services — remains a challenge. Physical and agentic AI offer new ways to close that gap, from digital twins for infrastructure planning to vision and service agents, while keeping local governments in control of how sensitive data is processed and used. Building on initiatives announced at GTC Berlin , NVIDIA and its partners are expanding physical AI and AI agents to cities worldwide. Shared computing infrastructure gives city departments, neighboring municipalities and local developers a common foundation to build on — extending services without each organization having to acquire and manage resources of their own. From resident services to vision agents, cities are adopting NVIDIA agentic AI to deliver faster, more responsive public services. City teams don’t need a massive infrastructure investment to get started building these AI services: depending on the workload, NVIDIA RTX workstations or a small GPU system may be enough. In Spain, 1MillionBot combines open source ALIA models trained at the Barcelona Supercomputing Center with NVIDIA Nemotron and other models in resident-service agents for Madrid Digital (Comunidad de Madrid), Administració Oberta de Catalunya and 150+ deployments across Spain, handling municipal procedures, appointment requests, urban-planning incidents and service inquiries. In the San Francisco Bay Area , LiveX is bringing its AI City vision to life with NVIDIA Cosmos world models and Nemotron open models, and Omniverse and Metropolis libraries on NVIDIA RTX PRO GPUs. The interactive, conversational AI hosts understand people’s needs, provide answers and take action, and can be tailored to local languages and service needs in airports, hospitals, local events and other public spaces. Vision AI agents can turn existing city camera feeds into operational insights, helping teams identify mobility and safety issues and coordinate emergency responses across city services. In Wrocław, Poland , K2K is building shared AI infrastructure using NVIDIA accelerated computing, NVIDIA Cosmos world reasoning models, and NVIDIA Metropolis Blueprint for video search and summarization (VSS) to transform existing camera streams into actionable intelligence for mobility, safety and event response — using the same infrastructure across several city functions. In Malaysia , ITMAX bundles infrastructure and agentic AI applications into long-term managed services for cities, including for traffic management. Built with reference to Cosmos, Nemotron and the Metropolis VSS blueprint, ITMAX’s SamurAI V2 vision agents are scaling on NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPUs to support 17,000+ cameras by 2027. ITMAX integrates TeraSim, an open source traffic simulation platform from Laplace Intelligence , to test signal timing, reducing peak-hour corridor travel times by up to 26%. Plan and Operate Critical Infrastructure With Digital Twins Beyond public-facing services, digital twins can help cities expedite infrastructure planning, minimizing disruption to local communities. City digital twins can also serve as a real-time operational simulation to facilitate faster decision-making. At Dangote’s Lekki refinery in Nigeria, Honeywell Technologies’ Forge Plant Cognition uses Nemotron-powered AI agents to understand operational data. A digital twin of the plant and its processes, built using Omniverse libraries, is also planned to support simulation and training. The platform, built on Dell PowerEdge servers with NVIDIA RTX PRO accelerators, helps operators identify bottlenecks, anticipate equipment and process issues, and optimize plant performance. In Taiwan , Linker Vision and Dutch architecture firm MVRDV are using NVIDIA Omniverse and Nemotron to build environmental, social and governance agents that can assess the environmental impact of various urban planning scenarios, simulating 15-year outcomes of an urban forest canopy in 10 minutes — increasing design iteration speed from two weeks per iteration to less than an hour. Cities can extend AI to more services by building on infrastructure already in place and adding capacity. Shared resources and managed services can help extend those capabilities across departments and municipalities. At Morocco’s Tanger Med port, Cires Technologies is expanding a sovereign AI factory for planned applications in worker safety, congestion analysis, cargo routing and port operations. Cires Technologies is also building an ecosystem of application providers to develop local models and applications for ports and cities. Beyond city services, Barcelona Supercomputing Center’s AI Factory Accelerator Programme gives startups access to sovereign computing, technical support and training. BSC AI Factory also supports research and innovation for startups — spanning agriculture, medical imaging, knowledge access and speech services. Learn how NVIDIA and its ecosystem are bringing physical AI, agentic AI and local AI factories to cities worldwide at Smart City Expo World Congress, running Nov. 3-5 in Barcelona, where NVIDIA Vice President of EMEA Paolo Guglielmini will deliver a keynote address followed by a panel moderated by Charbel Aoun, director of smart city and spaces for EMEA at NVIDIA. events.title: Chalmers promises to be 'helpful' on inflation but rejects blame for rate hike
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Government will play 'helpful role' on inflation but not at fault, Jim Chalmers says Jim Chalmers pointed to evidence that public sector demand was easing. ( ABC News: Ian Cutmore ) Jim Chalmers says the government's budget is "not what's putting upward pressure on inflation" after a fifth rate hike this year. The Reserve Bank made the widely expected move on rates. The government has promised fresh savings in the mid-year budget update next month. Treasurer Jim Chalmers has again denied his budget is the cause of persistent inflation, after the Reserve Bank raised interest rates for the fifth time this year. Facing political pressure over the level of government spending, the treasurer seized on the bank's assessment that public sector demand was "weaker than expected" in early 2026, the period when inflation began its resurgence. "Public demand growth has eased quite substantially at a time when private demand has tripled," he said. "Our budgets are not what's putting upward pressure on inflation, but we can play a helpful role and that's what we intend to do." RBA lifts interest rates to try to dampen inflation The RBA lifts interest rates to the highest level in 18 years in a majority decision by its board. Mr Chalmers has promised fresh savings in next month's mid-year budget update, but could not say whether the savings would be enough to outweigh new spending, a feat the Albanese government has not managed in any of the five years it has overseen. "We take responsibility for our part of the fight against inflation," he said. "We're helping with the cost of living at the same time as we manage the budget responsibly." Reserve Bank Governor Michele Bullock maintained her longstanding practice of avoiding direct comment on the government's budget, saying overall demand, combining public and private, remained too high across the economy. "It's up to the government, the elected officials, to decide what they want to do with the budget," she said. "Independence is a two-way street. I don't tell them what to do with fiscal policy. They don't tell me what to do with interest rates." Public demand eases, but question marks over role of NDIS Ms Bullock said the decision on rates, which was not unanimous, was motivated by the ongoing consequences of the Middle East and domestic factors. The main domestic driver, though not the sole one, has been artificial intelligence investment. The bank's updated forecasts predict business investment will grow by 12 per cent this year and public demand by just 2.1 per cent. The "weaker" public result was partly due to "the ending of some temporary cost-of-living measures", a staff note explained. Also cited was a "moderation" in spending on defence, disability and aged care. The largest single category of savings by far under the Albanese government has been to the National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS), with $36 billion saved over four years in the May budget alone. But fresh doubts have been raised over whether that saving can be achieved, after the publication of preliminary findings from the Australian Government Actuary that the $36 billion figure was subject to "considerable uncertainty". Though cautioning that he did not have "sufficient detail" to draw a firm conclusion about the costings, actuary Guy Thorburn noted several risks, including an assumption of the numbers of children with autism entering the scheme not yet borne out by reality. The government has not been specific about where further savings will be found in the budget. Finance Minister Katy Gallagher said she was "looking across government" for ways to cut back, but that these would be "difficult decisions". "We have to respond to the economic circumstances we face … [But] we're also mindful of the fact we need to support people through this as well," she said. "I hear a lot of calls for cuts to government spending, I don't hear as many specifics about where." Could government spending cuts fight inflation? The Reserve Bank is tipped to increase interest rates tomorrow because of an ongoing concern that inflation is not under control. But is there an alternative? Shadow Treasurer Tim Wilson said the government had a "spending addiction" and was fuelling inflation. "[It] will never pull in its belt, but it keeps telling Australians to pull in theirs. It stokes inflation, taxes inflation and spends inflation," he said. While public demand is growing much slower than private demand in the Reserve Bank's forecasts, the bank does expect it to grow faster than the economy overall.

events.title: Open models can do 90% of agentic work at a twentieth of the cost of a frontier LLM: Gartner
events.summary: For-profit model-makers, many of which are spending billions on AI infrastructure, will be chasing revenue from just ten percent of steps involved in agentic AI workflows, according to analyst firm Gartner. “Nine in 10 agent workflow steps are routine, and open-weight models handle them at parity for a quarter of the price of the cheapest closed model,” the firm’s senior director Mark Petty and group vice president Raymond Paquet wrote last week in new document titled “Open-Weight Models Will Run 90% of Enterprise Agentic Workflow Steps.” “Typical operational workflows involve hundreds of routine executions, such as classification, tool calling, passing, validating and reconciling data,” the pair observe, before suggesting open-weight models “can handle hundreds of these routine steps for every one that needs frontier reasoning.” “Against the cheapest closed model at the same score, the open model costs a quarter as much. Against a frontier model run on every step, it costs as little as a twentieth,” the pair add. Those are the best-case numbers, because the analysts admit “Current open models can be more verbose and retry more often, so the saving per task against a frontier model is closer to five or six times.” That’s still a lovely saving, but the analysts rate it as the welcome by-product of moving to open models rather than an end in itself. “Years of workflow history are a large part of what an acquirer pays for in a SaaS company and every routine step sent to a frontier API moves a slice of it outside your perimeter,” the pair wrote. “Open-weights preserve your control. The cost saving is a bonus.” The two analysts therefore offer the following strategic planning assumption: “By 2030, 90% of enterprise operational agent workflow steps will execute on open-weight models.” They argue that enterprises will mostly adopt domain-specific open-weight models, because they do well “in scenarios where a small number of highly stable steps run millions of times a month.” Most models, however, are already commodities. Harnesses, the tools that run agents and manage agents, are the source of value in AI products, because one of their roles is to route work to the most appropriate model for a job, without users noticing any impact. A good harness saves money, imposes strong guardrails, and manages agent fleets. Less powerful harnesses leave users with more to do. The paper suggests frontier models will continue to have a role as the engine of research and development and are effectively capital expense. Open-weight models become an operational expense after frontier models do the heavy lifting. ®

events.title: Victorian farmers blindsided by approval of 155-turbine wind farm ahead of election
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Victorian farmers blindsided by wind farm approval on eve of election caretaker period A 155-turbine wind farm has been approved for Victoria's north. ( ABC Great Southern: Andrew Chounding ) The Victorian government has approved the controversial Meering West Wind Farm, which could include up to 155 turbines, a day before entering caretaker mode. More than 100 objections had been lodged and neighbouring farmers say their concerns have been ignored. The project's future could hinge on the November 28 state election, with the Coalition pledging to scrap the VNI West transmission line the project intends to connect to. The Victorian government has signed off on a large wind and battery project for the state's north, on the eve of entering caretaker mode ahead of this month's state election. Planning Minister Sonya Kilkenny signed off on a planning permit for the Meering West Wind Farm on Monday, just a day before the caretaker period came into effect. The facility to be built at Meering West, about 140km north-west of Bendigo, would be one of Australia's largest, incorporating up to 155 wind turbines. Construction on the project, which would deliver 1.3 gigawatts of generation capacity and 1,000 megawatt-hours of battery energy storage, is due to start in 2029. Like other similar facilities, it has been deeply controversial among local residents, with many farmers rallying against its approval. The timing of the approval is further complicated by the facility's intention to tap into the VNI West transmission line, which is yet to be built and would be scrapped if the Victorian Coalition came to government. Tyler Nelson is one of many neighbouring farmers who have objected to the project. He said he was not surprised the government had signed off on it at the last minute. "I'm very disappointed, but at the same time I can't say I'm shocked with the behaviour of the Labor government," he said. "It's well established that there are a lot of projects being rushed through at the 11th hour and there's been a pretty poor process involved for quite some time." Tyler Nelson is among the many farmers who oppose the Meering West wind farm. ( Supplied: Tyler Nelson ) Mr Nelson said he and other neighbours had been unaware of the project until it was well advanced. "Most neighbours and those affected found out pretty late in the piece, once there were contracts and caveats in place," he said. Mr Nelson said more than 100 people had objected to the project, with concerns including noise, shadow, flicker, land devaluation, fire risk and impacts on the natural environment. He said their objections and requests, including removing turbines from the project footprint close to objecting neighbours, had not been adopted. The wind farm at Meering West would have 1.3 gigawatts of generation capacity. ( Supplied: Pixabay / JACLOU-DL / License /File ) Mr Nelson was reluctant to comment on the community divisions the project had created. "I've tried not to let it affect me, but it's difficult not to," he said. "Communities that usually stand together and talk, when that's taken away, it seems a bit odd." Victoria's election is nearly here — it's time to have Your Say Before Victorians head to the polls on November 28, we want to hear about what matters to you most. Given the Coalition has committed to scrap VNI West, Mr Nelson said he hoped there would be a change of government on November 28, but he was not convinced it would leave the Meering West project dead in the water. "It would be nice to think that is the case, but what we're learning is we never know what's happening with backroom deals," he said. "Yes, scrapping VNI West is a good move by the Coalition, but what does it mean for this project? "It's my understanding that [project proponent Virya] will continue to develop on somehow, but I don't know what that looks like." The Victorian government, Meering West Wind Farm representatives and developer Virya were contacted for comment.

events.title: Widening inequality, stagnant pay – Britain urgently needs Labour’s hard-won workers’ rights | Polly Toynbee
events.summary: Widening inequality, stagnant pay – Britain urgently needs Labour’s hard-won workers’ rights The British Social Attitudes survey reveals record levels of dissatisfaction. But still Kemi Badenoch and the business lobby want to take us backwards B ritain is unhappier at work than since records began. The British Social Attitudes survey , the nation’s long-running annual pulse-taker, finds growing job dissatisfaction in its report, published today. People complain of a lack of flexibility in working hours, a lack of career advancement – and, of course, a lack of pay rises. Who is surprised? Pay stagnation over the last decade is unprecedented since Napoleonic times, the economist Paul Johnson told me, but then corrected himself: “You might as well say ever.” Worse, over the last year pay inequality has jumped up for the first time in a decade, says the Resolution Foundation’s Mike Brewer. Pay for the top 10% rose by 7.3% but only by 1.1% for the bottom 10%. Why? The national living wage has stopped rising faster than median pay, and top pay has taken off again. This gap in pay rises is the highest ever recorded. As ever, the wealth gap is even wider, the top 1% owning more than the whole bottom half. When incomes are rising, people may forget Britain’s extreme inequality , the highest in western Europe, which has never fallen after taking off stratospherically in the 1980s. But in these moribund times, most see no upturn on the horizon. In high-growth 2006, only 25% of people told the BSA survey the government should shrink the gap between rich and poor; now it’s 53% . Let’s have no more politicians’ pieties about working hard and playing by the rules when “hard-working” people feel under-rewarded, with their expectation of career advancement having fallen from 35% to 26%. Rags to riches, tea boy to boardroom stories belong to grandparents’ folk memories of the 1950s and 60s, when steep upward mobility, even for early school leavers, came from an escalation in white-collar, admin, skilled and managerial jobs. For the statistics and personal stories of opportunities for the bright but unqualified, see social historian David Kynaston’s phenomenal book Deep into the Sixties . Alan Sugar, the poster boy for that lost world, was a Hackney market trader who became a billionaire. But look how he sees young people now , accusing them of “a lack of hunger, wanting a quick fix, not wanting to put the graft in and get there through hard work”. His TV series The Apprentice may influence his generation to despise young people, ignorant as they may be of what has changed since their day. Yet the work ethic is as strong as ever, says Prof John Curtice, editor of this week’s BSA findings. People feel that work matters beyond money: only 4% would choose not to work if they could, and just 2% of young people – they are not feckless and idle. The world of work has reversed, perversely: young people are more educated, with the exam results to prove it, yet have less chance than their parents of making progress. They are likely to earn and own less. That’s a recipe for social disaster. As job satisfaction falls to its lowest in the BSA survey’s records, “The proportion willing to work harder than required to help their employer succeed has fallen to its lowest-ever level over the past decade.” What to do when improving growth, productivity and pay eludes governments throughout Europe? Labour’s best hope of easing this national discouragement is by rolling out better working rights now. This flagship policy in its 2024 manifesto brings greater control over hours and increased protection from heavy-handed employers. The BSA finds 61% think it important to be able to decide their own working hours, yet only 31% say they can in their job. That affects everyone, in jobs high and low, anxiously calculating childcare, school drop-off times, counting every £1 in commuting costs from a home chosen as cheaper because it’s further away. A management’s sudden arbitrary edict to return to the office – I came across a case this weekend – upends everything in precariously balanced household finances. Far stronger rights to request flexible hours or more working from home come in next year, when employers must give highly specific business reasons for refusal, not simply their belief that working from the office is better, in face-to-face consultations where employees can bring a union rep or a fellow worker. Last Friday new working rights came into force , letting trade union reps visit every workplace to recruit – every KFC and McDonald’s, every care home, every office high and low – to bring employees together to discuss their working lives without fear of reprisal. Joining a union will open up new avenues for employees to resolve their discontents. Banning exploitative zero-hours arrangements and introducing guaranteed contracts, so workers always know their schedule and what they will earn, will remove one extreme of bad employment practice.

events.title: Hope for house hunters amid slump as realtor warns optimism premature
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Perth property price slump provides glimmer of hope for homebuyers Vanessa Bray says a drop in Perth house prices has given her hope of finding a home for her family. ( ABC News: Madigan Landry ) Home buyers are hopeful a drop in Perth property prices will help them break into the market. New data shows the city's median dwelling value has fallen to $942,018, but that is still 68 per cent higher than it was five years ago. A Perth realtor warns the optimism of those trying to buy a home may be premature, saying the figures do not represent the true state of the housing market. After years of searching for a home as Perth property prices continued to rise at an unprecedented rate, Vanessa Bray finally feels like she has a fighting chance of securing one. The single mum has been buoyed by new figures showing Australia is tracking towards its biggest housing market downturn in 40 years, with Perth's house prices dropping 5.7 per cent over the last three months. Data from property research group Cotality shows Perth's median dwelling price has fallen to $942,018 — a drop of nearly $100,000 since peaking at more than $1 million in April. Meanwhile, economists at the Commonwealth Bank today released an updated forecast predicting Perth property prices would plummet 18 per cent from that April peak, before prices begin to stabilise in the second half of 2027. For Ms Bray, the easing market spells hope of finding a home for her and her sons. Vanessa Bray is feeling a lot more positive about buying a home in light of recent data. ( ABC News: Madigan Landry ) "I can't even begin to describe the relief that I feel for myself and my kids that we could maybe have a home of our own," she said. "It's close. I feel like it will happen instead of the despair that I had that it was never going to happen." National house prices have fallen for a seventh consecutive month, according to property research group Cotality. Ms Bray has been looking for a family home since she and her partner separated four years ago. She needs to find something in their school catchment while staying under the $850,000 cap needed to qualify for the federal government's Help to Buy Scheme. Ms Bray said her experience of trying to buy a home had been '"devastating" and like being on a "rollercoaster". "[I've gone from] thinking, 'right, this could finally be it. I'm going to make it. I'm going to have long-term security for me and my kids' to the devastation of 'I've missed out again'," she said. Perth's median dwelling price has fallen by almost $100,000 in six months. ( ABC News: Gian De Poloni ) While the recent slump in prices represents a glimmer of hope for those trying to break into the market, the softening represents a small dent in the meteoric rise in Perth's property prices, which have risen 93 per cent in a decade, including 68 per cent in the last five years. Perth realtor Kyle Peters warned the optimism of those trying to enter the market could be premature. Mr Peters said the recent figures were not a good representation of the true state of Australia's housing market. "It would be an interesting anomaly that a housing market would crash when we have a housing crisis and don't have enough houses for people to live in," Mr Peters said. "At the rate things were ramping up before, there needed to be some abatement, but certainly we [still] have a housing shortage." REIWA president Rob Mandanici said even if prices did not continue to fall on the same trajectory, the slowing market still provided benefits for those entering the market. REIWA President Rob Mandanici says the easing should give buyers some breathing space. ( ABC News: Madigan Landry ) "They can take a little bit more time to make that purchasing decision and not feel that immense pressure to rush into a decision," he said. "The buyers themselves haven't disappeared, they've become more selective." House prices are falling all around the country. ( ABC News: Charlotte Wilkes ) Mr Mandanici said there was no doubt Australia was experiencing "a little bit of a market slowdown", but said the dip in prices did not amount to a crash. "We are seeing some prices across multiple Perth suburbs pull back, but a lot of those suburbs are coming off highs," he said. "We've got a lot of buyers sitting on the sidelines and I think today's interest rate decision will just give buyers the certainty that they want moving forward." On Tuesday the Reserve Bank increased interest rates by 0.25 percentage points, lifting the cash rate to 4.85 per cent, the highest it has been since 2008.

events.title: Aramco posts 34% jump in third-quarter profit despite attacks on energy infrastructure
events.summary: Saudi Arabia's Aramco , the world's largest oil-producing company, has reported a 34 per cent annual increase in its third-quarter net income despite disruption in the Strait of Hormuz and attacks on energy infrastructure in the kingdom. Net profit for the three months to the end of September rose to 135.94 billion Saudi riyals ($36.25 billion), up from 101 billion riyals for the same period last year, Aramco said on Tuesday in a statement to the Tadawul stock exchange, where its shares are traded. “Geopolitical uncertainty and attacks on key energy facilities continued to amplify the global energy supply crisis in the third quarter of 2026, with serious implications for global energy security,” Aramco president and chief executive Amin Nasser said. “Despite challenges, the flexibility of our system and the strength of a supply network built over decades enabled us to continue delivering reliably to our customers through this extraordinary period.” Aramco's board approved a third-quarter base dividend of $21.9 billion, a 3.5 per cent year-on-year increase, which will be paid in the fourth quarter of this year. Revenue boost The annual quarterly increase was driven by higher revenue despite volatile global energy markets, where prices shifted according to geopolitical headlines. Total revenue for the reporting period rose to $140.5 billion, up from $111.6 billion recorded for the third quarter of 2025. “The increase in revenue was predominantly driven by higher prices of refined and chemical products and crude oil, partially offset by lower volumes sold of crude oil and refined and chemical products,” Aramco said. The company's increased quarterly income provides a boost for Saudi Arabia, the Arab world’s biggest economy, which still relies heavily on the sale of hydrocarbons for revenue. Aramco, Opec’s biggest oil producer and the main driver of Saudi Arabia's industrial sector, has faced waves of missile and drone attacks from Yemen’s Houthi militants that have put pressure on government revenue. In October, a Houthi missile attack damaged Saudi Aramco’s headquarters in Dhahran. The attack caused a fire in an administrative building in the complex. Several crude refining facilities, including those in Jazan in the west and Riyadh, have also been attacked in recent weeks, raising fresh concerns about Saudi Arabia’s energy industry and Aramco’s ability to continue supplying crude oil to its global clientele. The disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, where Iranian attacks on vessels rose in October to the highest level since the US Iran-war began on February 28, is adding to oil exporters’ woes. Overseas storage To avoid Hormuz, Saudi Arabia has ramped up crude shipments from its main export hub at Ras Tanura. The kingdom has relied on its East-West pipeline to pump crude to its Red Sea port. However, the pipeline was temporarily shut down after missiles launched from Iraqi territory damaged a pumping station. Saudi Arabia, which is also facing a Houthi-enforced maritime blockade, is exploring more routes to keep servicing its customers in Asia. “We continue to explore additional overseas storage capacity and alternative export routes to further strengthen our global supply network,” Mr Nasser said. While the East-West pipeline provides export flexibility, the company remains focused on operations and will continue to invest in projects, Aramco said. Production started at the company's Zuluf crude oil increment project in October. Major upstream projects, including Jafurah phase two, the Fadhili Gas Plant expansion, and the Dammam development project, remain on track, the company said. Aramco's capital expenditure of $10.5 billion in the third quarter is, however, lower than the $12.6 billion reported for the same period in 2025. “Backed by our strong balance sheet, we remain focused on the disciplined execution of priority projects … to unlock new opportunities,” Mr Nasser said. “This is how we will continue to meet the world’s evolving energy needs and deliver value for our shareholders and customers.”

events.title: Adnoc Gas to supply TotalEnergies with up to 1.6 million tonnes of LNG in five-year deal
events.summary: Adnoc Gas has signed a five-year agreement to supply up to 1.6 million tonnes of liquefied natural gas to France's TotalEnergies, as the Abu Dhabi company expands its share of the global LNG market. The deal builds on a long-standing partnership between the two companies and reflects growing demand for LNG and confidence in Adnoc’s ability to deliver reliable supplies, the company said on Tuesday. “ Global demand for LNG continues to grow, and Adnoc Gas is well-positioned to capture that opportunity,” said Fatema Al Nuaimi, chief executive of Adnoc Gas. “This agreement reflects the strength of our LNG business, the competitiveness of our supply offering and our ability to secure long-term partnerships that support growth, enhance resilience and create lasting value for shareholders.” Adnoc Gas has continued to execute its long-term growth strategy this year, despite operational constraints. The company awarded $8.2 billion in engineering, procurement and construction contracts, part of its largest capital investment, for the second and third phases of the Rich Gas Development project – $3.9 billion for Phase 2, and $4.3 billion for Phase 3, the company said in August. These contracts build on Phase 1, announced in June 2025. The Rich Gas Development is a multi-phase, $13.2 billion capital investment programme by Adnoc Gas to expand gas processing and liquid recovery infrastructure across the UAE. The latest move strengthens Adnoc Gas’s commercial position at a time when demand for LNG is rising across Europe and Asia. Asia remains the main destination for LNG, accounting for about 65 per cent of global imports in 2025, while Europe has become a major buyer as it replaces Russian pipeline gas and manages storage needs, according to the International Energy Agency’s latest gas market report. “Thanks to its perfect location between Europe and Asia, this new supply will enable TotalEnergies to confirm its position as one of the main LNG portfolio suppliers,” said Stephane Michel, president of gas, renewables and power at TotalEnergies. TotalEnergies is both a shareholder in Adnoc Gas and a partner in the Ruwais LNG project. Adnoc Gas said it expects the planned integration of the Ruwais LNG project to significantly increase its production capacity, supporting its ambition to become one of the world’s leading LNG suppliers. The agreement between Adnoc Gas and TotalEnergies comes as Adnoc scales up a new global LNG marketing and trading platform that combines the marketing activities of Adnoc Gas and investment arm XRG with the trading capabilities of Adnoc Trading . The platform is aiming to reach 47 million tonnes per annum of marketable LNG beyond 2030, a level intended to place it among the world’s leading LNG marketing and trading businesses, Adnoc Gas said on Tuesday. Adnoc Gas supplies about 60 per cent of the UAE’s sales gas needs and supplies end-customers in more than 20 countries.

events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Kate McClymont denies 'profit motive' behind articles detailing Alan Jones allegations Investigative journalist Kate McClymont's stories kicked off a police investigation into broadcaster Alan Jones. ( ABC News: Ethan Rix ) Journalist Kate McClymont has given evidence in the Alan Jones trial where she was questioned about whether her reporting on Mr Jones was profit-driven. Ms McClymont spoke with three of the five complainants in the trial for stories published in late 2023 and early 2024. Mr Jones's team has also accused her of "introducing" the words "go the grope" in her interview with one complainant. The journalist whose work sparked a police investigation into broadcaster Alan Jones has been questioned about whether she had a "profit motive" to run a series of stories about the former 2GB radio host allegedly indecently assaulting young men. Kate McClymont gave evidence on day 55 of Mr Jones's criminal trial at the NSW Local Court, where he has pleaded not guilty to 21 counts of indecent assault and sexual touching. NSW Sexual Violence Helpline on 1800 424 017 NSW Victims Services on 1800 633 063 Bravehearts (support for child sexual abuse survivors) on 1800 272 831 Child Protection Helpline on 132 111 MARS Australia (for men affected by rape and sexual abuse) on (07) 3857 1222 National Survivors Foundation on 1300 124 433 Full Stop Australia on 1800 385 578. The court has heard Ms McClymont, who is a multiple Walkley Award-winning journalist and the Sydney Morning Herald's chief investigative reporter, spoke to three of the five complainants in the trial for stories published in late 2023 and early 2024. The defence has sought to poke holes in Ms McClymont's original reporting of the allegations against Mr Jones, some of which have since been explored during days of evidence in his criminal trial. Mr Jones's team has also accused the journalist of "introducing" the words "go the grope" in her interview with one complainant, and has suggested her reporting influenced the allegations other complainants made later. Mr Jones's barrister started her cross-examination of the reporter on Tuesday. ( ABC News: Ethan Rix ) Defence barrister Gabrielle Bashir SC probed Ms McClymont about why she wrote the stories, suggesting to her that there was a "profit motive" in writing articles about a high-profile person. "The story has to sell papers, doesn't it?" Ms Bashir asked. "That's not my problem," Ms McClymont replied. "It is correct to say that higher readership numbers encourage advertisers to invest in advertising with the paper?" Ms Bashir asked. "As a general proposition, yes, but that is not my role." Ms McClymont agreed Mr Jones was viewed "by some people" as "conservative leaning". "Alan Jones is a very public figure in New South Wales? He's a divisive figure?" Ms Bashir proposed. "If you say so," Ms McClymont replied. The journalist was also asked whether any money or benefit was paid to any alleged victim of Mr Jones in exchange for their stories, which she denied. Mr Jones has pleaded not guilty to 21 counts of indecent assault and sexual touching relating to five men. ( ABC News: Abbey Haberecht ) Ms McClymont confirmed she spoke to and published the allegations of three of the complainants in this criminal trial. She said she had no contact with two other complainants, the high-profile athlete known as Complainant M and a former up-and-coming athlete known as Complainant J. Mr Jones's lawyers have argued throughout the trial that Ms McClymont is on one side of a media rivalry which was set on "destroying" Mr Jones. Clip of McClymont's interview played to court McClymont gives evidence in Alan Jones trial — as it happened The reporter published a series of stories from late 2023 that contained accounts from a number of men who alleged Mr Jones indecently assaulted them. The court was played a snippet of an interview Ms McClymont conducted with Complainant C in 2023, in which he described allegations of being touched by Mr Jones in a car. "He would go the grope?" Ms McClymont can be heard asking the man. "He'd go the grope," Complainant C said in reply. That phrase became part of the headline of Ms McClymont's first article about Mr Jones, which was published in December 2023. Under questioning, the journalist agreed she "introduced" the words but said her interview subject repeated them, so she used them. "You used those words and then he repeated them?" Ms Bashir asked. "And when you used those words, you knew that would be a catchy quote?

events.title: ‘It brings soul into this sterile world’: the Birmingham clubbers fighting to save their patch – and Britain’s nightlife

events.title: Architect creates open source replacement for VM migration tool VMware has hidden
events.summary: A cloud architect has created an open source alternative to VMware’s Virtual Disk Development Kit (VDDK), which the virtualization giant recently withdrew from public downloads. VMware describes VDDK as “a set of libraries and utilities that enable software developers to create applications that can access and manipulate virtual disks” and “a valuable tool for developers of storage and backup applications.” Users, along with VMware’s rivals, had another use for VDDK: migrating VMs to alternative virtualization platforms. In August, VMware restricted access to VDDK downloads to its partners, meaning VMware customers couldn’t access the tool and some of its rivals’ migration tools became less effective. Cloud architect Andrija Panić decided to do something about it. “Many tools that have nothing in common except VMware use the same small library to read a virtual machine’s disks: virt-v2v and nbdkit, the importers in Forklift/MTV, Proxmox VE and Apache CloudStack, and countless in-house scripts,” he told The Register by email. “When public VDDK downloads ended, all of them became harder to install and run.” “I didn’t think it was fair that people’s ability to move or protect their own data should depend on a download page.” He describes the project as “an independent drop-in for libvixDiskLib.so.8.0.3, the disk library that VMware backup and migration tools load to read virtual disks. It was written from scratch, using only public documentation and black-box testing, and contains no VMware code.” Panić told The Register he wrote the tool in Go, with a thin C layer that exposes exactly the same C interface, library name and symbol versions as VMware’s code. The tool cannot write disks, just read them for backup and migration purposes. In his email to The Register , Panić said he has successfully tested OpenVDDK on vSphere versions 6.7 U3, 7.0.3, 8.0.3, 9.1.1. He said that tests in his lab with the latter version, accessing OpenVDDK through vCenter and on a standalone ESXi host, saw every disk read match. “Independent testers have reported successful use with Forklift (VMware to KubeVirt, cold and warm), MTV on OpenShift (cold and warm), a Proxmox VE pipeline and custom nbdkit-based tools,” the architect told The Register . “I've received reports of production use, including a German cloud provider migrating a large file server with V2K Migrate and a US-based company migrating to Apache CloudStack/KVM.” Panić was at pains to point out that the reports of successful use are “not independently audited customer endorsements or a guarantee of suitability for every production environment.” As is often the case with FOSS tools. OpenVDDK is not the only option for migrating away from VMware without VDDK. KVM-based OpenNebula has a tool called OneSwap that it says has a 96 percent success rate. Nutanix recently tweaked its “Move” migration tool so it can do the job without VDDK. Red Hat is working on a fix but has provided details of a workaround . Panić made OpenVDDK available under an Apache license, so perhaps Red Hat and others will find it useful as they re-jig their VM migration tools. ®

events.title: Here’s who is falling in line for Trump’s “Super Intelligence” loyalty test
events.summary: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here . At the end of September, President Trump signed an executive order that contained just one directive, ordering government agencies to rebrand what they had been calling artificial intelligence as “Super Intelligence.” That term beat out other contenders, including “Extreme Intelligence” and “Supreme Intelligence,” offered by the president in a poll on X a couple of weeks earlier.  Rebrands are, of course, now a White House tradition: Trump has changed names to project US dominance of certain bodies of water (the Gulf of America and Lake America), to signal new institutional priorities (Department of War), or simply to leave his mark on storied places (see the ongoing fight over renaming the Kennedy Center).  The stated reason for this name change is that today’s AI systems “amplify human ingenuity” rather than merely “imitate” intelligence, and the government’s terminology should reflect that. But if this rebrand follows the pattern of others, its effects will extend beyond government.  It will turn a choice of words into a political loyalty test: Those who use the new term demonstrate allegiance to the administration, and those who don’t become marks for attacks (recall that the Trump administration barred the Associated Press from some White House press events after the news outlet did not adopt the term “Gulf of America”).  But most Americans go months without ever pondering what to call the major lake between New York and Canada. AI, on the other hand, is at the center of our national conversation and a technology two-thirds of Americans report interacting with multiple times a week. It might be the boldest rebrand yet.  So one month in, who’s on board? Let’s start with the government itself. The term “Super Intelligence”—or simply “SI”—now appears more often on government solicitations, like a new request by Immigration and Customs Enforcement for companies to build “SI-powered” surveillance for ICE detention facilities. The new term has been swapped in silently on most government websites. Some, including that of the National Institutes of Health, now include a banner warning visitors they might see both the new and the old terms during the transition period. There have been hiccups. A day after the rebrand order, the Pentagon announced an ambitious new initiative to study the future of warfare, called Project Meridian; it used the old terminology. A Federal Trade Commission press release last week used “superintelligence” instead of the two-word, capitalized version ordered by the president, and recent press releases from Health and Human Services show no sign of the new language.  The term “AI” will likely stick around given the countless AI-related offices, initiatives, and programs that have sprung up in recent years, like the Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office at the Pentagon (the executive order says it doesn’t apply to previously issued regulations or documents). As for government employees, it appears to be taking time for “SI” rather than “AI” to roll off the tongue. One researcher at a national lab I interviewed a few weeks ago used “AI” repeatedly before sheepishly acknowledging the slip-up. Even Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth used “AI” in an interview on October 3.  But Trump’s other rebrands suggest the goal isn’t merely to change the government’s vocabulary. It’s to change how the rest of us speak, too. In the past couple of weeks, most of President Trump’s posts on Truth Social have been endorsements for candidates in the midterms. But on October 27 he took a break from electioneering to criticize the Wall Street Journal for not using “Super Intelligence,” “the name which virtually everyone else is using, or soon will be.” He suggested that a new rule will soon go further than the executive order to outright ban “artificial intelligence” from government documents.  But the Wall Street Journal is not alone: Even Newsmax, an outlet whose founder described it as “supportive of the President and his policies,” isn’t using the president’s preferred term.   Are Big Tech executives falling in line? It’s complicated. The same day that President Trump signed the rebranding order, he also released a nonbinding statement on AI safety, the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, signed by six of the most powerful people in tech: Sundar Pichai of Google, Dario Amodei of Anthropic, Mark Zuckerberg of Meta, Greg Brockman of OpenAI, Elon Musk of xAI, and Jensen Huang of Nvidia. But even among this group—three members of which attended Trump’s inauguration—the term has not caught on.  In an analysis of third-quarter earnings calls, CNBC reported that only Zuckerberg and Musk used the term consistently. But Zuckerberg doesn’t quite count: Meta has been saying “superintelligence” since last year anyway. Musk’s companies seem to use the term the most—and he even pledged to rename SpaceXAI to SpaceXSI. Musk himself still mixes SI and AI when posting on X.  Executives from Amazon, Microsoft, and Alphabet used “AI” in their calls, though Microsoft’s recent letter to shareholders referred to the “Super Intelligence era.” Huang has referenced the term but still uses AI too . One objection to this rebranding project is that it will cost time and taxpayer dollars. It is Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff’s prerogative to decide that SIForce is a better name than AIForce and direct his company to implement that change. But government employees are now spending time writing guides on how departments should navigate the rebrand. And, per the executive order , leaders of federal agencies will be required to put their heads together to draft a new legislative definition of “Super Intelligence” to be run by the president by the end of this month. But I’m more worried about what this does to our national conversation about AI than I am about the potential waste of time and money. Surprisingly often I overhear strangers at a grocery store or coffee shop who have struck up a conversation about AI. The substance of the conversation is rarely uplifting—they most often talk about a jobs apocalypse or AI-powered warfare—but what is heartening is how often I see a widespread desire among people to have a say in how this technology transforms their lives.  People may have wildly different feelings about AI, including outright hostility, but those differences don’t yet map neatly onto the partisan divisions that make it awkward for strangers to discuss immigration or climate change. If “Super Intelligence” turns into a loyalty test, this will cease to be the case. events.title: Interest rates highest since 2008 as inflation forecast to stay high
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts RBA lifts interest rates to highest level in 18 years to try to dampen inflation The RBA's monetary policy board has increased interest rates for the fifth time in 2026. ( Reuters: Jason Reed ) The Reserve Bank's monetary policy board has lifted interest rates by 0.25 percentage points. The decision lifts the cash rate target to 4.85 per cent, up from 4.60 per cent. It is the highest cash rate since late 2008. It is the fifth interest rate increase in 2026, and the RBA has left the door open for more rate hikes. The Reserve Bank has lifted interest rates to their highest level in 18 years, while acknowledging it will take much longer to drag inflation down than it was expecting a few months ago. It has increased rates by 0.25 percentage points, which lifts the cash rate target to 4.85 per cent, up from 4.60 per cent. The cash rate has not been this high in Australia since late 2008. It is the fifth time the bank has lifted rates in 2026. The brutal redistribution at the heart of the RBA's interest rate policy RBA officials argue the hit to borrowers' income isn't the main way rate rises lower inflation. But they often omit a key fact. The RBA board's decision to lift rates was not unanimous. Six members voted to increase the cash rate target by 25 basis points to 4.85 per cent, while three members voted to leave the cash rate target unchanged at 4.60 per cent. The majority decision will be another blow to households with mortgages. But individuals who have high-interest savings accounts will see their savings accruing more interest after today's decision, if their bank applies higher rates to their accounts. In a statement , the RBA board said inflation was now forecast to remain high throughout much of 2027 and was not expected to fall below 3 per cent until late 2027, which is "around three quarters later than previously forecast". "This presents upside risks to inflation expectations," it said. In recent weeks, RBA officials have been signalling their intention to lift rates at today's meeting, arguing that they can not afford to see peoples' inflation expectations drift higher. The RBA wants annual inflation in consumer prices to be around 2.5 per cent on average over the cycle. "There is an increasing share of businesses who are thinking that maybe 3 to 3.5 per cent is the new normal [for inflation]," RBA deputy governor Andrew Hauser warned last month . It takes between 12 and 18 months for a change in interest rates to flow completely through the economy, so we will not know what total impact this rate hike will have on economic activity until 2028. Economy slowing, house prices falling, unemployment rising The RBA Monetary Policy Board said the cumulative rate hikes this year have tightened financial conditions in Australia. It says the economy is slowing, housing prices have fallen significantly this year, and the unemployment rate has risen. Why housing's the great Australian talking point Why are Australians obsessed with property? Because we have to be. And there are big reasons why it's always on our minds. Its new economic forecasts see growth in output slowing even further over the coming year, which is expected to reduce capacity pressures and help return inflation to target. It says employment is expected to keep growing, but the unemployment rate is projected to rise by more than expected. In August, it was forecasting the unemployment rate to average 4.8 per cent in the December quarter of 2028, but now it was forecasting it to average 5.1 per cent in that period. The unemployment rate is currently 4.7 per cent . But the RBA board has also acknowledged that there continue to be "heightened uncertainties" about the outlook for inflation and the economy. "The Middle East conflict remains unresolved, and there are scenarios where inflation is higher and activity lower than forecast," it warned. "Global oil supply disruptions are maintaining upward pressure on global and domestic energy prices and inflation. "A period of prolonged uncertainty may also cause growth to be lower overseas and in Australia. "To date, however, growth in Australia's major trading partners has been stronger than expected, as the boost from AI-related investment has outweighed the adverse effects of the Middle East conflict," it said. Is the RBA pushing the economy into recession? In her post-meeting press conference, RBA governor Michele Bullock left the door open for more rate increases. She was then asked if the RBA was risking pushing Australia's economy into recession with more rate hikes.

events.title: Toyota shows off SoC that stores model weights and its OS on integrated memory
events.summary: Japanese carmaker Toyota has decided to have a crack at the market for AI processors. Toyota is the major shareholder in a company called AISIN, a manufacturer of automotive components. Both companies are aware that cars are increasingly reliant on tech like image recognition, and that robotics and other forms of “physical AI” will need parts that overlap with cars. AISIN thinks existing chips aren’t a good fit for such roles, because they rely on external memory to store AI models and then generate a lot of traffic between a processor and the model. That traffic, the company contends, makes image recognition and other on-device uses of AI less effective. DRAM is also currently vastly expensive. The company’s response is a system-on-chip built on a 16nm FinFET process, an Arm Cortex A53 dual-core CPU, plus an Arm MaliG31 GPU. The chip includes built-in STT-MRAM, which stores both model weights and an operating system. AISIN and its research partners at Tohoku University say that approach means the chip can go from power-on to kernel startup in 65.7 milliseconds – 38 times faster than is possible if using external memory – and run the Tiny YOLOv3 object detection algorithm on the chip. “To effectively utilize the limited on-chip memory capacity, a hybrid multiplication architecture combining 8-bit and 16-bit multiplication was developed” according to a machine translation of Tohoku University’s announcement [PDF]. “By combining 16x16, 16x8, and 8x8 bit multiplication, the amount of weight data for the AI model was reduced by 53 percent, from 17.7MB to 9.36MB, while maintaining 16-bit precision.” AISIN is an established parts supplier and already sells to Toyota and other automakers but hasn’t said if or when it can get this chip into production. Meanwhile, the likes of Nvidia and Qualcomm very much want to sell their silicon to carmakers, and position themselves as sources of tech and AI smarts that existing automotive supply chain participants can’t match. ®

events.title: EQT seeks joint AI and data centre deals with Saudi and UAE sovereign investors
events.summary: EQT , Europe’s biggest private markets investment firm, is in talks with sovereign investors in the UAE and Saudi Arabia to explore joint artificial intelligence and infrastructure investment opportunities in the Arab world’s top two economies, its global chair has said. The company with $400 billion in assets, which has been raising funds from Gulf investors for decades, is keen to now deploy capital in the region , home to some of the biggest sovereign wealth funds in the world, Jean Eric Salata, told The National . “Here [in the UAE] I would say, and we've also been talking to Saudis as well, looking at opportunities there. Those are the two big areas that we're working on right now,” Mr Salata said of the continuing AI co-investment conversations with sovereign investors. “We're most excited about, which I think aligns with the strategic goals of the UAE, is the whole infrastructure, particularly data infrastructure and data centres, where we have globally one of the largest footprints.” The Stockholm private equity company plans to expand its AI infrastructure footprint in the Gulf through its portfolio firm EdgeConneX, which owns more than 106 data centres across 25 countries, he said. AI opportunity EQT, which currently manages more than $100 billion in digital and energy assets across markets, is the latest global investor looking to the rapidly developing AI and digital infrastructure sector in the region. AI has become a central plank of economic diversification efforts of the oil-rich Gulf economies that have already announced mega AI infrastructure projects. The UAE is leading the way with a planned five-gigawatt UAE-US AI campus in Abu Dhabi, which includes Stargate UAE – a massive 1GW computing cluster anchored by a $20 billion data centre investment. UAE Tech investors Khazna and G42 are working on these projects alongside global leaders such as OpenAI, Oracle, Nvidia and Cisco, and investors such as SoftBank. Saudi Arabia, the largest Arab economy, has rolled out Project Transcendence, a $100 billion scheme to scale domestic AI and data infrastructure. The kingdom’s $1 trillion Public Investment Fund has also set up Humain to build out national cloud infrastructure in the country. Qatar’s sovereign arm, the Qatar Investment Authority, has also launched Qai, a $20 billion AI infrastructure partnership, to build out domestic GPU and data centre footprints. Since last year the three Gulf states have announced AI investment plans worth $120 billion, which exceeded 5 per cent of their gross domestic product, according to International Monetary Fund estimates. The sheer scale of investment required for AI development and data centres creates a huge opportunity for global investors such as EQT. The $1.3 trillion Blackstone Group has already struck a $3 billion deal with Saudi Arabia’s Humain, while tech giant Microsoft has committed over $10 billion towards data centres and related infrastructure across UAE, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and Kuwait through to 2030. “There are many conversations that are ongoing right now with potential partners, both here [in the UAE] and elsewhere in the region,” Mr Salata said. “This is a sector that is capital constrained and is really, if you think about the AI build-out, the core, the key constraint in building the infrastructure is actually physical. It's the physical constraint around chips, energy, and data centres.” There is no shortage of demand for compute, hence a very strong investment case for building the power generation capacity and rolling out data infrastructure, he said. “I think that's where a lot of investment opportunity is right now for providers of long-term capital that can invest on a 15-year investment horizon,” he said. UAE SWF partnerships EQT opened an office in Abu Dhabi’s ADGM in September, joining the roster of trillion-dollar investors and asset managers including BlackRock, State Street, Blackstone Group, PGIM , Nuveen and Capital Group . A base in Abu Dhabi gives global investors opportunities to expand in the region and work closely with sovereign funds, large family offices and institutional partners. EQT is already working closely with the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority, and Mr Salata said the firm is keen to expand that relationship. “They are one of our most important partners, and we're very excited to be working with them in, I would say, ever-increasing dimensions. We not only manage investments for Adia in our funds, but we also do a lot of co-investing together,” Mr Salata said. Adia is one of EQT’s largest co-underwriters in some of the European firm’s largest deals to take companies private in Europe. In June, Adia, along with Abu Dhabi’s $385 billion sovereign investment arm Mubadala Development Company, joined EQT’s £9.5 billion acquisition bid for the UK’s Intertek Group. Over the years, EQT has executed several co-investment deals with Mubadala, including the 2022 acquisition of Envirotainer, a biopharmaceutical industry solutions company. In 2025, Mubadala took a $600 million stake in Nord Anglia Education, and has been “a significant partner of ours all over the world”, he said. Deeping ties Establishing its first Middle East office in Abu Dhabi, Mr Salata said, was necessary to deepen its ties to the region, where it has active relationships with “many of the other sovereign wealth funds”. “The plan is to continue to develop those relationships regionally and use this office as a base to access them on a more regular basis,” he said. Forty EQT portfolio companies already have a presence in the Gulf, and with a local footprint, it expects more investments from regional sovereign investors to flow into those companies. “The logical place for us to start is with our existing portfolio companies,” Mr Salata said. “We really want to try and figure out how we can become more deeply involved in the investment ecosystem here,” he said. Over time EQT plans to bring more of its portfolio companies to the Gulf, and Mr Salata believes that the number will grow two or three-fold over the five to 10-year horizon. The sectors it seeks to invest in are “very much aligned with some of the longer-term trends in the region”, including infrastructure, education and health care, as well as technology and energy, where “the government policy is supportive”, he added.

events.title: Christmas 2026 stamps unveiled by Royal Mail
events.summary: Two stamps from the Royal Mail's annual Christmas collection Royal Mail has unveiled its Christmas stamps for this year - featuring scenes from the Nativity. The series of five stamps have been jointly created by graphic designer Gareth Howat and illustrator Rebecca Sutherland. The stamps depict familiar scenes of Mary and Joseph travelling, baby Jesus, an angel, the shepherds and the Three Wise Men. This year's collection marks the 60th anniversary of the first-ever Christmas special stamp. Sutherland said it was an "absolute honour" to be given the opportunity to illustrate the Christmas stamps for the Royal Mail. She said she has loved stamps since she was a child and had even collected them. "Being asked to create a set myself feels incredibly special," she added. The Christmas stamps from recent years have featured snowy scenes of UK cathedrals, or lyrics from famous carols - although 2025 also showed scenes from the Nativity. The first Christmas stamp collection came out in December 1966 after a children's art competition was announced by the then-postmaster Tony Benn. David Gold, of Royal Mail, said: "We hope this year's Christmas stamps will add an extra touch of festive magic to the millions of greetings sent to family and friends at home and around the world." events.title: Tech Firms Dismantle Botnet That Turned 1.3M TV Boxes Into Proxies
events.summary: Google said today it worked with industry partners to dismantle a botnet made up of more than 1.3 million Android TV set-top boxes that ship with malicious software which secretly rents the user’s Internet connection out to strangers and conducts advertising fraud. Experts involved in the takedown say the action is likely to sever the botnet’s access to more than 10 million additional compromised systems, including other Internet of Things (IoT) products such as Android-based healthcare devices and karaoke machines. A report from the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said Google has severed ties with Videostrong Technology Co. , a TV box manufacturer in China that GTIG and other industry experts concluded was responsible for including malware that enrolled more than 1.3 million set-top boxes in a botnet dubbed “ XCPE ” (named after one of the malware’s core code components). The global distribution of XCPE botnet infections. Image: Google Threat Intelligence Group. The report said the XCPE botnet loaded the user’s device with software that makes their Internet address available for resale by multiple “residential proxy” services, which allow customers to rent Internet addresses as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. As detailed in several stories here over the past year , residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects. “Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices,” the GTIG post reads, noting that Google took legal action to take down the domains and servers Videostrong used to control the botnet and install additional malware. “A device manufacturer intentionally infecting their users with malware is an unacceptable breach of trust, and represents a serious risk to those users. Without users’ knowledge or consent, infected devices were offered as a distribution mechanism for a wide array of criminal actors.” The report notes that while TV boxes made up the the majority of the botnet, the same XCPE malware was found in other Android-based IoT products, including telehealth devices, karaoke machines, and even digital signage systems . Google said it requires all Android device makers to pass compatibility and security tests to ensure their products don’t harm users, but that Videostrong nevertheless found a way to load their malicious software immediately after a user boots up one of these devices for the first time (Google says it has since addressed that weakness). The GTIG report calls out a number of residential proxy providers whose software development kits were routinely downloaded by devices infected by the XCPE botnet. Those include AppSalt , also known as Honeygain , which is owned by the Vilnius, Lithuania-based Oxylabs . In October 2026, Oxylabs was relaunched under a new brand called Source , after receiving $130 million in funding from private equity firm Warburg Pincus that reportedly valued the business at $3.6 billion. Oxylabs did not respond to a request for comment. Another provider linked to the botnet was NetNut , a once sprawling residential proxy company operated by the publicly-traded Israeli company Alarum Technologies . In July 2026, the FBI worked with industry partners to seize hundreds of domains associated with NetNut , saying the company was responsible for operating a separate botnet called Popa that enslaved TV boxes as residential proxies. Other proxy providers named in the GTIG report include EarnFM , Traffmonetizer , Jaguar , LINKFOG , BMW/IPWeb and GaGaNode . Google’s announcement credits a number of industry partners, including Synthient , a startup that tracks proxy providers. In January 2026, Synthient published research into the rapid spread of the Kimwolf botnet, which at the time was hammering networks worldwide with record-smashing DDoS attacks . Synthient documented how Kimwolf infected millions of Android set-top boxes virtually overnight, using a widespread vulnerability in these residential proxy services to compromise other Android-based devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting TV box users. Synthient’s research caused dozens of residential proxy providers to patch their networks, which helped to fragment the Kimwolf botnet into much smaller pieces that made its incessant and disruptive DDoS attacks far easier for network operators to manage. It also attracted the attention of the Motion Picture Association (MPA), a trade group representing the major Hollywood studios, which partnered with Synthient to purchase and tear apart a number of popular Android TV set-top boxes — including some that were being infected by Kimwolf and other IoT botnets. In a report published today, Synthient examined a popular, pre-infected TV box sold under the brand MECOOL by a publicly traded company in China called Skyworth Technology , concluding that MECOOL also bundled the malware from Videostrong Technology Co. and likewise installed AppSalt/Honeygain and other proxy components. The MECOOL storefront and marketing. Image: Synthient.com. Synthient founder Ben Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity that Videostrong’s malware also distributed software for the proxy service Grass . In our November 2025 story, “ Is Your Android TV Streaming Box Part of a Botnet? ” we quoted a researcher from Censys who found the popular Superbox TV streaming device bundled Grass’s residential proxy software. We also quoted the Grass founder, who denied any affiliation with the TV box maker. That November 2025 story noted that Superbox and similar Android TV set-top boxes gain new customers primarily by engaging influencers on Tiktok and other social networks who praise the product’s ability to offer hundreds of (pirated) pay TV streaming services for a one-time fee. Likewise, Synthient’s report observes that the MECOOL set-top boxes exploded in popularity after the product was mentioned in 2023 by the Youtube channel Linus Tech Tips, which has an audience of nearly 17 million subscribers [Linus Tech Tips said in a statement shared with Synthient that it has since updated the video to explicitly frame the product as a scam and have removed all associated affiliate links]. The popular Youtube channel Linus Tech Tips discussing MECOOL TV streaming boxes. The GTIG report estimates the XCPE botnet takedown should sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices, noting that the various proxy and ad fraud affiliates of Videostrong “each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE.” Synthient’s Brundage echoed that conclusion, calling the 1.3 million number “highly conservative.” “The scale

events.title: HashKey Adopts Tokenised Deposit for Cross-Market Treasury and Liquidity Management on Standard Chartered's Blockchain Platform
events.summary: [The content of this article has been produced by our advertising partner.] Hong Kong, November 2, 2026 — HashKey Group (3887.HK), a leading Asian digital asset company, today announced that, its is among the first institutional clients to adopt Standard Chartered’s newly launched institutional tokenised deposit solution. HashKey is using the solution to support its institutional treasury management and settlement use cases. Tokenized deposits are the digital representations of commercial bank deposits on the blockchain. Built on Standard Chartered’s blockchain infrastructure, they enable eligible clients, such as HashKey to use their bank deposit balances within an approved blockchain-based environment, while retaining the characteristics of commercial bank money. By combining the trust of bank deposits with blockchain-enabled programmability, speed and extended availability, Standard Chartered’s tokenized deposits can facilitate near real-time movement of funds, and support more efficient cross-border liquidity management with extended availability. For HashKey, which operates across multiple jurisdictions, the ability to move liquidity across markets outside traditional banking hours is particularly important. While digital asset activity takes place around the clock, the movement of funds between HashKey’s entities has traditionally been constrained by banking cut-off times. Tokenised deposits help bridge this gap by enabling near real-time, extended-hours movement of funds, giving HashKey greater flexibility to manage treasury positions across markets and entities, reduce funding friction and deploy working capital more efficiently in support of its global operations. Haiyang Ru, CEO of the HashKey Exchange BG, stated: "As more assets move on-chain, fund and settlement systems also need to evolve synchronously. The significance of tokenized deposits lies in connecting funds within the banking system more directly to the on-chain environment. Being among the first institutional clients to adopt Standard Chartered’s newly launched tokenised deposit solution is an important step in strengthening HashKey’s institutional financial infrastructure. We look forward to exploring more efficient fund-flowing methods with global financial institutions, providing more comprehensive infrastructure support for institutions participating in on-chain finance." Mark Willis, Head of Emerging Payments, Transaction Services and Digital Assets, Standard Chartered, said: "Tokenised deposits can play an important role in connecting commercial bank money with the digital asset ecosystem, giving clients greater flexibility in how they move and manage liquidity across markets. Our work with HashKey demonstrates how this technology can support near real-time, extended-hours movement of funds, helping clients manage treasury and liquidity more efficiently while supporting their digital asset activities. This is about bringing the trust of bank deposits together with the speed and programmability of blockchain to solve real-world treasury needs." In recent years, HashKey has continuously promoted the construction of institutional-grade digital asset infrastructure, expanding its business network with its "Asia Interconnected" strategy, and deepening its business layout and financial connections in major Asian markets. Relying on the group's cross-jurisdiction compliant license layout, institutional customer service capabilities, and continuously expanding global financial institution partnership network, HashKey continues to expand channels for institutional funds to enter the digital asset market, enhancing cross-market capital management, trading, and settlement capabilities. Based on HashKey's long-term business experience in serving institutions and professional investors, HashKey will further improve its global treasury management capabilities, strengthen the infrastructure connection between the traditional financial system and the digital asset market, and provide more efficient fund-flowing support for tokenized assets and other on-chain financial applications. In the future, HashKey will continue to deepen cooperation with global financial institutions, explore the practical applications of tokenized deposits in institutional business, and promote the further connection between the traditional financial system and on-chain financial markets. HashKey Group（“HashKey”, the Company, Stock Code: 3887.HK） is a leading digital asset company in Asia with a global footprint, providing end-to-end financial infrastructure, technology and investment management to create a digital assets ecosystem. The Company offers a licensed digital asset platform to provide transaction facilitation services, on-chain services, and asset management services. We are a leading international banking group, with a presence in 55 of the world’s most dynamic markets.

events.title: Fox-Roku deal poised to clear Justice Department scrutiny under consent decree
events.summary: The Scoop Fox’s $22 billion acquisition of Roku is poised to clear Justice Department scrutiny and move forward under a consent decree, according to people familiar with the deliberations, despite efforts from a right-wing ally of President Donald Trump to hold up the deal. It’s unclear what a consent decree would entail, or what terms are being considered. It’s possible the DOJ could change course, the people said. Fox declined to comment. Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward also declined to comment on the deal. “However, we can affirm that this DOJ under President Trump’s leadership will continue to prioritize affordability for all Americans across our economy,” he said in a statement. The deal, which would unite Fox’s content empire of news and sports with Roku’s dominant connected-TV operating system, had worried rivals who fear that Fox will favor its own content. Roku’s free, ad-supported channel also competes for viewers and content with Tubi, which Fox owns. Fox CEO Lachlan Murdoch has said his “expectation” is to run the two businesses separately while selling advertising across them. Semafor first reported in September that antitrust regulators were widening the inquiry into the deal, days before the two companies confirmed the deeper probe, known as a “second request.” That enhanced scrutiny came in part because of pressure from Newsmax majority owner Chris Ruddy, who bills himself as a Trump confidant and has had a long-running spat with Fox owner Rupert Murdoch, Semafor later reported. Rohan’s view Ruddy, briefly a reporter for Murdoch’s New York Post in the 1990s, has been feuding with Fox for more than a year over streaming access to his media assets. Murdoch’s camp has previously dismissed Newsmax’s efforts as a bid to “sue their way out of their own competitive failures,” and Murdoch himself has dined with Trump more than once. But it’s clear that Ruddy has been a headache for the Murdoch clan. Investors have fretted about the possibility that Fox’s deal for Roku could get tied up as a result of Ruddy’s efforts. Those worries were exacerbated after Fox ousted business anchor Maria Bartiromo following an internal investigation into allegations she leaked internal network information and communications to the Trump administration, a claim her lawyers have disputed. But if the deal goes through, it’s more evidence that the Murdoch name still carries a fair amount of weight in Washington.
